@space|Space
The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of all the stuff in our solar system. Every planet, moon and asteroid is just the leftovers.
About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun, which is still only an average-sized star.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, so you always see the Sun as it looked a few minutes ago.
The light hitting your face today may have started its journey out of the Sun's core tens of thousands of years ago.
Every second, the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of itself into pure energy. It is slowly losing weight.
The Sun's outer layer is over a million degrees C, hundreds of times hotter than the surface underneath it. Nobody is fully sure why.
The Sun is not on fire. It shines the same way a hydrogen bomb explodes, just held together by its own gravity.
The Sun is not solid, so different parts spin at different speeds: about 25 days at the middle and 35 days near the poles.
A single dark spot on the Sun can be bigger than the whole Earth.
In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell up so much it may swallow Mercury and Venus, and maybe even Earth.
The Sun is too small to explode. It will end as a white dwarf, a cooling ember about the size of Earth.
The Sun is slowly getting brighter. In about a billion years it may be hot enough to boil away Earth's oceans.
The Sun constantly blows a wind of particles into space at around 1.5 million kilometres per hour.
Total solar eclipses work because the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and also about 400 times farther away.
The Moon drifts about 4 centimetres farther from Earth every year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Because the Moon is drifting away, total solar eclipses will one day stop happening forever. Enjoy them while they last.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, so it is roughly middle-aged.
The Sun drags us around the galaxy at about 830,000 kilometres per hour, and one lap still takes about 230 million years.
The last time Earth was on this side of the galaxy, the first dinosaurs were just showing up.
In 1859 a solar storm made telegraph wires spark, and the northern lights were seen as far south as the Caribbean.
A NASA spacecraft, Parker Solar Probe, has flown through the Sun's outer atmosphere. It is the closest we have ever come to touching the Sun.
Parker Solar Probe is the fastest thing humans have ever built: fast enough to fly from New York to Tokyo in about a minute.
A day on Venus is longer than its year. It spins so slowly that it goes around the Sun before it turns around once.
On Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east, because the planet spins backwards.
Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun. Its thick air traps heat, at about 465 degrees C.
Standing on Venus would feel like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean, because its air is so heavy.
Venus has clouds of sulfuric acid, the stuff in car batteries. Its acid rain evaporates before it reaches the ground.
A Soviet probe landed on Venus in 1982 and survived just 2 hours before the heat and pressure destroyed it.
Venus is so bright that on a very dark night it can make you cast a faint shadow.
Mercury has almost no air to hold heat, so its day side bakes at 430 degrees C while its night side freezes at -180 degrees C.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, yet it has ice hiding in craters near its poles where sunlight never reaches.
On Mercury, a single sunrise to the next sunrise takes 176 Earth days, two of its whole years.
Mercury is shrinking. As its insides cool, the planet wrinkles like a drying apple, leaving cliffs hundreds of kilometres long.
Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, heavier for its size than even the giants.
Earth's spin is slowing down. About 400 million years ago, long before dinosaurs, a day lasted only about 22 hours.
Right now you are flying around the Sun at about 107,000 kilometres per hour, without feeling a thing.
Earth's magnetic north and south poles have swapped places many times. The last swap was about 780,000 years ago.
Tonnes of space dust fall on Earth every day, so some of the dust in your home may have come from space.
The Moon always shows us the same face, because it spins exactly once every time it goes around Earth.
The far side of the Moon is not dark. It gets just as much sunshine as our side; we just never get to see it from Earth.
All the other planets of the solar system could fit side by side in the gap between Earth and the Moon.
The Moon was probably made when a planet the size of Mars smashed into the young Earth, about 4.5 billion years ago.
The astronauts' footprints on the Moon could last for millions of years, because there is no wind or rain to wipe them away.
Only 12 people have ever walked on the Moon, and the last one left in 1972.
In 1969 astronauts crashed a used lunar module into the Moon on purpose, and instruments felt the Moon ring like a bell for almost an hour.
Apollo astronauts said Moon dust smelled like burnt gunpowder.
The Moon looks bigger near the horizon, but it is an illusion. Cover it with your fingertip and it is the same size.
The full Moon looks bright, but the Sun is about 400,000 times brighter.
The Moon pulls on the ground as well as the sea. The land under your feet rises and falls by tens of centimetres twice a day.
Our days keep getting longer, by about 1.7 thousandths of a second every century, mostly because the Moon acts like a brake.
Mars has a volcano about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest, called Olympus Mons.
The giant Martian volcano Olympus Mons is so wide that if you stood on its edge, the top would be hidden over the horizon.
Mars has a canyon as long as the United States is wide. It would make the Grand Canyon look like a crack in the pavement.
On Mars the sky is butterscotch by day, and the sunsets are blue.
Mars is red because its ground is full of iron oxide. The whole planet is basically rusty.
A day on Mars is only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
Mars has a moon, Phobos, that is slowly falling toward it and will probably break apart or crash in about 50 million years.
Dust storms on Mars can grow until they cover the whole planet for weeks.
You could jump nearly three times higher on Mars than on Earth, because its gravity is so weak.
Mars once had rivers and lakes. Rovers have found smooth pebbles that were tumbled by running water.
A Mars rover called Opportunity was built to last 90 days. It kept going for over 14 years.
In 2021 a tiny helicopter called Ingenuity flew on Mars, the first powered flight on another planet. It was meant to fly 5 times and flew 72.
A scrap of fabric from the Wright brothers' first airplane flew on Mars, tucked inside the Ingenuity helicopter.
Mars has ice caps like Earth, but in winter they get a frosting of frozen carbon dioxide, which is dry ice.
Some rocks found on Earth came from Mars. Huge impacts blasted them off Mars and they eventually landed here.
The NASA rover Curiosity is the size of a car and was lowered onto Mars on ropes from a hovering rocket crane.
In movies, asteroid belts are crowded. In real life, the asteroids are so far apart you would be lucky to see even one.
All the asteroids in the main asteroid belt put together weigh only about 3 percent as much as our Moon.
Bright white spots on Ceres, the biggest asteroid, turned out to be salt left behind by water seeping up from below.
Jupiter is so big that all the other planets in the solar system could fit inside it, with room to spare.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for at least 190 years, and maybe much longer.
Jupiter spins faster than any other planet. A day there lasts less than 10 hours.
Jupiter has no solid surface. If you tried to land, you would just sink through thicker and thicker gas until it crushed you.
Deep inside Jupiter, hydrogen is squeezed so hard it turns into a liquid metal that conducts electricity.
Earth is drifting away from the Sun by about 1.5 centimetres a year, probably because the Sun keeps losing mass and its grip slowly weakens.
In 1994 the pieces of a broken comet crashed into Jupiter, leaving dark scars bigger than Earth.
Jupiter has faint rings, too thin and dark to see with a backyard telescope.
Jupiter's moon Io has hundreds of active volcanoes, making it the most volcanic place in the solar system.
Volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io can shoot plumes hundreds of kilometres up into space.
Io is squeezed and stretched by Jupiter's gravity so much that its ground bulges up and down by about 100 metres.
Jupiter's moon Europa hides a salty ocean under its ice that may hold twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.
Europa's hidden ocean is one of the best places in the solar system to look for alien life.
Jupiter's moon Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury. If it orbited the Sun on its own, we would call it a planet.
Ganymede is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, and it even has its own little auroras.
Jupiter's moon Callisto is one of the most cratered objects known, with a surface that has barely changed in 4 billion years.
When Galileo spotted four moons circling Jupiter in 1610, it proved not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.
As of 2024, Jupiter has 95 officially known moons, and astronomers keep finding more.
Jupiter's auroras are hundreds of times more powerful than Earth's northern lights.
Jupiter's magnetic bubble is so huge that if we could see it, it would look bigger than the full Moon in our sky.
Saturn is less dense than water. If you could find a bathtub big enough, Saturn would float.
Saturn's rings are about 280,000 kilometres across but in many places only about 10 metres thick. For their width, that is far thinner than paper.
Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of ice, from tiny grains to pieces as big as a house.
Saturn's rings may be surprisingly young, possibly formed while dinosaurs roamed Earth, though scientists still argue about it.
Saturn's rings are slowly raining down onto the planet, and may be gone in a few hundred million years.
Saturn has a giant six-sided storm at its north pole, more than twice as wide as the whole Earth.
Winds on Saturn can blow at about 1,800 kilometres per hour, much faster than any hurricane on Earth.
Saturn spins so fast that it is visibly squashed: about 10 percent wider at the middle than from pole to pole.
Saturn's moon Titan has rain, rivers, lakes and seas, but they are made of liquid methane and ethane, not water.
Titan's air is thicker than Earth's and its gravity is weak, so a person could fly there by flapping strapped-on wings.
In 2005 the Huygens probe landed on Saturn's moon Titan, the farthest landing ever made by a spacecraft.
Saturn's moon Enceladus shoots fountains of water ice out into space from cracks near its south pole.
The ice sprayed by Saturn's moon Enceladus helps make one of Saturn's rings.
Enceladus is the shiniest object in the solar system, reflecting almost all the sunlight that hits it.
Saturn's moon Iapetus has one side as dark as coal and the other as bright as snow.
Saturn's moon Mimas has a giant crater that makes it look just like the Death Star.
Saturn's moon Pan is shaped like a ravioli, or a flying saucer, because it gathers ring material around its middle.
As of 2025, Saturn has over 270 known moons, more than any other planet.
The Cassini spacecraft ended its mission in 2017 by diving into Saturn on purpose, so it could never contaminate a moon that might hold life.
Uranus spins on its side, tipped over so far that it rolls around the Sun like a ball.
Because Uranus is tipped over, each of its poles gets about 42 years of daylight followed by 42 years of darkness.
The first photo of Earth from space was taken in 1946 by a camera on a captured German V-2 rocket launched from New Mexico.
Herschel wanted to name Uranus after King George III. For a while, some people called it "George's Star".
Uranus is the coldest planet, dropping to about -224 degrees C, even colder than Neptune which is farther out.
Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants. Deep inside they may be hot, slushy oceans of water, ammonia and methane.
Uranus has faint rings and moons named after characters from Shakespeare, like Miranda, Oberon and Titania.
Uranus's moon Miranda has a cliff about 20 kilometres high. A fall from the top would take about 12 minutes.
Neptune was found using maths before anyone saw it. Astronomers predicted where it should be from the way Uranus wobbled.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 kilometres per hour.
Neptune takes about 165 years to go around the Sun. It finished its first orbit since its discovery only in 2011.
Neptune's moon Triton orbits backwards and has geysers that spray dark material kilometres into its thin air.
Triton is probably a captured dwarf planet, grabbed by Neptune's gravity long ago.
Triton is slowly spiralling in toward Neptune and may one day be torn apart into a ring.
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune: Voyager 2, in 1986 and 1989.
Pluto is smaller than our Moon. It is even narrower than the United States.
A year on Pluto lasts 248 Earth years. Since it was discovered in 1930, it has not yet finished one orbit.
Pluto has a giant heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice, discovered by the New Horizons probe in 2015.
Pluto has mountains made of water ice as tall as the Rocky Mountains.
Pluto and its biggest moon Charon always face each other, like two dancers locked eye to eye.
Charon is so big compared to Pluto that the two orbit a point in empty space between them.
Pluto's sky is blue, because of a thin haze high in its atmosphere.
The New Horizons probe that flew past Pluto carries some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the man who discovered Pluto.
Pluto was named by an 11-year-old girl from England, Venetia Burney, in 1930.
Sunlight on Pluto is so dim that noon there looks about as bright as Earth just after sunset.
Eris, a dwarf planet beyond Pluto, is almost the same size as Pluto and about a quarter heavier.
The dwarf planet Haumea spins so fast, once every 4 hours, that it is stretched into an egg shape.
The farthest object ever visited by a spacecraft is Arrokoth, a space rock shaped like a snowman, about 6.6 billion kilometres away.
Moon dust is sharp like tiny shards of glass, because no wind or water has ever smoothed it. It scratched Apollo visors and wore through boot layers.
Far beyond Pluto, the Sun may be wrapped in the Oort Cloud, trillions of icy comets reaching a good part of the way to the nearest star.
The Moon is slowly shrinking as its insides cool. It has shrunk by about 50 metres around its middle, wrinkling its surface and setting off moonquakes.
Some scientists think an undiscovered large planet, Planet Nine, may orbit far beyond Neptune, but no one has found it.
Comets are dirty snowballs of ice, dust and rock. Their tails can stretch for millions of kilometres.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, so when it heads back out into space, it travels tail first.
Comets have two tails: a curved one of dust and a straight, bluish one of electrically charged gas.
Halley's Comet comes back every 75 to 76 years. It was last seen in 1986 and will return in 2061.
Most shooting stars are made by specks of dust no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up in our air.
Meteor showers happen when Earth ploughs through trails of dust left behind by comets.
In 2014 the Rosetta mission's Philae lander touched down on a comet, the first landing on one ever.
A NASA spacecraft brought back a sample of the asteroid Bennu in 2023, and it contained building blocks of life.
In 2022 NASA crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid on purpose, and it changed the asteroid's orbit, the first test of planetary defence.
The dinosaurs were wiped out after an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico, 66 million years ago.
In 2013 a meteor exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, shattering windows across the city and injuring about 1,500 people.
The first person confirmed to be hit by a meteorite was Ann Hodges of Alabama in 1954. It crashed through her roof, bounced off a radio and bruised her hip.
Most meteorites are older than any rock on Earth, about 4.5 billion years old.
Some meteorites contain tiny grains of stardust that are older than the Sun itself.
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches, by most estimates.
Most stars you see at night are bigger and brighter than the Sun. The many small, dim stars are too faint to see without a telescope.
Most of the stars you can see without a telescope are within a few thousand light years, a tiny corner of our galaxy.
On a clear, dark night, a person can see only about 2,500 to 5,000 stars with the naked eye, not millions.
Stars twinkle because of moving air in Earth's atmosphere. Seen from space, they shine perfectly steadily.
Planets usually do not twinkle like stars, because they look like tiny discs rather than single points of light.
A star's colour tells its temperature: red stars are the coolest, and blue-white stars are the hottest.
Red dwarfs, the most common stars, burn so slowly they can last for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed.
Point Nemo, the most remote spot in the ocean, is a graveyard for old spacecraft. The nearest people are often astronauts passing overhead.
Big stars live fast and die young. A star 20 times heavier than the Sun may last only around 10 million years.
The star Betelgeuse in Orion is so big that if it replaced the Sun, it would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
Betelgeuse will explode as a supernova someday, maybe within the next 100,000 years. It will be bright enough to see in daylight.
Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, has a tiny partner: a white dwarf about the size of Earth but as heavy as the Sun.
A teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
The North Star, Polaris, will not always be the North Star. Earth's axis wobbles, and in about 12,000 years Vega will take its place.
A full Moon is about 10 times brighter than a half Moon, not twice, because the shadows on its rough surface vanish when sunlight hits it head on.
About half of Sun-like stars have at least one partner star. Our single Sun is not as typical as you might think.
Polaris is not a single star but a family of at least three stars.
Every atom of gold on Earth was made in a violent event in space, such as two dead stars smashing together.
The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.
The hydrogen in your body is about as old as the universe itself, made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
When a huge star dies in a supernova, it can briefly outshine its entire galaxy of billions of stars.
In 1054, Chinese astronomers saw a new star so bright it was visible in daylight for 23 days. It was a supernova.
The exploded star seen in 1054 left behind the Crab Nebula, which is still expanding at over 1,000 kilometres per second.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres wide, the size of a city.
A sugar-cube-sized piece of neutron star would weigh about as much as all the people on Earth put together.
Some neutron stars spin over 700 times a second, faster than a kitchen blender.
The first pulsar, found in 1967, sent such regular blips that scientists jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for Little Green Men.
Magnetars are neutron stars with magnetic fields so strong they could wipe your credit card from halfway to the Moon.
In 2004 a burst from a magnetar 50,000 light years away was strong enough to disturb Earth's upper atmosphere.
A neutron star's gravity is so strong that a mountain on it would be only millimetres tall.
Some dead stars called white dwarfs crystallize as they cool, a bit like a diamond the size of Earth.
A black hole is not a hole. It is a huge amount of matter squeezed into a tiny space, with gravity so strong not even light escapes.
If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep orbiting exactly as it does now. It would just get very cold.
To turn Earth into a black hole, you would have to squeeze it down to about the size of a marble.
Near a black hole, time slows down. Someone falling in would seem to freeze at the edge to anyone watching from far away.
Falling into a small black hole, you would be stretched like spaghetti. Scientists really call it spaghettification.
In 1967 the big space powers signed a treaty agreeing that no country can claim the Moon or any planet as its own.
The first-ever picture of a black hole was released in 2019. It showed a glowing ring around the giant black hole in galaxy M87.
The black hole in galaxy M87 is about 6.5 billion times heavier than the Sun.
The Milky Way has a giant black hole at its centre, Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times heavier than the Sun.
A photo of the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy was released in 2022, taken by telescopes linked across the whole Earth.
Some black holes weigh billions of Suns. Astronomers still are not sure how they grew so big so fast.
Physics predicts that black holes slowly leak energy, called Hawking radiation. Given unimaginable time, they may evaporate.
Black holes can spin. Some are thought to spin at close to the speed of light at their edges.
In 2015 scientists detected two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light years away, by sensing ripples in space itself.
The first ripples in space ever detected changed the length of a 4 kilometre detector by about a thousandth of the width of a proton.
When two black holes merged in 2015, for a split second they released more power than all the stars in the universe combined.
Some black holes are caught eating stars. When a star gets too close, it is shredded and its gas swirls in, glowing brightly.
Quasars are the blazing hearts of distant galaxies, powered by gas falling into giant black holes. Some outshine whole galaxies by thousands of times.
Some black holes shoot jets of matter at nearly the speed of light, stretching farther than their whole galaxy.
There may be around 100 million black holes scattered through our galaxy alone.
As of 2024, the nearest known black hole, Gaia BH1, is about 1,500 light years away. Do not worry, it is much too far to hurt us.
The Sun is often called an average star, but it is bigger and brighter than about 9 in 10 stars in the Milky Way, most of which are small red dwarfs.
The Sun is actually white. It looks yellow from Earth because our air scatters away some of its blue light.
Stars are born in huge clouds of gas and dust, like the Pillars of Creation, where clumps collapse under their own gravity.
The Orion Nebula, a star nursery, is visible as a fuzzy patch with the naked eye in Orion's sword.
The tallest Pillar of Creation is about 4 light years tall. Even light would need 4 years to climb it.
The spacesuits worn on the Moon were made by Playtex, a company famous for bras, and stitched together by skilled seamstresses.
Light from the Sun takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune, but over 4 years to reach the nearest star.
If the Sun were the size of a grain of sand, the nearest star would be another grain of sand about 30 kilometres away.
If the Sun were shrunk to the size of a red blood cell, the Milky Way would still be about as wide as the United States.
Some stars are racing out of our galaxy for good, flung away at millions of kilometres per hour by the black hole at its centre.
Vega spins so fast that it bulges at the middle and its equator is cooler and darker than its poles.
At NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, engineers eat lucky peanuts during big mission moments, a tradition that began after a 1964 Moon probe finally worked.
Until 1924, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the entire universe. Then Edwin Hubble proved that other galaxies exist.
The faint star Proxima Centauri has at least one planet roughly Earth's size, in the zone where water could be liquid.
Astronomers have found a planet orbiting a dead star, a pulsar, before they found any planet around a normal star like the Sun.
Some stars produce flares so strong that they can be thousands of times brighter than the biggest flares on our Sun.
Eta Carinae, a monster star system about 7,500 light years away, had a giant outburst in the 1840s and became the second brightest star in the sky.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, has somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars.
The Milky Way is about 100,000 light years across. Light, the fastest thing there is, takes 100,000 years to cross it.
We live in the Milky Way, so we can only see it edge-on, as a faint band of light stretching across a dark sky.
About a third of all people, including most people in North America, cannot see the Milky Way from home because of light pollution.
The Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy are heading toward each other, but a 2025 study put the chance of a merger in the next 10 billion years at about 50-50.
When galaxies collide, their stars almost never hit each other. The gaps between stars are just too enormous.
The Andromeda galaxy is the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye, about 2.5 million light years away.
The light from Andromeda that you see tonight left it when early human ancestors were walking in Africa.
If your eyes could see it, the Andromeda galaxy would look several times wider than the full Moon in our sky.
The Milky Way is slowly eating smaller galaxies. Streams of stars from swallowed galaxies still wrap around it.
Our solar system sits in a quiet suburb of the Milky Way, about halfway out from the centre.
The Milky Way has a warped shape, a bit like a vinyl record left out in the sun.
Two of the Milky Way's companion galaxies, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, can be seen by eye from the Southern Hemisphere.
Scientists think about 85 percent of all matter in the universe is dark matter, which we cannot see or touch and have never directly detected.
Ordinary matter, everything made of atoms, is only about 5 percent of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy.
The expansion of the universe is speeding up, pushed by a mysterious something scientists call dark energy.
Galaxies spin so fast that they should fly apart. Unseen dark matter is the leading explanation for what holds them together.
There are probably hundreds of billions to around two trillion galaxies in the observable universe.
The James Webb telescope's first deep photo showed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
NASA's newest space toilet, sent to the space station in 2020, cost about 23 million dollars.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, only about three times older than Earth.
The Big Bang was not an explosion in space. It was space itself starting to expand everywhere at once.
The universe has no centre. Every galaxy sees the others moving away from it, like raisins in rising bread dough.
For decades Russian cosmonauts carried a special pistol in their survival kit, in case they landed in the wild near wolves or bears.
The observable universe is about 93 billion light years across, even though it is only 13.8 billion years old, because space kept stretching.
Some distant galaxies are moving away from us faster than light. Space itself can stretch faster than light can travel through it.
Some of the static on old analogue TVs came from the Big Bang: the faint glow left over from the birth of the universe.
The afterglow of the Big Bang was first found by accident in 1964, by two scientists who at first blamed pigeon droppings in their antenna.
The universe was so hot and dense at first that for about 380,000 years, light could not travel freely through it.
For roughly the first hundred million years after the Big Bang there were no stars at all. Astronomers call it the cosmic dark ages.
The first atoms in the universe were almost all hydrogen and helium. Everything heavier was made later, in stars.
The farther you look into space, the further back in time you see. Telescopes are time machines.
As of 2025, the James Webb Space Telescope has spotted galaxies that existed when the universe was less than 300 million years old.
In the far future, other galaxies will race so far away that astronomers in the Milky Way will no longer be able to see them.
The universe is mostly empty. Spread its atoms out evenly and you would get about one atom for every 4 cubic metres.
Between galaxy clusters there are enormous empty voids, some hundreds of millions of light years across.
Galaxies are strung together in a vast cosmic web of filaments, like the strands of a gigantic spider's web.
Gravity from huge galaxy clusters can bend light like a lens, letting us see galaxies hidden behind them.
Our Milky Way belongs to a group of over 50 galaxies, and that group is part of a supercluster of about 100,000 galaxies called Laniakea.
Laniakea, the name of our home supercluster, means "immeasurable heaven" in Hawaiian.
The Sombrero galaxy looks just like a giant Mexican hat floating in space.
Dwarf galaxies can have just a few thousand stars, fewer than a big city has people.
There are more galaxies in the universe than there are people on Earth, by a long way.
Space is not perfectly cold. The leftover glow from the Big Bang keeps it at about -270 degrees C.
The coldest known natural place in the universe is the Boomerang Nebula, at about -272 degrees C, colder than empty space.
Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched so much by the expanding universe that it has turned from visible light into infrared.
Physicists are still not sure whether the universe goes on forever or curves back on itself. As far as we can measure, it looks flat.
There are giant clouds of alcohol in space. One near the centre of our galaxy holds enough to fill about 400 trillion trillion pints.
A cloud near the centre of the Milky Way contains a chemical called ethyl formate, which gives raspberries their flavour.
Astronauts coming in from spacewalks say space has a smell, a bit like seared steak, hot metal or welding fumes.
Astronomers once measured the average colour of the universe. It is a beige shade they nicknamed cosmic latte.
Most of the light in the universe is not starlight but the faint microwave glow from the Big Bang.
Every second, about 65 billion tiny particles called neutrinos from the Sun pass through each square centimetre of your body.
Pluto was officially a planet for 76 years, from its discovery in 1930 until astronomers voted to call it a dwarf planet in 2006.
Particles from space called cosmic rays hit your body all the time. Some are moving at nearly the speed of light.
A cosmic ray called the Oh-My-God particle, seen in 1991, hit with as much energy as a baseball thrown at about 90 kilometres per hour.
Some astronauts see flashes of light with their eyes closed. Scientists think it is cosmic rays zipping through their eyes.
Astronomers have found a cloud of water vapour around a distant black hole holding about 140 trillion times all the water in Earth's oceans.
There is no up or down in space, so some astronauts get space sick until their brain gets used to it.
The Whirlpool galaxy is caught in a slow dance with a smaller galaxy that is tugging on one of its spiral arms.
The Milky Way's spiral arms are not solid. Stars drift in and out of them like cars passing through a traffic jam.
The universe might end with everything spread so thin and cold that nothing ever happens again. Scientists call it the heat death.
Some galaxies stopped making new stars billions of years ago. Astronomers call them red and dead.
Galaxy collisions can set off a burst of star formation, with stars being born hundreds of times faster than in our galaxy.
The gas between galaxies in big clusters can be hotter than 50 million degrees C.
If the Milky Way were shrunk to the size of a dinner plate, the observable universe would be a ball about 200 kilometres across.
Earth is wrapped in a faint glowing cloud of hydrogen that stretches out past the Moon, so in a way the Moon flies through our outer atmosphere.
A star nicknamed Methuselah once seemed to be older than the universe itself. Newer measurements put it at about 12 billion years old, just under the limit.
Earth is spinning, orbiting the Sun, circling the galaxy and flying through the universe, all at the same time, without you feeling any of it.
Relative to the Big Bang's afterglow, our galaxy is moving at about 2 million kilometres per hour.
Helium was found on the Sun before it was found on Earth. Its name comes from Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.
Stars in the Milky Way's centre are packed so tightly that the night sky there would be ablaze with bright stars.
Astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.
The International Space Station circles the whole Earth about every 90 minutes, at roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour.
The International Space Station is about the size of a football field and is often called the most expensive single object ever built.
People have lived on the International Space Station without a break since November 2000.
Astronauts grow up to about 5 centimetres taller in space, because their spines stretch out without gravity. They shrink back on Earth.
In space, tears do not fall. They gather into a wobbly ball of water stuck to your eye.
Astronauts on the space station drink water recycled from their own sweat and urine. They say it tastes fine.
Astronauts cannot burp properly in space, because without gravity the gas and food in the stomach do not separate.
Astronauts lose bone and muscle in space, so they must exercise about two hours every day to stay strong.
Flames in space form round blue balls instead of pointed flickering shapes, because hot air does not rise without gravity.
Astronauts sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall, so they do not float around and bump into things.
Bread is rarely flown to space because crumbs float away and could get into equipment. Astronauts use tortillas instead.
In 1965 an astronaut smuggled a corned beef sandwich into space. The crumbs caused a fuss back on Earth.
Salt and pepper on the space station come as liquids, because loose grains would float off and clog air vents.
A toilet on the space station uses airflow instead of gravity, sucking waste away like a vacuum cleaner.
Many astronauts say food tastes blander in space, partly because fluids shift into the head and stuff up their noses.
Without gravity, fluids drift up toward an astronaut's head, giving them puffy faces and skinny legs, sometimes called bird legs.
Many astronauts' eyesight changes in space, because fluid pressure changes the shape of the back of their eyes.
Astronaut Scott Kelly spent nearly a year in space while his identical twin, Mark, stayed on Earth, so scientists could compare them.
The longest single spaceflight was about 437 days, by Russian doctor Valeri Polyakov in 1994 and 1995.
Sound needs air to travel, so out on a spacewalk astronauts can only talk to each other by radio.
A spacesuit is like a small personal spaceship, with its own air, cooling, power and radio.
Astronauts wear diapers under their spacesuits during launch and long spacewalks.
On a spacewalk, sunlit parts of the station can reach about 120 degrees C while shaded parts drop below -150 degrees C.
Astronauts train for spacewalks in a giant swimming pool, where floating feels a bit like weightlessness.
Astronauts on the space station are not weightless because there is no gravity. They are falling around Earth so fast they keep missing it.
At the height of the space station, gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground.
The planes used to train astronauts in weightlessness are nicknamed vomit comets.
Astronauts cut their hair with clippers attached to a vacuum hose, so the clippings do not float around the station.
Water on the space station forms floating blobs that astronauts can catch and drink straight out of the air.
In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. It was about the size of a beach ball.
Laika, a stray dog from the streets of Moscow, became the first animal to orbit Earth, in 1957.
In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. His flight around Earth lasted just 108 minutes.
Gagarin's famous words at launch were "Poyekhali!", which means "Let's go!" in Russian.
Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, flew in 1963 and orbited Earth 48 times.
In 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk. His suit swelled up so much he had to let air out to get back inside.
A modern smartphone has millions of times more computing power than the computer that guided Apollo 11 to the Moon.
Neil Armstrong had to steer past a field of boulders to land on the Moon, and touched down with less than a minute of fuel left.
The American flags planted on the Moon have probably been bleached white by decades of harsh sunlight.
Apollo astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of Moon rock.
Astronauts left a family photo, a golf ball and even a falcon feather on the Moon.
Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon. With no air, they hit the ground at the same time.
Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon in 1971, using a club head fixed to a tool handle.
Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists still bounce lasers off them to measure the Moon's distance to the centimetre.
The Apollo 13 crew had to fly around the Moon to get home after an oxygen tank exploded, and survived.
In 1970 the Apollo 13 crew travelled about 400,000 kilometres from Earth while swinging around the Moon, farther than any humans had gone before.
The Apollo 8 crew were the first humans to see the whole Earth as a ball, and the first to see the far side of the Moon.
The famous Earthrise photo was taken by an Apollo 8 astronaut on Christmas Eve 1968.
The Saturn V rocket that took astronauts to the Moon was taller than the Statue of Liberty.
As of 2025, Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object, over 25 billion kilometres away.
A signal from Voyager 1 takes nearly a full day to reach Earth, travelling at the speed of light.
Voyager 1 left the Sun's bubble of solar wind in 2012 and is now drifting in the space between the stars.
The Voyager golden records include greetings in 55 languages, whale songs, and music from Bach to Chuck Berry.
Voyager 1 took the Pale Blue Dot photo in 1990, showing Earth as a tiny speck from about 6 billion kilometres away.
Each Voyager probe has only about 69 kilobytes of memory, less than one small phone photo, yet both still work nearly 50 years later.
In about 40,000 years Voyager 1 will drift past another star, still about 1.6 light years away from it. It is not heading anywhere in particular.
The Pioneer 10 and 11 probes carry plaques with a drawing of a man and woman and a map showing where Earth is.
The Hubble Space Telescope launched with a mirror ground very slightly wrong, about 1/50th of a human hair, and astronauts fixed it in 1993.
Hubble has been orbiting Earth since 1990 and has been repaired and upgraded by astronauts five times.
The James Webb Space Telescope has a sunshield as big as a tennis court to keep its mirror extremely cold.
The James Webb telescope's mirror is coated with a thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared light so well.
The James Webb telescope orbits a point in space about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, about four times farther than the Moon.
Yuri Gagarin did not land inside his capsule. He ejected and parachuted down, a detail the Soviet Union kept quiet for years.
There are thousands of working satellites around Earth, and many thousands more pieces of space junk.
Even a fleck of paint in orbit hits with the force of a bullet. Space station windows have been chipped by tiny debris.
In 1979 the space station Skylab fell to Earth and scattered pieces across Western Australia.
To escape Earth's gravity completely, a spacecraft must reach about 40,000 kilometres per hour, fast enough to cross the Atlantic in under 10 minutes.
The Space Shuttle took only about 8 and a half minutes to get from the launch pad into orbit.
Space is closer than most people think: it starts about 100 kilometres up, an hour's drive if you could go straight up.
Rockets do not push against air. They work by throwing gas out of the back, which is why they work even better in space.
A Space Shuttle launch shook the ground for kilometres, and its pad used a flood of water to quiet the sound so it would not damage the shuttle.
As of 2025, SpaceX has launched and landed the same Falcon 9 rocket booster more than 25 times.
In 2018 SpaceX launched a red sports car into orbit around the Sun, with a dummy in a spacesuit at the wheel.
In 2001 Dennis Tito became the first space tourist, paying about 20 million dollars to visit the space station.
The first meal eaten on the Moon included bacon squares, peaches, sugar cookies and coffee.
Astronauts on the space station once grew lettuce in space and ate it, in 2015.
Mice, monkeys, spiders, fish, jellyfish and even a frog have all been sent into space for science.
In 1973 two spiders, Arabella and Anita, spun webs on the Skylab space station.
India's Mangalyaan probe reached Mars on its first try in 2014, for less money than some Hollywood space movies cost to make.
China's Chang'e 4 made the first ever landing on the far side of the Moon, in 2019.
In 2024 China's Chang'e 6 brought back the first samples ever collected from the Moon's far side.
Japan's Hayabusa2 probe fired a bullet-like projectile into an asteroid to collect samples, then brought them back to Earth.
Some space probes use nuclear batteries, because sunlight is far too weak to power them in the outer solar system.
Spacecraft use a planet's gravity as a slingshot to speed up for free, like a skateboarder grabbing a passing truck.
The New Horizons probe reached the Moon's distance in about 9 hours, faster than any spacecraft launched before it.
The Juno spacecraft orbiting Jupiter carries three small Lego figures: Galileo, and the Roman gods Jupiter and Juno.
The Galileo spacecraft was crashed into Jupiter on purpose in 2003 to avoid accidentally contaminating Europa.
In 2021 the Perseverance rover recorded the first sounds on Mars, including wind and the hum of the Ingenuity helicopter.
Sound travels slower on Mars than on Earth, and high and low notes travel at different speeds there.
The first planet found around a Sun-like star was discovered in 1995. As of 2025, astronomers know of over 6,000 planets beyond our solar system.
There may be more planets in our galaxy than stars, since most stars seem to have at least one.
On the planet HD 189733b, winds of thousands of kilometres per hour may whip sideways rain made of molten glass.
Some giant planets orbit so close to their stars that a year lasts less than one Earth day.
The exoplanet WASP-12b is so close to its star that it is being stretched into an egg shape and slowly eaten.
The planet TrES-2b reflects less than 1 percent of the light that hits it, making it darker than coal.
The giant asteroid Vesta has a mountain over 20 kilometres tall in the middle of a huge crater, rivalling Olympus Mons on Mars.
There may be billions of rogue planets in the Milky Way: worlds with no star at all, wandering alone in the dark between the stars.
The star TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-sized planets. From one of them, the others would look bigger than our Moon in the sky.
Some exoplanets are so hot that iron evaporates on their day side and may rain down as liquid iron at night.
The planet Kepler-16b orbits two stars, like Luke Skywalker's home world Tatooine. Standing there, you would see double sunsets.
The first exoplanet picture was taken in 2004. Most planets are lost in the glare of their star, millions of times brighter.
In 1977 a radio telescope picked up a strong signal so striking that an astronomer wrote "Wow!" next to it. It has never been heard again.
Since the 1960s, scientists have been listening for radio signals from alien civilizations. So far, nothing confirmed.
In 1974 scientists beamed a radio message toward a star cluster 25,000 light years away. Any reply would take 50,000 years.
Our own radio and TV broadcasts have been leaking into space for about a century, reaching thousands of stars.
The Fermi paradox asks: if the galaxy is so old and huge, why have we found no sign of aliens? Nobody knows the answer.
Microbes might survive a trip between planets inside rocks blasted off by impacts, so life could, in theory, hop from one world to another.
Some scientists think life could exist in the clouds of Venus, where temperatures and pressures are surprisingly Earth-like.
Saturn's moon Titan has the ingredients some scientists think could support strange life, in seas of liquid methane.
The northern lights happen when particles from the Sun crash into our air and make it glow, like a giant neon sign.
Green auroras come from oxygen high in the air. Rare red auroras come from oxygen even higher up.
In May 2024 a huge solar storm made auroras glow as far south as Mexico, in skies that almost never see them.
Auroras happen on other planets too. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune all have them.
Phone cameras often see auroras better than our eyes, because they collect faint light for longer.
During a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns red, because it is lit by all the sunsets and sunrises around Earth at once.
A total solar eclipse at any one spot lasts at most about 7 and a half minutes.
On average, any single spot on Earth sees a total solar eclipse only about once every 375 years.
During a total solar eclipse, the temperature can drop several degrees and birds may start their evening songs.
Ancient Babylonians predicted eclipses thousands of years ago, by noticing that they repeat in an 18-year pattern.
A blue moon is not blue. The name usually just means a second full Moon in the same calendar month.
Earth has some small temporary moons: little asteroids that get caught for a few months, then wander off again.
A near-Earth asteroid called Apophis will pass closer to Earth than some satellites in April 2029, visible to the naked eye. It will miss.
About once a year a car-sized asteroid hits our atmosphere, and it usually burns up or breaks apart before reaching the ground.
NASA tracks thousands of asteroids near Earth. None of the known big ones is on course to hit us for at least the next century.
Some meteorites are pieces of the Moon, knocked off by impacts and landed on Earth.
Shooting stars burn up about 80 to 100 kilometres above your head.
During the Leonid meteor storm of 1833, people saw so many shooting stars, many thousands an hour, that some thought the world was ending.
Big meteorites that land in deserts or Antarctica are easiest to find. Antarctica is the best meteorite-hunting place on Earth.
The Hoba meteorite in Namibia weighs about 60 tonnes, the largest single meteorite ever found. It has never been moved.
Galileo was put under house arrest for life for saying that the Earth goes around the Sun.
Ancient Greek scientist Eratosthenes measured the size of Earth over 2,000 years ago using shadows, a stick and some walking.
Over 2,000 years ago, a Greek astronomer named Aristarchus suggested that Earth goes around the Sun. Hardly anyone listened.
In 1610 Galileo saw Saturn's rings but thought they were two moons, or ears. His telescope was too blurry to see the truth.
Isaac Newton is said to have worked out gravity partly by wondering why apples fall but the Moon does not.
Ancient Egyptians lined up the Great Pyramid of Giza with true north almost perfectly, probably by watching the stars.
Stonehenge was built to line up with the sunrise on the summer solstice and the sunset on the winter solstice.
Uranus, the first planet found with a telescope, was spotted in 1781 by William Herschel, a music teacher and composer who stargazed as a hobby.
Caroline Herschel, William's sister, discovered eight comets and became the first woman paid as a scientist in Britain.
Venus has no small craters at all, because its thick air crushes or slows down small space rocks before they can reach the ground.
The constellations are not real groups. Stars in the same constellation can be wildly different distances from us.
Constellations slowly change shape over tens of thousands of years, because every star is moving.
There are 88 official constellations. Together they cover the entire sky like the countries on a map.
The Big Dipper is not a constellation by itself. It is part of a bigger one called the Great Bear.
Your zodiac sign is probably out of date. Earth's wobble has shifted the stars by about one sign since astrology was set up.
The Sun actually passes through 13 constellations a year, including Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer, which astrology leaves out.
The star patterns you see depend on where you live. People in Australia never see the North Star.
Dust devils on Mars can tower up to about 20 kilometres high and leave dark tracks across the ground.
Saturn's storms produce lightning thousands of times stronger than on Earth.
If you could drive a car to the Sun at highway speed, the trip would take over 150 years.
If you could drive to the Moon at highway speed, it would take about five or six months without a single stop.
If Earth were the size of a basketball, the Moon would be a tennis ball about 7 metres away.
If the Sun were as tall as a front door, Earth would be about the size of a coin, and Jupiter about the size of a basketball.
Jupiter is so massive that it does not really orbit the Sun's centre. The two circle a point just outside the Sun's surface.
Because of Saturn's tilt, its rings seem to vanish from Earth's view every 13 to 15 years when we see them exactly edge-on.
Saturn's moon Hyperion looks like a giant sponge, full of deep holes.
Saturn's moon Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
Some of Saturn's moons act like sheepdogs, herding the ice in its rings into thin, sharp strands.
Jupiter's moon Europa has a surface of ice so smooth that it has almost no big craters, meaning it is young and keeps being resurfaced.
Jupiter's moon Europa may spray water out into space, and a NASA probe called Europa Clipper is on its way to take a closer look.
Uranus smells like rotten eggs, scientists think, because its upper clouds contain hydrogen sulfide.
Neptune is a deep blue partly because of methane in its air, which soaks up red light.
Uranus was once hit by something so big that it may have knocked the whole planet onto its side.
A day on Venus is so long that a person on a bicycle could keep pace with the sunset, if they could survive the heat.
On Mercury, at certain spots, the Sun rises, stops, goes backwards and then rises again, all in the same morning.
Earth is the only planet not named after a god or goddess. Its name comes from old words meaning ground or soil.
The Moon has no weather and almost no air, so the sky there is black even in the middle of the day.
On the Moon, the temperature swings from about 120 degrees C in the day to about -130 degrees C at night.
A lunar day, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about a month on Earth: two weeks of sunshine, then two weeks of night.
On the Moon you would weigh about one sixth of what you weigh on Earth, so a 60 kilogram person would feel like 10 kilograms.
Earth seen from the Moon goes through phases, just like the Moon does for us, and it barely moves in the lunar sky.
From the Moon, Earth looks about four times wider than the full Moon looks from Earth.
The Moon has lava tubes, huge underground tunnels that future astronauts might one day use as shelters.
There are craters near the Moon's poles that may not have seen a single ray of sunlight for billions of years.
The Moon's south pole is a top target for new missions, because water ice there could be turned into drinking water and rocket fuel.
India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023, making India the fourth country to land softly on the Moon.
Astronauts in orbit see Earth's glowing cities at night, and can easily spot huge fishing fleets with bright lights at sea.
Seen from space, Earth's atmosphere looks like a thin blue line, thinner compared to Earth than the skin of an apple.
From the space station, astronauts can see lightning flashing inside storms and spreading across hundreds of kilometres.
Space radiation is one of the biggest dangers for a trip to Mars. A round trip could expose astronauts to many years' worth of Earth radiation.
A trip to Mars would take about 6 to 9 months each way with today's rockets.
Radio messages between Earth and Mars take between about 3 and 22 minutes each way, so a live chat is impossible.
When Mars and Earth are on opposite sides of the Sun, the Sun blocks radio contact, and missions pause for about two weeks.
Spacecraft sent to Mars must be cleaned carefully so Earth germs do not hitch a ride and fool scientists looking for Martian life.
Before Apollo 11, NASA made the astronauts sign autographs that their families could sell if they did not come home.
The Apollo 11 astronauts had to fill in a customs form when they came back from the Moon, listing Moon rocks and Moon dust.
After returning from the Moon, the Apollo 11 crew were kept in quarantine for three weeks in case they had brought back Moon germs.
There are three small Moon buggies, the Apollo rovers, still parked on the Moon where astronauts left them.
In 1971 an astronaut left a small aluminium sculpture and plaque on the Moon honouring astronauts who had died.
In 1984 astronaut Bruce McCandless flew untethered about 100 metres from the Space Shuttle using a jetpack, a human satellite.
The Kennedy Space Center's giant Vehicle Assembly Building is so tall that clouds can form inside it on humid days, NASA says.
Plants grown in space send their roots wandering in odd directions, because there is no down to grow toward.
After months in space, some astronauts back on Earth say they let go of a cup in mid-air, expecting it to float.
Without gravity, sweat does not drip off astronauts. It builds up as a layer of water on the skin.
Astronauts on the space station clean themselves with no-rinse shampoo and wet towels, since a shower would just make floating blobs.
The space station's air is constantly pushed around by fans. Without them, a sleeping astronaut could be surrounded by their own breathed-out carbon dioxide.
The Apollo astronauts traveled to the Moon in a capsule with roughly the inside space of a large car.
The crew of Apollo 10 flew faster than any other humans in history, at about 40,000 kilometres per hour on the way home.
Voyager 1's radio has about the power of a fridge light bulb, yet giant antennas on Earth still hear it from over 24 billion kilometres away.
It would take a beam of light about 4 years to reach the nearest star, but it would take Voyager 1 more than 70,000 years.
Every two years Mars seems to drift backwards in our sky for about two months, as Earth overtakes it like a faster car on a racetrack.
Almost everything in the solar system spins and orbits in the same direction, a fingerprint of the swirling cloud that made it.
Earth and the other planets formed from dust grains that stuck together, growing into pebbles, boulders and eventually worlds.
Water on Earth may have been brought partly by asteroids and comets that crashed into the young planet.
Some of the water you drink may be older than the Sun, formed as ice in space before the solar system existed.
On average, the closest planet to Earth is not Venus or Mars but Mercury, because it never strays far from the Sun.
On one giant planet, Kepler-13Ab, astronomers think it may snow titanium dioxide, the white stuff in sunscreen.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is shrinking. In the 1800s it was about three Earths wide; today it is closer to just one.
In 2013 astronaut Chris Hadfield recorded David Bowie's Space Oddity on the space station, the first music video made in space.
While Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon, Michael Collins circled alone, cut off from every human whenever he passed behind it.
When a switch broke on Apollo 11's lander, Buzz Aldrin pushed the circuit breaker in with a felt-tip pen so they could leave the Moon.
The Moon looks bright white at night, but its surface is really dark grey, about as dark as worn asphalt.
Leonardo da Vinci worked out over 500 years ago that the faint glow on the dark part of the Moon was light reflected from Earth.
The first living things to travel around the Moon were two tortoises, on a Soviet probe in 1968. They came back to Earth alive.
Comet Hale-Bopp stayed visible to the naked eye for about 18 months in 1996 and 1997, longer than any other comet on record.
Only one person has been buried on the Moon: geologist Eugene Shoemaker, whose ashes were crashed onto it by a NASA probe in 1999.
On the first American spacewalk, in 1965, Ed White lost a spare glove, which floated off to circle Earth on its own.
In 2008 an astronaut lost a tool bag on a spacewalk. It circled Earth for months and could be seen from the ground with binoculars.
The International Space Station sometimes has to fire its engines to dodge pieces of space junk.
You can see the International Space Station without a telescope. It looks like a very bright star gliding across the sky in a few minutes.
Mars's two moons, Phobos and Deimos, are named after Greek words for fear and dread.
Uranus is the only planet named after a Greek god. All the others take their names from Roman gods.
The distant dwarf planet Sedna takes about 11,000 years to go around the Sun once.
In 2017 astronomers spotted Oumuamua, the first object ever seen visiting our solar system from another star.
Gas around a giant black hole in the Perseus galaxy cluster carries a sound wave, a B flat about 57 octaves below middle C.
When two neutron stars collided in 2017, they made an amount of gold several times heavier than the whole Earth, scientists estimate.
There are more trees on Earth, about 3 trillion, than there are stars in the Milky Way.
Tree seeds flew around the Moon on Apollo 14 in 1971. The Moon trees grown from them still stand in places across the United States.
Cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev was in space when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, so he came home to a different country.
You would weigh about two and a half times as much at the cloud tops of Jupiter as you do on Earth.
NASA plans to send a car-sized flying drone called Dragonfly to explore Saturn's moon Titan in the 2030s.
A star called S2 whips around the black hole at the centre of our galaxy every 16 years, at up to almost 3 percent of the speed of light.
The night sky is dark partly because the universe had a beginning. Light from very distant stars has not had time to reach us yet.
Venus shines so brightly near the horizon that it is one of the things people most often mistake for a UFO.
An astronaut's heart becomes slightly rounder during a long stay in space, then returns to its normal shape back on Earth.
@animals|Animals
A giraffe's tongue can be about 45 to 50 centimeters long, and it is dark blue-black, likely to protect it from sunburn while feeding.
Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as humans: seven. Each one can be over 25 centimeters long.
A giraffe's heart weighs about 11 kilograms and pumps hard enough to push blood two meters up its neck to the brain.
Newborn giraffes drop about 1.5 meters to the ground at birth and can usually stand within an hour.
Elephants can hear rumbles too low for human ears and may pick up these calls from several kilometers away.
An elephant's trunk has no bones but contains tens of thousands of muscle units, enough to pick up a single peanut.
African elephants flap their huge ears to cool down: the ears are full of blood vessels that release body heat.
Elephants can sense vibrations in the ground through their feet, which may help them detect distant herds.
An adult African elephant can drink well over 100 liters of water in a single day.
Elephants are pregnant for about 22 months, the longest pregnancy of any living land animal.
Asian elephants have passed the mirror test, recognizing their own reflection, a skill few animals share.
A hippo's sweat is a reddish oily fluid that acts like sunscreen and may help fight germs.
Hippos cannot really swim. In deep water they bounce along the bottom, pushing off with their feet.
Despite their bulk, hippos can run about 30 kilometers per hour over short distances on land.
A cheetah can go from 0 to about 100 kilometers per hour in roughly three seconds, faster than many sports cars.
Cheetahs cannot roar. Instead they chirp, purr and make bird-like yelps to call each other.
The black tear marks under a cheetah's eyes may cut glare from the sun, like a football player's eye black.
A lion's roar can be heard up to about 8 kilometers away on a still night.
Lions can sleep or rest for up to 20 hours a day, saving energy for short bursts of hunting.
A lion's tail ends in a tuft of hair that hides a small, hard spur, and nobody is quite sure what it is for.
No two tigers have the same stripe pattern, and the stripes are on their skin too, not just their fur.
A tiger sees about six times better than you in the dark, which is why it hunts mostly at night.
Tigers are strong swimmers and often cool off by lounging in rivers and lakes.
A snow leopard can leap roughly six times its own body length in a single bound.
Snow leopards wrap their long, thick tails around their faces like a scarf to stay warm while they sleep.
Polar bears have black skin under their fur, and each hair is actually transparent, not white.
A polar bear can smell a seal through snow from far away and may sniff out a seal's breathing hole nearly a kilometer off.
Grizzly bears can run at about 55 kilometers per hour, faster than an Olympic sprinter.
During hibernation, black bears can go months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating.
A giant panda spends up to 14 hours a day eating and can munch through more than 12 kilograms of bamboo daily.
Giant pandas have a special wrist bone that works like a thumb, helping them grip bamboo stalks.
A newborn giant panda is about 1/900th the size of its mother, roughly the weight of a stick of butter.
Red pandas are not closely related to giant pandas; they sit in a family all their own.
Koalas sleep up to 18 to 22 hours a day because their eucalyptus diet gives them very little energy.
Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that they could confuse a crime scene investigator.
A baby kangaroo is born about the size of a jelly bean and crawls up into its mother's pouch.
Red kangaroos can cover about 8 meters in a single hop and reach speeds over 50 kilometers per hour.
Kangaroos cannot easily walk backwards: their big tail and long feet are built for hopping forward.
Wombats produce cube-shaped poop, which they stack on rocks and logs to mark their territory.
A wombat's pouch faces backwards, so dirt does not get in when the mother digs.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs and has no nipples: its babies lap milk from patches of skin.
Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind legs that can cause severe pain in humans.
A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nose shut, sensing the tiny electric signals of its prey with its bill.
Echidnas, like platypuses, are egg-laying mammals, and a baby echidna is called a puggle.
Sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, giving them a greenish camouflage.
A sloth climbs down from its tree only about once a week, mainly to go to the toilet.
Sloths can hold their breath for up to 40 minutes by slowing their heart rate.
Three-toed sloths can turn their heads about 270 degrees, thanks to extra bones in their necks.
An armadillo can hold its breath for around six minutes and may walk across the bottom of a stream.
The nine-banded armadillo almost always gives birth to identical quadruplets from a single egg.
Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, and the scales are made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its body and is anchored near its pelvis.
Aardvarks can dig a burrow so fast that they may vanish underground in a few minutes.
Naked mole-rats can survive about 18 minutes with no oxygen at all, by switching their bodies to run on a different sugar, like plants do.
Naked mole-rats can live over 30 years, roughly ten times longer than mice of similar size.
Naked mole-rats live in colonies with a single breeding queen, much like bees or ants.
Star-nosed moles have 22 fleshy tentacles on their nose and can identify and eat food in a quarter of a second.
A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines, and each one is really a stiff, hollow hair.
Porcupines cannot shoot their quills, but the quills detach easily and have tiny barbs that work their way in.
A beaver's front teeth never stop growing and are orange because they contain iron, which makes them tougher.
A beaver can hold its breath for about 15 minutes and has see-through eyelids that work like swimming goggles.
The longest known beaver dam, in Canada, is about 850 meters long, long enough to spot in satellite photos.
Squirrels plant thousands of trees by accident: many nuts they bury are never dug up again.
Gray squirrels sometimes pretend to bury a nut to fool other animals that may be watching.
Prairie dogs have complex alarm calls that seem to describe a predator's type, size and even color.
Chipmunks can stuff their cheek pouches until they are about three times the size of their head.
A capybara is the world's largest rodent and can weigh over 60 kilograms, about as much as an adult human.
Capybaras can sleep in water, keeping just their nose above the surface.
Rats can tread water for days and can survive being flushed down a toilet.
A rat can fall from the height of a five-story building and walk away unhurt.
A house mouse can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil, because its skull is the only part that needs to fit.
Rabbits can see nearly 360 degrees around them without turning their heads.
Rabbits eat some of their own droppings, special soft ones, so their food passes through them twice and they get every last bit of goodness.
A happy rabbit may leap into the air and twist its body, a move called a binky.
Snowshoe hares turn white in winter and brown in summer, triggered by changing day length.
The jackrabbit can leap about 3 meters in one bound and run up to about 65 kilometers per hour.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Flying squirrels and sugar gliders only glide.
About one in every five kinds of mammal on Earth is a bat. There are over 1,400 bat species.
Vampire bats share blood meals with roost mates who failed to feed, and they remember who helped them.
Vampire bats can run, jump and hop along the ground on their folded wings.
A single little brown bat can catch hundreds of insects in an hour of hunting.
Some fruit bats have wingspans of up to about 1.5 meters, longer than many people are tall.
Bumblebee bats from Thailand weigh about 2 grams, less than a penny, making them among the smallest mammals.
The Etruscan shrew weighs under 2 grams, and its heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute.
A shrew must eat roughly its own body weight in food every day or it will starve.
A single cave in Texas holds around 15 million bats every summer, so many that their nightly exit shows up on weather radar.
Mexican free-tailed bats can reach speeds of around 160 kilometers per hour in level flight.
Gorillas share about 98 percent of their DNA with humans, and some have learned hundreds of sign language signs.
Chimpanzees make tools: they strip leaves off twigs and poke them into termite mounds to fish out a snack.
Orangutans make a fresh bed of branches high in the trees almost every single night.
Orangutans have been seen using big leaves as umbrellas when it rains.
A wild orangutan in Indonesia was seen treating a wound on its face with a chewed-up medicinal plant.
Bonobos often calm down tense moments with hugs and cuddles instead of fights.
Howler monkeys are so loud that their calls can carry about 5 kilometers through the rainforest.
Japanese macaques in snowy mountains soak in natural hot springs to stay warm in winter.
Some capuchin monkeys crack open hard nuts by smashing them with stones on a rock, like a hammer and anvil.
A tarsier's eyes are each as big as its brain, so it cannot move them and turns its head instead.
Aye-ayes tap on tree bark with a long, skinny middle finger and listen for hollow tunnels where grubs hide.
Ring-tailed lemurs hold stink fights, rubbing smelly scent on their tails and waving them at rivals.
A dog's sense of smell is roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times sharper than a human's.
No two dogs have the same nose print: the bumpy pattern on a dog's nose is as unique as your fingerprint.
Dogs can be trained to sniff out diseases, including some cancers and low blood sugar in people with diabetes.
A dog's nose is wet partly because the moisture helps catch scent particles from the air.
Dogs often turn in circles before lying down, a habit that may come from wild ancestors flattening grass into a bed.
Dalmatian puppies are born pure white; their spots appear in the first few weeks.
The Basenji, an African dog breed, does not bark. It makes a yodel-like sound instead.
Greyhounds can reach about 70 kilometers per hour, making them the fastest dog breed.
Puppies are born deaf and blind, and their ears and eyes open after about two weeks.
Dogs can understand pointing, something even our closest cousins, chimpanzees, struggle with.
Cats spend about two thirds of their lives asleep, so a 9-year-old cat has been awake for only about three years.
A cat's purr vibrates at a low hum, and cats purr when stressed or hurt as well as when happy.
Cats cannot taste sweetness at all: the gene for tasting sugar is broken in every cat, from house cats to tigers.
Adult cats rarely meow at each other. They mostly meow to talk to humans.
A cat has 32 muscles in each ear and can swivel them independently, like satellite dishes.
Cats almost always land on their feet thanks to a twisting reflex they develop by about seven weeks old.
Most cats are lactose intolerant, so a saucer of milk can actually give them an upset tummy.
Cats have a third eyelid, a thin membrane that sweeps across the eye to protect it.
The first cat in space was a French cat named Felicette, who flew in 1963 and returned safely.
Your pet cat shares about 95 percent of its DNA with a tiger, which explains a lot about the pouncing.
Horses cannot breathe through their mouths at all, only through their noses, even when galloping flat out.
Horses can sleep standing up thanks to a locking system in their legs, but they need to lie down for deep sleep.
A horse's eyes are among the largest of any land mammal, each one bigger than a golf ball.
Horses have nearly 360-degree vision, with small blind spots right in front of and behind them.
A newborn foal can usually stand and walk within about an hour, and trot after its mother soon after.
Zebra stripes may help keep biting flies away: flies seem to have trouble landing on them.
Every zebra has a unique stripe pattern, and foals may learn to recognize their mother's stripes.
Cows have best friends, and they get stressed when separated from them.
Alpacas and llamas share communal toilet spots, and a whole herd will line up to use the same dung pile.
A dairy cow can produce around 25 to 30 liters of milk a day, about 100 glasses.
Pigs barely sweat at all, so they roll in mud to cool down, and the mud doubles as sunscreen and bug spray.
Pigs can sniff out truffles buried underground, which is why French truffle hunters have used them for centuries.
Goats have rectangular pupils, which give them a wide view to watch for predators.
Goats have regional accents: their bleats change depending on the group they live with.
Sheep can recognize at least 50 different sheep faces and remember them for about two years.
Sheep can learn to recognize human faces from photos, and in one study they picked out celebrities like Barack Obama.
A single merino sheep, called Chris, was found in Australia carrying over 40 kilograms of wool.
Llamas and alpacas spit when annoyed, but usually at each other, not at people.
A thirsty camel can gulp down over 100 liters of water in about 10 minutes, roughly a bathtub full.
A camel's hump stores fat, not water, which it can break down for energy when food is scarce.
Camels have three eyelids, two rows of eyelashes and nostrils they can squeeze shut, all to keep out blowing sand.
Reindeer eyes change color with the seasons, golden in summer and blue in winter.
Reindeer knees make a clicking sound as they walk, which may help a herd stay together in a blizzard.
Moose are excellent swimmers and can dive about 6 meters deep to eat water plants.
A moose's antlers can span about 1.8 meters, wider than most people are tall, and they fall off every winter.
Deer antlers are among the fastest-growing tissues known, growing up to about 2.5 centimeters a day.
Pronghorn can run about 88 kilometers per hour, and they can keep up a fast pace for many kilometers.
The pronghorn may run so fast because it once had to escape the American cheetah, now extinct.
White rhino calves run in front of their mothers, while black rhino calves trot behind theirs.
White rhinos are not white. Their name may come from a mistranslation of a Dutch word meaning wide, for their mouth.
Rhinos have poor eyesight and may not see a person standing about 30 meters away if they stay still.
A rhino may weigh as much as a car, yet it can charge at around 50 kilometers per hour.
The okapi looks like a zebra mixed with a horse but is actually the giraffe's closest living relative.
An okapi's tongue is long enough to lick its own eyelids and clean its ears.
Hyenas look like dogs, but they are actually more closely related to cats and mongooses.
Spotted hyena jaws are strong enough to crunch through bones and eat them.
Meerkats take turns standing guard on high spots and give alarm calls when danger appears.
Honey badgers are famously fearless and will fight lions, leopards and venomous snakes.
Skunks can spray their smelly defense up to about 3 meters, and the smell can be noticed over a kilometer away.
Spotted skunks do a handstand before spraying, as a warning to back off.
Raccoons have very sensitive front paws, and wetting them may make their sense of touch even sharper.
Opossums have 50 teeth, more than any other land mammal in North America.
When threatened, an opossum can play dead for hours, even drooling and giving off a foul smell.
River otters can pinch their ears and nostrils shut to keep the water out while they swim.
A wolf pack is usually just a family: a mother, a father and their pups of different ages.
A hungry wolf can wolf down around 9 kilograms of meat in one meal, then go days without eating again.
Arctic foxes stay cozy at minus 50 degrees Celsius thanks to fur so thick it even covers the soles of their feet.
A diving peregrine falcon can top 300 kilometers per hour, making it the fastest animal on Earth.
Hummingbirds can hover in place and even fly backwards, something almost no other bird can do.
A hummingbird's heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute while it zips between flowers.
Some hummingbirds flap their wings around 50 to 80 times every second, which is why they hum.
At night, hummingbirds can drop into a deep chill called torpor, cooling their bodies to save energy until morning.
The bee hummingbird of Cuba is the smallest bird in the world, about 5 centimeters long and lighter than a dime.
A hummingbird's nest can be about the size of a walnut shell, held together with spider silk.
Ostriches lay the biggest eggs of any living bird: one egg weighs about as much as two dozen chicken eggs.
An ostrich's eye is about the size of a billiard ball and bigger than its own brain.
Ostriches can sprint at about 70 kilometers per hour, faster than any other bird on land.
A kick from an ostrich, with its long-clawed toes, is powerful enough to kill a lion.
Emus can sprint at nearly 50 kilometers per hour, taking strides almost 3 meters long.
Male emus sit on the eggs for about eight weeks, barely eating or drinking the whole time.
The kiwi lays one of the biggest eggs compared with its body size, up to about 20 percent of the mother's weight.
The kiwi is the only bird with nostrils at the tip of its beak, which it uses to sniff out worms underground.
The kakapo of New Zealand is the world's heaviest parrot and cannot fly, so it climbs trees instead.
Kakapo smell of honey or musty flowers, a scent that sadly helped predators find them.
The kea, a parrot from New Zealand's mountains, is famous for pulling rubber off car windshields.
Keas can solve puzzles and seem to understand probability, choosing the jar more likely to hold a treat.
Some parrots name their chicks: parents give each one a unique call that sticks for life.
Parrots can live a very long time: some large parrots reach 60 years or more in captivity.
A cockatoo named Snowball can dance to the beat of music, a skill once thought to be uniquely human.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember people who treated them badly for years.
Crows have been seen holding what look like funerals, gathering around a dead crow to learn about danger.
New Caledonian crows bend twigs into hooks to pull grubs out of holes.
Ravens can mimic sounds, including car engines, toilets flushing and human words.
Clark's nutcrackers bury tens of thousands of seeds each autumn and find many of them months later under snow.
Owls cannot move their eyes, so they twist their heads up to about 270 degrees instead.
Burrowing owls spread animal dung around their burrow entrances, which lures beetles right to their front door.
A barn owl can catch a mouse in total darkness using its hearing alone, no light needed.
In many owls, one ear sits higher than the other, helping them pinpoint sounds up and down.
Owl feathers have soft fringed edges that silence the air, so prey cannot hear them coming.
A single barn owl can eat around a thousand mice and voles in a year, which is why farmers love them.
Snowy owls can swallow a lemming whole and later spit up the bones and fur as a pellet.
An eagle can spot a rabbit from about 3 kilometers away, roughly the length of 30 football fields.
A bald eagle's nest can weigh over a ton, and one in Florida was measured at about 3 meters wide.
The harpy eagle's back talons can be as long as a grizzly bear's claws.
Vultures have such strong stomach acid that they can eat rotten meat that would sicken other animals.
The turkey vulture finds dead animals by smell, a rare skill among birds.
A bearded vulture's diet is mostly bone: it drops big bones onto rocks to smash them into bite-size pieces.
One Andean condor was tracked flying over 170 kilometers in five hours while barely flapping its wings.
The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying roughly 70,000 kilometers a year pole to pole.
Hummingbirds cannot walk or hop: their tiny feet are only good for perching, so they fly even to shuffle along a branch.
In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,500 kilometers nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days, without eating or resting.
