Common swifts can stay airborne for about 10 months straight, eating and even sleeping on the wing.
Frigatebirds can sleep in flight, sometimes resting one half of their brain at a time.
Albatrosses can glide for hours without flapping and may circle the globe in under two months.
In late 2024, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom laid an egg at about 74 years old. She is the oldest known wild bird.
The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 3.5 meters.
Many migrating birds sense Earth's magnetic field, and robins may actually see it as a faint pattern over their vision.
Some migrating birds use the stars to find their way, learning the night sky when they are young.
Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas at over 7,000 meters, where the air holds less than half the oxygen at sea level.
Flamingos are born gray. They turn pink from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.
Flamingos can only eat with their heads upside down, filtering food through their beaks.
Flamingos often stand on one leg, and they are actually more stable that way than on two.
A woodpecker can peck about 20 times a second, and its long tongue wraps around its skull.
Penguins cannot fly in air, but they fly underwater, beating their wings like flippers.
Emperor penguin dads keep an egg on their feet for about two months in the Antarctic winter, eating nothing.
Huddles of thousands of emperor penguins take turns moving into the warm middle and out to the cold edge.
The common poorwill is the only bird known to truly hibernate, sleeping for weeks in desert rock crevices during cold spells.
Male Adelie penguins give pebbles to females to help build their nests, and some steal pebbles from neighbors.
Pigeons can recognize themselves in a mirror and can even tell paintings by Monet from ones by Picasso.
Homing pigeons can find their way back home from over 1,000 kilometers away.
Birds are living dinosaurs, and chickens are among the closest living relatives of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Chickens have more than 20 different calls, including separate alarms for danger from the sky and on the ground.
There are more chickens on Earth than any other bird, roughly 25 billion at any time.
A hen turns her egg about 50 times a day to keep the chick from sticking to the shell.
Turkeys can see in color and have a field of view of about 270 degrees.
A turkey's head and neck can change color, from red to blue or white, with its mood.
Ducks have waterproof feathers thanks to an oil gland near their tail that they spread with their beaks.
Ducklings bond with the first moving thing they see after hatching and follow it everywhere.
Ducks' feet do not freeze on ice because warm blood flowing down passes right beside cold blood coming back up and warms it.
Swans can have a wingspan of over 2 meters, and mute swan pairs often stay together for many years.
Geese fly in a V formation to save energy, each bird riding the air lifted by the one ahead.
Pelicans can hold about three times more in their beak pouch than in their stomach.
The shoebill stork can stand totally still for hours waiting for a fish, then lunges in an instant.
Lyrebirds can mimic almost any sound they hear, including chainsaws, car alarms and camera shutters.
Male bowerbirds build elaborate stick houses decorated with colorful objects, sorted by color, to impress females.

Cuckoos lay their eggs in other birds' nests, and the cuckoo chick pushes the host's own eggs out.
Oxpeckers ride on rhinos and buffalo, eating ticks, and sound an alarm when danger approaches.
Hoatzin chicks have claws on their wings, which help them climb back up into trees.
Some bird species, like the pitohui of New Guinea, have poisonous feathers and skin.
Male sage grouse puff up yellow air sacs on their chests and pop them to impress females.
Chameleons change color mostly to show mood and signal to rivals, not just to blend in.
A chameleon's tongue can shoot out at its prey in a fraction of a second and be longer than its own body.
Chameleon eyes can move independently, so one can look forward while the other looks back.
Some chameleons are so small they can sit on the tip of a matchstick.
Geckos can walk up glass thanks to millions of tiny hairs on their toes that stick by sheer closeness.
Tokay geckos are named after their loud call, which sounds like someone shouting to-kay in the middle of the night.
Many lizards can drop their tail to escape a predator, and the tail keeps wriggling to distract it.
The horned lizard can squirt blood from its eyes to scare off coyotes and dogs.
The basilisk lizard can run across water on its hind legs, earning it the nickname Jesus Christ lizard.
The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard alive, growing to about 3 meters long.
A Komodo dragon can eat up to 80 percent of its body weight in one meal.
Female Komodo dragons can sometimes have babies without a male, through virgin birth.
Marine iguanas of the Galapagos sneeze salt out of their noses after feeding in the sea.
Marine iguanas can actually shrink in body length during hard times when food is scarce.
The thorny devil of Australia drinks through its skin: tiny grooves carry water to its mouth.
Some skinks have bright blue tongues that they flash to startle predators.
The flying dragon lizard glides between trees on wing-like flaps of skin stretched over its ribs.
Some big snakes can go a year or more without eating, living off the energy from one huge meal.
Snakes smell with their tongues, flicking them to pick up scent and pressing them to a sensor in the mouth.
Pit vipers, pythons and boas can see the body heat of their prey in total darkness.
Snakes have no eyelids. Instead, a clear scale covers and protects each eye.
Egg-eating snakes swallow bird eggs whole, crack them with spiky bones inside their throat, then spit out the folded shell.
Reticulated pythons are the world's longest snakes, with some over 6 meters long.
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth, and a big one can weigh over 90 kilograms, more than most grown men.
King cobras are the only snakes that build nests, piling up leaves for their eggs and guarding them.
A king cobra can rise up so high that it can look an adult human in the eye.
Black mambas can slither at about 15 to 20 kilometers per hour, among the fastest snakes on Earth.
Spitting cobras can aim venom at an attacker's eyes from about 2 meters away.
The inland taipan of Australia has the most toxic venom of any land snake, but it is very shy.
Some snakes in Asia, called flying snakes, flatten their bodies and glide from tree to tree.
Rattlesnakes are born without a rattle; a new segment is added every time they shed their skin.
Hognose snakes play dead dramatically, rolling over, sticking out their tongues and even releasing a bad smell.
Garter snakes gather in Manitoba by the tens of thousands each spring, the biggest snake gathering on Earth.
A snake sheds its skin in one piece, often turned inside out like a sock.
The Brahminy blind snake is so small it is often mistaken for an earthworm, and all known ones are female.
The Gaboon viper has the longest fangs of any snake, up to about 5 centimeters, and it hides on the forest floor looking just like dead leaves.
Saltwater crocodiles have the strongest bite ever measured in a living animal.
A crocodile's jaw closes with huge force, but the muscles that open it are so weak a rubber band can hold it shut.
Crocodiles burn energy so slowly that they can go months without a meal when food is scarce.
Crocodiles swallow stones, which may help them grind food or stay balanced in the water.
Crocodiles cannot stick out their tongues, because the tongue is held down along the floor of the mouth by a thin skin.
Baby crocodiles chirp from inside their eggs to tell their mother it is time to dig them out.
Crocodile mothers gently carry their hatchlings to the water inside their huge jaws.
Crocodiles have salt glands on their tongues that let them live in the sea, while alligators mostly stick to fresh water.
Alligators have been seen balancing sticks on their snouts during bird nesting season, possibly as bait.
Gharials have extremely long, thin snouts packed with over 100 sharp teeth for catching fish.
A tortoise's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to its ribs and spine, so it can never crawl out of it.
Jonathan, a giant tortoise on the island of St Helena, hatched around 1832 and was still alive in 2025, the oldest known land animal.
A turtle's shell has nerves, so turtles can feel it when you touch it.
Box turtles can close their shells completely thanks to a hinge on the bottom shell.
Some freshwater turtles can breathe through their bottoms, absorbing oxygen from water while they hibernate.
The alligator snapping turtle lures fish with a pink, worm-shaped flap on its tongue.
Galapagos tortoises can survive about a year without food or water, which sadly made them easy food for sailors long ago.
Tuataras have a third eye on the top of their head, which is covered by skin in adults.
Wood frogs freeze solid in winter, their heart stops, and they thaw back to life in spring.
Glass frogs have see-through bellies: you can watch their heart beating inside.
Some glass frogs hide their red blood in their liver while they sleep, making them nearly invisible.
A golden poison frog carries enough toxin to kill about 10 adult humans.
Poison dart frogs raised in zoos are harmless: their poison comes from the bugs they eat in the wild.
The Goliath frog of West Africa can grow over 30 centimeters long and weigh over 3 kilograms, as much as a newborn baby.
As of 2024, the smallest known frog is a Brazilian flea toad about 7 millimeters long, small enough to sit on your fingernail with room to spare.
Frogs do not drink with their mouths: they soak up water through their skin, mostly through a patch on their belly.
Frogs use their eyes to help them swallow: they pull their eyeballs down into their head to push food down.
Some frogs can glide: Wallace's flying frog spreads its webbed feet like parachutes.
The Surinam toad raises its babies inside pockets in the skin of its back, and tiny toads pop out.
Cane toads were brought to Australia to eat beetles, and they spread across the country instead.
Axolotls can regrow lost legs, tails, and even parts of their heart, spine and brain.

The Chinese giant salamander is the largest amphibian on Earth, reaching about 1.8 meters long.
The olm, a cave salamander, can live about 100 years and go roughly 10 years without eating.

The Iberian ribbed newt pushes its own sharp ribs through its skin as poisonous spikes when grabbed.

A fennec fox's huge ears help it hear prey moving under the sand and release heat in the desert.
Chinchillas have such thick fur, about 50 to 80 hairs per follicle, that fleas cannot easily live in it.

Sugar gliders are tiny marsupials that glide between trees on thin skin flaps, like living kites.

Tapirs have short trunk-like snouts that they use like a snorkel when swimming.

Jaguars have the strongest bite of any big cat for their size and can bite straight through turtle shells.

Pumas have more names than almost any other animal, including cougar, mountain lion and catamount.

African wild dogs vote by sneezing: the more sneezes, the more likely the pack is to go hunting.
African wild dog packs succeed in roughly 60 to 90 percent of their hunts, far more often than lions.
Coyotes have learned to live in big cities like Chicago and Los Angeles, often without being noticed.
A wolverine can smell food buried under several meters of snow, then dig straight down to it.

Elephants have one of the best noses in the animal world and can smell water from several kilometers away.

Dogs see the world mostly in blues and yellows, and reds look like dull browns to them.

Horses use facial expressions to communicate and can read human facial expressions too.
Horses can remember people who were kind to them, even after years apart.
Starlings swirl in giant flocks called murmurations, thousands of birds turning together by watching their nearest neighbors.
Around 1890, about 100 European starlings were set free in New York's Central Park, and their descendants now number in the tens of millions across North America.
Weaver birds tie real knots with grass to build hanging nests, and young males get better with practice.
Sociable weavers build giant shared nests that can house hundreds of birds and last for a century.
The tailorbird sews leaves together into a pouch for its nest, poking holes with its beak and threading plant fibers.
Honeyguide birds lead people to wild bees' nests, and in Mozambique they answer a special call that honey hunters make.
The cassowary has a dagger-like claw on each foot up to about 12 centimeters long and can be dangerous to people.
Cassowaries are one of the few birds that spread big rainforest seeds, which pass through them whole.
The secretary bird kills snakes by stomping on them with kicks faster than the blink of an eye.
Roadrunners can sprint at about 30 kilometers per hour and are fast enough to catch and eat rattlesnakes.
Puffins can hold a dozen or more small fish in their beaks at once, thanks to a spiny tongue that pins them.
A kingfisher dives into water with barely a splash, and its beak shape inspired the nose of Japan's bullet train.
Female hornbills seal themselves inside a tree hole with mud, and the male feeds her through a slit for weeks.
The potoo bird hides by sitting perfectly still on a broken branch, looking just like part of the tree.
Oilbirds live in caves and find their way in the dark with clicking echoes, much like bats.
Some swiftlets build nests entirely out of their own hardened saliva, which people make into bird's nest soup.
A toucan's huge beak is light and hollow inside, and it works like a radiator to release body heat.
Macaws in the Amazon gather in crowds to eat clay from riverbanks, possibly for the salt it contains.
Canaries were once taken down coal mines because they react to dangerous gases before people do.
Male budgies can learn hundreds of words, and one named Puck was credited with a vocabulary of over 1,700 words.
Blue jays can copy the screams of hawks, perhaps to warn others or to scare birds away from food.
Northern mockingbirds can learn around 200 different songs, including car alarms and other birds.
A male nightingale can know around 200 different songs, and city nightingales sing louder to be heard over traffic.
Shrikes impale their prey on thorns and barbed wire, building a pantry of insects, lizards and mice.
The American dipper walks along the bottom of fast streams to hunt insects, fully underwater.
Ptarmigans grow feathers on their feet in winter, which work as both boots and snowshoes.
Male birds-of-paradise perform wild courtship dances, some turning into strange shapes like a black oval with a smile.
The red-capped manakin attracts females by sliding backwards along a branch like a moonwalk.
The club-winged manakin makes a violin-like hum by rubbing special wing feathers together over 100 times a second.
Hoopoe chicks defend themselves by squirting stinky poop at intruders.
Wild budgies in Australia fly across the outback in flocks that can number in the thousands, turning the sky green and yellow.
Chickadees add new brain cells each autumn, possibly to help remember where they hid thousands of seeds.
Black-capped chickadees add more dee notes to their alarm call when the predator is more dangerous.
Woodpeckers drum on trees and even metal gutters not only to find food but to announce their territory.
Acorn woodpeckers drill thousands of holes in a single tree and store an acorn in each one.
Hummingbirds can see colors that humans cannot, mixing ultraviolet light with ordinary colors.
Pigeons can see ultraviolet light and may sense very low sounds, like distant storms, that we cannot hear.
A woodcock's eyes sit so far back on its head that it can see behind itself, and it has a full circle of vision.
A bird's feathers can weigh more than its whole skeleton, because its bones are so light and hollow.
A swan can have around 25,000 feathers, while a tiny hummingbird has only about 1,000.
Great grey owls can hear a vole moving under about 60 centimeters of snow, then plunge in feet-first to grab it.
Hawks and eagles see colors more vividly than people and can spot details about four to eight times farther.
A peregrine falcon has little bony cones in its nostrils that are thought to tame the blast of air during its dive.
Peregrine falcons now nest on skyscrapers in many cities, treating ledges like cliffs and pigeons as dinner.
Ospreys turn the fish they catch head-first to make them more streamlined in flight.
Golden eagles have been trained in Mongolia for centuries to hunt foxes alongside their human partners.
Bald eagles are not actually bald: their name comes from an old word meaning white-headed.
A young bald eagle has brown head feathers and only gets its white head at around five years old.
Cattle egrets follow cows and tractors to snap up the insects they stir up.
Sandhill cranes perform bouncing dances with wing flaps and leaps, and pairs often dance together.
Crane couples sing duets called unison calls, which can be heard several kilometers away.
Storks have almost no voice and communicate by loudly clattering their beaks together.
Ruby-throated hummingbirds fly about 800 kilometers nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico during migration.
Before migrating, some songbirds nearly double their body weight in fat to fuel the trip.
Blackpoll warblers, which weigh about as much as two coins, fly nonstop over the Atlantic for up to three days.
Migrating birds can make a mistake called reverse migration and turn up thousands of kilometers off course.
A goose can fly over 1,000 kilometers in a single day during migration.
The ostrich has just two toes on each foot, fewer than any other bird.
Blue jays are not truly blue: their feathers have no blue pigment and only look blue because of the way they scatter light.
Male cardinals get their red color from pigments in the berries and seeds they eat.
Baby pigeons are rarely seen because they stay in the nest until they are almost adult-sized.
Mute swans are not really mute: they hiss, snort and grunt, and their wings make a loud throbbing hum in flight.
Pigeons and flamingos both feed their chicks a milk made in their throats, and flamingo milk can be bright red.
A mother hen clucks to her chicks while they are still inside the eggs, and the chicks peep back.
Chickens are smarter than they look: they can recognize and remember over 100 other chickens by face.
Roosters crow on an inner clock, not only at sunrise, and the top rooster usually crows first.
A duck's bill is packed with touch sensors, letting it find food in muddy water without seeing it.
A binturong, a furry tree-dweller from Asia, smells like buttered popcorn, thanks to the same chemical that flavors the snack.
Sun bears have tongues up to about 25 centimeters long, perfect for licking honey out of beehives.
Sloth bears close their nostrils and suck up termites like a vacuum cleaner, loud enough to hear 100 meters away.
A polar bear was tracked swimming for nine days straight, covering about 690 kilometers.
Brown bears catch salmon leaping up waterfalls, sometimes snatching them right out of the air.
Clouded leopards can climb down trees head-first, and even hang upside down from branches by their back feet.
Pallas's cats have round pupils instead of slits and fluffy fur so thick they look grumpy all year round.
Every wolf has its own howl, and scientists can tell individual wolves apart by their voices.
Spotted hyenas giggle when stressed, and their giggles carry clues about their age and rank.
Lions with darker manes tend to be healthier and are more attractive to lionesses.
Giraffes hum to each other at night, a low drone that scientists only discovered in 2015.
A yawning hippo is not sleepy: it is showing off its huge tusks as a warning.
White rhinos leave dung piles that work like a message board, telling other rhinos who passed by.
The fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar is the only primate known to hibernate, for up to seven months.
A bushbaby, a tiny primate, can leap over 2 meters straight up, many times its own height.
Colugos can glide over 100 meters between trees on a furry skin cape that stretches to the tips of their tails.
Pikas gather piles of grass and flowers in summer and dry them into haystacks to eat through the winter.
Moles bite the heads of earthworms to paralyze them and keep hundreds alive in underground pantries.
Some badger setts are used by generation after generation of badgers for over a hundred years.
A kinkajou can turn its back feet backwards so it can run up and down tree trunks with ease.
Coatis hold their striped tails straight up like flags so the group can keep together in tall grass.
Gila monsters may eat only a handful of meals a year, and a diabetes medicine was developed from a hormone in their spit.
Green anoles change from bright green to brown depending on mood and temperature.
Some whiptail lizards are all female: they reproduce without males, laying eggs that hatch into clones.
Geckos have no eyelids, so many of them lick their eyeballs to keep them clean.
The armadillo lizard grabs its tail in its mouth and curls into a spiky ring when threatened.
The frilled lizard opens a huge umbrella of skin around its neck and hisses to scare predators.
Painted turtles can survive months under frozen ponds with almost no oxygen.
Gopher tortoise burrows shelter hundreds of other kinds of animals, from snakes to frogs to owls.
Darwin's frog dads carry tadpoles inside their vocal sac until tiny froglets hop out of their mouths.
The hellbender, a giant salamander nicknamed snot otter, breathes mostly through wrinkly folds of skin.
Superb fairywren mothers teach a secret password call to chicks while they are still in the egg.
Chinstrap penguins take over 10,000 micro-naps a day, each only about four seconds long.
A peacock's famous train is not its tail: it is made of extra-long feathers growing from its back, covering a short real tail.
Cockatoos in Sydney learned to open garbage bin lids, and the trick spread from suburb to suburb.
Crows in Japan drop walnuts onto busy roads, let cars crack them, then grab the nuts at a red light.
Green herons drop bits of bread or insects on the water as bait, then grab the fish that come to eat.
Baby burrowing owls hiss like rattlesnakes to scare away animals poking into their burrows.
A killdeer pretends to have a broken wing, limping away to lead predators far from its nest.
Some vultures and storks cool down on hot days by peeing on their own legs and letting it evaporate.
The kori bustard is one of the heaviest birds able to fly, with large males weighing about 18 kilograms.
A kookaburra's call sounds like loud laughter, and families laugh together at dawn to mark their territory.
Hachiko, a dog in Japan, waited at a train station for his owner every day for about nine years after the man died.
A chimpanzee named Ham flew into space in 1961, months before any American astronaut.
A cat named Creme Puff lived to 38 years old, the oldest cat on record.
An Australian cattle dog named Bluey lived to 29 years old, one of the oldest dogs ever recorded.
For about 20 years, a cat named Stubbs was the honorary mayor of a small town in Alaska.
Many all-white cats with blue eyes are born deaf, because the gene for white fur can also affect the inner ear.
Female cats are more likely to be right-pawed, while male cats are more likely to be left-pawed.
Most calico and tortoiseshell cats are female, because the genes for those colors ride on the X chromosome.
Rabbits gently grind their teeth when content, a sound owners call a bunny purr.
Pet hamsters can run several kilometers in a single night on their exercise wheels.
Gerbils thump the ground with their back feet to warn the colony of danger.
A rat named Magawa sniffed out over 100 land mines and unexploded bombs in Cambodia and won a gold medal for bravery.
Crows and ravens have been filmed sliding down snowy roofs and slopes again and again, apparently just for fun.
Young elephants suck their trunks for comfort, much like a human baby sucks its thumb.
An elephant's trunk can hold about 8 liters of water at once, which it sprays into its mouth or over its back.
@body|Human body
Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, which adds up to roughly 2.5 billion beats in an average lifetime.
The back of your eye is the only place a doctor can look straight at your blood vessels and a nerve without making a single cut.
Over a long life, your heart pumps enough blood to fill dozens of Olympic swimming pools.
As far as scientists know, humans are the only animals that cry tears because of their feelings.
Your body makes roughly 2 to 3 million new red blood cells every second, just to replace the ones wearing out.
A red blood cell lives about four months, travelling round and round your body the whole time before it is recycled.
A drop of blood about the size of a pinhead holds roughly 5 million red blood cells.
Red blood cells throw away their own core when they mature, freeing up space to carry more oxygen.
Your tiniest blood vessels are so narrow that red blood cells must squeeze through them one at a time, bending like soft little discs.
Blood is never blue inside you. Even blood heading back to the heart is dark red; veins only look blue through your skin.
Your heart has its own built-in spark plug, so it can keep beating for a while even after it is removed from the body.
Charles Darwin called blushing the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions.
Your biggest artery, the aorta, is about as wide as a garden hose.
The lub-dub sound of a heartbeat is not the muscle squeezing. It is the sound of heart valves snapping shut.
An adult heart is roughly the size of a large fist and weighs about as much as a can of soda.
An average adult carries about 5 liters of blood, roughly as much as two big bottles of soda and a bit more.
Try humming with your mouth shut and your nose pinched: the hum dies almost at once, because the air has nowhere to go.
The tiny cell fragments that plug a cut and help blood clot live only about a week to ten days.
Your brain has no pain sensors of its own, so surgeons can operate on it while the patient is awake and chatting.
Some blood is so rare that fewer than a hundred people in the world are known to have it. Doctors nicknamed it golden blood.
The valves in your leg veins work like one-way doors, and every step you take squeezes blood back up toward your heart.
Before birth, a baby gets oxygen from its mother because its blood grabs oxygen even more tightly than hers does.
Before birth, a small hole in the heart lets blood skip the lungs. It usually seals up soon after the baby's first breaths.
A newborn's heart races along at about twice the speed of an adult's.
Your heart never fully rests. It only relaxes for a split second between each beat, for your whole life.
Your heart muscle barely renews itself: in adults, less than 1 percent of its cells are replaced each year.
Fallout from Cold War nuclear bomb tests left a time stamp in everyone's cells, which let scientists work out how old different body parts really are.
The first person to measure blood pressure stuck a tall glass tube into a horse's artery, and the blood shot up over 2.5 meters.
For centuries doctors thought the liver kept making fresh blood. Only in the 1600s did someone show the same blood goes round and round.
White blood cells can squeeze out through the walls of blood vessels to chase down germs hiding in your tissues.
The most common white blood cells are short-lived soldiers that survive only hours to a few days.
Your spleen acts as a quality inspector, pulling old and worn-out red blood cells out of circulation.
You can live without your spleen. Other organs take over most of its work.
Your body recycles the iron from old red blood cells to build new ones instead of throwing it away.
A bruise changes from purple to green to yellow because your body is breaking down the blood trapped under the skin.
The arteries that feed the heart itself are only about as wide as a drinking straw.
Doctors have been able to transplant a human heart from one person to another since 1967.
In 1929 a young doctor slid a thin tube through a vein in his own arm all the way into his heart, then walked to the X-ray room to prove it.
The first man to get an implanted pacemaker went on to have 26 of them and outlived both the surgeon and the inventor.
Donated red blood cells keep in the fridge for about six weeks, but donated platelets last less than a week.
After you give blood, the liquid part is replaced within a day or two, but the red cells take several weeks to rebuild.
Carbon monoxide is so dangerous because your blood grabs it about 200 times more eagerly than it grabs oxygen.
Your heart is really two pumps side by side: one sends blood through your lungs, the other sends it everywhere else.
The left side of your heart has much thicker walls than the right, because it has to push blood all the way to your toes.
Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, like bunches of grapes too small to see.
Spread out flat, the inside surface of your lungs would cover something close to a badminton court.
You take roughly 20,000 breaths every day without thinking about a single one.
Your left lung is smaller than your right one, because it has a notch to make room for your heart.
The urge to breathe when you hold your breath comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up, not from running out of oxygen.
Hiccups are sudden spasms of the muscle under your lungs. The hic sound is your vocal cords slamming shut right after.
An American man named Charles Osborne hiccuped for 68 years straight, from 1922 to 1990.
Droplets from a big sneeze can travel several meters, much farther than scientists once believed.
Your airways are lined with tiny hairs that beat over ten times a second, sweeping mucus up toward your throat like an escalator.
Most of the time you breathe mainly through one nostril, and your nose quietly switches sides every few hours.
When you talk, your vocal cords vibrate hundreds of times every second.
Your lungs never fully empty. Even after the biggest breath out, about a liter of air stays inside to keep them from collapsing.
Before birth a baby's lungs are full of fluid, which is squeezed out and soaked up as it takes its first breaths.
Healthy lungs hold so much air that a piece of lung tissue floats in water.
You breathe in roughly 10,000 liters of air a day, enough to fill about 50 bathtubs.
You were born with around 300 bones and bony bits. Many fuse together as you grow, leaving about 206 in an adult.
More than half of all your bones are in your hands and feet.
The smallest bone in your body sits deep in your ear and is smaller than a grain of rice.
Your thigh bone is the longest bone you have, roughly a quarter of your total height.
Your skeleton is constantly rebuilt from the inside, so you get roughly a brand new one about every ten years.
Bone can withstand more squeezing pressure than ordinary concrete.
There is one bone in your throat that does not touch any other bone. It floats there, holding up your tongue.
Babies have kneecaps, but they are soft cartilage that does not turn into bone until the age of about three to five.
The soft spots on a baby's head let its skull squeeze and overlap during birth.
Astronauts can lose about 1 percent of the bone in their hips and spine for every month they spend in space.
You are a little taller in the morning than at bedtime, because the cushions in your spine squash down during the day.
Astronauts grow up to about 3 percent taller in space, since there is no gravity squashing their spine.
Your bones store about 99 percent of all the calcium in your body.
The funny bone is not a bone at all. It is a nerve that runs right under the skin at your elbow.
Your teeth are not bones. Tooth enamel is the hardest substance your body makes.
Tooth enamel has no living cells, so once it is worn away your body cannot grow it back.
Your adult teeth are already hiding in your jaw while your baby teeth are in use. Kids' X-rays show two rows stacked up.
Your skull is not one bone. It is 22 bones, most of them locked together by wiggly seams.
Humans and giraffes have the same number of neck bones: seven. A giraffe's are just much, much longer.
Your tailbone is the leftover of a tail. Early human embryos even have a little tail for a few weeks.
You have more than 600 muscles, and together they make up roughly a third of your body weight.
Your biggest muscle is the one you sit on. It does its hardest work when you climb stairs or stand up from a chair.
The smallest muscle in your body is in your ear, and it is only about a millimeter long.
Muscles can only pull, never push. Every move you make uses muscles working in pairs, one pulling each way.
Goosebumps are tiny muscles yanking your hairs upright. In furry animals that trick puffs up the coat to keep warm or look bigger.
Your tongue is not one muscle but a bundle of eight working together.
Stiffness after death happens because muscles run out of the fuel they need to let go.
Shivering is your muscles twitching on purpose to make heat, like a built-in furnace.
Your skin is your biggest organ. Peeled off and laid flat, an adult's would cover about 2 square meters.
You shed millions of dead skin cells every hour, yet you almost never notice a single flake.
The outer layer of your skin is completely replaced about every month or two, as new cells rise up from below.
The skin on your eyelids is only about half a millimeter thick, while the soles of your feet are several times thicker.
Your fingerprints formed months before you were born, and apart from growing bigger they stay the same for the rest of your life.
Even identical twins, who share the same DNA, have different fingerprints.
You have somewhere between 2 and 4 million sweat glands spread across your skin.
In hot weather, some athletes sweat away more than 2 liters of water in a single hour.
Fresh sweat barely smells at all. The smell comes from bacteria on your skin munching on it.
Whether your earwax is wet and sticky or dry and flaky depends mostly on a single gene, the same one that affects underarm smell.
Newborn babies do not seem to taste salt at all; the ability shows up at around four months old.
You have about as many hair follicles on your body as a chimpanzee. Most of yours just grow hairs too fine to notice.
You have around 100,000 hairs on your head, and losing 50 to 100 of them a day is perfectly normal.
Hair on your head grows about a centimeter a month, so roughly the length of a ruler every two years.
Some people can grow hair past their waist and others cannot, because each hair grows for a set number of years before it falls out.
Eyebrows stay short because each eyebrow hair only grows for a few months before it drops out and is replaced.
A fingernail takes about six months to grow from base to tip. A big toenail can take more than a year.
Young babies placed in water automatically hold their breath and make swimming movements, a reflex that fades within months.
Hair does not turn gray once it has grown. New hairs come out gray because the color-making cells in the root have stopped working.
Stress really can turn hair gray, and a study found that some gray hairs can even regain their color when the stress goes away.
Only about 1 to 2 percent of people in the world have naturally red hair.
People of every skin color have about the same number of pigment cells. What differs is how much pigment those cells make.
Your skin makes vitamin D when sunlight hits it, so in a way you are partly solar powered.
Wrinkly bath fingers are not just soggy skin. Your nerves actively shrink blood vessels to make them, and people with certain nerve damage do not wrinkle.
Lips look red because their skin is so thin that you can see the blood vessels underneath.
Your lips have no sweat glands and no oil glands, which is why they dry out so easily.
Tattoos stay put because cleanup cells in your skin swallow the ink and hold it. When those cells die, new ones swallow the same ink.
Scars cannot grow hair or sweat, because the skin that forms them is a quick patch job.
A newborn's grip reflex is so strong that some babies can briefly hang from a bar by their hands alone.
Your palms and soles never tan as much as the rest of you, whatever your skin color.
Nails, hair and rhino horns are all made of the same tough protein.
The pale half-moon at the base of your fingernail is the visible edge of the nail's root.
Peeling skin after a sunburn is your body throwing away cells that the sun damaged so badly they self-destructed.
Most adults have somewhere between 10 and 40 moles, and many of them appear during childhood and the teen years.
In a few people, lightly scratching the skin leaves a raised red line, so you could literally write words on their arm.
Tiny mites live in the hair roots of your eyelashes and face. Most adults have them and never know.
A single healthy hair can hold up something like 50 to 100 grams before it snaps.
Straight or curly hair depends on the shape of the hole it grows from: round holes make straight hair, flatter ones make curls.
Your eyes can tell apart something like a million different colors.
Each eye has a blind spot where its nerve connects. You never notice it because the gap gets filled in for you.
The back of each eye has about 120 million cells for dim light and only about 6 million for color.
In total darkness, a single cell in your eye can respond to just one particle of light.
The picture landing on the back of your eye is upside down. It only looks right side up because it gets flipped for you.
Newborn babies see only blurry shapes. Their vision sharpens and color fills in over the first few months.
The clear front window of your eye has no blood vessels at all. It takes its oxygen straight from the air.
The front of your eye is packed with more nerve endings than almost anywhere else, which is why one speck of dust feels huge.
Tears drain through tiny holes at the inner corners of your eyelids and into your nose, which is why crying makes your nose run.
Your body makes three kinds of tears: everyday ones to keep eyes wet, flood tears to wash out onions or dust, and crying tears.
About 1 in 12 men are color blind, but only about 1 in 200 women.
Some women may have an extra type of color cell in their eyes, which could let them see shades of color most people cannot.
Young people can hear much higher sounds than older adults. Some ringtones are pitched so high that only teenagers can hear them.
Your inner ear has only about 15,000 sound-sensing hair cells each, and once they are lost they do not grow back.
The part of your ear that turns sound into nerve signals is a spiral tube about the size of a pea, shaped like a snail shell.
Your sense of balance comes from three little fluid-filled loops in each ear, set at right angles like the corner of a box.
You feel dizzy after spinning because the fluid in your inner ear keeps swirling after you stop.
Tiny crystals in your inner ear sense gravity. When some come loose and drift, they can make the whole room seem to spin.
Your voice sounds weird on recordings because normally you hear it partly through the bones of your own skull, which makes it sound deeper.
Koala fingerprints are so much like human ones that even under a microscope they are hard to tell apart.
The skin inside your ear canal slowly creeps outward like a conveyor belt, carrying old wax with it.
Your nose has around 400 different types of smell detectors, which work in combinations to tell smells apart.
The nerve cells that detect smells are replaced every month or two, something most nerve cells in your body can never do.
Pinch your nose and an apple and a raw onion become surprisingly hard to tell apart. Most of flavor is really smell.
Taste buds are replaced about every week or two, which is why a burnt tongue recovers quickly.
You have thousands of taste buds, and not only on your tongue. Some are on the roof of your mouth and in your throat.
The tongue map from school is wrong. Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can sense sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savory.
Savory, or umami, was only recognized as a basic taste in the 20th century, after a Japanese chemist pulled it out of seaweed soup.
Whether cilantro tastes like soap to you is partly down to the genes for your smell detectors.
Some people find certain bitter chemicals unbearably strong, while others taste nothing at all, and it largely comes down to one gene.
In experiments, people could feel wrinkles just 13 nanometers high with their fingertips, thousands of times thinner than a hair.
Itch has its own nerve wiring, separate from pain. Scratching works by making a small pain that drowns the itch out.
You cannot tickle yourself, because your body predicts your own touch and turns down the surprise.
A few people are born unable to feel pain at all, which is dangerous because they can be badly hurt without knowing.
You can touch your nose with your eyes shut thanks to sensors in your muscles that always know where your limbs are.
You have far more than five senses: balance, body position, temperature, pain and even a full bladder are senses too.
Your pupils can widen to about four times their width in the dark to let in more light.
Your eyes take around 20 to 30 minutes to fully adjust to the dark.
The lens inside your eye keeps adding layers all your life, like an onion. It stiffens too, which is why many people need reading glasses after 40.
Floaters are bits of gel or cells drifting in the fluid inside your eye, casting shadows that you see as squiggles.
Rubbing your closed eyes makes you see colors and sparks because the pressure tricks your eye into firing as if it saw light.
Blue eyes have no blue pigment. They look blue for the same reason the sky does: the way light scatters.
Many babies are born with blue or gray eyes that darken over their first year as pigment builds up.
Your pupil is not a thing at all. It is a hole, and it looks black because light goes in and very little comes back out.
Humans have unusually big, bright whites of the eyes, which may help us see where other people are looking.
Your small intestine is several meters long, coiled up and folded to fit inside your belly.
The inside of your gut is covered in millions of tiny finger-like bumps that give it about as much surface as half a badminton court.
Your stomach does not digest itself because it coats its walls with thick mucus and replaces its lining every few days.
People are about 30 times more likely to laugh when they are with others than when they are alone.
You could swallow food while hanging upside down, because muscles squeeze food down to your stomach in waves.
A meal usually takes one to three days to travel all the way through you.
About 9 out of 10 people are right-handed, and ancient tools and cave art suggest it has been that way for a very long time.
Your body is made of roughly 30 trillion of its own cells, and most of them are red blood cells.
On a perfectly dark night, your eyes could spot a candle flame about 2.5 kilometers away, not the 48 kilometers often claimed.
A British girl named Donna Griffiths sneezed almost nonstop for 976 days, from 1981 to 1983.
Your gut has its own nervous system of hundreds of millions of nerve cells, so it can run digestion on its own.
About 90 percent of the body's serotonin, a famous brain chemical, is actually made in your gut.
An empty stomach is about the size of a fist, but it can stretch to hold a liter or more.
Stomach rumbles are just your gut muscles pushing gas and liquid along, and they happen whether you are hungry or not.
You make between half a liter and a liter and a half of saliva every day.
Chew a piece of plain bread long enough and it starts to taste sweet, because your spit turns its starch into sugar.
Your liver is your biggest internal organ, weighing about as much as a big bag of sugar, and it does hundreds of different jobs.
The liver can regrow. A person can donate part of theirs, and both pieces grow back toward full size within months.
Poop is brown because of leftovers from your old red blood cells, broken down by your liver and gut.
Around 9 liters of liquid pass through your gut every day, including your own spit and digestive juices, and almost all of it is soaked back up.
Poop is mostly water, and a big part of the solid rest is bacteria.
Most people pass gas between about 13 and 21 times a day, including while they sleep.
Most of the gas you pass has no smell at all. The stink comes from tiny traces of sulfur.
The appendix, long thought useless, may be a safe house where good gut bacteria shelter and regrow after an illness.
You can live without your gallbladder. The liver keeps making the bile it used to store.
In the 1800s a man was left with a hole into his stomach after a gunshot, and a doctor studied digestion through it for years.
A little flap folds over your windpipe every time you swallow, so food goes down the right pipe.
Young babies can breathe and suckle almost at the same time because their voice box sits higher in the throat than an adult's.
Being able to digest milk as a grown-up is a recent twist in human history. About two thirds of adults worldwide do it poorly.
Your kidneys filter about 180 liters of fluid a day, yet you only pee out about 1 or 2 liters. The rest goes back into your blood.
Each kidney contains about a million tiny filters, packed into an organ about the size of a fist.
Your kidneys are small, but about a fifth of all the blood your heart pumps goes straight through them.

You can live a normal life with just one kidney, which is why healthy people can donate one.
The first successful organ transplant was a kidney, given by one identical twin to the other in 1954.
Asparagus makes some people's pee smell, but not everyone can smell it, and that comes down to genes.
Beets can turn some people's pee pink or red. It looks alarming but it is harmless.
An adult bladder can comfortably hold about two cups of liquid.
You spend about a third of your life asleep, which for many people adds up to more than 25 years.
In dream sleep, most of your muscles switch off completely, which stops you from acting out your dreams.
Your body temperature drops at night and hits its lowest point in the early hours of the morning.
Babies spend about half their sleep in dream sleep. Adults spend only about a fifth.
Newborn babies sleep 14 to 17 hours a day, in short bits around the clock.
Much of your body's growth hormone is released while you are in deep sleep, so a lot of growing happens at night.
In 1964 a 17-year-old stayed awake for about 11 days straight for a school science fair project.
Your body clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours, so daylight has to reset it every morning.
Sleepwalkers are not acting out dreams. Sleepwalking happens in deep sleep, when you usually are not dreaming.
A night's sleep comes in waves: you go through about four to six cycles, each lasting roughly 90 minutes.
That sudden jolt as you drift off, like falling off a step, is very common and has a name: a hypnic jerk.
Sleep paralysis, waking up unable to move for a moment, happens when the body's dream-sleep freeze lingers after you wake.
Sounds wake sleeping people far more easily than smells do, which is one reason smoke alarms beep.
Every person starts out as a single cell about as wide as a human hair.
Heart muscle cells in a lab dish start beating on their own, and cells that touch soon fall into step with each other.
A baby's heart starts beating about three weeks after conception, when the whole embryo is smaller than a grain of rice.
In the womb your hands were webbed. The skin between your fingers melted away before you were born.
A newborn baby has only about a cup of blood in its whole body.
Babies grow about 25 centimeters in their first year, faster than they ever will again.
Most babies triple their birth weight by their first birthday.
Many studies have found that children grow a little faster in spring and summer than in autumn and winter.
After about age 40, most people slowly start to shrink, losing roughly a centimeter every decade.
Your ears keep getting a little longer as you age, as skin and cartilage slowly sag.
Once the growth zones at the ends of your bones close after puberty, you cannot get any taller.
Doctors can estimate a child's age from an X-ray of their hand, by looking at how far their bones have grown.
Wisdom teeth usually show up between about 17 and 25, if they appear at all. Some people are born without them.
A newborn is about three quarters water, compared with about 60 percent for an adult.
As of 2026, the longest confirmed human life lasted 122 years. The French woman who lived it was born before the Eiffel Tower was built.
Newborn babies usually cry without tears for their first few weeks.
Babies in the womb grow a fine coat of fuzzy hair, which usually falls out before birth.
The placenta is an organ your body grows for a few months during pregnancy and then throws away.

In rare cases, twins can have different fathers, when two eggs are released and fertilized separately.
Babies hiccup in the womb, and many mothers can feel the rhythmic little jumps.

Babies in the womb can taste what their mother eats. In one study, babies whose mothers drank carrot juice liked carrot flavor more later.

During pregnancy the womb can stretch to hundreds of times its original size.
Pregnancy can make a woman's feet permanently longer, because hormones loosen the ligaments in the arches.
Babies yawn in the womb, and ultrasound scans have caught them doing it months before birth.
A girl is born with all the eggs she will ever have, and she had the most of them, millions, months before she was even born.
The egg that made you formed inside your mother while she was still a baby inside your grandmother.
A man's body makes roughly 1,500 sperm every second, which adds up to millions every day.
Your body replaces around 330 billion cells a day, mostly blood and gut cells, which is about 1 percent of you.
Some people faint at the sight of blood because their heart rate and blood pressure suddenly drop, a reaction few other fears cause.
Your immune system can make billions of different antibodies, so it is ready for germs it has never even met.
A fever is not just a symptom. The extra heat slows down some germs and speeds up your immune cells.
Pus is mostly the bodies of white blood cells that died fighting an infection.
People who survived the 1918 flu still had defenses against it in their blood nearly 90 years later.
In a rare condition, a tiny gap in the bone of the inner ear lets people hear their own eyeballs moving.
A few people sneeze uncontrollably after a big meal, a rare reflex that doctors jokingly named snatiation.
A newborn's brain is only about a quarter to a third of its adult size, and it roughly doubles during the first year.

Your lymph system has no heart to pump it. Its fluid gets pushed along mostly by your muscles squeezing as you move.
Some immune cells are called macrophages, which means big eaters, because they swallow germs whole.
Breast milk carries antibodies from the mother that help protect a newborn while its own defenses grow up.
The idea that you lose most of your body heat through your head is a myth; it loses heat about as fast as any other bare skin.
The redness and warmth around a cut come from extra blood rushing in, bringing immune cells to the scene.
The T in T cells stands for thymus, a gland in your chest where these immune cells go to school.
The gland that trains your immune cells is biggest in childhood and slowly shrinks and turns to fat as you age.
The gut holds more immune cells than any other part of your body.
For every white blood cell in your blood, there are roughly 500 to 1,000 red ones.
Centuries before vaccines, people in China, India and Africa protected themselves by deliberately catching a mild dose of smallpox.
In 1721 an enslaved man named Onesimus taught Boston how Africans protected themselves from smallpox, helping fight an epidemic.
One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for about 60 years and found no more arthritis in it than in the other.
Shaving does not make hair grow back thicker or darker; the cut tip just feels blunt and stubbly as it grows out.
Before anesthesia, speed was everything. One famous surgeon in the 1840s could take off a leg in under three minutes.
Laughing gas was a party trick for decades before a dentist realised it could stop people feeling pain.
One of the first X-ray pictures ever taken shows the bones of a woman's hand, with her wedding ring floating on one finger.

Hair and nails do not keep growing after death; the skin dries out and pulls back, which only makes them look longer.

A tiny bone behind the knee, the fabella, has become about three times more common over the last century, and no one is sure why.

A man paralysed by polio in 1952 lived inside an iron lung breathing machine for more than 70 years, and still earned a law degree.
Medieval anatomy books were full of errors because the most famous ancient doctor, Galen, mostly dissected monkeys and pigs.

Gray's Anatomy, the medical textbook, was first published in 1858 and is still being updated today.

@history|History
Oxford University was already teaching students around 1096, more than 200 years before the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was even founded.
Vikings almost certainly never wore horned helmets. The horns were dreamed up by 19th century costume designers, especially for Wagner's operas.
Vikings reached North America around the year 1000, nearly 500 years before Columbus, and built a camp in Newfoundland you can still visit.
According to the sagas, Erik the Red named icy Greenland "green" on purpose, to make settlers want to move there.
In 1830 Louis Antoine was king of France for about 20 minutes, the time between his father giving up the throne and him doing the same.
Abraham Lincoln is the only US president to hold a patent, for a device to lift riverboats over sandbars.
In the 800s a Viking named Halfdan carved his name in runes on a balcony rail of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, and you can still read it.
Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was finished in the year 537 and stayed the biggest cathedral in the world for almost a thousand years.
The Roman Empire did not end in 476. Its eastern half carried on from Constantinople for nearly another thousand years, until 1453.
The people we call Byzantines never used that word. They called themselves Romans right up to the end in 1453.
Mansa Musa of Mali gave away so much gold on his trip to Mecca in 1324 that gold lost value in Cairo for years afterward.
Great Zimbabwe, an African stone city built centuries ago, has walls about 11 meters tall stacked without any mortar at all.
In Ethiopia around the 1200s, builders carved whole churches straight down into solid rock, like sculptures you can walk inside.
A coin from Kilwa, a medieval trading city in East Africa, was found on a beach island off northern Australia in 1944.
Most of the Great Wall of China you see in photos was built by the Ming dynasty, much of it only around 500 years ago.
China was using paper money about 600 years before Europe printed its first banknotes.
The oldest dated printed book in the world is a Buddhist scroll from China, printed in the year 868.
A Chinese inventor made movable type out of baked clay around 1040, about 400 years before Gutenberg's printing press.
The oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type is Korean, from 1377, almost 80 years older than the Gutenberg Bible.
The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel, was written by a Japanese court lady about a thousand years ago.
The word "algorithm" comes from the name of a Persian mathematician who worked in Baghdad in the 800s.
Charlemagne ruled much of Europe and loved learning, yet he tried to learn to write so late that he never really managed it.
After 1066, England's kings and nobles spoke French for about 300 years, while ordinary people kept speaking English.
Thanks to the Norman Conquest, English has "cow" and "pig" for the animals in the field, but French-based "beef" and "pork" for the meat.
The famous Bayeux Tapestry is not actually a tapestry. It is embroidery, and it is almost 70 meters long.
Magna Carta, the famous charter of rights from 1215, was cancelled by the Pope only about ten weeks after it was sealed.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
Joan of Arc was only about 19 when she died, and a church court later reversed her conviction and declared her innocent.
The Black Death killed somewhere between a third and half of everyone in Europe in just four years, from 1347 to 1351.
The Ottoman Empire lasted about 600 years, from around 1299 to 1922, so it began in the age of knights and ended after the First World War.
Machu Picchu was built around 1450 and abandoned barely a hundred years later, so it was lived in for only about four generations.
The Inca road network was about 40,000 km long, roughly enough to wrap once around the whole Earth.
When the Spanish arrived, the Aztec capital probably had over 200,000 people, likely bigger than any city in Spain at the time.
The Aztecs used cacao beans as money. One record from the 1540s says a turkey cost about 100 beans.
For the Aztecs, chocolate was a bitter, frothy drink often spiced with chili, nothing like a sweet candy bar.
The people of Easter Island carved nearly 1,000 giant moai statues and moved some weighing as much as a dozen elephants.
New Zealand was one of the last big places on Earth people reached, settled by Polynesian sailors only around 1250 to 1300.
Leonardo da Vinci never handed over the Mona Lisa. He kept working on it for years and still had it with him when he died.
In 1992 the Catholic Church formally admitted it had been wrong to condemn Galileo, 359 years after his trial.
Isaac Newton spent his later years running England's Royal Mint and personally hunting down coin forgers.
Columbus didn't prove the Earth was round. Educated people already knew that. He just thought it was much smaller than it is.
Columbus died in 1506 still insisting the lands he had reached were part of Asia.
America got its name from a 1507 German map. Only one copy survives, and the US Library of Congress paid 10 million dollars for it.
Magellan's crew made the first trip around the world, but Magellan didn't. He died in the Philippines halfway through.
Only 18 men of roughly 270 made it home from Magellan's voyage around the world, on a single battered ship.
Chinese admiral Zheng He led fleets of hundreds of ships across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s, decades before Columbus sailed.
Before 1492 Italy had no tomatoes, Ireland had no potatoes, and India and Thailand had no chili peppers. They all came from the Americas.
In the 1630s Dutch tulip craze, a single rare tulip bulb could sell for more than a skilled worker earned in a whole year.
Tulips reached the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire, where they had long been a favorite flower of the sultans.
Around 20,000 workers spent roughly 20 years building the Taj Mahal as a tomb for the emperor's beloved wife.
The man who built the Taj Mahal was later locked up by his own son and spent his last years in a fort looking out at it.
The Mughal emperor Akbar ruled most of India and built a huge library, yet he is believed to have never learned to read.
Shakespeare and Cervantes are often said to have died on the same day in 1616, but their countries used different calendars, so they were about 11 days apart.
When Britain changed calendars in 1752, people went to bed on 2 September and woke up on 14 September.
Russia's October Revolution of 1917 actually happened in November by the calendar most of the world used.
Sweden tried to change calendars slowly, got muddled, and ended up with a 30 February in 1712.
For over 200 years Japan almost shut itself off, letting Europeans trade only through Dutch merchants on one tiny artificial island in Nagasaki.
Peter the Great put a tax on beards in Russia, and bearded men had to carry a token proving they had paid it.
Peter the Great traveled through Europe under a fake name and worked in Dutch shipyards to learn how to build ships.
The Great Fire of London in 1666 burned down over 13,000 houses, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded.
Queen Elizabeth I ruled England for 44 years and never married, which was almost unthinkable for a queen of her time.
More ships of the Spanish Armada were wrecked by storms off Scotland and Ireland than by English cannons.
The Viking Age is usually dated from a raid on a quiet island monastery in England in 793.
Sweden has turned up tens of thousands of Arab silver coins, brought home by Viking traders who sailed down Russian rivers.
Iceland's parliament, the Althing, first met in 930 in an open field, making it one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
Women in Viking Age Scandinavia could own property and could divorce their husbands, rights many European women got only centuries later.
King Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway all at once in the early 1000s, a North Sea empire run by a Viking.
The story of King Cnut ordering the tide to stop was first told to show he knew even a king couldn't control the sea.
The Mongol Empire became the largest connected land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.
The Mongols had a pony express 600 years before America's, with relay stations where riders swapped horses and kept going.
Genghis Khan was born with the name Temujin. "Genghis Khan" was a title he took in 1206.
The Mongols tried to invade Japan twice, and both times storms wrecked their fleets. The Japanese called them kamikaze, "divine wind".
Kublai Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, became emperor of China and built his capital where Beijing stands today.
Marco Polo's famous travel book was dictated while he was a prisoner of war in Genoa, to a writer in the cell with him.
Ibn Battuta, a traveler from Morocco, covered about 120,000 km in the 1300s, much farther than Marco Polo.
Soviet scientists opened the tomb of the conqueror Timur in 1941 and confirmed he really was lame, just like his nickname said.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 is thought to be the shortest war in history. It lasted less than an hour.
Around the year 750, the Chinese capital Chang'an may have been the biggest city on Earth, with about a million people.
Wu Zetian is the only woman in over 2,000 years of Chinese history who ruled as emperor in her own name.
Chinese sailors were steering with magnetic compasses by around 1100, long before Europeans used them at sea.
Around 1090, a Chinese engineer built a clock tower over 10 meters tall, driven by a giant water wheel.
China picked its government officials through written exams for about 1,300 years, until the system was scrapped in 1905.
China's last emperor, Puyi, took the throne when he was two years old and later worked in a botanical garden in Beijing.
In 1443 King Sejong of Korea invented a whole new alphabet, Hangul, so ordinary people could learn to read in days instead of years.
A Japanese temple-building company founded in the year 578 kept going on its own for over 1,400 years, until 2006.
The haiku poet Basho once set off on foot and walked about 2,400 km across Japan, writing as he went.
Japan's first railway opened in 1872, less than 20 years after the country ended two centuries of near isolation.
In 1876 Japan banned samurai from carrying swords in public, ending a symbol that had lasted for centuries.
Abraham Lincoln's son Robert was saved from falling under a train by Edwin Booth, the brother of the man who later shot his father.
The famous Fibonacci sequence first appeared in a European book of 1202, as a puzzle about breeding rabbits.
In early chess the queen was a weak piece that moved one square diagonally. She became the most powerful piece only in the late 1400s.
Around the year 1020, a scientist in Cairo explained that we see because light enters our eyes, not because eyes shoot out rays.
A medical textbook written by the Persian doctor Avicenna around 1025 was still used in European universities in the 1600s.
Muslim rulers held parts of Spain for nearly 800 years, from 711 until Granada fell in 1492.
1492 was a busy year for Spain: Granada fell, Spain's Jews were expelled, and Columbus set sail, all within months.
The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land. In 1204 the crusaders attacked Constantinople, a Christian city, instead.
The so-called Children's Crusade of 1212 was probably mostly poor young people and peasants, and none of them reached the Holy Land.
Richard the Lionheart was king of England for ten years but spent only about six months of it actually in England.
On his way home from crusade, Richard the Lionheart was kidnapped and held for a ransom worth about three years of England's royal income.
The US government kept paying a pension for a Civil War soldier until 2020, to his daughter Irene Triplett, who died that year aged 90.
In medieval and early modern Europe, courts sometimes put animals on trial, including pigs, rats and even insects.
In 1457 the King of Scotland banned golf and football because men were playing them instead of practicing archery.
An English monk named Eilmer reportedly strapped on wings and glided about 200 meters off a tower around the year 1010.
Eyeglasses were invented in Italy around 1286, and suddenly older monks and scholars could keep reading for decades longer.
Cologne Cathedral was started in 1248 and finished in 1880. Builders worked on it, on and off, for over 600 years.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to lean while it was still being built, and finishing it took about 200 years.
A full suit of medieval plate armor weighed about 15 to 25 kg, so a knight could run, roll and climb onto his horse without help.
Cambridge University was started in 1209 by scholars who fled Oxford after a fight with the townspeople.
By the year 1500, only about 50 years after Gutenberg, European printers had produced millions of books.
Florence's Medici family ran a bank with branches across Europe and gave the Catholic Church several popes.
The dome of Florence Cathedral, finished in 1436, is still the largest brick dome ever built, raised without a wooden frame to hold it up.
In 1494 Spain and Portugal drew a line down the Atlantic and split the newly found lands between them. That's why Brazilians speak Portuguese.
Cortes didn't conquer the Aztecs with a few hundred Spaniards alone. Tens of thousands of local allies who hated Aztec rule fought with him.
Around 1600, Potosi, a silver-mining town high in the Bolivian Andes, was one of the biggest cities in the world.
For 250 years, Spanish galleons sailed between Mexico and the Philippines, carrying American silver that mostly ended up in China.
The Mayflower Pilgrims meant to land near the Hudson River but ended up in Massachusetts in 1620.
Pocahontas traveled to England in 1616, met the royal court, and is buried there, in a churchyard in Gravesend.
President Ulysses S. Grant was reportedly stopped by a Washington police officer in 1872 for driving his horse and carriage too fast.
In 1667 the Dutch let England keep Manhattan, and in return kept Run, a tiny Indonesian island prized for its nutmeg.
Wall Street in New York is named after a real wall the Dutch settlers built there in the 1650s.
Captain Cook's first great voyage was partly a science trip, sent to Tahiti to watch the planet Venus pass in front of the Sun in 1769.
In 1642 Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sailed all the way around mainland Australia without ever seeing it, though he did find Tasmania.
Most of the American Declaration of Independence was signed on 2 August 1776, not on 4 July.
John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration of Independence.
George Washington's false teeth were not wooden. They were made of ivory, metal and real human teeth, and he had just one tooth of his own left by 1789.
In 1926 President Calvin Coolidge was sent a raccoon to cook for Thanksgiving. He kept it as a pet instead and named her Rebecca.
As a boy, Benjamin Franklin invented wooden swim fins for his hands, and he is in the International Swimming Hall of Fame.
When revolutionaries stormed the Bastille prison in 1789, they found only seven prisoners inside.
Revolutionary France tried decimal time: 10 hours a day, 100 minutes an hour. People hated it and it was dropped after about 17 months.
The French Revolution renamed the months with names like "Fog," "Frost" and "Heat," and gave weeks 10 days.
Napoleon was about 1.69 m tall, normal for his time. The "short" idea came partly from French inches being longer than English ones.
In 1803 Napoleon sold the US a huge slice of North America for 15 million dollars, nearly doubling the size of the country overnight.
When Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798, he brought along over 160 scientists and scholars to study the country.
The Rosetta Stone was found by French soldiers in 1799, but ended up in the British Museum because Britain won the war.
Nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs for over 1,400 years, until Champollion cracked them in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone.
When Napoleon escaped from exile in 1815, the soldiers sent to arrest him switched sides and marched with him to Paris.
Haiti, in 1804, became the first country founded by people who had freed themselves from slavery.
Simon Bolivar helped free six of today's countries from Spanish rule, and one of them, Bolivia, is named after him.
In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon and moved to Brazil, so Rio de Janeiro became the capital of a European empire.
In 1829 a steam locomotive called Rocket hit about 48 km/h, faster than any stagecoach, and won a contest to run the first intercity railway.
Before railways, every town kept its own time by the Sun, so clocks in Bristol ran about 10 minutes behind London's.
US railroads switched to time zones on 18 November 1883, which people called "the day of two noons".
Queen Victoria's first message over the transatlantic telegraph cable in 1858 took about 16 hours to send. The cable died weeks later.
Benjamin Franklin never asked for the turkey to be America's national bird, but he did call the bald eagle "a bird of bad moral character" in a letter.
London's "Great Stink" of 1858 made the River Thames smell so bad that Parliament paid for a new sewer system, and much of it is still in use today.
Paul Revere never shouted "The British are coming!" on his famous ride. His mission was secret, and colonists still saw themselves as British.
In 1854 Dr. John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London to one water pump and stopped it by having the pump's handle removed.
In 1847 a doctor showed that washing hands saved the lives of many new mothers, but his colleagues laughed at him.
Queen Victoria used chloroform during the birth of her eighth child in 1853, which helped make pain relief in childbirth acceptable.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair and was only supposed to stand for 20 years.
In 1884 showman P.T. Barnum marched 21 elephants across the new Brooklyn Bridge to prove it was safe.
At the first modern Olympics in 1896, winners got silver medals. Second place got bronze, and there was no gold at all.
Tug of war used to be an official Olympic sport, with medals handed out for it at five Games between 1900 and 1920.
For decades the Olympics gave out medals for painting, music, poetry and architecture, until 1948.
The man who first crossed the line in the 1904 Olympic marathon had ridden part of the way in a car.
In 1835 a New York newspaper claimed astronomers had spotted bat-winged people on the Moon. Many readers believed it.
The first photograph of a real scene, taken around 1826 in France, needed the camera to stare at it for hours, possibly days.
Alexander Graham Bell wanted people to answer the phone by saying "Ahoy!" Edison's suggestion, "Hello," won.
The first speeding ticket was handed out in England in 1896, to a man going about 13 km/h in a 3 km/h zone.
A British law of 1865 made some motor vehicles crawl at walking pace in towns, with a person walking in front waving a red flag.
The California gold rush turned San Francisco from a village of about 1,000 people in 1848 into a city of over 25,000 by the end of 1849.
In 1909 Louis Bleriot flew across the English Channel in about 37 minutes, in a plane with no cockpit cover.
The Titanic carried lifeboats for only about half the people on board, and that was perfectly legal at the time.
On Christmas 1914, British and German soldiers in WWI climbed out of their trenches, swapped gifts and even played football.
World War I officially stopped at 11 o'clock on the 11th day of the 11th month of 1918.
Tanks were first called "water tanks" in WWI to fool spies into thinking they were water carriers, and the name stuck.
A carrier pigeon named Cher Ami delivered a message in 1918 that helped rescue nearly 200 trapped American soldiers.
In 1914 French soldiers were rushed to the Battle of the Marne in hundreds of Paris taxis.
The treaty ending WWI was signed in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors, the same room where Germany had proclaimed its empire in 1871.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all women the right to vote.
Swiss women could not vote in national elections until 1971, the year Disney World opened.
One Swiss region only let women vote in local elections in 1990, and only because a court forced it to.
The flu pandemic of 1918 infected roughly a third of everyone on Earth, far more people than fought in WWI.
In 1942 Britain recruited some of its WWII codebreakers through a newspaper crossword that had to be solved in under 12 minutes.
The codebreakers at Bletchley Park kept their war work secret for about 30 years, even from their own families.
Abraham Lincoln grew his famous beard after an 11-year-old girl named Grace Bedell wrote to him saying it would help him win votes.
Before D-Day, the Allies built a fake army with inflatable tanks and made-up radio chatter to fool Germany about where they'd land.
Navajo Code Talkers sent US Marine messages in their own language during WWII, and the enemy never cracked it.
Wojtek, a bear adopted by Polish soldiers in WWII, was officially enlisted and helped carry heavy crates of ammunition.
In 1943 Britain fooled Germany by letting fake invasion plans wash up in Spain with a dead man dressed as an invented officer, complete with love letters.
Japanese soldier Hiroo Onoda hid in a Philippine jungle until 1974, and only gave up when his old commander flew out to order him to stand down.
Duct tape was developed during WWII to keep moisture out of ammunition boxes, and soldiers soon used it to fix everything.
Martin Van Buren was the first US president born a US citizen, and he grew up speaking Dutch, not English, in his New York hometown.
Winston Churchill won the Nobel Prize, not for peace, but for literature, in 1953.
During WWII the future Queen Elizabeth II trained as a truck mechanic and driver in the British army.
From 1908 to 1940 you could order a whole house from the Sears catalog. It arrived by train as a kit of numbered pieces, and about 70,000 were sold.
Gagarin didn't land inside his capsule. He bailed out and came down on his own parachute, a detail the Soviets hid for years.
Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space in 1963, had worked in a textile factory and loved skydiving.
During WWII the best gems of Britain's Crown Jewels were hidden in a biscuit tin, buried under Windsor Castle in case of a German invasion.
The Apollo 11 astronauts couldn't get life insurance, so they signed hundreds of envelopes for their families to sell if they didn't return.
Only twelve people have ever walked on the Moon, and all of them did it between 1969 and 1972.
The flag planted by Apollo 11 was blown over by the rocket blast when the lunar module took off.
The crew of Apollo 13 went farther from Earth than any humans before or since, while trying to get home safely.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 partly because an East German official mistakenly told reporters new travel rules started "immediately".
Stewardess Violet Jessop survived the Titanic sinking in 1912, a crash of its sister ship before that, and the sinking of a third sister ship in 1916.
The first photo of a person, taken in Paris in 1838, shows a man having his boots polished. He was the only one who stood still long enough.
The oldest surviving film, shot in Leeds, England, in 1888, lasts about two seconds and shows a few people walking around a garden.
The very first Academy Awards ceremony, in 1929, lasted about 15 minutes, and the winners had been announced months earlier.
In 1859 a settler released about 24 rabbits in Australia so he could hunt them. Within decades there were hundreds of millions.
Mount Rushmore was meant to show the four presidents down to their waists, but the money ran out and work stopped in 1941.
Gandhi was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize five times but never won it, which the Nobel committee later called its greatest omission.
In 1930 Gandhi walked about 390 km to the sea to make his own salt, protesting a British tax on salt.
Months before Rosa Parks, a 15-year-old named Claudette Colvin also refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery.
The mass panic over the 1938 War of the Worlds radio show was hugely exaggerated by newspapers. Few people were actually fooled.
During US Prohibition, doctors could still write prescriptions for whiskey as medicine.
US President William Henry Harrison gave the longest inauguration speech ever in 1841 and died just 31 days into his term.
Abraham Lincoln is in the National Wrestling Hall of Fame. He was a skilled wrestler as a young man in Illinois.
The US Secret Service was set up in 1865, just after Lincoln's death, to catch money forgers. Guarding presidents came decades later.
In 1912 Theodore Roosevelt was shot before a speech and gave the speech anyway, for about 90 minutes. A folded speech had slowed the bullet.
In 1814 British troops set fire to the White House during a war with the United States.
One of the most famous battles of the War of 1812, at New Orleans, was fought two weeks after the peace treaty was signed. The news hadn't arrived yet.
The Pony Express is famous, but it only ran for about 18 months before the telegraph put it out of business.
The US bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars, about 2 cents an acre.
During the Klondike gold rush, prospectors had to haul about a tonne of supplies over a steep mountain pass to be allowed in.
After British troops burned the Library of Congress in 1814, Thomas Jefferson sold the nation his own 6,487 books to start it again.
Marie Curie is the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry.
Albert Einstein was offered the job of President of Israel in 1952. He politely said no.
Britain had a window tax from 1696 to 1851, and people bricked up windows to pay less. You can still see them on old houses.
In 1647 England's Puritan-led Parliament abolished Christmas celebrations, and they stayed banned until 1660.
The colony of Massachusetts made it illegal to celebrate Christmas from 1659 to 1681.
