In medieval England, bakers who sold short loaves could be fined, so many are said to have added a 13th loaf to be safe. Hence the baker's dozen.
In the Middle Ages, rich and poor were told by law what clothes and colors they were allowed to wear, depending on their rank.
Venice's gondolas are black partly because of laws in the 1500s against showing off with fancy, colorful boats.
Japan's shoguns forced their lords to live every other year in the capital, Edo, so they were too busy and too broke to rebel.
In the 1600s English coffeehouses were nicknamed "penny universities": for a penny's coffee you could join clever conversations.
Lloyd's of London, one of the world's biggest insurance markets, started in a coffee house in the 1680s.
King Charles II tried to shut down all of England's coffeehouses in 1675, but people were so angry he gave up in about 11 days.
An Ottoman sultan banned coffee in the 1630s and is said to have prowled Istanbul in disguise to catch people drinking it.
The Boston Tea Party in 1773 dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbor, enough to make millions of cups.
Tea was so expensive in 1700s Britain that families kept it in locked boxes so the servants couldn't help themselves.
Pineapples were so rare in 1700s Britain that people rented them for the evening to show off at dinner parties.
Ketchup started out as a salty fermented fish sauce from Southeast Asia. Tomatoes came much later.
When an Englishman brought back the habit of eating with a fork from Italy around 1608, people made fun of him for it.
High heels were first worn by men. Persian horsemen used them to keep their feet in the stirrups, and European noblemen copied them.
Louis XIV of France wore red-heeled shoes and only let nobles in his favor wear them too.
Louis XIV became king at age four and reigned for 72 years, longer than any other monarch of a major European country.
In 1833 the "Ice King" Frederic Tudor shipped New England ice all the way to India, and much of it arrived without melting.
In 1932 the Australian army went to war against emus with machine guns, and the emus pretty much won.
The Pig War of 1859 between the US and Britain, over an island border, had just one casualty: a pig.
In 1325 soldiers from Modena stole a wooden bucket from rival Bologna. Modena still keeps it, centuries later, as a trophy.
In the summer of 1518, dozens of people in Strasbourg started dancing in the streets and couldn't stop for days.
In 1814 a giant vat burst at a London brewery and sent a flood of over a million liters of beer through the streets.
In 1919 a giant tank burst in Boston and a wave of molasses about as tall as a house rushed through the streets.
Texas was its own country for almost 10 years, from 1836 to 1845, with its own president, money and diplomats.
California was briefly an independent republic for about 25 days in 1846, with a bear on its flag.
Vermont was an independent republic for 14 years before it became the 14th US state in 1791.
Mozart wrote his first symphony when he was about 8, an age when most kids are still learning their times tables.
The composer Vivaldi was a Catholic priest, nicknamed "the Red Priest" because of his red hair.
As a young man, J.S. Bach walked about 400 km to hear a famous organist play, and stayed months longer than he was allowed.
Handel composed his famous Messiah, over two hours of music, in about 24 days in 1741.
Charles Darwin almost wasn't allowed on his famous voyage because the captain didn't like the shape of his nose.
Charles Darwin and Abraham Lincoln were born on the very same day, 12 February 1809.
At Cambridge, Charles Darwin belonged to a "Glutton Club" that tried eating unusual animals like hawks and owls.
Thomas Jefferson made his own version of the Bible by cutting out the verses he liked with a razor and gluing them into a new book.
As a young officer, Napoleon wrote a short romantic novel called Clisson and Eugenie. It was only published long after his death.
The first person to go over Niagara Falls in a barrel, in 1901, was Annie Edson Taylor, a 63-year-old teacher. She survived with only a cut on her head.
Vincent van Gogh painted around 900 paintings in about ten years but sold very few of them in his lifetime.
In 1926 crime writer Agatha Christie vanished for 11 days, sparking a nationwide search. She turned up at a hotel under another name.
At age 12, Charles Dickens was sent to work in a factory pasting labels on pots of shoe polish while his father was in debtors' prison.
In 1863 Harriet Tubman helped lead a raid during the US Civil War that freed more than 700 enslaved people in a single night.
Frederick Douglass is often called the most photographed American of the 1800s. He used photos to fight racist cartoons.
Sacagawea crossed much of North America with the Lewis and Clark expedition while carrying her baby son.
Lewis and Clark crossed the American West and back over two years, and only one man in their group died, probably of appendicitis.
After the mutiny on the Bounty in 1789, Captain Bligh sailed an overcrowded open boat about 6,700 km to safety.
Hokusai made his famous Great Wave print when he was about 70 years old, and he wrote that nothing he drew before 70 was worth noticing.
The Japanese artist Hokusai changed his name more than 30 times during his life.
The Persian ruler Nader Shah carried off India's jewel-covered Peacock Throne in 1739.
The Koh-i-Noor diamond passed between Mughal, Persian, Afghan and Sikh rulers before ending up with Queen Victoria.
Hong Kong was handed back to China at midnight on 1 July 1997, after 156 years of British rule.
Macau, handed from Portugal to China in 1999, was the last European colony in Asia.
In 1793 the Chinese emperor told a British envoy that China had no need for anything Britain made.
The King of Siam once offered to send elephants to the United States. Lincoln politely said no, thanks.
The marching bands of the Ottoman army were so striking that composers like Mozart and Beethoven wrote music imitating them.
Suleiman the Magnificent ruled the Ottoman Empire for 46 years and also wrote poetry under a pen name.
Hurrem, a captive from what is now Ukraine, rose to become the wife of Ottoman sultan Suleiman, breaking centuries of royal tradition.
The great square of Isfahan in Iran, built around 1600, is so huge that polo matches were once played in it.
The Asante people of Ghana keep a sacred Golden Stool that holds the soul of the nation. No one is allowed to sit on it.
Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, in today's Angola, fought off Portuguese conquest for decades in the 1600s.
In the 1860s Mexico had an emperor from Austria, Maximilian, who was put on the throne with the help of a French army.
Bolivia lost its coastline to Chile in a war in the 1880s but still has a navy, which trains on Lake Titicaca.
Lima's San Marcos University in Peru, founded in 1551, is 85 years older than Harvard University.
Harvard University is older than calculus, which Newton and Leibniz worked out decades after Harvard opened in 1636.
In 1835, under Andrew Jackson, the United States paid off its entire national debt, the only time that has ever happened.
Hawaii was an independent kingdom, and its royal palace had electric lights before the White House did.
The way we number years, "AD," was invented by a monk in the year 525, who probably got the date of Jesus's birth wrong by a few years.
A giant Bible made in England around the year 700 needed the skins of about 500 calves for its pages.
The medieval "Devil's Bible" in Sweden is so huge it weighs about 75 kg, as much as a grown man.
Bored medieval monks sometimes scribbled complaints in the margins of books, like "my hand is tired" or "the ink is thin".
The Voynich manuscript, made in the early 1400s, is written in a mystery script that nobody has ever been able to read.
The Republic of Venice lasted about 1,100 years, until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
A medieval abbess, Hildegard of Bingen, composed music, wrote about medicine and even invented her own secret language.
Christine de Pizan, born in 1364, is often called the first woman in Europe to earn her living as a writer.
Eleanor of Aquitaine was queen of France, then divorced and became queen of England. Two of her sons became English kings.
After England's king was executed in 1649, the new government melted down almost all the medieval crown jewels.
In 1671 Colonel Blood grabbed the Crown Jewels from the Tower of London and was caught running off with them. The king then pardoned him.
Since the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, the cellars of Britain's Parliament are still searched before each State Opening.
Around the year 552, two monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of China to the Byzantine Empire, reportedly hidden inside hollow walking sticks.
The Byzantines had a secret weapon called Greek fire that kept burning even on water. Its recipe was so well guarded it's now lost.
Empress Theodora, one of the most powerful women in Byzantine history, started out as an actress, a job seen as scandalous at the time.
The White House was officially called the Executive Mansion until 1901, when Theodore Roosevelt put "White House" on his letterhead.
Baghdad had paper mills around the year 800, centuries before Europe made its own paper.
Around the year 800 the caliph of Baghdad sent Charlemagne a real elephant named Abul-Abbas, which walked and sailed all the way to Germany.
Many bright stars have Arabic names, like Betelgeuse, Aldebaran and Altair, given by medieval Muslim astronomers.
In the 1420s the astronomer-prince Ulugh Beg measured the length of the year in Samarkand and was off by less than a minute.
In the 1200s the Chinese city of Hangzhou was one of the largest and richest cities in the world, with over a million people by some estimates.
China's Yongle Encyclopedia, finished in 1408, filled over 11,000 volumes and stayed the world's largest for about 600 years.
Less than 4 percent of the giant Yongle Encyclopedia survives today. The rest was lost to fire, war and looting.
In 1717 a German king traded 600 of his soldiers to a neighbor for 151 pieces of Chinese porcelain.
Tibet's Potala Palace, mostly built in the 1600s, is 13 stories tall and has around 1,000 rooms.
Japan's Himeji Castle has stood since 1609 and survived the bombings of WWII almost untouched.
Japan's Horyu-ji temple has wooden buildings from around the year 700, among the oldest wooden buildings in the world.
In the 1200s Korean monks carved the entire Buddhist scriptures onto over 81,000 wooden printing blocks, and they all still survive.
Borobudur in Java, built around the year 800, is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, made of about 2 million stone blocks.
In Bagan, Myanmar, rulers and townspeople built over 10,000 temples between the 1000s and 1200s. More than 2,000 still stand.
The Golden Temple in Amritsar has served free meals to anyone who comes since the 1500s, and today it can feed up to 100,000 people a day.
In the 1730s a maharaja in Jaipur built a stone sundial about 27 meters tall that tells the time to within a couple of seconds.
Tipu Sultan of Mysore fired iron-cased rockets at British troops in the 1790s, and Britain copied them for its own army.
Around 1800 the British East India Company, a business, had a private army about twice the size of Britain's own army.
Queen Victoria made white wedding dresses fashionable when she wore one in 1840. Before that, brides wore all sorts of colors.
The first Christmas card was sent in England in 1843, and printed copies were sold for a shilling each.
In Victorian London, the mail was delivered up to 12 times a day, so people could swap several letters before dinner.
Between 1913 and 1915, a few American parents sent their children by parcel post, until the post office banned it.
At London's Great Exhibition of 1851, over 800,000 visitors paid a penny to use its new flushing toilets, which may be where "spend a penny" comes from.
London's Underground, the world's first, opened in 1863 with steam trains puffing through its tunnels.
Big Ben is not the name of the famous London clock tower. It's the nickname of the great bell inside it.
Victorian wallpapers and dresses were often colored with a bright green dye that contained arsenic.
Mount Everest is named after George Everest, a British surveyor who pronounced his name "EVE-rest" and never saw the mountain.
In 1612 the Dutch drained a whole lake with windmills and turned it into farmland lying below sea level.
Catherine the Great, empress of Russia, was born a German princess and didn't speak Russian until she was a teenager.
In 1768 Catherine the Great had herself inoculated against smallpox, to show her people it was safe.
In the 1720s Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought an early smallpox prevention method from Istanbul to England, and tried it on her children.
The Trans-Siberian Railway, finished in 1916, runs about 9,300 km, crossing eight time zones.
From 1397 to 1523, Denmark, Norway and Sweden were united under one ruler, starting with a queen named Margaret.
Henry VIII's warship Mary Rose sank in 1545 and was lifted from the seabed in 1982, watched live on TV by millions.
Queen Christina of Sweden gave up her throne in 1654, converted to Catholicism and moved to Rome.
The US Virgin Islands used to be Danish. Denmark sold them to the United States in 1917.
In 1791 Poland passed one of the first written national constitutions in the world, second only to the United States.
Poland vanished from the map for 123 years after its neighbors carved it up in 1795. It came back in 1918.
Prague's astronomical clock was installed in 1410 and is the oldest one still working.
In 1618 angry nobles threw two officials out of a castle window in Prague. They fell about 20 meters and survived.
The Holy Roman Empire lasted about a thousand years, though the writer Voltaire joked it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.
Empress Maria Theresa of Austria had 16 children. One of them was Marie Antoinette, the future queen of France.
Marie Antoinette almost certainly never said "Let them eat cake." The line was in a book written when she was a child.
Bram Stoker borrowed the name Dracula from Vlad III, a real prince of Wallachia in the 1400s, though Vlad was no vampire.
Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored Portugal's great voyages of exploration but did not sail on them himself.
Bartolomeu Dias named Africa's southern tip the "Cape of Storms," but the king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.
In 1860 Garibaldi conquered Sicily and southern Italy with about a thousand volunteers wearing red shirts.
Vatican City only became an independent country in 1929, making it younger than many people's grandparents.
Neuschwanstein, the fairy-tale castle built by King Ludwig II of Bavaria, inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
Britain's George V and Germany's Kaiser Wilhelm II, enemies in WWI, were first cousins, both grandsons of Queen Victoria.
The British royal family changed its German-sounding name to Windsor in 1917, in the middle of a war with Germany.
The Romanovs ruled Russia for 300 years, and their reign began in the Ipatiev Monastery in 1613 and ended in the Ipatiev House in 1918.
Soviet space dogs Belka and Strelka orbited Earth in 1960 and came home safely. One of Strelka's puppies was given to the Kennedys.
Britain printed millions of "Keep Calm and Carry On" posters in 1939 but barely used them. A bookshop rediscovered one in 2000 and made it famous.
Winston Churchill's mother was American, born in Brooklyn, and in 1963 he was made an honorary citizen of the United States.
Queen Elizabeth II sent her first email in 1976, from an army research base in England, decades before most people had heard of email.
The 1953 coronation of Elizabeth II was the first to be shown live on TV, and many British families bought their first television to watch it.
Pirates almost never made prisoners walk the plank. The idea comes mostly from later stories, novels and plays.
The sandwich is named after an 18th century Earl of Sandwich who liked to eat meat between bread without leaving his work or game.
Cardigans and Wellington boots are named after a British general and a duke from the 1800s.
In 1887 a Polish eye doctor invented Esperanto, a whole new language meant to help the world's people understand each other.
Many pirate crews of the early 1700s voted for their captains and signed written rules, including set payouts for injured crew members.
Ching Shih led one of history's biggest pirate fleets, hundreds of ships off China in the early 1800s, then made a deal for a pardon and retired.
The Hindenburg airship, which flew in the 1930s, was more than three times as long as a jumbo jet.
Roald Amundsen beat Robert Falcon Scott to the South Pole by about five weeks in 1911, partly thanks to sled dogs.
When Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by Antarctic ice in 1915, every one of his 28 men survived.
Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic in 1932, five years to the day after Lindbergh's flight.
Alcock and Brown flew nonstop across the Atlantic in 1919, eight years before Lindbergh, and landed nose-first in an Irish bog.
Bessie Coleman couldn't find an American flight school that would teach a Black woman, so she learned French and got her license in France in 1921.
The game Monopoly began as The Landlord's Game, invented by a woman named Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show the problems with greedy landlords.
The first crossword puzzle was printed in a New York newspaper in 1913. It was shaped like a diamond.
Around 1100, Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, may have had as many people as London did at the time.
Pueblo Bonito, a stone "great house" in New Mexico, had about 650 rooms around 1100. Nothing bigger was built in North America until the 1800s.
Horses had died out in the Americas thousands of years ago. The Spanish brought them back in the 1490s.
The great pyramid at Chichen Itza has 91 steps on each of its four sides, plus the top platform: 365, one for each day of the year.
People in Mexico and Central America were making bouncy rubber balls for their ball games thousands of years before Europeans knew rubber.
In 1958 the famous Hope Diamond was sent to the Smithsonian museum by ordinary registered mail, wrapped in plain brown paper.
In 1989 Pepsi got 17 old Soviet submarines and three warships in exchange for soda. It sold them off for scrap.
Sliced bread was first sold in 1928, in a small town in Missouri. Before that, everyone sliced their own.
Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. were born in the same year, 1929, only months apart.
France carried out its last execution by guillotine in 1977, the same year the first Star Wars film came out.
The Russian space station Mir stayed in orbit for 15 years, much longer than it was designed to last.
In 1571 England passed a law making everyone over six wear a woolen cap on Sundays and holidays, to help the wool trade.
Henry VIII's "Groom of the Stool" helped the king on the toilet, and was one of the most trusted and powerful men at court.
The legend that Britain will fall if the ravens leave the Tower of London probably only dates from Victorian times.
Since the Middle Ages, the British monarch has owned unmarked mute swans on open water, and the ones on parts of the Thames are still counted every summer.
Since the 1300s, any whale or sturgeon caught off England's coast has been a "royal fish" that belongs to the monarch.
From 1645 China's rulers required men to shave the front of their heads and wear a long braid, on pain of severe punishment.
A Japanese shogun in the 1680s passed so many laws protecting animals, especially dogs, that he was nicknamed the Dog Shogun.
Venice had stone "lion's mouths" in its walls where citizens could slip in anonymous letters reporting crimes.
During plague outbreaks in the 1600s, Florence's wine sellers used tiny "wine windows" in walls to sell wine without touching anyone.
Liechtenstein sent 80 soldiers to a war in 1866 and 81 came back. Nobody had been hurt, and an Austrian officer came home with them.
In 1154 a Muslim scholar made a famous world map for the Christian king of Sicily. It puts south at the top.
On 3 September 1967 all of Sweden switched from driving on the left to driving on the right, starting at 5 a.m. on a single morning.
The walls and ditches around Benin City in today's Nigeria were once described as the longest earthworks of the pre-machine age.
The famous "Benin Bronzes" of West Africa are misnamed: most of them are made of brass, not bronze.
The marathon is 42.195 km because the 1908 London Olympic race was laid out to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box.
The story of Sundiata, founder of the Mali Empire, has been passed down by storytelling families called griots for over 700 years.
The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 by the British and Maori chiefs, exists in English and Maori versions that don't say quite the same thing.
Over 700 convicts sailed to Australia on the First Fleet in 1788. One of the youngest was a 9-year-old chimney sweep.
In the 1000s the Chola kings of southern India sent naval raids all the way to Southeast Asia.
Nalanda, an ancient Buddhist university in India, had thousands of students and teachers long before Oxford existed.
Visitors in the 1500s compared Vijayanagara in southern India to Rome and called it one of the richest cities they had ever seen.
The walls of the Alhambra palace in Spain are covered in carved Arabic poems, some of them praising the building itself.
On Friday 13 October 1307, the King of France had the Knights Templar arrested all across his kingdom.
Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris took almost 200 years to build, so nobody who saw it started lived to see it finished.
The University of Bologna, founded in 1088, is the oldest university in the Western world, and it has never closed since.
In 1086 William the Conqueror's officials counted England's land, mills and even pigs in a survey later called the Domesday Book.
In 1569 the map maker Gerardus Mercator drew the map that still makes Greenland look as big as Africa, though Africa is 14 times larger.
Humans first saw Antarctica only in 1820, after people had already been flying in hot air balloons for decades.
Coca-Cola was invented in 1886 by a pharmacist in Atlanta and first sold as a medicinal drink.
Levi Strauss and tailor Jacob Davis patented riveted blue jeans in 1873, designed as tough work trousers for miners and laborers.
Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison and became president of South Africa four years after he was released.
Byzantine royal babies were born in a palace room lined with purple stone, so they were called "born in the purple".
In the 1620s Cornelius Drebbel built the first known navigable submarine, rowed under the River Thames.
In 1797 Andre-Jacques Garnerin made the first parachute jump from a balloon, using a silk canopy.
After a big graphite deposit was found in England in the 1500s, it was so valuable that miners were searched when leaving work.
China was using toilet paper by the 500s. In 1393 the emperor's court used sheets about 60 by 90 cm.
In 1299 Florence banned bankers from using Arabic numerals in their account books, because they were too easy to alter.
Denmark's flag has been used since at least the 1300s, making it the oldest national flag still in use.
The 50-star US flag design is credited to a 17-year-old who made it for a school project in 1958. He said his teacher gave him a B minus.
In WWII an American shipyard built a cargo ship in under five days, start to finish.
During WWII Britain spread the story that carrots helped pilots see in the dark, partly to hide that they were using radar.
Britain kept rationing food until 1954, nine years after WWII ended. Candy rationing ended only in 1953.
Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, yet said he had to ride the freight elevator to his own celebration in New York.
At the 1948 "Austerity Olympics" in London, athletes were asked to bring their own towels.
At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, the horse events were held in Sweden because of Australia's strict animal quarantine rules.
In 1966 the football World Cup trophy was stolen in England, and a dog named Pickles found it under a hedge.
Only 13 teams played in the first football World Cup in 1930, and European teams spent about two weeks on a ship to reach Uruguay.
Basketball was invented in 1891 with peach baskets nailed to a balcony, and someone had to fetch the ball after each basket.
Golf courses have 18 holes because St Andrews in Scotland cut its course from 22 holes to 18 in 1764, and everyone copied it.
In 1967 Kathrine Switzer ran the Boston Marathon when women weren't officially allowed, and an official tried to grab her number.
Timbuktu was a great center of learning in the 1400s and 1500s, and families there still guard huge collections of old manuscripts.
In the 1520s King Afonso of Kongo wrote letters to the King of Portugal complaining about the slave trade.
Brasilia was built from scratch in about 41 months and became Brazil's new capital in 1960.
In 1881 King Kalakaua of Hawaii became the first reigning monarch to travel all the way around the world.
The captured Inca emperor Atahualpa offered to fill a large room with gold, and twice over with silver, to win his freedom.
The Aztecs farmed on "floating gardens" built up in shallow lakes, and some are still farmed today in Mexico City.
The burial place of Genghis Khan is still unknown, despite centuries of searching.
In 1854 Commodore Perry brought Japan a working miniature steam train as a gift, and officials took turns riding it.
In 1441 Korea set up a nationwide network of rain gauges, two centuries before Europe measured rainfall that way.
The Philippines are named after King Philip II of Spain, who was still a prince when explorers named the islands after him in 1543.
A map drawn by an Ottoman admiral in 1513 is one of the oldest surviving maps to show part of the Americas.
Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, begun in the 1450s, is one of the oldest covered markets in the world, with thousands of shops.
Babur, founder of India's Mughal Empire, wrote in his diary that India sadly lacked good grapes and melons.
Concorde flew from London to New York in about 3.5 hours, so by the local clocks passengers landed before the time they took off.
The 1969 Moon landing was watched live by an estimated 600 million people, about one in every six people on Earth at the time.
The Titanic's wreck was found in 1985 by an explorer who was on a secret US Navy mission to inspect two lost submarines.
The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, made the first dry-land link between Britain and mainland Europe since the Ice Age.
LEGO comes from the Danish words "leg godt," meaning "play well." The company started out making wooden toys in the 1930s.
In 1962 Decca Records turned down the Beatles, reportedly saying that guitar groups were on their way out.
Before alarm clocks were common, "knocker-uppers" were paid to tap on workers' bedroom windows with long poles to wake them up.
The tin can was invented around 1810, but a handy can opener only came about 50 years later. People used hammers and chisels.
In 1890 Edison sold talking dolls with tiny record players inside. They broke easily, sounded eerie, and were pulled within weeks.
The world's first traffic light went up outside Parliament in London in 1868. It was lit by gas and exploded about a month later.
The pirate Blackbeard is said to have tucked slow-burning fuses under his hat before battle, so smoke curled around his face.
Playing cards reached Europe in the 1370s, probably carried over from the Islamic world.
Norse settlers lived in Greenland for about 450 years before their farms mysteriously emptied out in the 1400s.
Dublin, the capital of Ireland, was founded as a Viking trading base in the 800s.
The name Russia probably comes from the Rus, traders and warriors with Scandinavian roots who ruled Kyiv over a thousand years ago.
The Normans who conquered England in 1066 were descended from Vikings. "Norman" simply means "Northman".
William the Conqueror was crowned on Christmas Day 1066 in Westminster Abbey, where almost every English monarch since has been crowned.
Old London Bridge was lined with houses and shops for centuries, some of them up to seven stories tall.
The Swahili word "safari," meaning a journey, comes from Arabic, a leftover of centuries of trade across the Indian Ocean.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the top of Mount Everest in 1953 and stayed only about 15 minutes.
@sea|Sea life
Greenland sharks may live for around 400 years, making them the longest-lived vertebrates known to science.
Greenland sharks grow about 1 centimeter a year and may not be ready to have babies until they are over 100 years old.
Sharks have been around for more than 400 million years, which means they are older than trees.
A whale shark can grow to about 18 meters long, yet it feeds mostly on tiny plankton, fish eggs and small fish.
Every whale shark has its own pattern of spots, and scientists tell them apart using software first made to map the stars.
Sharks can feel the tiny electric buzz of a fish's heartbeat, so a prey animal hiding under the sand still gives itself away.
Hammerhead sharks have eyes so far apart that they can see above and below themselves at the same time.
Some female sharks in aquariums have had babies with no male around at all, a kind of virgin birth.
Baby sand tiger sharks eat their brothers and sisters inside their mother, so usually just two pups are born, one from each womb.
Shark skin is covered in tiny teeth instead of normal scales, so it feels like sandpaper if you stroke it the wrong way.
A shark can lose and regrow thousands of teeth in its lifetime, with new rows constantly moving forward like a conveyor belt.
Great white sharks can raise their body temperature well above the surrounding water, which helps them hunt in cold seas.
The cookiecutter shark bites perfectly round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna, and has even left marks on submarine rubber.
The goblin shark can launch its jaws forward out of its mouth to snatch prey, one of the fastest jaw strikes known in sharks.
The shortfin mako is often called the fastest shark, with bursts estimated at around 70 kilometers per hour.
Tiger sharks are famous for eating almost anything, and license plates, tires and tin cans have been found in their stomachs.
Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found more than 3,000 kilometers up the Amazon River.
Great whites and makos must keep swimming to breathe, but nurse sharks can lie still on the seafloor and pump water over their gills.
Venice, Florida, calls itself the shark tooth capital of the world, because fossil shark teeth wash up on its beaches by the thousands.
The epaulette shark can walk on its fins across reef flats and survive for hours in low-oxygen tide pools.
The swell shark gulps seawater to inflate its body to about twice its size, wedging itself tightly into rocky crevices.
The megamouth shark was unknown to science until 1976, when one got tangled in a ship's sea anchor near Hawaii.
Lemon sharks often return to give birth in the same nursery lagoon where they themselves were born.
Basking sharks filter around 2,000 tonnes of water an hour through their gills while cruising with their mouths wide open.
The largest known shark, the extinct megalodon, had teeth about as long as a human hand.
Thresher sharks stun schools of fish by whipping their enormous tail, which can be as long as the rest of their body.
Frilled sharks have about 300 needle-sharp teeth arranged in rows and look almost unchanged from ancient fossil relatives.
The spined pygmy shark grows to only about 20 centimeters long, small enough to hold in your hand.
Manta rays have the biggest brains for their size of any fish, and some have acted as if they recognized themselves in a mirror.
Giant manta rays can have a wingspan of about 7 meters, wider than a typical car is long.
Mobula rays leap out of the water by the hundreds, sometimes flipping in midair, and scientists still debate why.
A sawfish uses its long toothed snout to slash through schools of fish and to sense prey buried in the sand.
Electric rays can deliver shocks of up to about 200 volts to stun prey, and ancient Greeks used them to numb pain.
One kind of electric eel, described in 2019, can zap with up to 860 volts, and electric eels are really knifefish, not true eels.
Stingrays can find crabs and clams buried under the sand by sensing the faint electricity their bodies give off.
The ocean sunfish is the heaviest fish with a bony skeleton, and some weigh over 2,000 kilograms, as much as a car.
A single ocean sunfish can produce around 300 million eggs at once, more than any other known vertebrate.
Ocean sunfish lie flat at the surface so seabirds can pick parasites off their skin.
Sailfish can raise their huge sail-like back fin and flash new colors in seconds while herding schools of sardines.
Swordfish have a built-in heater that warms their eyes and brain, keeping their vision sharp in the cold deep sea.
Atlantic bluefin tuna can swim across an entire ocean, traveling between the Gulf of Mexico and the Mediterranean Sea.
A single Pacific bluefin tuna sold for over 3 million US dollars at a Tokyo auction in 2019.
The coelacanth was thought to have died out with the dinosaurs until a living one was caught off South Africa in 1938.
Coelacanths are believed to live up to about 100 years and carry their young for around five years before giving birth.
The Australian lungfish can breathe air with a lung, and its DNA is about 14 times longer than a human's.
African lungfish can survive for years buried in dried mud, wrapped in a cocoon of mucus, waiting for the rains to return.
Mudskippers are fish that spend much of their time out of water, skipping across mudflats and breathing through their skin.
The four-eyed fish has eyes split in two, so it can see above and below the waterline at the same time.
The archerfish knocks insects off overhanging leaves by shooting precise jets of water from its mouth.
Flying fish can glide more than 200 meters through the air by spreading their large winglike fins.
Clownfish are all born male, and when the dominant female of a group dies, the largest male turns into a female.
Clownfish coat themselves in mucus that keeps their host sea anemone from stinging them.
Parrotfish crunch up coral and poop out fine white sand, so a lot of the sand on tropical beaches has been through a parrotfish.
Some parrotfish sleep inside a bubble of mucus they blow around themselves each night, which may hide their scent from predators.
Reef fish visit cleaner wrasse at cleaning stations, and even big predators open their mouths and let the tiny cleaners inside.
Pufferfish blow themselves up like a spiky balloon by gulping water fast, turning into a ball too big for most predators to swallow.
Many pufferfish carry a poison over a thousand times deadlier than cyanide, yet in Japan specially licensed chefs serve them as a delicacy.
Male white-spotted pufferfish spend about a week carving huge geometric circles in the sand with their fins to attract a mate.
A male seahorse can give birth to more than a thousand babies at once, popping them out of his belly pouch.
Seahorses have no stomach, so food passes through them quickly and they must eat almost constantly.
Seahorses are among the slowest swimming fish, with the dwarf seahorse moving only about 1.5 meters an hour.
The leafy seadragon is covered in leaf-shaped flaps that make it look exactly like drifting seaweed.
Stonefish are the most venomous fish known, and their spines can inject venom through a beach shoe.
Lionfish invaded the Atlantic from the Pacific, and in one experiment a single lionfish wiped out nearly 80 percent of the young fish on a small reef in five weeks.
Some frogfish swallow prey in about 6 milliseconds, among the fastest feeding strikes of any vertebrate.
Remoras have a suction cup on top of their head, which is really a fin, and use it to hitch free rides on sharks and whales.
Flounders are born with an eye on each side, but one eye migrates across the head so both end up on top.
The Atlantic salmon can leap waterfalls more than 3 meters high on its journey upstream to spawn.
Pacific salmon find their way back to the stream where they hatched, partly by remembering its smell.
Pacific salmon die soon after spawning, and their bodies feed the forests, with salmon nutrients found in streamside trees.
European eels are thought to swim thousands of kilometers to the Sargasso Sea to breed, yet no one has ever seen them spawn in the wild.
Some European eels have lived over 80 years in captivity, and one famous eel in a Swedish well was said to live over 150.
Hagfish can produce buckets of slime in seconds, clogging the gills of predators that try to bite them.
Hagfish can tie their own bodies into knots to scrape off slime or to tear food apart.
Hagfish slime threads are so fine and strong that scientists have studied them for making fabrics.
Lampreys have no jaws, just a round sucking mouth full of teeth, and they have barely changed in over 300 million years.
Some fish living in Indonesian swamps are fully grown at about 8 millimeters long, small enough to sit on a fingernail.
The oarfish can reach over 8 meters long and is thought to have inspired many sea serpent legends.
Herring seem to talk to each other by farting: they release bubbles from their rear ends that make a high-pitched ticking sound.
Plainfin midshipman fish hum so loudly at night while courting that houseboat owners have mistaken them for machinery.
A goliath grouper can weigh over 300 kilograms and uses a booming sound to warn off intruders.
Pistol shrimp snap their claw so fast it makes a bubble that collapses with one of the loudest bangs in the sea, plus a tiny flash of light.
Mantis shrimp punch with the acceleration of a small bullet, hitting hard enough to crack aquarium glass.
A blue whale's heart weighs around 180 kilograms, and during a deep dive it can slow down to just two beats a minute.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur.
A blue whale's tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant, and its mouth could hold a crowd of people.
A blue whale can eat around 16 tonnes of tiny krill in a single day during feeding season.
Blue whale calves drink hundreds of liters of milk a day and gain roughly 90 kilograms every day.
Blue whale calls are so deep and powerful that they can travel hundreds of kilometers underwater, and most are too low for humans to hear.
Bowhead whales can live for over 200 years, and old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found in living whales.
A bowhead whale can smash through sea ice about 60 centimeters thick with its huge head to make a breathing hole.
Sperm whales have the biggest brain of any animal that has ever lived, more than five times heavier than a human brain.
Sperm whales can dive deeper than 2 kilometers and hold their breath for over an hour while hunting squid.
Sperm whales sleep upright, floating vertically near the surface in groups like giant motionless logs.
Sperm whale clicks are the loudest sounds made by any animal, and divers close by have described feeling them buzz through their bodies.
Ambergris, a waxy lump from sperm whale guts, washes up on beaches and has long been prized by perfume makers.
Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving record: nearly 3 kilometers deep and one dive lasting over 3 hours.
Humpback whales blow rings of bubbles around fish, trapping them in a shimmering net before lunging up through the middle.
Male humpback whales sing long, complex songs, and a new song can spread across a whole ocean's population within a couple of years.
Humpback whales migrate up to about 8,000 kilometers each way between their feeding and breeding grounds.
Humpback whales have been filmed rescuing seals and other animals from attacking orcas, and no one knows exactly why.
Gray whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, about 16,000 to 20,000 kilometers round trip.
The giant combs that filter-feeding whales use to strain food are made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
A whale's blow is not a fountain of seawater but warm breath condensing into a cloud, like your breath on a cold day.
Whales evolved from four-legged land animals, and their closest living relatives today are hippos.
Some whales still carry tiny leftover hip bones inside their bodies from ancestors that walked on land.
When a whale dies and sinks, its body can feed a whole community of deep-sea creatures for decades.
Whale poop is rich in iron and feeds tiny ocean plants that make a large share of the oxygen we breathe.
Narwhal tusks are actually a tooth that grows through the upper lip and can reach about 3 meters long.
A narwhal's tusk spirals counterclockwise and is packed with millions of nerve endings.
Beluga whales are nicknamed sea canaries because of their chirps, whistles and clicks.
Belugas can squish and reshape the big round bump on their forehead, which may help them aim their clicks and calls.
A beluga named NOC at a US Navy program learned to mimic human speech so well that a diver thought someone was talking to him.
Killer whales are not really whales in the usual sense: they are the biggest member of the dolphin family.
Orcas are one of the very few animals besides humans whose females go through menopause, and the grandmothers lead their families to food.
Different orca families speak in their own dialects of calls, passed down through generations.
Some orcas team up to swim at an ice floe side by side, making a wave that washes the resting seal right off into the water.
Orcas have been seen killing great white sharks to eat only their livers, scaring other great whites away from the area.
Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half awake to breathe and watch for danger.
Bottlenose dolphins give themselves signature whistles that work like names, and they respond when they hear their own.
Dolphins can find fish hiding under the sand just by bouncing sound off them, then dive headfirst into the seafloor to grab them.
Bottlenose dolphins have been seen deliberately chewing pufferfish, possibly to get a mild buzz from the toxin.
Spinner dolphins can leap out of the water and spin up to seven times before splashing back down.
River dolphins in the Amazon are bright pink, and their color gets pinker when they get excited.
Common dolphins can travel in super-groups of thousands, churning the sea white as they move.
A manatee's closest living relative on land is the elephant, and both have fingernails on their flippers or feet.
Manatees grow new teeth all their lives: worn molars fall out at the front as fresh ones slide in from the back.
A dugong can eat around 30 kilograms of seagrass a day, grazing the seafloor like an underwater cow.
Sailors may have mistaken manatees and dugongs for mermaids, and Columbus wrote that mermaids were not as pretty as painted.
Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they do not drift apart, a habit called rafting.
Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to about a million hairs per square inch.
Sea otters keep a favorite rock in a pouch of skin under their arm and use it to crack open shellfish.
By eating sea urchins, sea otters protect entire kelp forests from being chewed down to bare rock.
An elephant seal can dive more than 2 kilometers deep and stay under for nearly two hours.
Male elephant seals can weigh up to about 4 tonnes, roughly as much as two cars.
Weddell seals live under the Antarctic ice and keep their breathing holes open by sawing at the ice with their teeth.
A leopard seal once spent days bringing penguins to an underwater photographer, as if trying to teach him to hunt.
Walruses use their tusks like ice picks to haul their huge bodies out of the water onto the ice.
A walrus can suck a clam out of its shell with such force that it leaves the empty shell behind.
Harbor seals can sense the wake left by a fish that swam past seconds earlier, just with their whiskers.
Fur seal pups and their mothers can find each other among thousands on a crowded beach by their voices.
A sea lion named Ronan learned to bob her head in time to music, a skill once thought to belong only to humans and parrots.
Leatherback sea turtles can dive over 1,000 meters deep, deeper than many submarines can go.
Leatherback turtles mainly eat jellyfish and have spiky throats lined with backward-pointing spines to keep them down.
Leatherback turtles can weigh as much as 900 kilograms and swim over 16,000 kilometers between their feeding and nesting grounds.
Sea turtle eggs become male or female depending on the sand's temperature, with warm nests making mostly females.
On the warming beaches of the northern Great Barrier Reef, over 99 percent of young green sea turtles are now female.
Sea turtles return to nest on the same beach where they hatched, sometimes decades later, guided partly by Earth's magnetic field.
Green sea turtles get their name from the green color of their fat, not their shells.
Sea turtles cry salty tears, which is how they get rid of the extra salt from seawater.
Loggerhead hatchlings may ride ocean currents for years, crossing the entire Atlantic before returning to coasts.
Hawksbill sea turtles eat sponges filled with glass-like spikes that would be harmful to most animals.
Marine iguanas of the Galapagos are the only lizards that feed in the sea, diving to graze on seaweed.
Sea snakes cannot drink salt water, so they sip the thin layer of fresh rainwater that floats on top of the sea after a storm.
Some sea snakes can breathe partly through their skin, staying underwater for hours.
Emperor penguins can dive over 500 meters deep and hold their breath for more than 20 minutes.
Rockhopper penguins get around by bouncing with both feet together, hopping up rocky shores instead of waddling.
Gentoo penguins are the fastest swimming penguins, reaching about 36 kilometers per hour underwater.
Penguins can drink salt water because a gland above their eyes filters the salt out of their blood.
A young albatross may spend several years at sea without ever touching land before it returns to the island where it hatched.
Herring gull chicks peck at the red spot on their parent's beak, and that peck makes the parent cough up food for them.
A puffin's beak is only bright and colorful in the breeding season: afterwards the colored outer plates fall off and it turns dull.
An octopus has three hearts, and the main one stops beating while it swims, which may be why octopuses would rather crawl.
Octopus blood is blue, not red, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of the iron that makes our blood red.
About two thirds of an octopus's brain cells are in its arms, so each arm can partly think for itself and keeps reacting to touch even after being cut off.
Octopus suckers can taste whatever they touch, so an octopus tastes its food just by grabbing it.
An octopus can squeeze its whole body through any hole bigger than its beak, the only hard part it has.
Octopuses have escaped aquarium tanks, crawled across floors and slipped down drainpipes back to the sea.
Veined octopuses carry coconut shell halves around and hide inside them, one of the first known cases of tool use by an octopus.
The mimic octopus can impersonate a lionfish, a sea snake and a flatfish to scare off predators.
A female octopus guards her eggs without eating until they hatch, and one deep-sea mother guarded hers for four and a half years.
Some octopuses have been seen punching fish while hunting with them, seemingly for no reward at all.
Octopuses can change color and skin texture in a fraction of a second, even though they are thought to be colorblind.
In Australia scientists found an underwater spot nicknamed Octlantis, where gloomy octopuses live together like a tiny town.
The giant Pacific octopus can have an arm span of about 6 meters and lives only about three to five years.
Thousands of brooding octopus mothers gather near warm springs on the deep seafloor off California, a place nicknamed the Octopus Garden.
The blue-ringed octopus is about the size of a golf ball but carries enough venom to kill over 20 adult humans.
Cuttlefish can flash moving stripes of color across their bodies, which may hypnotize the crabs and shrimp they hunt.
Cuttlefish have W-shaped pupils, which may help them see clearly in water where light comes from above.
The cuttlebone found on beaches is the internal shell of a cuttlefish, which it fills with gas to float like a submarine.
Male giant cuttlefish sometimes disguise themselves as females to sneak past bigger males and reach a mate.
The colossal squid has the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, each about the size of a soccer ball.
The first video of a living colossal squid in the wild was only filmed in 2025, a baby in the deep sea near the South Sandwich Islands.
Giant squid can reach around 12 meters long, and the first live one was not photographed until 2004.
Sperm whales often carry round scars from the toothed suckers of giant squid they have fought.
The vampire squid lives in water with almost no oxygen and eats marine snow, the sinking dead stuff from above.
Despite its name, the vampire squid sucks no blood and can turn itself inside out like a cloak when threatened.
Humboldt squid hunt in packs, flash red and white, and can grow nearly 2 meters long.
Some squid can launch themselves out of the water and glide through the air for over 30 meters.
Octopuses and squid can rewrite parts of their own genetic instructions on the fly, possibly to keep their nerves working in cold water.
The chambered nautilus has changed little in hundreds of millions of years and can have around 90 arms with no suckers.
The paper nautilus is actually an octopus, and the female builds a thin papery shell to carry her eggs.
Jellyfish have no brain, no heart, no bones and no blood, and are about 95 percent water.
Jellyfish have drifted through the oceans for over 500 million years, longer than dinosaurs, sharks or trees.
The immortal jellyfish can turn back into a baby polyp when stressed or old, restarting its life cycle again and again.
A lion's mane jellyfish found in 1870 had tentacles about 37 meters long, longer than a blue whale.
Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, and some of them have lenses, retinas and corneas like ours.
The sting of an Australian box jellyfish can kill a person within minutes, making it among the deadliest animals in the sea.
The Irukandji jellyfish is about the size of a fingernail but its sting can cause severe pain and a racing heart.
A jellyfish can still sting after it dies, so a dead one washed up on the beach is still worth stepping around.
The Portuguese man o' war is not a single jellyfish but a colony of many tiny animals working together as one.
Upside-down jellyfish lie on the seafloor with their tentacles up, farming algae that grow inside their bodies.
Moon jellyfish have been sent into space, and those that developed in orbit had trouble telling which way was down on Earth.
In Palau's Jellyfish Lake, millions of golden jellyfish migrate across the lake every day following the sun.
Comb jellies are not true jellyfish, and they shimmer with rainbows as tiny hairlike combs beat along their bodies.
Some comb jellies have no permanent anus, and one opens up only when they need to poop.
The by-the-wind sailor is a little blue animal with a built-in sail that drifts across the ocean wherever the wind blows.
Sea turtles, sunfish and some seabirds eat jellyfish, and plastic bags floating in the sea can look like a jelly meal to them.
Corals are animals, not plants, and each coral head is made of thousands of tiny creatures called polyps.
Corals get most of their color from tiny algae living inside them, and when the water gets too hot they throw them out and turn ghostly white.
Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but are home to about a quarter of all known marine species.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things and can be seen from space.
On a few nights each year, many corals on a reef release their eggs and sperm at the same time, like an underwater snowstorm.
Some deep-sea black corals have been dated to over 4,000 years old, among the oldest living animals known.
Some coral reefs grow in cold, pitch-dark water hundreds of meters deep, like the huge reefs off Norway, with no sunlight at all.
Corals glow in vivid colors under blue light, and some may use their fluorescence like a sunscreen.
Sea anemones are close relatives of jellyfish, basically a jellyfish turned upside down and stuck to a rock.
Some sea anemones can live for decades, and scientists have found few signs that they ever grow old.
Sponges have no organs, no nerves and no muscles, yet they are animals, and among the oldest kinds on Earth.
If you push a living sponge through a sieve, its separated cells can crawl back together and rebuild the sponge.
A single sponge the size of a basketball can filter thousands of liters of seawater a day.
Some glass sponges on the Antarctic seafloor are thought to be over 10,000 years old, alive since the end of the last ice age.
The Venus flower basket is a glass sponge whose skeleton traps a pair of shrimp for life, and in Japan it became a wedding gift.
Starfish have no blood and no brain, and they move by pumping seawater through hundreds of tiny tube feet.
A starfish eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and digesting its prey outside its body.
Many starfish can regrow lost arms, and some can grow a whole new body from a single arm.
Starfish have a simple eye at the tip of each arm, letting them sense light and dark shapes.
The crown-of-thorns starfish can eat its way across a coral reef, killing huge areas during population booms.
Sea urchins have no eyes, but scientists think their whole spiny body may work like one big eye.
Sea urchin teeth sharpen themselves as they wear down, and they can grind holes into solid rock.
Sea cucumbers can shoot out their own guts to tangle predators, then grow new ones.
Some fish called pearlfish live inside sea cucumbers, entering and leaving through the cucumber's rear end.
Sea cucumbers breathe through their bottoms, pumping water in and out of their rear ends.
A sea cucumber can turn its body from soft and floppy to stiff like a board in seconds.
Brittle stars can drop an arm to escape a predator and run away surprisingly fast for a starfish relative.
Sea lilies, relatives of starfish, can crawl across the seafloor on their arms to escape hungry sea urchins.
Sea squirts start life as swimming tadpole-like larvae, then settle down and absorb most of their own brain.
Giant clams can grow over 1 meter wide, weigh over 200 kilograms and live for more than 100 years.
Giant clams cannot trap divers, because the largest ones close their shells too slowly and cannot shut completely.
Scallops have up to about 200 tiny eyes along the edge of their shell, each with a mirror inside to focus light.
Scallops swim by clapping their shells together, jetting through the water in jerky zigzags.
An ocean quahog clam named Ming was about 507 years old, alive since before Shakespeare was born.
Mussels hold on to rocks in crashing waves with strong threads glued down by a superglue that works underwater.
A pearl forms when an oyster coats an annoying bit of grit or tissue with layer after layer of the same shiny stuff that lines its shell.
A single oyster can filter around 190 liters of water a day, cleaning bays as it feeds.
The cone snail harpoons fish with a venomous tooth, and some cone snail venom is strong enough to kill a person.
A powerful hospital painkiller was made from cone snail venom, and it is far stronger than morphine.
Sea slugs come in neon colors and patterns as bright as candy, often to warn predators that they taste terrible.
The blue dragon sea slug eats Portuguese man o' war and stores their stinging cells to use as its own weapon.
The Japanese spider crab has legs that can span about 3.7 meters, wider than a small car is long.
Hermit crabs line up by size next to an empty shell and swap homes in a chain, each moving into the next bigger shell.
Coconut crabs are the biggest animals without a backbone that live on land, strong enough to crack open coconuts with their claws.
Every year tens of millions of red crabs march from the forest to the sea on Christmas Island, covering roads and bridges.
Horseshoe crabs have bright blue blood, and it is used to check that vaccines and medicines are free of harmful bacteria.
Horseshoe crabs are not really crabs: they are more closely related to spiders and scorpions.
Horseshoe crabs have ten eyes, including light sensors on their tail, and have been around for over 400 million years.
Lobsters taste their food with their legs and smell with tiny hairs on their antennae, flicking them like a snake's tongue.
American lobsters may live more than 100 years in the wild, and they keep growing for as long as they live.
Lobsters were once so common in New England that they were seen as poor people's food and even fed to prisoners.
Spiny lobsters migrate in long single-file lines across the seafloor, each touching the one in front with its antennae.
Mantis shrimp have about 12 kinds of color-sensing cells, compared with our three, yet tests show they are worse than us at telling similar colors apart.
Mantis shrimp can see polarized light, a hidden pattern of light that humans cannot see at all.
Some mantis shrimp pairs stay together for 20 years, sharing a burrow and hunting duties.
Antarctic krill swarms can be so dense that they turn the sea red and can be seen from space.
All the Antarctic krill in the ocean together may weigh about as much as all the people on Earth.
Krill can shrink their bodies when food runs out and survive over 200 days without eating.
Barnacles stand on their heads inside their shells and kick food into their mouths with their feathery legs.
The skeleton shrimp looks like a tiny stick insect, clinging to seaweed with its back legs while it waves its claws in the water.
Some barnacles live only on whales, riding along for their whole lives across entire oceans.
Gooseneck barnacles were once believed to hatch into geese, which is how the barnacle goose got its name.
Copepods, tiny shrimp-like animals smaller than a grain of rice, may be the most numerous animals on Earth.
Every night, countless sea creatures swim up from the deep to feed at the surface, then sink back by dawn, the biggest migration on Earth.
Boxer crabs hold small sea anemones in their claws like stinging pom-poms to fight off enemies.
Decorator crabs glue bits of sponge, seaweed and anemones onto their shells to create living disguises.
Fiddler crab males wave one giant claw, which can make up about half their body weight, to attract females.
Bright red Sally Lightfoot crabs in the Galapagos pick ticks off the skin of marine iguanas, which lie still and let them.
Gulf corvina fish spawn in such huge crowds that their croaking chorus is as loud as a stadium full of cheering fans.
Yeti crabs on deep-sea vents grow bacteria on their hairy arms, then wave them around and eat their own farm.
The deepest part of the ocean, the Challenger Deep, is about 11 kilometers down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the water pressure is over 1,000 times stronger than at the surface.
Until 2019, only three people had ever been to the deepest point of the ocean, while twelve had walked on the Moon.
Scientists estimate that most of the species living in the ocean have never been discovered or named.
As of 2024, only about a quarter of the seafloor has been mapped in detail, so we have better maps of Mars than of our own ocean bottom.
In 2022, a snailfish was filmed swimming about 8,300 meters deep off Japan, the deepest fish ever recorded.
Amphipods, little shrimp-like scavengers, live at the very bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers down.
Plastic has been found in the guts of tiny creatures living at the bottom of the deepest ocean trenches.
In some deep-sea anglerfish, the tiny male bites onto a female and fuses to her body for life, sharing her blood.
The glowing lure dangling in front of a deep-sea anglerfish's mouth gets its light from bacteria living inside it.
The black swallower can eat a fish more than twice its own length, storing it in a stomach that balloons out.
The gulper eel has a huge mouth that unhinges like a pelican's pouch, far bigger than the rest of its body.
The barreleye fish has a see-through head, and its glowing green eyes look straight up through its clear forehead.
The blobfish looks like a sad pile of jelly only when brought to the surface; in the deep sea it looks like a normal fish.
The viperfish has fangs so long they do not fit inside its mouth, so they stick out past its face even when it is closed.
The fangtooth fish has the biggest teeth for its size of any known fish, so big it needs pockets in its head to close its mouth.
Tripod fish stand on the seafloor on three long fins like stilts, waiting for food to drift past.
The giant isopod is a deep-sea cousin of the garden pill bug that can grow about as long as a house cat.
One giant isopod in a Japanese aquarium refused food for over five years and still lived.
The Dumbo octopus is named after the Disney elephant because its fins look like big flapping ears.
Dumbo octopuses live deeper than any other known octopus, recorded around 7,000 meters down.
The deep-sea dragonfish makes red light, which most other deep-sea animals cannot see, like a secret flashlight.
Hydrothermal vents on the seafloor blast out water hotter than 350 degrees Celsius, yet animals thrive right beside them.
Giant tube worms can grow over 2 meters long and get their bright red color from blood like ours.
The Pompeii worm lives in tubes on scalding vent chimneys and is one of the most heat-tolerant animals known.
The scaly-foot snail on deep-sea vents builds its shell and armor scales partly out of iron.
Life at deep-sea vents runs on chemicals instead of sunlight, a discovery from 1977 that changed ideas about where life can exist.
Zombie worms have no mouth or stomach and drill into the bones of dead whales on the seafloor to feed.
Deep-sea brine pools are underwater lakes so salty that fish that swim in by mistake can die.
The deep-sea glass squid is almost completely transparent, so predators can see right through it.
The giant siphonophore, a deep-sea string of many tiny clones living as one, can stretch about 40 meters, longer than a blue whale.
Sea angels are tiny see-through snails with wing-like feet that flap through icy seas, and they hunt sea butterflies.
The ping-pong tree sponge is a meat-eating sponge from the deep sea that traps tiny animals on its sticky glass balls.
About three quarters of the animals in the open ocean, from the surface to the deep, can make their own light.
Many deep-sea animals are red, because red light does not reach the deep, making them nearly invisible.
Lanternfish are among the most common fish on Earth, and their glowing spots form patterns unique to each species.
The deep-sea snipe eel has a long, thin beak whose two halves curve apart at the tip, so it can never fully close its mouth.
The cookiecutter shark glows on its belly except for a dark band that may look like a small fish to its prey.
Glowing waves on some beaches come from tiny plankton that flash blue when the water is disturbed.
Sailors have long told of milky seas that glow for miles at night, and satellites have since spotted one about as big as Iceland.
The vampire squid can squirt out a cloud of glowing mucus to confuse predators instead of ink.
Tiny glowing sea creatures called sea fireflies were dried by Japanese soldiers in World War II, then wetted to make a dim light for reading.
Firefly squid gather in Toyama Bay, Japan, every spring, lighting the water with millions of blue lights.
A glowing protein from the crystal jellyfish is now used in labs worldwide to light up cells and won a Nobel Prize.
Some shrimp spew glowing liquid from their mouths to blind and confuse predators.
The deep-sea fish called the stoplight loosejaw has a jaw with no floor, letting it snap up prey fast.
Pyrosomes are glowing tubes made of thousands of tiny animals, and some are big enough for a person to swim into.
The Atolla jellyfish flashes a spinning ring of blue light that may call bigger predators to attack whatever is attacking it.
The ocean's twilight zone, between about 200 and 1,000 meters deep, may hold more fish by weight than all the rest of the sea.
Tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton make roughly half of the oxygen on Earth, so every other breath you take comes from the sea.
One tiny ocean microbe is so common that it may make up to a fifth of the oxygen we breathe, yet it was only discovered in the 1980s.
A single teaspoon of seawater can hold millions of bacteria and tens of millions of viruses.
Giant kelp can grow up to about 60 centimeters in a single day, making kelp forests some of the fastest-growing on Earth.
Kelp is not a plant but a giant seaweed, and it uses gas-filled bulbs to float its leaves toward the sunlight.
Seagrass meadows can store carbon up to about 35 times faster than tropical rainforests can.
A single seagrass plant in Shark Bay, Australia, has cloned itself across about 180 square kilometers, making it the largest known plant.
A clump of Mediterranean seagrass is thought to be many thousands of years old, among the oldest living things on Earth.
The Sargasso Sea is the only sea with no coastline, defined by ocean currents and floating mats of golden seaweed.
Baby sea turtles hide and feed in floating seaweed rafts during their lost years far out at sea.
The ocean holds about 97 percent of all the water on Earth, so the lakes, rivers and ice we know are only a tiny bit.
Seawater holds millions of tonnes of dissolved gold, but it is so spread out that nobody has found a way to collect it.
If all the salt in the ocean were spread over the land, it would form a layer taller than a 40-story building.
The longest mountain range on Earth is under the sea: the mid-ocean ridge runs about 65,000 kilometers around the planet.
Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, which is why whales can hear each other across huge distances.
A great ocean conveyor belt of currents moves water around the globe, and one drop may take about 1,000 years to finish the loop.
The Gulf Stream carries more than 100 times as much water as all the world's rivers put together.
Giant rogue waves were dismissed as sailors' tall tales until an oil platform measured one about 25 meters high in 1995.
In 2020 a surfer rode a wave about 26 meters tall at Nazare, Portugal, a world record at the time.
Most water in the deep sea stays just a few degrees above freezing all year round, colder than your fridge.
Sea ice is mostly fresh, because the salt gets squeezed out as seawater freezes.
Brinicles are underwater icicles of super-cold salty water that grow down from sea ice and freeze sea creatures in their path.
There are more than 100,000 seamounts, underwater mountains, and most of them have never been explored.
In 2023 scientists discovered a hidden world of worms, snails and other animals living in caves beneath deep-sea hot springs.
Goldfish can remember things for months and can be trained to push levers, swim through hoops and respond to sounds.
Goldfish released into the wild can grow to the size of a football and take over lakes.
Piranhas are mostly scavengers and timid fish, and many stories of them stripping animals in seconds are exaggerated.
Red-bellied piranhas bark, croak and grunt at each other, a bit like tiny underwater dogs warning each other off.
Some killifish in Africa live in puddles that dry up every year, so they hatch, grow up, breed and die in just a few months.
Saltwater fish lose water to the salty sea, so they drink seawater constantly and push the salt out through their gills.
The arapaima of the Amazon can grow about 3 meters long and must come up to gulp air, so it can actually drown if held underwater.
Arapaima scales are so tough that people in the Amazon use them as nail files, and piranha teeth cannot bite through them.
The Mekong giant catfish can weigh about as much as a grizzly bear, and one caught in 2005 weighed 293 kilograms.
A giant freshwater stingray caught in Cambodia in 2022 weighed about 300 kilograms, the largest freshwater fish on record.
Catfish are swimming tongues, with taste buds covering their entire bodies, and a big one may have more than 100,000.
Some catfish can walk across land on their fins and breathe air for hours, crossing from pond to pond.
The candiru is a tiny Amazon catfish that sneaks into the gills of bigger fish to drink their blood.
Mexican blind cavefish have lost their eyes completely, and their cousins living in rivers still have them.
The Devils Hole pupfish lives in just one small pool in a Nevada desert cave, one of the tiniest homes of any wild animal with a backbone.
Electric catfish from Africa can deliver shocks of up to about 350 volts, enough to stun fish and give a person a nasty jolt.
Wild axolotls live in just one area of canals around Mexico City and are critically endangered.
The goliath tigerfish of Africa's Congo River has big dagger-like teeth and can weigh over 50 kilograms.
The male stickleback builds a nest of plants glued together with a sticky thread made in its kidneys, then fans fresh water over the eggs.
Electric fish in murky rivers sense their surroundings with weak electric fields, like a built-in radar.
Sea lampreys invaded the Great Lakes through canals and nearly wiped out the lake trout there.
Sturgeon have been around since the time of the dinosaurs and some can live over 100 years.
Beluga sturgeon can grow over 7 meters long, and their eggs are sold as some of the most expensive caviar.
Paddlefish use their long flat snouts to sense the tiny electric signals of plankton in murky water.
Gars can breathe air with a lung-like swim bladder and have armor scales once used as arrowheads.
The climbing perch can wriggle across dry land from pond to pond and survive out of water for days.
Mosquito fish can each eat hundreds of mosquito larvae a day and have been released around the world to fight malaria.
Bettas, or Siamese fighting fish, build floating nests of bubbles where the father guards the eggs.
Cichlid fish in Africa's Lake Malawi have split into hundreds of species in just a few million years.
Mouthbrooding cichlid mothers carry their eggs and babies in their mouths and do not eat until they leave.
Some cuckoo catfish sneak their eggs into the mouths of mouthbrooding cichlids, and the babies eat the cichlid's own young.
Zebrafish can regrow damaged heart muscle, spinal cord and even parts of their eyes.
Lake Baikal's golomyanka fish has no scales and is so fatty that it is partly see-through.
Lake Baikal in Siberia has its own seals, living more than 1,000 kilometers from the nearest ocean, and no one knows exactly how they got there.
The hairy frogfish looks like a walking ball of fuzz and blends in perfectly with algae-covered rocks.
The sarcastic fringehead settles fights by opening its enormous mouth and pressing it against a rival's like a kiss.
Some deep-sea dragonfish have see-through teeth, which may keep their prey from spotting the danger until it is too late.
The Antarctic icefish has no red blood cells, and its blood is almost clear like water.
Antarctic fish have natural antifreeze in their blood that keeps them from freezing in water below 0 degrees Celsius.
The mudskipper builds a burrow in mud and carries mouthfuls of air down into it to keep its eggs breathing.
The leaping blenny spends its life out of water on rocks splashed by waves, hopping away from the sea.
Garden eels live in huge colonies with their tails in the sand, swaying like grass and ducking down when danger comes.
Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat that shoots forward to drag prey down, like the creature in Alien.
Coral trout point at hidden prey with their bodies, a kind of gesture once thought only apes and humans used.
Tuskfish smash clams against rocks to open them, a rare example of tool use in fish.
Damselfish farm their own patches of algae, weeding out unwanted kinds and chasing off grazers.
Triggerfish blow jets of water at sea urchins to flip them over and attack their soft undersides.
Boxfish have a hard bony box for a body, and their shape inspired a car designed by Mercedes-Benz.
The ocean sunfish's babies start out the size of a pinhead and grow up to about 60 million times heavier.
The red-lipped batfish, a kind of anglerfish, walks along the seafloor on its fins and looks like it is wearing bright red lipstick.
Moray eels and cleaner shrimp work together: the shrimp picks food scraps from the eel's teeth.
In a typical year, cows kill more people in the United States alone than sharks kill in the whole world.
Humans kill roughly 100 million sharks a year, while sharks kill only about five to ten people.
Great white sharks were found to travel from South Africa to Australia and back in about nine months, over 20,000 kilometers.
Great white sharks sometimes gather at a spot in the middle of the Pacific nicknamed the White Shark Cafe, and scientists are still not sure why.
Whale sharks can dive nearly 2 kilometers deep, even though they spend lots of time near the surface.
Sharks have no bones, so most of what is left of ancient sharks is just teeth, millions of them in fossil beds.
Some sharks glow in the dark, and swell sharks shine bright green to each other in a pattern only other sharks can see.
A whale shark's skin can be about 10 centimeters thick, among the thickest of any animal.
Wobbegong sharks look like shaggy rugs on the seafloor, with fringes around their mouths that look like seaweed.
Port Jackson sharks lay spiral-shaped egg cases, which their mothers may wedge into rocky cracks to keep them safe.
Empty shark and ray egg cases that wash up on beaches are nicknamed mermaid's purses.
Pacific sleeper sharks have been found with the beaks of giant squid in their stomachs, though no one knows how they catch them.
Some sharks can smell blood diluted to about one part in a million, like a drop in a bathtub, but not a single drop from miles away.
Whale shark mothers can carry around 300 pups at once, at different stages of growth.
Tiger sharks get their name from the dark stripes they are born with, which fade as they grow up.
The Greenland shark's eyes often host a parasite that dangles from them, which may partly blind it.
Some manta rays visit cleaning stations on reefs and remember them, returning to the same spot for years.
Ray babies are born rolled up like burritos, unrolling as soon as they enter the water.
The giant oceanic manta ray has no stinger, and despite its huge size it is harmless to people.
Cownose rays migrate in schools of thousands, turning the sea brown with their bodies.
The great hammerhead often swims tilted on its side, which saves energy because its tall back fin works like a wing.
Sperm whales nap in short bursts of about 10 to 15 minutes, adding up to only a couple of hours a day.
Right whales got their name because whalers thought they were the right whale to hunt: slow, close to shore and floating when killed.
Fin whales are the second largest animals on Earth and can swim faster than many ships, around 40 kilometers per hour.
A fin whale's calls are so loud and low that scientists have used them to scan the rock layers under the seafloor.
The pygmy right whale is so rarely seen that it was once thought to belong to a group of whales believed extinct.
Omura's whale, about as long as a bus, was only named as a new species in 2003 and was not filmed alive in the wild until 2015.
In a single gulp, a blue whale can swallow a mouthful of water and krill bigger than its own body.
Humpback whale flippers can be about a third as long as their bodies, up to about 5 meters, the longest flippers of any whale.
The bumps on humpback whale flippers inspired wind turbine and fan blades that work better.
A whale's earwax builds up in layers every year, like tree rings, and scientists can read its life story from them.
Killer whales have been seen wearing dead salmon on their heads like hats, a trend that came and went in 1987.
Since 2020, a group of orcas off Spain and Portugal has been ramming sailboats' rudders, and scientists still do not know why.
Beluga whales shed their skin every summer by rubbing and rolling on gravel in shallow river mouths.
The vaquita, the world's smallest porpoise, lives only in Mexico's Gulf of California, and fewer than a dozen were thought to be left in 2024.
The Yangtze river dolphin was declared functionally extinct in 2006, the first dolphin species lost to human activity.
Some dolphins team up with fishermen in Brazil, signaling when to throw nets, and both sides catch more fish.
Bottlenose dolphins can recognize the whistles of old companions even after 20 years apart.
New Zealand's Hector's dolphin is one of the smallest dolphins, with a rounded fin often compared to a Mickey Mouse ear.
Risso's dolphins are covered with white scars from squid and from playing rough with each other.
A dolphin's skin peels off and renews itself about every two hours, keeping it super smooth for swimming.
The crabeater seal mostly eats krill, not crabs, and may be one of the most common large mammals on Earth.
Male hooded seals can blow a red balloon out of one nostril to show off to females.
Bearded seal songs are long trilling calls that can be heard underwater over 20 kilometers away.
Elephant seals sleep only about two hours a day at sea, napping in short spirals as they sink.
Male Steller sea lions can weigh over a tonne, about as much as a small car, and roar like lions on their beaches.
Sea otters have no blubber and stay warm by eating about a quarter of their body weight every day.
Female sea otters float on their backs with their pups on their bellies, like a living raft.
Manatees get sick in water colder than about 20 degrees Celsius, so in winter they crowd into warm springs and the warm water near power plants.
Manatees use their flexible lips like hands to grab and pull plants into their mouths.
Steller's sea cow was a giant relative of manatees, about 8 meters long, hunted to extinction within 27 years of its discovery.
Sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells like many land turtles can.
A sea turtle hatchling has only about a one in a thousand chance of surviving to adulthood.
Sea turtle hatchlings find the sea by heading toward the brightest horizon, which is why beach lights can lead them astray.
Olive ridley sea turtles nest in mass arrivals, with hundreds of thousands coming ashore on the same beach over a few days.
Sea turtles have been around for over 100 million years, swimming alongside the dinosaurs.
The hawksbill turtle's beak is shaped like a bird's, perfect for picking food out of cracks in coral.
A sea turtle can slow its heart to just one beat every nine minutes to save oxygen.
Northern gannets dive into the sea at around 85 kilometers per hour, folding their wings just before they hit the water.
Brown pelicans dive headfirst from up to about 20 meters, with air sacs under their skin cushioning the impact.
