Sooty shearwaters fly a giant figure-eight loop around the Pacific Ocean every year, covering about 64,000 kilometers.
Male frigatebirds puff up a giant red throat pouch like a balloon to attract females flying overhead.
Albatrosses can sniff out food from many kilometers away, following the smell of fish oil across the open ocean.
Albatross couples often stay together for life and greet each other with an elaborate dance after months apart.
Cormorants have feathers that soak up water, helping them dive, so they stand with wings spread to dry off afterward.
Penguin poop stains on Antarctic ice are so big that scientists find penguin colonies from space by spotting them.
Macaroni penguins are named after an 18th-century fashion craze for flashy feathered hats, not after the pasta.
A king penguin can recognize its chick's voice among thousands of shrieking birds in a crowded colony.
Galapagos penguins live right on the equator, the only penguins whose range reaches the northern hemisphere.
Little penguins, also called fairy penguins, stand only about 33 centimeters tall and parade up Australian beaches at dusk.
Harp seal pups nurse for only about 12 days, but the milk is so rich they gain over 2 kilograms a day before their mothers leave.
Ringed seal mothers dig snow caves on top of the sea ice to hide their newborn pups from polar bears.
Seahorses mate for the season and greet each other every morning with a little dance, changing colors together.
Pygmy seahorses are smaller than a fingernail and match the color and bumps of the coral they live on so well they were found by accident.
A seahorse can move each eye on its own, looking forward and backward at the same time.
The weedy seadragon is found only in southern Australia, and its babies hatch from eggs stuck under the father's tail.
Moray eels can tie themselves in knots, sliding the knot along their body to get a better grip as they tear food apart.
Electric eels can leap out of the water to shock threats above the surface, as described by explorer Alexander von Humboldt.
Some electric eels hunt together in groups, herding small fish before zapping them.
A school of sardines can stretch for kilometers, and during South Africa's sardine run it attracts dolphins, sharks, whales and birds.
Fish in a school can turn all at once because they feel each other's movements through a line of sensors along their sides.
Atlantic cod were once so plentiful off Canada that early explorers said you could catch them by lowering a basket into the sea.
The flying gurnard has huge winglike fins it spreads like a fan, and it walks on the seafloor using fingerlike rays.
The sea robin fish walks on six little legs, which are actually fin spines that can also taste food in the sand.
Eels start life as see-through, leaf-shaped babies that drift across the ocean for months before reaching the coast.
Glass eels, baby eels so clear you can see their insides, are among the most expensive seafood by weight in the world.
Pacific lampreys climb waterfalls and even dam walls by sucking on with their mouths and inching their way up.
Grunion fish lay their eggs on California beaches at night, wriggling out of the waves onto the wet sand.
Coral reef fish larvae can hear and smell their way back to a reef after drifting in the open ocean for weeks.
Playing healthy reef sounds through underwater speakers helped draw young fish back to damaged reefs in an experiment.
Coral reefs work like natural sea walls, soaking up about 97 percent of the energy of the waves before they reach the shore.
Brain corals can live for hundreds of years, and their growth bands record the history of ocean temperatures.
Scientists are raising heat-resistant corals in nurseries and planting them back on damaged reefs, like underwater gardeners.
Christmas tree worms live on corals and look like tiny colorful fir trees, vanishing into their tubes in a blink when startled.
The bobbit worm hides in the sand and can grow up to about 3 meters long, snapping at passing fish with scissor jaws.
Fireworms are covered in bristles that break off in your skin and burn like fiberglass, which is how they got their name.
The Antarctic scale worm has a mouth with golden fanged jaws that it shoots out of its body to grab food.
One ribbon worm washed up in Scotland was reported to be over 50 meters long, longer than a blue whale, though its stretchy body is hard to measure.
Those curly piles of sand you see on beaches at low tide are the poop of lugworms living in burrows underneath.
Sea spiders are so thin that their guts and reproductive organs extend down into their legs.
Antarctic sea spiders can grow as wide as a dinner plate, much bigger than their relatives in warmer seas.
A Japanese sea slug can cut off its own head and grow a whole new body from it within weeks.
The sea butterfly is a tiny swimming snail with wing-like feet that flaps through the water.
Sea hares are giant sea slugs that squirt purple ink when disturbed and can weigh up to about 14 kilograms.
The Spanish dancer sea slug swims by flapping its bright red body like a flamenco dancer's swirling skirt.
Abalone shells are made of tiny tiles stacked like bricks, making them about 3,000 times tougher than the chalky mineral they are made from.
Limpets have the strongest known biological material in their teeth, stronger than spider silk.
Octopuses sometimes sleep with their colors flickering, and scientists suspect they might be dreaming.
Whale sharks have tiny teeth covering their eyeballs, armor that protects their eyes, and they can pull their eyes back into their heads.
Lobsters pee out of their faces and squirt it at each other to send messages during fights and courtship.
Most crabs walk sideways because their leg joints bend outward, but a few kinds, like some spider crabs, can walk forward.
Sea turtles can sleep underwater for several hours at a time by slowing down and needing very little oxygen.
Grey seals clap their flippers underwater, making a loud crack like a gunshot to warn off rivals and impress mates.
Baby dolphins are usually born tail first, which helps keep them from drowning during birth.
Blue whale milk can be about 35 to 50 percent fat, so thick it has been compared to cottage cheese.
A shrimp's heart is in its head, tucked inside the shell just behind its eyes, along with most of its other organs.
The brown ink artists call sepia was originally made from the ink of cuttlefish.
A great white shark's oily liver can make up about a quarter of its body weight and helps keep it from sinking.
Seahorse tails are square instead of round, which makes them tougher to crush and better at gripping.
The bristlemouth, a fish the size of your finger, may be the most common animal with a backbone on Earth, numbering in the hundreds of trillions.
Scientists worked out the age of Greenland sharks by carbon-dating the centers of their eye lenses, which form before they are born.
The bumps on a humpback whale's head each have a hair growing out of it, because whales are mammals and have hair.
Adult green sea turtles eat mostly seagrass, grazing it like underwater lawnmowers and keeping the meadows healthy.
Only about one in two million lobsters is born bright blue, thanks to a rare genetic quirk.
Sockeye salmon turn from silver to bright red before spawning, and the males grow a hump and a hooked jaw.
Many oysters change from male to female and sometimes back again during their lives.
Narwhals are born dark gray, turn spotted as they grow, and the oldest ones become almost completely white.
Walruses can sleep floating upright at sea by inflating pouches in their throats like a built-in life jacket.
Hermit crabs that cannot find a good shell sometimes move into bottle caps, plastic cups and other trash.
The sea pen is a feather-shaped colony of tiny animals that glows with a green light when it is touched.
@mind|Mind
Your brain is only about 2 percent of your body weight, yet it burns roughly 20 percent of your energy, even while you rest.
Your whole brain runs on about 20 watts of power, roughly the same as a dim light bulb.
Thinking really hard barely burns extra calories: your brain uses almost as much energy daydreaming as solving a puzzle.
The small lump at the back of your brain holds about 4 out of every 5 of your brain cells.
Some patients play the violin or guitar during their own brain surgery, so doctors can avoid damaging their musical skills.
Your fastest nerve signals zip along at around 430 kilometers per hour, faster than a Formula 1 car.
Signals for a dull, aching pain travel at about walking speed, which is why a stubbed toe hurts a moment after the bump.
Your brain floats in fluid, which makes it feel about as heavy as a few sugar cubes instead of a bag of flour.
In mice, the gaps between brain cells widen by about 60 percent during sleep, which may help wash out waste, though scientists still debate how much.
Ironed flat, the wrinkly outer surface of your brain would cover roughly the area of a full newspaper page.
Your brain's thinking layer is only 2 to 4 millimeters thick, about as thin as a few credit cards stacked together.
In 1848, Phineas Gage survived an iron rod blasting through his skull, but his friends said his personality changed so much he was "no longer Gage".
After brain surgery in 1953, Henry Molaison could never form a new long-term memory, yet he still got better at new hand skills he did not remember practicing.
Clive Wearing, a musician with severe amnesia, forgets everything within seconds, yet he can still play the piano beautifully.
After Einstein died, the doctor doing his autopsy took his brain home and kept pieces of it in jars for decades.
Einstein's brain was actually a little smaller than the average man's brain, so size is not everything.
In people whose brain halves were surgically separated, the talking half will confidently make up reasons for things the other half did.
Your eye has a blind spot where there are no light sensors at all, but your brain fills in the hole so you never notice it.
You blink about 15 to 20 times a minute, yet your brain edits out the blackouts so the world never flickers.
Every time your eyes dart to a new spot, your brain switches off your vision for a split second, and you never notice.
Your eyes jump around three times every second; the smooth view you see is stitched together by your brain.
Your retina receives an upside-down picture of the world, and your brain flips it the right way up.
A psychologist in the 1890s wore goggles that turned the world upside down, and after a few days it started to feel normal.
Stroke a rubber hand and someone's hidden real hand at the same time, and within minutes many people feel the rubber hand is theirs.
Sugar does not make kids hyper: mothers told their son had eaten sugar rated him more hyperactive, though he had only had a sugar-free drink.
A cheap mirror box, which reflects the healthy arm, has eased pain in missing limbs for some people by tricking the brain.
Around 4 percent of people have synesthesia, where senses blend, like seeing colors when they hear music or read numbers.
For a few people, certain words have tastes: hearing a name might fill their mouth with the flavor of bacon or chocolate.
About 1 in 50 people have face blindness, and some cannot recognize their own family or even themselves in photos.
Oliver Sacks, a famous neurologist with face blindness, once apologized to a bearded man who turned out to be his own reflection.
A rare brain condition makes people believe a loved one has been swapped for an identical-looking impostor.
Some people with a rare condition called Cotard delusion are convinced that they are already dead.
Some people blinded by brain damage can still dodge objects and point to things they swear they cannot see.
A man blinded by strokes walked down a hallway full of boxes and chairs without bumping into a single one.
A woman who lost her sense of motion saw the world as still photos; pouring tea was hard because the liquid looked frozen.
Two squares on a checkerboard image can be the exact same gray, yet one looks dark and the other light, because your brain corrects for a shadow.
In 2015 one photo of a dress split the internet into "blue and black" and "white and gold" because brains guessed the lighting differently.
In one experiment, about half of people giving directions to a stranger did not notice when the stranger was swapped for a different person.
Asked to count basketball passes in a video, about half of people completely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the middle.
When expert doctors searched lung scans, most missed a picture of a gorilla hidden in the scan, 48 times bigger than what they were looking for.
In a noisy room you can suddenly hear your own name across the room, even from a conversation you were not listening to.
You cannot tickle yourself because your brain predicts how your own fingers will feel and turns the sensation down.
Fake pills can make your brain release its own natural painkillers, which is part of why placebos really work.
In some studies, sugar pills still helped people feel better even when they were told up front the pills were fake.
People warned that a sugar pill may cause side effects often report getting those side effects.
People who fell backward 31 meters into a safety net thought their own fall lasted about a third longer than it really did.
When you first glance at a ticking clock, the second hand can seem to freeze for longer than a second.
Smell is the only sense that goes almost straight to the brain's memory and emotion areas, skipping the usual relay station.
A smell can yank back a memory from early childhood more strongly than a photo or a word can, studies suggest.
The maddening tip-of-the-tongue feeling hits most people about once a week, and more often as they get older.
About two out of three people say they have felt deja vu, and it tends to happen less as people age.
Every time you remember something, your brain rebuilds it, and it can quietly change a detail before storing it again.
The idea that you use only 10 percent of your brain is a myth: brain scans show nearly every part of it is active over the course of a day.
A week after watching a car crash video, people who heard the word "smashed" were twice as likely to remember broken glass that was never there.
In experiments, about a quarter of adults came to "remember" being lost in a shopping mall as a child, which never happened.
People's vivid memories of where they were on 9/11 changed over the years as much as ordinary memories, while feeling just as certain.
Most forgetting happens within the first day after you learn something, then it slows down dramatically.
Studying in short sessions spread over several days beats one long cramming session, and it is one of the most solid findings in learning science.
Quizzing yourself on something sticks in memory far better than rereading your notes over and over.
Your short-term memory can juggle only about four chunks at once, which is why phone numbers are split into groups.
A few dozen people in the world can tell you what they did on almost any day of their lives, and what day of the week it was.
A Russian man studied for decades could recall lists from years earlier, and his real struggle was learning to forget.
Memory champions remember things by imagining them placed around a familiar house, a trick used since ancient Greece.
Ordinary people who practiced the memory palace trick for six weeks more than doubled how many words they could remember.
London taxi drivers, who memorize about 25,000 streets, have a bigger memory region in their brains than most people.
Almost nobody can remember anything from before about age 3 or 4, even though babies learn at an incredible pace.
Shown 10,000 photos for a few seconds each, people later recognized most of them, a 1973 study found.
Walking through a doorway can make you forget why you came into the room, because your brain files the old room as a finished scene.
People who sleep after learning remember more than people who stay awake for the same amount of time.
When rats sleep, their brains replay the mazes they ran that day, often in fast-forward.
While you dream, most of your muscles are paralyzed, so you do not act out your dreams.
Some people wake up still paralyzed from dreaming and briefly feel a scary presence in the room, a common experience called sleep paralysis.
In 1964, a teenager named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about 11 days straight, a record watched by scientists.
You will spend about a third of your whole life asleep, roughly 25 years for a typical lifespan.
People who know they are dreaming can send signals to scientists from inside the dream by moving their eyes in a planned pattern.
In a 2021 study, scientists asked sleeping people simple math problems, and some answered correctly from inside their dreams.
Most dreams vanish from memory within minutes of waking, unless you write them down right away.
Holding a pen in your teeth to force a smile was famously said to make cartoons funnier, but a big 2016 retest found no effect.
People in a remote Papua New Guinea village with no contact with Western media recognized the same basic facial expressions of emotion as Americans.
Your brain can react with fear to an angry or scared face flashed so fast that you never consciously see it.
A woman known as S.M., whose fear centers were damaged, seems to feel almost no fear and walks up to snakes with curiosity.
People who lose their emotions through brain damage can still reason perfectly, yet struggle for ages to pick a date for an appointment.
Losing 100 dollars hurts roughly twice as much as winning 100 dollars feels good, studies suggest.
People given a free mug wanted about twice as much money to sell it as other people were willing to pay for it.

Once you know how something turned out, you tend to believe you saw it coming all along, even when you did not.
People value furniture they assembled themselves more than identical pieces built by others, a quirk called the IKEA effect.
A famous study found shoppers bought more jam when offered 6 flavors than 24, but later research found too much choice does not always backfire.
Students predicted they would finish their thesis in about 34 days; on average it took them 56.

Shark attacks and plane crashes feel more dangerous than they are, because dramatic stories are easier to remember.

Adding a deliberately bad third option can make people pick the pricier of two others, a trick menus and subscriptions use.
You tend to like things more just because you have seen them before, even if you do not remember seeing them.
You probably prefer your face in the mirror, while your friends prefer your face in photos: each likes the version they see most.
Students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt thought half the room noticed; in reality, only about a quarter did.

In the 1960s, about two thirds of ordinary people kept giving what they believed were dangerous electric shocks just because a scientist told them to.

People start favoring their own team even when the teams were picked by a coin toss.
Children who watched an adult punch an inflatable clown doll were much more likely to beat it up themselves.

Asking someone to do you a favor can make them like you more, a trick Benjamin Franklin used on a rival.
Many college students privately disliked heavy drinking but wrongly believed everyone else loved it.
Canned laughter really works: people rate the same jokes as funnier when they can hear other people laughing along.
Faces tend to look more attractive in a group photo than on their own, studies suggest.
You judge whether a stranger's face looks trustworthy in about a tenth of a second, and looking longer mostly just makes you more confident.
Humans can keep up about 150 meaningful relationships, according to a famous estimate based on brain size, though the number is debated.
Yawning is so contagious that just reading about yawns can make you yawn. Are you yawning yet?
You are about 30 times more likely to laugh when you are with other people than when you are alone.

Rocks hundreds of kilometers down may hold as much water as all the oceans, or more, locked inside their crystals.
Diamonds form about 150 km underground and shoot up to the surface in rare, extremely fast volcanic eruptions.
Most natural diamonds are 1 to 3.5 billion years old, so the diamond in a ring is often older than the first plants on land.
Tiny zircon crystals from Australia's Jack Hills are about 4.4 billion years old, the oldest known pieces of Earth.
The biggest gem diamond ever found, the Cullinan, weighed about 620 grams, more than a can of soup.
Australia digs up about 95 percent of the world's precious opal, much of it near outback towns where people live underground to escape the heat.
Emeralds and aquamarines are the same mineral; tiny traces of different metals make one green and the other sea blue.
Amethyst is plain quartz that turned purple thanks to a bit of iron and natural radiation in the ground.
Squeeze a quartz crystal and it makes a tiny bit of electricity, which is how quartz watches keep time.
Diamond is not just a bit harder than ruby: it is about four times harder, even though hardness scales put them side by side.
The softest mineral, talc, is so soft you can scratch it with your fingernail, and it was long the main ingredient in baby powder.
A cave in Mexico holds natural crystals up to about 12 m long, longer than a city bus.

Vietnam's Son Doong cave is so huge it has its own clouds and a forest growing inside where the roof fell in.
In 2010 a round sinkhole about 20 m wide and 90 m deep opened in Guatemala City, swallowing a three-story building.
A rare sandstone called itacolumite can bend like a thick rubber slab, because its grains are only loosely locked together.
The deepest known cave on Earth plunges more than 2 km below its entrance, about five Empire State Buildings stacked up.
Most caves are carved by rainwater that turned slightly acidic, like a very weak soda, dissolving limestone over ages.
A huge share of all the gold ever mined, perhaps a third or more, came from one region of South Africa, the Witwatersrand around Johannesburg.
As of 2023, all the gold ever mined in history would fit in a cube about 22 m on each side, about as tall as a seven-story building.
Most of Earth's gold probably sank into the core long ago; the gold we mine may have arrived later on meteorites.
In Iran's Zagros Mountains, salt squeezes up from deep underground and flows slowly downhill like a glacier made of salt.
Petrified wood is a tree turned to stone: minerals slowly replaced the wood bit by bit, so even its growth rings can still be seen.
In 2012 an undersea volcano near New Zealand made a floating raft of pumice rock bigger than a large city.
The tall rock spires of Utah's Bryce Canyon are carved mostly by ice, as water freezes and thaws in their cracks on about 200 days a year.
Opal flashes rainbow colors because it is packed with tiny, neatly stacked silica balls that split white light into colors.
The first compasses used lodestone, a rock that is naturally magnetic, possibly magnetized by lightning strikes.
When lightning hits sand, it can melt it into a hollow glass tube in a split second, a rock called a fulgurite.
As of 2024, scientists had named more than 6,000 kinds of minerals, and around 100 brand-new ones are recognized every year.
About two thirds of Earth's minerals may only exist because living things filled the air with oxygen.
Almost half of the rock in Earth's crust, by weight, is oxygen, locked inside the stone.
The most common mineral on Earth lies so deep that nobody had seen a natural sample until one turned up in a meteorite.
Some rocks in northern Canada are about 4 billion years old, formed when Earth was still a young planet.
Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo canyon is the deepest on Earth, plunging over 5 km in places, more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.
Given enough heat, pressure and millions of years, solid rock can bend and fold like ribbon candy.
The walls of the Grand Canyon show rocks spanning nearly 2 billion years of Earth's history.
In the Grand Canyon, one rock layer sits right on another over a billion years older; the time in between is simply missing.
The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon nearly 2 km deep in just the last 5 to 6 million years.
The Appalachian Mountains may once have been as tall as the Himalayas, before hundreds of millions of years of rain wore them down.
As mountains wear away, they slowly float back up, a bit like an iceberg rising as its top melts.
Parts of Scandinavia are still rising almost 1 cm a year, springing back after the weight of Ice Age glaciers melted away.
Mountains have roots: under the Himalayas the crust is about 70 km thick, roughly twice as thick as normal.
The Tibetan Plateau is so high that its average height, over 4,500 m, is nearly as tall as the highest peak in the Alps.
The San Andreas Fault creeps a few centimeters a year, so Los Angeles is slowly sliding toward San Francisco.
In 200 to 300 million years, the continents are expected to crash together again into a new supercontinent.
If you dropped Mount Everest into the deepest part of the ocean, its peak would still be more than 2 km underwater.

The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest dry land on Earth, more than 430 m below sea level, and it keeps dropping.
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface.
Lake Baikal is about 25 million years old, the oldest lake on Earth, and it is still slowly getting wider.
Australia's Lake Hillier is naturally bubblegum pink, colored by salt-loving algae and microbes, and its water stays pink even in a glass.
There are about 1,350 volcanoes on land that could erupt again, and many more hidden under the oceans.
Most of Earth's volcanic eruptions happen on the deep seafloor, where almost nobody ever sees them.
Runny Hawaiian lava is about 1,150 degrees C, hot enough to glow bright orange even in daylight.
In 1943 a volcano suddenly started in a Mexican farmer's cornfield and grew over 300 m tall within a year.
In 1963 a brand-new island called Surtsey rose out of the sea off Iceland during an eruption.
The blast from Krakatoa in 1883 sent a pressure wave that circled the entire planet several times.

When Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, its haze cooled the whole planet by about half a degree C for a year or so.
Yellowstone's last super-eruption, about 630,000 years ago, spread ash across much of what is now the United States.

Yellowstone's Steamboat Geyser, the tallest active geyser on Earth, can blast water over 90 m into the air.
Lava from Congo's Nyiragongo volcano is so runny that in 1977 it raced downhill at about 60 km/h.

Volcanoes can make their own lightning, as ash particles rub together and build up static electricity.

Flowing lava can crust over on top and keep running underneath, leaving behind tunnels big enough to walk through.
Avalanches of hot volcanic gas and rock can race down a mountainside at hundreds of km/h, far faster than anyone can run.
Volcanic ash is not soft like fireplace ash: it is made of tiny shards of sharp rock and glass.
In 2010 a fairly small eruption in Iceland shut down much of Europe's air travel for about six days.
The 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption threw its plume about 57 km high, the tallest ever measured, more than halfway to space.

At night, Indonesia's Kawah Ijen volcano glows with electric blue flames from burning sulfur gas.
Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai erupts black lava that turns white within days, and at about 500 degrees C it is the coolest lava known.
Much of the air and water on early Earth probably came bubbling out of volcanoes.
About 90 percent of the world's earthquakes and 75 percent of its active volcanoes ring the Pacific Ocean, in the Ring of Fire.
Iceland gets nearly all of its home heating from hot water and steam rising from the ground.
Instruments around the world pick up about 55 earthquakes every day, and many more are too small to notice.
Each step up the earthquake scale means about 32 times more energy, so a magnitude 9 is about 1,000 times stronger than a 7.
The biggest earthquake ever recorded struck Chile in 1960, with a magnitude of about 9.5.
The 2011 earthquake in Japan moved part of the country's coast about 5 m to the east in a few minutes.
The 2011 earthquake in Japan sped up Earth's spin, shortening the day by about 1.8 millionths of a second.
During the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake, the ground ripped open along about 1,300 km, and the shaking lasted around 8 to 10 minutes.
During huge earthquakes in Missouri in 1811 and 1812, parts of the Mississippi River briefly seemed to flow backward.
People have reported strange glowing lights in the sky during some earthquakes, and scientists still debate what causes them.
Some earthquakes happen in slow motion, slipping over days or weeks so gently that no one feels a thing.
People can cause earthquakes too: filling giant reservoirs and pumping wastewater underground have both triggered quakes.
Strong shaking can turn wet, sandy ground into something like quicksand, letting whole buildings tip over.
The first waves from an earthquake rush through rock at about 6 km per second, more than 15 times faster than sound in air.
Earthquake alerts on phones can arrive seconds before the shaking does, because radio signals travel faster than shaking ground.
After a giant earthquake, the whole planet rings like a bell for days, vibrating too slowly for anyone to hear.

The 1964 Alaska earthquake lifted some ground about 11 m and made water slosh in swimming pools as far away as Texas.
The 2011 earthquake in Japan made the water in fjords in Norway slosh back and forth, about 8,000 km away.
The 2011 tsunami from Japan broke icebergs off an Antarctic ice shelf about 13,000 km away.
In the open ocean a tsunami can travel at around 800 km/h, as fast as a jet plane.

Just before a tsunami arrives, the sea can suddenly pull back and expose the seafloor, a warning to run for high ground.

Some buildings sit on giant rubber pads, so during an earthquake the ground shakes beneath while the building barely moves.
Mount Vesuvius has erupted many times since it buried Pompeii, and about 3 million people now live in its shadow.

When volcanoes erupt beneath Iceland's glaciers, melted ice can burst out in sudden floods that sweep away roads and bridges.
Volcanic eruptions can launch rocks the size of cars, called volcanic bombs, that twist into shape as they fly.
Some volcanoes have lakes of boiling lava inside their craters that bubble for years or even decades.
A volcano can stay quiet for centuries and still be active: Vesuvius looked like a green, peaceful mountain before 79 AD.
If Earth's surface were smoothed perfectly flat, the oceans would cover the whole planet about 2.7 km deep.
The ocean holds about 97 percent of Earth's water; less than 1 percent is fresh water people can easily get to.
If all the salt in the oceans were spread over the land, it would make a layer over 150 m thick, as tall as a 40-story building.
Below about 1,000 m, the ocean is completely dark: no sunlight ever reaches most of the water on Earth.
The oceans have soaked up about 90 percent of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases in recent decades.
The Atlantic Ocean is saltier than the Pacific, partly because winds carry water evaporated from it over Central America to the Pacific.

In Canada's Bay of Fundy the tide rises and falls up to about 16 m, the height of a five-story building, twice a day.

The Moon's pull lifts not just the oceans but the solid ground: the land under you rises and falls by up to about 30 cm every day.

Hundreds of millions of years ago a day lasted only about 22 hours, because Earth spun faster back then.

Swells from storms near Antarctica can travel over 10,000 km across the Pacific before breaking on the shores of Alaska.
Ocean waves do not carry water across the sea: each bit of water mostly moves in a circle as the wave's energy passes through.

A special layer of the ocean traps sound so well that a noise made in it can be heard thousands of kilometers away.

The deep seafloor has lakes of extra-salty water so heavy they sit on the bottom with their own shorelines and waves.
The biggest waterfall on Earth is hidden underwater between Greenland and Iceland, where cold water plunges about 3.5 km.

Seawater has become about 30 percent more acidic since the 1800s, as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.
The Amazon River pours about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

A water molecule that evaporates stays in the sky for only about 9 days on average before falling back as rain or snow.

The Mediterranean Sea almost completely dried up about 6 million years ago, leaving a deep salty basin.

The Red Sea is a baby ocean: Africa and Arabia are pulling apart, and it widens by about a centimeter a year.

Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 40 to 50 times every second, over a billion flashes a year.
A bolt of lightning heats the air to around 30,000 degrees C, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Thunder is the sound of air exploding outward after lightning heats it in a split second.

Hail falls mostly in spring and summer, not winter, because only warm-weather thunderstorms have updrafts strong enough to hold it up.
At any given moment, nearly 2,000 thunderstorms are rumbling somewhere on Earth.
Ball lightning, glowing orbs that drift through the air during storms, has been reported for centuries and is still not understood.

Rocks in Death Valley slide across the desert floor on their own, pushed by wind on thin sheets of ice, leaving long trails.
The puddle you see on a hot road is a mirage: hot air near the ground bends light from the sky toward your eyes.
Namibia's Namib is thought to be the oldest desert on Earth, dry for tens of millions of years.
Ethiopia's Danakil Depression is one of the hottest places on Earth, with bright yellow and green pools of acid and salt.
Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat on Earth and so flat that it is used to check satellite measurements.

If you stand on the equator, Earth's spin is carrying you east at about 1,670 km/h, faster than a passenger jet.
Earth races around the Sun at about 107,000 km/h, so you travel roughly 2.5 million km every day without leaving your chair.
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of northern winter: seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance.
Earth actually turns once in about 23 hours and 56 minutes; the extra 4 minutes of a day come from our trip around the Sun.
Melting polar ice is moving water toward the equator, which is making Earth's days very slightly longer.
Pumping huge amounts of groundwater shifted Earth's spin axis by about 80 cm between 1993 and 2010.
China's Three Gorges Dam holds so much water that it slows Earth's spin by a tiny fraction of a millionth of a second each day.
Earth's geographic poles do not stay put: they wander in a small loop a few meters wide every year or so.
Thousands of tonnes of space dust fall onto Earth every year, so a little of the dust in your home may come from space.
Earth leaks about 90 tonnes of gas into space every day, mostly light hydrogen and helium escaping from the top of the air.
Arizona's Meteor Crater, over 1 km wide, was blasted out about 50,000 years ago by an iron meteorite only about 50 m across.

South Africa's Vredefort crater is about 2 billion years old and was probably around 300 km wide, the largest confirmed on Earth.
More meteorites are found in Antarctica than anywhere else, because dark rocks are easy to spot on white ice.
Some meteorites found on Earth are chunks of Mars and the Moon, knocked loose by giant impacts and sent flying to us.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country, about 243,000 km, enough to wrap around the equator about six times.
The Hawaiian islands were built one by one as the seafloor slid over a fixed hot spot, like a conveyor belt over a blowtorch.
A sharp bend in the chain of undersea Hawaiian volcanoes shows that the Pacific seafloor changed direction about 47 million years ago.
Scientists say there is an eighth continent, Zealandia, but about 94 percent of it is underwater, with New Zealand sticking out.
In 2015 a new island appeared in Tonga between two old ones; in 2022 the same volcano blew most of it away.
Australia's Finke River may be the oldest river on Earth, following roughly the same path for hundreds of millions of years.
Some rivers cut right through mountain ranges because the river was there first and kept carving as the mountains rose.
The Congo River is the deepest river on Earth, plunging more than 200 m deep in places.
In Brazil, the dark Rio Negro and the sandy Amazon meet and flow side by side for kilometers without mixing.
In the Philippines, a river flows about 8 km through a cave under a mountain, and boats can paddle into it.

The spray from Victoria Falls in Africa rises so high that it can be seen from tens of kilometers away.
In Antarctica, a waterfall called Blood Falls pours out bright red, stained by iron-rich salty water rusting in the air.
Behind a small waterfall in New York State, a natural gas leak keeps a little flame burning, called Eternal Flame Falls.
In Turkmenistan, a gas-filled crater nicknamed the Door to Hell has been burning since about 1971.
A coal fire has been burning under the town of Centralia, Pennsylvania, since 1962, and most residents moved away.
In Australia a coal seam deep underground has been burning for roughly 6,000 years, the oldest known fire on Earth.
At Pamukkale in Turkey, hot spring water has built bright white terraces of stone that look like frozen waterfalls.
Northern Ireland's Giant's Causeway is made of about 40,000 stone columns, many with six sides, formed by cooling lava.
China's Rainbow Mountains are striped in red, yellow and orange by layers of minerals in the rock.
The Eye of the Sahara is a ring-shaped rock structure about 40 km wide, so large that astronauts use it as a landmark.
Utah's Arches National Park has more than 2,000 natural stone arches, carved by water, ice and wind.
China's deepest sinkhole, Xiaozhai Tiankeng, plunges about 660 m, deep enough to swallow most skyscrapers.
Belize's Great Blue Hole was once a dry cave; it flooded when sea levels rose after the last Ice Age.
Azerbaijan has hundreds of mud volcanoes that burp up cold mud and gas, more than any other country.
In Indonesia, a mud volcano named Lusi started erupting in 2006 and buried whole villages in mud.
Some clays in Norway and Canada can suddenly turn from solid ground into a liquid, letting whole hillsides flow away.
Mount Kilimanjaro sits only about 330 km from the equator, yet its summit has glaciers and snow.
In 2020, China and Nepal agreed that Mount Everest is 8,848.86 m tall, a bit higher than the old official number.

Canada's Mount Thor has a cliff that drops about 1,250 m, the greatest straight vertical drop of any cliff on Earth.
Mountains make their own deserts: air dumps its rain on one side, leaving the far side dry, an effect called a rain shadow.
Tanzania's Lake Natron is so salty and alkaline that birds that die in it can end up crusted in minerals, like chalky statues.
Most of Earth's carbon is not in the air or in living things but locked inside rocks like limestone.
The deepest point of land on Earth is hidden under Antarctic ice: the rock beneath Denman Glacier lies about 3.5 km below sea level.
Earth is the only planet we know of where the surface is broken into moving plates.
Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, thanks to its big heavy metal core.
The deeper you dig, the hotter it gets: rock typically warms by about 25 to 30 degrees C for every kilometer down.
In South Africa's deepest gold mines, about 4 km down, the rock is so hot that miners rely on ice slurry to cool the tunnels.
Peru has a river hot enough to scald, with stretches of water around 90 degrees C, heated by underground hot water.
Canada's Spotted Lake turns into hundreds of colorful pools each summer as its water dries up and leaves minerals behind.
Hawaii has a green sand beach, colored by tiny crystals of a mineral called olivine washed out of a volcanic cone.
Black sand beaches are made of volcanic rock and glass, broken down by waves crashing on lava.
Snow has fallen in the Sahara Desert several times in recent years, dusting orange dunes with white.
On calm, freezing rivers, ice can form giant spinning disks called ice circles that slowly rotate in the current.

On very cold nights, glittering ice crystals can float in clear air, a sight called diamond dust.

Common world maps make Greenland look about as big as Africa, but Africa is really about 14 times larger.
Fresh snow reflects up to about 90 percent of sunlight, which is why it can cause sunburn and snow blindness.
Cities can be several degrees warmer than the countryside at night, because concrete and asphalt soak up and slowly release heat.
On cold, still nights, sound can carry much farther, because a layer of warm air above bends it back down to the ground.

Rivers of water vapor flowing through the sky, called atmospheric rivers, can carry many times the flow of the Mississippi River.
A five-day weather forecast is now right about 90 percent of the time, much better than a few decades ago.
The idea of the butterfly effect came from weather: a meteorologist found that tiny changes in his model led to completely different forecasts.
The Moon probably formed when a planet about the size of Mars smashed into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
Earth is the only planet in our solar system not named after a Greek or Roman god; its name comes from old words for the ground.
Australia is wider than the Moon: it stretches about 4,000 km from east to west, while the Moon is about 3,500 km across.

Lumps of metal on the deep seafloor grow so slowly that they add only a few millimeters every million years.

In 1929 a giant underwater avalanche off Canada raced down the seafloor and snapped transatlantic telegraph cables one after another.
Mount Everest is on the move, drifting a few centimeters northeast every year as India keeps pushing into Asia.
Geologists count ice as a mineral, so a glacier is technically a giant river of moving rock.
The shape of a snowflake depends on the temperature: around minus 5 degrees C they grow as needles, around minus 15 as flat stars.
It takes about a million tiny cloud droplets clumping together to build just one ordinary raindrop.
Clouds need specks of dust, sea salt or smoke to form around; without them water vapor would struggle to make droplets.
Tornadoes have touched down on every continent except Antarctica, even in places like England and New Zealand.
Weather scientists fly airplanes straight into hurricanes on purpose to measure them from the inside.
Most lightning flashes over land, even though oceans cover most of the planet, because land heats up faster and builds stronger storms.

Wind can shove sheets of lake ice onto the shore, piling up walls of broken ice several meters tall.
Thin lake ice can make eerie sci-fi sounds, like laser guns in a space movie, when it cracks or someone skates on it.
In Canada's Abraham Lake, bubbles of gas freeze into stacks of white disks trapped in clear blue ice.
The mantle makes up about 84 percent of Earth's volume, far more than the crust and core put together.

Earth's inner core grows by roughly a millimeter a year as the liquid metal around it slowly freezes.
A weak spot in Earth's magnetic field over the South Atlantic lets space radiation through, glitching satellites that pass over it.
A flip of Earth's magnetic field does not happen overnight; it takes hundreds to thousands of years.
The seafloor is striped like a barcode by rocks that froze while Earth's magnetic field pointed different ways, a key clue that continents move.
When Alfred Wegener said in 1912 that continents drift, many geologists scoffed; the proof came about 50 years later.
South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces, because they were once joined.
Rocks in the mountains of Scotland match rocks in North America's Appalachians, because they were once one mountain range.
Some earthquakes start as deep as about 700 km inside Earth, where rock is hot and squeezed.
Some glaciers suddenly surge, flowing up to about 100 times faster than normal for months.

Antarctica's Mount Erebus has a lake of lava inside its crater and puffs out tiny specks of gold in its gas.

At the end of the last Ice Age, a lake in Montana burst its ice dam many times, unleashing floods ten times the flow of every river on Earth.
The English Channel was partly carved by giant floods that burst out of a glacial lake about 450,000 years ago.
On average, Earth's land stands only about 840 m above sea level, while the average ocean is more than four times deeper.
The Bermuda Triangle has no more shipwrecks or plane crashes than other busy stretches of ocean, according to insurers and the US Coast Guard.
Every bit of seafloor eventually gets recycled back into the planet, like a giant conveyor belt that takes about 200 million years.
A grain of beach sand may be millions of years old, worn down from rocks that were once part of mountains.
Wind-blown dust has piled up in China's Loess Plateau in layers up to about 300 m thick.
Nature can take a few hundred years or more to make just 1 cm of new soil, but a single storm can wash it away.
Crack open a plain-looking round rock called a geode and you may find a hollow lined with sparkling crystals.
A single crystal of beryl found in Madagascar was about 18 m long and weighed roughly 380 tonnes.
Jade is not one stone but two different minerals that look alike, and for centuries no one could tell them apart.
The blue-violet gem tanzanite has been found in only one small area on Earth, near Mount Kilimanjaro.
The gem alexandrite looks green in daylight and turns red under lamplight, like two gems in one.
Some minerals glow in bright colors under ultraviolet light; the mineral fluorite gave its name to the word fluorescence.
Tiny droplets of mercury, a metal that is liquid at room temperature, can be found naturally inside some rocks.

Cut and polish an iron meteorite and it shows a crisscross pattern that can only form by cooling over millions of years in space.
In Libya's desert lie chunks of yellow natural glass, and a piece of it was carved into a jewel on Tutankhamun's necklace.
Moldavite is a green glass gem formed about 15 million years ago when a meteorite impact melted rock and flung it far away.
Hurricanes need ocean water of about 26 degrees C or warmer, and they quickly weaken once they move over land.
In foggy deserts like Chile's coast, people catch drinking water with big nets that comb droplets out of the fog.
Arica in northern Chile averages less than 1 mm of rain a year, one of the driest cities on Earth.
The saying red sky at night, sailor's delight has some truth: in many places weather moves from west to east.
Cloud droplets can stay liquid down to about minus 40 degrees C if there is nothing for them to freeze onto.
Outside the tropics, most rain starts out as snow high in the clouds and melts on the way down.
In 2023 the sea off southern Florida reached about 38 degrees C, as warm as a hot tub, one of the hottest ocean readings ever.
Twin satellites can weigh melting ice and shrinking underground water from space by measuring tiny changes in Earth's gravity.
Parts of Mexico City are sinking by up to about 50 cm a year, because water is pumped out of the ground beneath it.
During storms, wind can push Lake Erie's water so hard that one end rises several meters higher than the other.
Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are joined by a wide strait at the same water level, so technically they are one giant lake.
Storms on Lake Superior can whip up waves taller than 8 m, as big as many ocean waves.
Cold winds crossing the warmer Great Lakes can dump more than a meter of snow on towns downwind in a day or two.
Oregon's Crater Lake fills the hole left by a volcano that collapsed about 7,700 years ago, and its water comes almost only from rain and snow.
Under Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula lie flooded cave systems hundreds of kilometers long, entered through water-filled sinkholes.
Nevada's Fly Geyser was accidentally created when a well was drilled in 1964, and minerals have built it into a colorful mound.
Iceland's Strokkur geyser erupts every few minutes, shooting boiling water about 20 m into the air.
Every geyser in the world is named after Geysir in Iceland, whose name comes from an old word meaning to gush.
The Andes run about 7,000 km down South America, the longest mountain range on any continent.
The Alps were pushed up as Africa slowly crashed into Europe, and the collision is still going on.
The ocean floor is dotted with tens of thousands of underwater mountains taller than 1 km, most of them never visited.
Ice cores from Greenland show that the climate has sometimes jumped by several degrees in just a few decades.
If Earth's 4.5 billion year history were squeezed into one day, humans would show up only in the last few seconds before midnight.
Borneo's Sarawak Chamber is one of the largest cave rooms on Earth, big enough to hold dozens of jumbo jets.
Dripping water in caves can roll tiny grains into smooth round stones called cave pearls.
Austria's Eisriesenwelt is the largest known ice cave, with frozen passages running for about 42 km inside a mountain.
Hawaii's Kazumura Cave is a tunnel left by flowing lava, running about 65 km, the longest lava tube known.
Near the equator lies a belt of calm, sticky air called the doldrums, where sailing ships could be stuck for weeks.
Trade winds were named after an old English word for a steady path, not for commerce, though they did carry sailing ships across the Atlantic.
Italy's Stromboli volcano has been erupting almost nonstop for thousands of years, earning the name Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.
Hawaii's Kilauea volcano erupted almost continuously for 35 years, from 1983 to 2018.
On any given day, around 40 to 50 volcanoes are erupting somewhere on Earth, most of them far from any city.
When Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, its top collapsed in the biggest landslide ever recorded, and the mountain lost about 400 m of height.
Yellowstone is not overdue for a giant eruption: volcanoes do not erupt on a schedule, and scientists see no sign of one coming.
There is no such thing as earthquake weather: earthquakes start kilometers underground, where weather cannot reach.
California will not fall into the ocean: along the San Andreas Fault the land slides sideways, not down into the sea.
The Pacific Ocean is so big that all of Earth's land could fit inside it, with room to spare.
In 2021 National Geographic began recognizing a fifth ocean, the Southern Ocean, swirling around Antarctica.
The Sargasso Sea is the only sea with no coastline; its edges are drawn only by ocean currents.
The salt in the sea comes from rocks: rain slowly dissolves minerals on land, and rivers carry them to the ocean.
Foam cups sent to the deep sea come back shrunk to the size of thimbles, crushed by the weight of the water.
Earth weighs about 6,000 billion billion tonnes, roughly 80 times as much as the Moon.
Earth is not a perfect sphere or even a smooth one: gravity makes its true shape lumpy, more like a slightly squashed potato.
Most tornadoes in the north spin counterclockwise, but a small number twist the other way.
Ojos del Salado on the border of Chile and Argentina is the highest volcano on Earth, rising nearly 6,900 m.
Glacier-fed lakes like Canada's Lake Louise glow turquoise because of rock flour, stone ground as fine as dust by moving ice.
The North Pole sits on floating sea ice over an ocean about 4 km deep, while the South Pole sits on ice nearly 3 km thick over land.
At the poles the Sun rises and sets just once a year, giving about six months of daylight followed by six months of night.

ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers, weighed about 30 tons and filled a room with roughly 17,000 glowing vacuum tubes.
ENIAC's first programmers were six women who had no manuals, so they taught themselves from the machine's wiring diagrams.
Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program in 1843, for a machine that was never actually built.
In 1991 a London museum finally built a calculating machine Charles Babbage designed in the 1840s. It worked perfectly, about 150 years late.
A shipwreck off Greece held a 2,000-year-old bronze gadget full of gears that predicted eclipses. It is called the oldest known computer.
Britain's wartime codebreaking computer Colossus was so secret that most of the machines were destroyed after the war, and the world only learned of it in the 1970s.
Long before machines, "computer" was a job title: rooms full of people, often women, were paid to do calculations by hand.
Some early computers stored their memory as sound waves bouncing back and forth inside tubes of liquid mercury.
The software that flew Apollo to the Moon was woven by hand: workers threaded wires through tiny magnetic rings to spell out the 1s and 0s.
The computer that landed Apollo 11 on the Moon had less memory than a single photo on your phone.
During the Apollo 11 landing the computer kept flashing overload alarms, but its clever software ignored minor jobs and kept landing.
Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote the Apollo Moon software; a famous photo shows her next to a stack of printed code as tall as she is.
IBM's first hard drive, from 1956, weighed about a ton and held about 5 million characters, less than a single song on your phone today.
In 2009 a South African company raced a carrier pigeon against its slow internet. The pigeon flew a memory card 80 km and arrived long before the upload finished.
Grace Hopper handed out pieces of wire about 30 cm long to show how far light travels in one billionth of a second.
In 1947 engineers found a real moth stuck in a computer and taped it in their logbook as a joke, because "bug" already meant a glitch.
Thomas Edison was already calling glitches in his inventions "bugs" in the 1870s, long before computers existed.
The Harvard Mark I computer of 1944 was about 51 feet long and contained roughly 500 miles of wire.
Some banks and governments still run on COBOL, a programming language older than the Moon landing. In 2020 New Jersey begged for volunteers who knew it.
The Y2K scare happened because early programmers saved precious memory by writing years with two digits, so 2000 could look like 1900.
Fixing the Y2K bug before the year 2000 cost an estimated $300 billion or more around the world.
Many computers count time in seconds since 1970, and older ones will run out of numbers on January 19, 2038, a problem nicknamed Y2K38.
When computer clocks hit 1,234,567,890 seconds since 1970, on February 13, 2009, programmers around the world threw parties to watch.
In one 1968 demo, Douglas Engelbart showed the mouse, clickable links, windows and video calls, decades before most people had a computer.
The first computer mouse was a carved wooden box with two metal wheels underneath and a single button on top.
Xerox built a computer with a mouse, windows and icons in 1973, more than ten years before the Macintosh made the idea famous.
After visiting Xerox's lab in 1979, Steve Jobs was so inspired by its mouse and windows that Apple built them into its next computers.
The Apple I sold in 1976 for $666.66 as a bare circuit board. You had to bring your own case, keyboard and screen.
Time magazine skipped its usual Person of the Year for 1982 and named the computer its "Machine of the Year" instead.
Apple's very first logo was not an apple shape but a detailed drawing of Isaac Newton sitting under an apple tree.
Apple's third co-founder, Ronald Wayne, sold his 10 percent share of the company in 1976 for $800. It later became worth billions.
Microsoft was born in 1975 in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and only moved to the Seattle area a few years later.
The system that launched Microsoft's empire, MS-DOS, began life as QDOS, short for "Quick and Dirty Operating System".
The first IBM PC, in 1981, came with about 16 kilobytes of memory. A cheap phone today has hundreds of thousands of times more.
The first microprocessor, Intel's 4004 from 1971, was made for a Japanese calculator and had about 2,300 tiny switches on it.
Nvidia's Blackwell AI chip, announced in 2024, packs about 208 billion tiny switches onto a piece of silicon you could hold in your palm.
The first transistor, built in 1947, was a clunky hand-made gadget of gold foil, a plastic wedge and a chunk of germanium.
Transistors are the most-produced human-made thing ever: an estimated 13 sextillion had been made by 2018.
The machines that make the most advanced computer chips are so big that each one ships in dozens of containers on several cargo planes.
Top chipmaking machines make their light by blasting tiny drops of molten tin with a laser 50,000 times a second, hotter than the Sun's surface.
The silicon in computer chips is purified until only about one atom in a billion is something else.
The garage in Palo Alto where Hewlett-Packard started in 1939 is now an official California historical landmark.
One of Hewlett-Packard's first customers was Walt Disney, which bought eight of their sound gadgets to make the movie Fantasia.
The Cray-1 supercomputer of 1976 was shaped like a C to keep its wires short, and its padded base doubled as a bench to sit on.
In 2006 Time magazine named "You" its Person of the Year, for everyone making things online, and put a shiny mirror-like panel on the cover.
Garry Kasparov actually beat IBM's Deep Blue in their first match in 1996. The computer only won the rematch a year later.
An old Mac alert sound was named "Sosumi", read "so sue me", a joke about the Beatles' record label Apple Corps suing Apple over its name.
AlphaGo once made a move so strange that experts thought it was a blunder. It turned out to be brilliant, and helped it win.
Lee Sedol, the best Go player of his era, retired in 2019, saying AI was something that "cannot be defeated".
When IBM's Watson won Jeopardy! in 2011, it famously answered "Toronto" to a question in the category "U.S. Cities".
In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a simple test for machine intelligence: can a computer chat so well that you can't tell it isn't human?
ELIZA, a very simple 1966 chatbot, just turned your words into questions, yet some people opened their hearts to it like a therapist.
In 1955, scientists proposed that about 10 researchers could make big progress on artificial intelligence in a single summer.
Science fiction writer Isaac Asimov invented the word "robotics" in a short story in 1941, two decades before the first factory robot went to work.
The first factory robot started work at a General Motors plant in 1961, doing a dangerous job: lifting hot pieces of freshly cast metal.
NASA's Curiosity rover sang "Happy Birthday" to itself on Mars in 2013 by vibrating one of its instruments at different notes.
When Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone in 2007, the name iPhone belonged to Cisco, which sued Apple the very next day. They soon agreed to share it.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has only about 70 KB of memory, less than one small photo, and still sends data from beyond the planets.
In 2024 NASA fixed a glitch on Voyager 1 from about 15 billion miles away by moving its software around a broken memory chip.
The first message ever sent over the early internet, in 1969, was supposed to be "LOGIN". The system crashed after "LO".
The inventor of email picked the @ sign for addresses in 1971 mostly because almost nobody used it for anything else.
A copy of the very first website, made by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991, can still be visited today at its original address, info.cern.ch.
When Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989, his boss scribbled on it: "Vague but exciting".
CERN gave the World Wide Web away for free in 1993. Nobody ever paid to use it, and nobody collected royalties.
The very first web server had a handwritten sticker warning "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!" so nobody switched off the web.
The first webcam pointed at a coffee pot in a Cambridge lab, so scientists could see if it was empty before making the trip to fetch a cup.
Nintendo Switch game cards taste horribly bitter on purpose. They are coated with a harmless chemical so children won't swallow them.
The first spam email was sent in 1978 to about 400 people on the early internet, advertising a new computer. People complained right away.
Junk email is called "spam" because of a Monty Python sketch where Vikings keep singing "Spam" until nobody can hear anything else.
The first item ever sold on eBay, in 1995, was a broken laser pointer. It went for $14.83 to a man who collected broken laser pointers.
In Japan, the PlayStation's circle button long meant yes and the X button meant no, the exact opposite of how most of the world used them.
Jeff Bezos first wanted to call Amazon "Cadabra", until his lawyer misheard it as "cadaver". He also considered calling it Relentless.
Before it was called Google, the search engine run by two Stanford students had a far less catchy name: BackRub.
Google's very first computer storage was housed in a homemade case built from Lego bricks.
In 1999 the search company Excite reportedly turned down a chance to buy Google for $750,000.
The first YouTube video, "Me at the zoo", is just 19 seconds long and shows a co-founder standing in front of elephants.
YouTube's founders have said the site began as an idea for a video dating website.
As of 2022, more than 500 hours of video were uploaded to YouTube every single minute.
The first tweet ever, "just setting up my twttr", sold as a digital collectible for about $2.9 million in 2021.
Twitter was first called "twttr", without vowels, because that was trendy for websites at the time.
The first text message ever sent, in 1992, said "Merry Christmas". It was typed on a computer because phones could not type yet.
The first emoji set, 176 tiny pictures made in Japan in 1999, is now part of the collection of New York's Museum of Modern Art.
When the hashtag was first suggested in 2007, Twitter reportedly told its inventor it was "for nerds" and would never catch on.
The first banner ad, in 1994, was clicked by an astonishing 44 percent of people who saw it. Today most ads get far under 1 percent.
The first .com web address ever registered was symbolics.com, in 1985, years before the World Wide Web existed.
About 99 percent of data crossing oceans travels through cables on the seabed, not through satellites.
Deep-sea internet cables can be about as thick as a garden hose, yet they carry data between whole continents.
Sharks have been filmed biting undersea internet cables, but ship anchors and fishing nets cause far more damage.
In 2011 a 75-year-old woman digging for scrap copper in Georgia cut a cable and knocked most of neighboring Armenia offline for hours.
In 2016 an accidental email to all of the NHS's roughly 840,000 staff started a "reply all" storm that jammed its email system.
CAPTCHA, the "prove you are human" test, stands for "Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart".
Typing squiggly CAPTCHA words once helped digitize old books and newspapers, because each word was one a computer could not read.
QR codes were invented in 1994 by a company in the Toyota group to keep track of car parts in factories.
The inventor of the QR code said the black and white stones of the board game Go helped inspire its design.
Wi-Fi owes part of its invention to Australian astronomers who were searching the sky for tiny exploding black holes.
Hollywood star Hedy Lamarr co-invented a radio "frequency hopping" system in 1942 to stop enemies jamming torpedoes, inspired partly by player pianos.
The first home video game console, the Magnavox Odyssey of 1972, came with plastic sheets you stuck on your TV because it couldn't draw backgrounds.
Wi-Fi doesn't actually stand for anything. A branding company made up the name as a catchy pun on "hi-fi".
Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a Viking king, and its logo combines his initials in ancient runes.
The first photo ever posted on the web, in 1992, showed a comedy pop band made up of women who worked at CERN.
One of the first secure online purchases ever, in 1994, was a Sting CD sold for $12.48 plus shipping.
Pizza Hut let people order pizza online in 1994 through a site called PizzaNet, back when few homes even had internet.
When an artist turned English Wikipedia into books in 2015, it came to more than 7,400 volumes of about 700 pages each.
In 2025 the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine passed one trillion saved web pages.
Google has said about 15 percent of the searches it sees every day have never been typed before.
Facebook's "Like" button was almost called the "Awesome" button, the name its creators used while building it.
Facebook is blue because Mark Zuckerberg is red-green colorblind, and blue is the color he sees best.
Instagram started as a check-in app called Burbn, and it had just 13 employees when Facebook bought it for $1 billion in 2012.
The first book ever sold on Amazon, in 1995, was a thick science title called Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies.
WhatsApp's co-founder signed the $19 billion sale at the door of the welfare office where he once lined up for food stamps.
WhatsApp co-founder Brian Acton was turned down for jobs at both Twitter and Facebook in 2009. Facebook later paid billions for his app.
In 2000 Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million. Blockbuster said no; it later went bust while Netflix boomed.
Netflix started out mailing DVDs in red envelopes, and it only sent its very last DVD in September 2023.
The screeching of a dial-up modem was two machines testing the phone line and agreeing how fast they could talk.
AOL's marketing chief once said that, at its peak, half of all CDs made in the world carried an AOL free trial.
The very first web browser could also edit pages, because its inventor wanted everyone to write the web, not just read it.
Undersea internet cables add up to about 1.4 million km, enough to wrap around the Earth about 35 times.
After watching the 1983 hacker movie WarGames, President Reagan asked his generals if it could really happen. It led to new US computer security rules.
Email is about 20 years older than the World Wide Web: people were emailing in 1971, and the web arrived in 1991.
In 2024, automated bots made up just over half of all traffic on the web, according to the security company Imperva.
By 2019 Google's Street View cars had driven over 10 million miles, about 400 trips around the Earth.
Google mapped part of the Arabian desert for Street View by strapping a camera to a camel.
In the Faroe Islands, locals strapped cameras to sheep to get Google to map their islands, calling it "Sheep View".
Google's homepage was so bare at first partly because, as Sergey Brin joked, they didn't have a webmaster and he didn't do HTML.
The first Google Doodle, in 1998, was a stick figure telling visitors the founders had gone to the Burning Man festival.
Gmail launched on April 1, 2004 with a huge 1 GB of free storage, so many people thought it was an April Fools' joke.
The tiny Pacific nation of Tuvalu owns the .tv web ending, and renting it out brings in a big share of its government's money.
The AI boom made the small Caribbean island of Anguilla rich in web money: it owns the .ai address ending.
As of 2024, about 5.5 billion people use the internet, roughly two-thirds of everyone on Earth.
Web cookies were invented in 1994 and named after "magic cookies", an old programmer's term for a little token passed between programs.
The programmer who wrote the code for the first pop-up ad, back in the 1990s, publicly said sorry for it in 2014.
The sideways smiley :-) was proposed in 1982 by a professor who wanted a way to mark jokes on an online message board.
The website for the 1996 movie Space Jam stayed online, almost untouched, for about 25 years.
On April Fools' Day 2008, YouTube rickrolled the whole world: every featured video on its homepage led to "Never Gonna Give You Up".
As of 2024, the "Baby Shark Dance" video has more YouTube views than there are people on Earth.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, more than 130 years ago, to make hand-painted playing cards.
In the 1960s Nintendo tried running a taxi company and selling instant rice before it found success with toys and games.
Mario's first name was Jumpman. He got the name Mario in the early 1980s, reportedly after the landlord of Nintendo's US warehouse.
Mario has a mustache and a cap because the tiny pixel graphics of 1981 couldn't draw a mouth or hair that looked right.
Before Mario became the world's most famous plumber, he started out in Donkey Kong as a carpenter.
Pac-Man's name comes from "paku paku", the Japanese sound for munching with your mouth opening and closing.
Pac-Man's creator said the character's shape was partly inspired by a pizza with one slice missing.
Each Pac-Man ghost hunts differently: the red one chases you, the pink one tries to get ahead of you, and the orange one wanders.
The highest possible Pac-Man score is 3,333,360, because level 256 turns into scrambled garbage that can't be finished.
Pac-Man's creator designed it partly to attract women to arcades, which were then full of shooting games.
Tetris was created in 1984 by a scientist at a Soviet research lab in Moscow, and he didn't earn money from it for about 12 years.
In 2023 a 13-year-old became the first person to "beat" the original Nintendo Tetris, by playing so far that the game crashed.
After playing Tetris for hours, many people see falling blocks when they close their eyes. Scientists call it the Tetris effect.
The famous Tetris music is based on "Korobeiniki", a Russian folk song from the 1800s about a peddler.
A Game Boy that was badly burned in a bombing during the Gulf War still works, and is on display at Nintendo's New York store.
Space Invaders' aliens speed up as you shoot them because the computer had fewer to draw. The designer liked it, so it stayed.
The first Pong arcade machine, tested in a bar in 1972, "broke" within days. It was just jammed full of quarters.
One of the very first video games, Tennis for Two in 1958, was played on a lab instrument screen at a science open day.
Atari really did bury truckloads of unsold E.T. game cartridges in a New Mexico landfill. Diggers found them in 2014.
The infamous Atari E.T. video game was made in about five weeks to be ready for Christmas 1982.
Minecraft is the best-selling video game ever, with more than 300 million copies sold as of 2023.
Minecraft began as a one-person project, and in 2014 Microsoft bought it for $2.5 billion.
A full Minecraft world is about seven times bigger than the surface of the entire Earth.
Minecraft's exploding Creeper was born from a coding mistake: its creator mixed up the height and length while building a pig.
The Legend of Zelda was inspired by its creator's childhood adventures exploring caves, lakes and forests around Kyoto.
In The Legend of Zelda, Zelda is the princess. The green-clad hero you play is called Link.
Sonic the Hedgehog's shoes were inspired by Michael Jackson's boots and the red and white of Santa Claus.
Pokemon was inspired by its creator's childhood hobby of collecting bugs in the fields around his home in Japan.
Pokemon is the highest-earning media franchise in the world, ahead of Star Wars and Mickey Mouse.
Pikachu's name combines "pika", the Japanese sound of a spark, and "chu", the sound a mouse makes.
In 1997 a Pokemon cartoon episode with flashing red and blue lights sent hundreds of Japanese children to hospital.
Pokemon Go was downloaded more than 500 million times within about two months of its 2016 launch.
Grand Theft Auto V made $1 billion in just three days in 2013, faster than any movie, book or game before it.
The made-up language spoken in The Sims, called Simlish, is improvised gibberish, so players everywhere hear the same nonsense.
In 2005 a virtual plague in World of Warcraft escaped into crowded cities and killed thousands of characters. Disease experts later studied it.
In 2014 one battle in the space game EVE Online destroyed virtual spaceships worth about $300,000 in real money.
In 2020 more than 12 million people attended a Travis Scott concert held inside the game Fortnite.
Combos in fighting games began as a bug in Street Fighter II. Players loved it, so it became a feature.
The famous cheat code Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right B A was added by a programmer who found his own game too hard.
Doom has been made to run on calculators, a smart fridge and even inside the plastic case of a pregnancy test.
In 2024 a student made Doom run on gut bacteria. Each frame took about 70 minutes, so a full game would take centuries.
As of 2024, the PlayStation 2 is the best-selling game console ever, with more than 160 million sold.
The first PlayStation began as a CD add-on for Nintendo. When Nintendo backed out, Sony built its own console.
A rare prototype of the "Nintendo PlayStation", a console that never launched, sold at auction in 2020 for about $360,000.
The original Xbox was nicknamed the "DirectX Box" by its creators, after the Windows software it was built on.
So many Wii remotes flew out of people's hands and into TV screens that Nintendo replaced the wrist straps with stronger ones.
To tell if you hit a duck in Duck Hunt, the screen flashed black with white boxes for a split second and the gun looked for the light.
In the arcade version of Duck Hunt, you can actually shoot the laughing dog. In the home version, you can't.
Blowing into old Nintendo cartridges never really fixed them. The moisture from your breath could even damage the metal contacts.
One of the first video game Easter eggs, in 1979, was a programmer's hidden name, because Atari refused to credit game makers.
Steve Wozniak designed the Atari game Breakout for Steve Jobs, who reportedly kept most of the bonus and told Woz it was just $700.
Angry Birds was the 52nd game made by its Finnish studio, which was close to going broke before it became a hit.
At its peak, Flappy Bird reportedly earned about $50,000 a day, but its creator pulled it from app stores in 2014.
Wordle was made by a software engineer as a gift for his partner who loved word games. The New York Times bought it in 2022.
In 2014 over a million people played the same game of Pokemon Red together by typing commands into a chat, and finished in 16 days.
In 2023 video games earned more money worldwide than movie theaters and recorded music combined.
Gamers aren't mostly kids: as of 2024, the average American video game player is about 36 years old.
Video game age ratings in the US exist because of a 1993 government hearing about violent games like Mortal Kombat.
In 2023 the Super Mario Bros. theme became the first video game music added to the US Library of Congress's recording registry.
In Super Mario Bros., the clouds and the bushes are the same picture, just colored differently.
The Legend of Zelda in 1986 was one of the first home console games with a battery inside so you could save your progress.
The Oregon Trail computer game was created in 1971 by three student teachers in Minnesota to make history lessons fun.
Windows came with Solitaire to secretly teach people how to drag and drop with a mouse, a new skill for most users at the time.
The version of Solitaire that shipped with Windows was written by a summer intern, who was never paid royalties for it.
Snake, the classic phone game, came built into hundreds of millions of Nokia phones.
The first video game tournament, held at Stanford in 1972, offered a year's subscription to Rolling Stone magazine as the prize.
The first handheld mobile phone call, in 1973, was made by a Motorola engineer who used it to call his rival at another company.
The first cell phone sold to the public, in 1983, was nicknamed "the brick". It cost $3,995, took about 10 hours to charge and gave 30 minutes of talk.
Sega's name comes from Service Games. The company started out bringing slot machines and jukeboxes to US military bases in Japan.
The first smartphone, IBM's Simon from 1994, had a touchscreen and apps, but its battery lasted only about an hour.
The first iPhone, in 2007, had no app store. Apps arrived a year later, starting with about 500 of them.
At the first iPhone demo, Steve Jobs followed a carefully planned "golden path" of steps because the prototype crashed so often.
The iPhone almost had a plastic screen. Weeks before launch, Steve Jobs saw keys scratching his prototype and demanded glass.
Your phone knows which way is up thanks to a microscopic weight on tiny springs, carved right into a chip.
Apple has said the chance that a random stranger could unlock your iPhone with their face is about one in a million.
To recognize your face, an iPhone's Face ID shines over 30,000 invisible dots of light onto it.
The Nokia 3310, launched in 2000, sold about 126 million units and was famous for surviving drops and lasting days on a charge.
Nokia began in 1865 as a paper mill in Finland, and before phones it also made rubber boots and car tires.
Samsung started in 1938 as a small shop selling dried fish, noodles and groceries.
Text messages were limited to 160 characters because an engineer typed out sample messages and found that was nearly always enough.
The QWERTY keyboard was designed for typewriters in the 1870s, and we still use it on phone screens that have no keys at all.
The first photo shared from a phone, in 1997, was of a software engineer's newborn daughter, sent from the maternity ward.
"Selfie" was named Word of the Year by Oxford Dictionaries in 2013, after its use jumped about 17,000 percent in a year.
A ton of old mobile phones contains far more gold than a ton of gold ore dug from a mine.
Atari is named after a word from the board game Go, used to warn that a stone is about to be captured, a bit like saying "check" in chess.
Android was first designed to run digital cameras before its makers switched to phones.
For about ten years, Android versions were named after sweets in alphabetical order: Cupcake, Donut, Eclair, Froyo and so on.
As of 2024, Android is the most used operating system in the world, ahead of Windows.
The first hard drive to hold a gigabyte, in 1980, was the size of a refrigerator, weighed about 250 kg and cost over $80,000.
The "save" icon in many programs is a floppy disk, an object many young people who click it have never seen.
The US military used 8-inch floppy disks in a system that helped run its nuclear forces until 2019.
Japan's government only finished scrapping rules requiring floppy disks for some official paperwork in 2024.
As recently as 2020, some Boeing 747 jets still got important software updates loaded from floppy disks.
A memory card smaller than your fingernail can now hold 1 terabyte, room for about 200,000 photos.
In theory, a single gram of DNA could store about 215 million gigabytes of data.
In 2020 GitHub stored copies of open-source code on special film inside an Arctic mine in Norway, meant to last 1,000 years.
In 2018 Microsoft sank a data center in the sea off Scotland. When they pulled it up two years later, its computers had failed less often than on land.
