In 2024 data centers used about 1.5 percent of all the world's electricity, according to the International Energy Agency.
Google once hired a herd of goats to mow the grass at its California headquarters.
A hard drive's reading head floats so close to the spinning disk that engineers compare it to a jumbo jet flying just millimeters off the ground.
The US Library of Congress, the national library, saved a copy of every public tweet sent from 2006 to 2017.
The first digital camera, built at Kodak in 1975, took 23 seconds to save one black-and-white picture to a cassette tape. Kodak went bankrupt in 2012.
The first Pong arcade machine came with just one line of instructions: "Avoid missing ball for high score".
The first digital photo ever scanned into a computer, in 1957, was a tiny picture of a scientist's baby son.
Linux began in 1991 as a student's hobby project that he said "won't be big". Today it runs every one of the world's top 500 supercomputers.
The Python programming language is named after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.
The programming language Java was first called Oak, after a tree outside its creator's office window.
JavaScript, which runs on almost every website, was created in just 10 days in 1995. Despite its name, it has almost nothing to do with Java.
BlackBerry phones were so addictive that people nicknamed them "CrackBerry", and a US dictionary made it its Word of the Year in 2006.
Linus Torvalds named his famous program Git after a British word for an unpleasant person, joking that he names his projects after himself.
One of the first PC viruses, Brain, was made in 1986 by two brothers in Pakistan, who put their names, address and phone number inside it.
One of the first computer worms, from 1971, was harmless. It just showed the message "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!" and moved on.
In 1988 a student's experiment accidentally slowed down about one in ten computers on the internet. He later became an MIT professor.
In 2000 the ILOVEYOU email virus spread to tens of millions of computers in days, because people couldn't resist opening a love letter.
In 1996 Europe's Ariane 5 rocket blew up about 40 seconds after launch because a number got too big for the space its software gave it.
In 2012 a trading company lost about $440 million in 45 minutes because of a software glitch, nearly destroying the firm.
In 1990 a single mistake in a line of code knocked out much of AT&T's long-distance phone network for about nine hours.
In 2024 one faulty software update from a security company crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounding flights around the world.
In 2015 US regulators ordered Boeing 787 jets to be rebooted regularly, because a software counter would overflow after 248 days of power.
In 2007 a group of F-22 fighter jets lost their navigation and communication computers when they crossed the International Date Line.
Microsoft Excel thinks February 29, 1900 was a real day. It wasn't, but the bug was copied on purpose from an older program to stay compatible.
Scientists renamed some human genes in 2020 because Excel kept turning their names, like SEPT1 and MARCH1, into dates.
In 1962 an MIT researcher pulled off one of the first password thefts: he printed the password file to get extra computer time.
For years, the most common password found in leaked password lists has been "123456".
Microsoft launched Windows 95 with the Rolling Stones' song "Start Me Up" and lit the Empire State Building in Windows colors.
The famous Windows XP wallpaper of a green hill and blue sky is a real photo, taken in 1996 in California wine country.
The engineer who invented Ctrl+Alt+Delete once joked on stage that he invented it, but Bill Gates made it famous.
Larry Tesler, who helped invent cut, copy and paste, had a car license plate that read NO MODES.
The tradition of making your first program print "Hello, World" comes from a programming book written in the 1970s.
In 2024 an engineer noticed logins were half a second too slow and uncovered a hidden backdoor that was about to spread to millions of computers.
In 2016 a programmer removed a tiny 11-line piece of shared code from the internet, and thousands of software projects around the world broke.
The arrow in Amazon's logo points from the A to the Z, to say it sells everything from A to Z. It also doubles as a smile.
Twitter's little blue bird logo had a name: Larry, after the basketball star Larry Bird.
There are joke programming languages whose code looks like abstract paintings, cooking recipes or scenes from a Shakespeare play.
NASA's Space Shuttle software was so carefully written that one version of the 420,000-line program had just one known error.
A modern car can run on around 100 million lines of code, more than many passenger jets.
The power symbol on your devices, a line poking into a circle, comes from 1 and 0, the computer digits for on and off.
The inventor of the GIF picture format said it should be pronounced "jif", like the peanut butter brand. Many people still disagree.
The Enigma machine had a tiny flaw: it could never turn a letter into itself. Codebreakers used that to help crack it.
Apple's product photos usually show the time 9:41, roughly the moment Steve Jobs first revealed the iPhone on stage in 2007.
Phone keypads have 1, 2, 3 along the top row, while calculators and computer number pads have 7, 8, 9 there instead.
In the Navajo code of World War II, a tank was called "tortoise" and a submarine "iron fish".
Some historians estimate that cracking the Enigma code shortened World War II in Europe by up to two years.
Type "do a barrel roll" into Google search and the whole results page spins around once.
Mary, Queen of Scots, lost her head in 1587 after her secret coded letters were cracked by her enemies.
The secret trick behind modern online encryption was first invented in Britain by government spies in the early 1970s, and kept hidden for decades.
The famous Cold War "red phone" between Washington and Moscow was never a phone. It was a teletype machine for written messages.
In 2010 a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas. At later prices, those coins were worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Nobody knows for sure who invented Bitcoin. Its creator used the name Satoshi Nakamoto and vanished from the internet in 2011.
A man in Wales threw away a hard drive holding about 8,000 bitcoins in 2013, and spent years trying to get permission to dig it out of a landfill.
Only 21 million bitcoins can ever exist, and millions of them are thought to be lost forever in forgotten wallets.
The very first Bitcoin record, made in 2009, contains a newspaper headline about governments bailing out banks.
Quantum computers are chilled to just above absolute zero, making them colder than outer space.
In 2019 Google said its quantum computer did in 200 seconds a task that would take a supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM said it would take only days.
GPS only works because of Einstein: without correcting for relativity, its satellites' clocks would put you off by about 10 km a day.
GPS was opened up for everyone after a passenger jet strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down in 1983.
Until 2000, the US military deliberately scrambled GPS for civilians, so it was accurate only to about 100 meters.
Your phone never talks to GPS satellites. It only listens to their signals and works out where you are by itself.
The first mobile phone call in Britain was made on New Year's Day 1985 by the comedian Ernie Wise, who rang the phone company's office.
As of 2025, more than half of all working satellites orbiting the Earth belong to SpaceX's Starlink.
TV satellites sit about 36,000 km up, where they circle at exactly the speed the Earth spins, so your dish can point at one fixed spot.
Science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke described satellites hovering over one spot to relay signals in 1945, 12 years before the first satellite.
A phone call bounced off a satellite 36,000 km up has about half a second of delay, because the signal travels more than 140,000 km there and back.
More than 30,000 pieces of space junk are tracked in orbit, and most of them move about ten times faster than a bullet.
In 1962 the Telstar satellite beamed the first live TV pictures across the Atlantic, and a pop song named after it hit No. 1.
ChatGPT reached about 100 million users roughly two months after it launched, the fastest growth of any consumer app up to then.
In 2023 a US lawyer was fined after submitting court papers citing cases that ChatGPT had made up entirely.
AI image generators were long famous for drawing people with too many or too few fingers.
In 2022 a picture made with an AI image generator won first prize in the digital art category of the Colorado State Fair.
An AI called AlphaFold predicted the shapes of about 200 million proteins, nearly every one known to science, and its creators won a Nobel Prize in 2024.
The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics went to two scientists whose early work on artificial brains made today's AI possible.
As of 2025, Waymo robotaxis give hundreds of thousands of paid rides a week in US cities with nobody in the driver's seat.
The Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing machine of the 1770s, beat famous people including Napoleon. A human chess master was hiding inside.
In 1958 the New York Times reported the Navy expected a new learning machine to one day walk, talk, see, write and be conscious.
Training the AI model GPT-3 is estimated to have used about as much electricity as 120 American homes use in a year.
In 2019 an AI called Pluribus beat top professional poker players at six-player Texas hold'em, a game full of bluffing.
Phones sold in Japan make a camera shutter sound that can't be switched off, a rule phone makers follow to discourage secret photos.
In 2019 a Japanese hotel staffed by robots "fired" about half of its 243 robots, because they annoyed guests more than they helped.
In 2017 a humanoid robot named Sophia was granted citizenship by Saudi Arabia, the first robot to be given a nationality.
A Buddhist temple in Japan has held funerals for broken Aibo robot dogs, with priests chanting for them.
Leonardo da Vinci sketched a robot knight around 1495 that could sit, stand and move its arms. Engineers built one from his notes in 2002.
A boy-shaped doll called The Writer, built in Switzerland in the 1770s, can still dip a quill in ink and write a custom message.
As of 2023, Amazon used more than 750,000 robots in its warehouses, carrying shelves of goods to human packers.
South Korea has the most factory robots in the world for its size, about one for every ten factory workers.
In 1994 a tiny math error in Intel's Pentium chip forced a recall that cost the company about $475 million.
In 1962 NASA destroyed its Mariner 1 probe minutes after launch because of a tiny missing symbol in its code, "the most expensive hyphen in history".
A software bug in a power company's alarm system helped cause the 2003 blackout that left about 50 million North Americans without power.
In 1983 a Soviet warning system mistook sunlight bouncing off clouds for incoming US missiles. Officer Stanislav Petrov decided it was a false alarm.
In 2012 Apple Maps misplaced the town of Mildura so badly that Australian police warned it was sending drivers into a remote national park.
In 2016 iPhones could freeze completely if you set their date back to January 1, 1970.
On December 31, 2008, thousands of Microsoft Zune music players froze at once because of a leap year bug.
In 2011 two pricing bots on Amazon kept outbidding each other until a book about flies was listed for over $23 million.
In 2010 the US stock market lost about a trillion dollars in value within minutes during a computer-driven "flash crash", then mostly bounced back.
In 2009 Google warned that every website on the internet might harm your computer, for about 40 minutes, because someone typed one wrong slash.
In 2020 a 17-year-old took over the Twitter accounts of Barack Obama, Elon Musk and others to run a bitcoin scam.
In 2018 Hawaii sent a false missile alert to every phone in the state after a worker clicked the wrong option, and the correction took 38 minutes.
In 1995, students recreated the entire room-sized ENIAC computer on a single chip smaller than a fingernail.
Before Apple, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak sold "blue boxes" that tricked phone networks into giving free calls.
Using one of his homemade phone-hacking boxes, Steve Wozniak once prank-called the Vatican pretending to be Henry Kissinger.
Apple, now one of the most valuable companies on Earth, was founded on April Fools' Day, April 1, 1976.
In 1997 Apple was reportedly within months of going bankrupt, and its old rival Microsoft invested $150 million to help save it.
Amazon's first desks were made from cheap wooden doors with legs attached, a habit the company kept for years.
Google's first office was a garage in Menlo Park rented from Susan Wojcicki, who later became the boss of YouTube.
Before Microsoft, Bill Gates and Paul Allen ran a company called Traf-O-Data that counted cars from traffic sensor tapes.
Bill Gates is often quoted as saying "640K ought to be enough for anybody", but there's no evidence he said it, and he denies it.
The Sony Walkman exists because one of Sony's founders wanted a way to listen to music on long plane flights.
Sony says the CD was made to hold about 74 minutes so that Beethoven's Ninth Symphony could fit on one disc.
Engineers fine-tuned the MP3 music format by listening to Suzanne Vega's song "Tom's Diner" over and over, earning her the nickname "mother of the MP3".
Apple sold the first iPod in 2001 with the slogan "1,000 songs in your pocket", when most people carried CDs holding about 15 songs each.
Napster, the music-sharing app that shook up the music business in 1999, was created by an 18-year-old college student.
In 1804 a French loom used cards with punched holes to weave patterns, an idea that inspired early computers.
Punched-card machines sped up counting the 1890 US census, and the company behind them later became part of IBM.
The inventor of the square pixel, Russell Kirsch, said near the end of his life that he regretted making pixels square.
Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated movie, took from about 45 minutes to 30 hours of computer time to draw each frame.
Steve Jobs bought the computer division that became Pixar from George Lucas for about $10 million. Disney bought it in 2006 for $7.4 billion.
The oldest known recording of computer music, made in 1951, has a computer in Alan Turing's Manchester lab playing "God Save the King".
In 1961 an IBM computer sang the song "Daisy Bell", which inspired the dying computer HAL in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Shift each letter of HAL, the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey, one step and you get IBM. Arthur C. Clarke insisted it was a coincidence.
Siri began as a spin-off from a US military-funded research project to build a virtual office assistant.
Amazon chose the name Alexa partly because its hard "x" sound is easy for computers to pick out, and as a nod to the Library of Alexandria.
The first cash machine, opened in London in 1967, used paper vouchers marked with a slightly radioactive substance instead of cards.
One of the first internet-connected devices was a Coca-Cola machine at a US university in 1982 that reported whether its drinks were cold.
In 1990 an engineer connected a toaster to the internet, so it could be switched on from a computer.
E-paper screens, like those in e-readers, can keep showing a picture with no power at all; they only use energy to change it.
The Sims began after its creator lost his home in a 1991 wildfire in California. Rebuilding his life gave him the idea for a game about everyday living.
The touchscreen was invented in 1965 by a British engineer working on air traffic control.
Phone touchscreens sense the electricity in your skin, which is why they ignore most gloves but can be tapped with a sausage.
In the first big race for self-driving cars, in 2004, no car finished. The best one managed about 7 miles of a 150-mile course.
As of 2024, an estimated 360 billion emails were being sent every day, and close to half of all email is spam.
In 2019 the web address voice.com sold for $30 million, more than many mansions, for one short everyday word.
The first band to perform live over the internet, in 1993, was a little-known group called Severe Tire Damage.
In 2005 Estonia became the first country to let everyone vote online in a nationwide election.
In 2010 Finland became one of the first countries to make access to broadband internet a legal right.
A 2016 leak showed that North Korea's own national internet had only about 28 websites.
Grace Hopper, the computing pioneer nicknamed "Amazing Grace", has a US Navy warship named after her.
In 2021 a fan found why Grand Theft Auto Online took minutes to load, cut it by about 70 percent, and got a $10,000 reward.
SimCity grew out of a helicopter game. Its creator had more fun building the city maps than bombing them, so he made a game just for building.
In 2010 a company spent about $300 million laying a straighter cable from Chicago to New York to shave 3 thousandths of a second off stock trades.
A sealed first-generation iPhone from 2007 sold at auction in 2023 for about $190,000.
Many people feel their phone vibrate in their pocket when it didn't. It's so common it has a name: phantom vibration syndrome.
The wheels of NASA's Curiosity rover have holes that spell "JPL" in Morse code, stamped into the Martian dirt as it drives.
The parachute that landed the Perseverance rover on Mars hid a secret coded message: "Dare mighty things".
In 2013 the International Space Station's laptops switched from Windows to Linux.
In 2008 a computer virus made it all the way to the International Space Station, carried on an astronaut's laptop.
The Altair 8800, a 1975 home computer kit, had no keyboard and no screen. You flipped switches to program it and read blinking lights.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote their first program for the Altair computer without ever seeing one. It worked the first time they tried it.
Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad was directed by Ridley Scott and shown nationally on TV just once, during the Super Bowl.
The signatures of the original Macintosh design team are moulded into the inside of the computer's plastic case.
The first big-selling portable computer, the Osborne 1 from 1981, weighed about 11 kg and had a screen smaller than a postcard.
The word "byte" is spelled with a y on purpose, so nobody would confuse it with "bit". Half a byte is jokingly called a "nibble".
AI pioneer Marvin Minsky invented the "useless machine": a box with a switch that, when you flip it on, pushes out a hand and turns itself off.
Alan Turing was a serious runner who finished a marathon in 2 hours 46 minutes, close to Olympic level at the time.
Alan Turing wrote one of the first chess programs before there was a computer to run it, so he played it by working out each move on paper.
Since 2021, codebreaker and computer pioneer Alan Turing has been on the Bank of England's 50 pound note.
Tim Berners-Lee has said he regrets the two slashes after "http:" in web addresses, because they were never really needed.
Tim Berners-Lee's parents both worked on one of the first computers ever sold, the Ferranti Mark 1.
"Google" was added to major English dictionaries as a verb in 2006, meaning to search the web.
Hotmail spread like wildfire because every email it sent ended with a little ad: "Get your free email at Hotmail".
"LOL" and "OMG" were officially added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2011, though "OMG" turned up in a letter as early as 1917.
One of the first home online shoppers was a 72-year-old grandmother in England who ordered groceries through her TV in 1984.
Mario has appeared in more than 200 video games since 1981, making him one of the busiest characters in entertainment history.
Luigi began as a simple copy of Mario in different colors, so two people could play together.
In 2022 a rare Pikachu Illustrator trading card sold for about $5.3 million, a world record for a Pokemon card.
As of 2024, speedrunners can finish the original Super Mario Bros. in under 5 minutes.
Since 2022, many iPhones can text emergency services through satellites when there's no phone signal at all.
The original American voice of Siri, Susan Bennett, recorded her lines in 2005 without knowing they would end up in millions of iPhones.
The famous Nokia ringtone comes from "Gran Vals", a classical guitar piece written in 1902.
The Windows 95 startup sound was composed by musician Brian Eno, who said he made it on a Mac.
The voice saying "You've got mail" on AOL belonged to a man who recorded it for about $200, and it was heard billions of times.
In 2019 Netflix alone made up about 15 percent of all the internet traffic flowing around the world.
In 2020 Netflix and YouTube lowered their video quality in Europe so the internet wouldn't get jammed during lockdowns.
The patent for the computer mouse, granted in 1970, didn't call it a mouse. It was an "X-Y position indicator for a display system".
In 2017 AlphaGo Zero learned Go entirely by playing itself for three days, then beat the version that defeated a world champion 100 games to 0.
Robots find chess easy but folding laundry incredibly hard, while for humans it's the other way round.
The company that made the Roomba vacuum also built bomb-disposal robots that searched the rubble of the World Trade Center.
In 2008 Honda's child-sized walking robot ASIMO stood on a podium and conducted the Detroit Symphony Orchestra.
In 1999 the US National Security Agency banned Furby toys from its offices, fearing they could record secrets. They couldn't.
The International Space Station circles the Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see about 16 sunrises a day.
Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, is the oldest human-made object still orbiting the Earth.
In the 1990s strong encryption software counted as a weapon under US export law, so a T-shirt printed with the code was legally a "munition".
To get his encryption software out of the US legally in the 1990s, its creator published the code as a printed book.
NASA's Mars Polar Lander probably crashed in 1999 because it mistook the jolt of its legs unfolding for touchdown and shut off its engines.
When the clocks changed in 2010, many iPhone alarms in Europe went off an hour late, making people late for work.
Sony's first product, made in 1946, was an electric rice cooker that often burned the rice.
Electronics giant LG started out in the 1940s making a face cream called Lucky Cream, long before it made TVs and phones.
Intel's founders first wanted to call their company "Moore Noyce", but dropped it because it sounded like "more noise".
The software company Adobe is named after a creek that ran behind one of its founders' houses.
The camera maker Canon got its name from Kwanon, its first camera, named after a Buddhist goddess of mercy.
Skype's name started as "Sky peer-to-peer", which became "Skyper", then Skype when that web address was taken.
Zoom went from about 10 million daily meeting participants in December 2019 to about 300 million in April 2020.
Some programmers solve bugs by explaining their code out loud, line by line, to a rubber duck. It's called rubber duck debugging.
From the late 1960s, children learned to program with a language called Logo by steering a robot "turtle" that drew lines on paper.
When Google Chrome can't reach the internet, pressing the space bar starts a hidden game where a little T. rex jumps over cactuses.
On Wikipedia, if you keep clicking the first link in an article, you will very often end up on the page for "Philosophy".
In 1969 a luxury store sold a "Kitchen Computer" for storing recipes for about $10,600. It came with a cutting board, and nobody is known to have bought one.
The first phone book, printed in 1878 in New Haven, Connecticut, listed about 50 names and no numbers at all. You asked the operator by name.
Clippy, Microsoft's talking paper clip helper, was so disliked that Microsoft later ran ads joking that it had been fired.
Steve Jobs named Apple's Lisa computer after his daughter, though for years the company claimed the name stood for something technical.
For years Steve Jobs drove a car with no license plates, by swapping it for a new leased one every six months.
Steve Jobs picked the name Apple partly because he was on a fruit diet, and partly because it came before Atari in the phone book.
At age 12, Elon Musk sold the code for a space video game he had written, called Blastar, for about $500.
Japanese researchers sent data through optical fiber at 402 terabits per second in 2024, fast enough to download thousands of movies in a second.
In 2006 Netflix offered $1 million to anyone who could improve its movie recommendations by 10 percent. A team won in 2009.
As of 2024, Google Translate works with more than 240 languages, including some spoken by only a few hundred thousand people.
In 2025 AI systems reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad, the world's toughest math contest for teenagers.
Surgical robots are so precise that surgeons have used them to peel a grape and stitch its skin back together.
In 2001 surgeons in New York used a robot to remove a patient's gallbladder in France, more than 6,000 km away.
In 2024 a robot solved a Rubik's Cube in about 0.3 seconds, roughly the time it takes you to blink.
Since late 2024 the European Union has required new phones sold there to charge with USB-C, which is why iPhones switched to it.
As of 2024 there are more than 3,700 official emoji, including a mosquito, a lungs icon and a moai statue from Easter Island.
In 2010 a computer worm called Stuxnet physically wrecked machines in an Iranian nuclear facility, one of the first cyberweapons to break real things.
In 2017 a 22-year-old researcher stopped the WannaCry cyberattack that hit hospitals around the world by registering a web address for about $11.
Hackers once broke into a casino's computer network through an internet-connected thermometer in its fish tank.
In 2015 hackers showed they could take over a Jeep on the highway from miles away, and Chrysler recalled 1.4 million vehicles.
The first telephone operators were teenage boys, but they were so rude and playful on the line that companies soon hired women instead.
In the 1980s home computer games came on cassette tapes, and loading one could take several minutes of screeching sounds.
In the 1980s some radio stations broadcast computer programs as screeching sounds, so listeners could record them on tape and load them.
Big tech companies still store huge archives on magnetic tape, which can last around 30 years sitting on a shelf.
The first face ever shown on television, in 1925, wasn't a person. John Logie Baird used a ventriloquist's dummy he called Stooky Bill.
The Apollo 11 Moon landing code is now online, and it's full of programmer jokes, like a routine named BURN_BABY_BURN.
NASA's Ingenuity helicopter flew on Mars using a processor first designed for smartphones.
Animal Crossing: New Horizons came out in March 2020, just as lockdowns began, and went on to sell more than 40 million copies.
A 2007 study found surgeons who played video games at least three hours a week made about a third fewer errors in keyhole surgery training.
In 2011 gamers playing a puzzle game called Foldit worked out the shape of a virus protein in about 10 days, after scientists had struggled for over a decade.
The United Nations has used Minecraft to let local people, including kids, redesign real parks and public spaces.
Microsoft Flight Simulator recreates the entire planet, every city and mountain, using satellite and map data streamed as you fly.
In 2020 a typo in map data put a 212-story skyscraper in a quiet Melbourne suburb in Microsoft Flight Simulator.
A 2004 report found that most of New York City's pedestrian crossing buttons had stopped working years earlier. Pressing them did nothing at all.
The word "hacker" first meant a clever tinkerer at MIT's model railroad club in the 1950s, not a computer criminal.
The first computer weather forecast, made on ENIAC in 1950, predicted 24 hours ahead and took about 24 hours to calculate.
Apollo astronauts carried slide rules, old-fashioned calculating sticks, as a backup in case their computers failed.
The first spreadsheet program, VisiCalc, was dreamed up by a student who was tired of redoing calculations by hand in class.
The first video call system for sale, AT&T's Picturephone from 1964, cost so much and showed such a tiny picture that almost nobody used it.
Google's logo repeats blue, red and yellow, then breaks the pattern with a green L on purpose, to show that Google doesn't follow the rules.
When the laser was invented in 1960, people joked it was "a solution looking for a problem". Now it reads barcodes, cuts metal and carries the internet.
Scientists tried for about 30 years to make a bright blue LED. The three who finally did won the 2014 Nobel Prize, because it made white LED lights possible.
The first TV remote control, from 1950, was attached to the TV by a long cable. It was called "Lazy Bones".
TV remotes got the nickname "clicker" because early ones worked by striking little metal rods, making a click and a sound only the TV could hear.
The small bumps on the F and J keys of a keyboard let you find the right place for your fingers without looking.
One of the first trackballs, built in the early 1950s for the Canadian Navy, used a five-pin bowling ball.
In 2014 NASA emailed the design for a wrench to the International Space Station, and astronauts 3D-printed it in orbit.
The first virtual reality headset, built in 1968, was so heavy it had to hang from the ceiling. It was nicknamed the Sword of Damocles.
Nintendo's Virtual Boy, a 1995 headset that showed games only in red, was such a flop that it was discontinued within about a year.
In the 1990s many schools banned Tamagotchi virtual pets because kids kept feeding and cleaning them during lessons.
In the movie E.T., the alien builds his "phone home" device partly out of a Speak & Spell, a talking toy from 1978.
The first digital watch, launched in 1972, cost $2,100, about as much as a small new car at the time.
In 1969 President Nixon phoned the Apollo 11 astronauts on the Moon, calling it the most historic phone call ever made.
Spell checkers once kept changing "cooperation" into "Cupertino", Apple's hometown, and the mistake slipped into official UN and EU documents.
In 1996 AOL's word filter blocked people from the English town of Scunthorpe, because a rude word is hidden inside its name.
The fictional Klingon alphabet from Star Trek was proposed for the world's official computer text standard, but it was turned down in 2001.
Tomb Raider's hero Lara Croft started out as a man. Her designer changed it partly because the character looked too much like Indiana Jones.
The plus-shaped D-pad on game controllers was invented at Nintendo in the early 1980s for a handheld Donkey Kong game.
In 2018 a portrait made by an AI program sold at Christie's auction house for $432,500.
In 2017 an AI combing through NASA telescope data found an eighth planet around a distant star, tying the record set by our own solar system.
The first Mars rover, Sojourner, landed in 1997 and was only about the size of a microwave oven.
The first remote-controlled rover on the Moon was the Soviet Lunokhod 1 in 1970, driven by a team on Earth with a delay of a few seconds.
In 2005 a trader in Japan meant to sell 1 share for 610,000 yen but sold 610,000 shares for 1 yen each, a typo that cost his firm about $225 million.
Shazam began in 2002 in the UK as a phone service: you dialed 2580, held your phone up to the music, and got the song's name by text.
Wikipedia began in 2001 as a side project of Nupedia, an encyclopedia written by experts that finished only about two dozen articles.
Apple's 1993 Newton tablet was so bad at reading handwriting that The Simpsons mocked it, turning "Beat up Martin" into "Eat up Martha".
The inventor of the PalmPilot carried a block of wood in his shirt pocket for months to test the right size for his gadget.
The unit for measuring how far a computer mouse moves is officially called a "mickey".
In 1998 Bill Gates was showing off Windows 98 live on stage when the computer crashed with a blue error screen. He joked it must be why it wasn't shipping yet.
In many US elevators the "door close" button does nothing for passengers. It mainly works when firefighters or staff turn on a special mode.
Contactless bank cards have no battery. They borrow power from the radio waves of the card reader for the instant they need it.
As of 2024, more than 60 million Raspberry Pi computers had been sold, each about the size of a credit card.
In 2018 engineers built a working computer smaller than a grain of rice, about 0.3 mm on each side.
If every person on Earth did one sum per second, it would take about 7 years to match what the El Capitan supercomputer does in one second.
In 2025 computers worked out the number pi to 300 trillion digits. Printed out, it would fill millions of books.
In 2024 a former chip engineer found the largest known prime number, over 41 million digits long, using computers rented over the internet.
A toy whistle once given away in cereal boxes played the exact note that phone networks used, letting phone hackers make free long-distance calls.
The first photo posted on Instagram, in 2010, was a picture of a dog near a taco stand.
Guinness World Records lists the Commodore 64, launched in 1982, as the best-selling single computer model ever, with millions sold.
Old-school computer speakers buzzed when a mobile phone nearby was about to ring, because they picked up the phone's radio signals.
Text messaging was added to early mobile networks as a minor extra. Almost nobody expected billions of people to use it every day.
@ancient|Ancient world
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Roman dinner guests brought their own napkins to parties and used them to carry home leftovers, an ancient doggy bag.
Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, a temple of giant carved stone pillars, is about 6,000 years older than Stonehenge.
The giant stone temple of Gobekli Tepe was built by hunter-gatherers, before anyone had farms, pottery, metal or the wheel.
If you have European or Asian roots, about 1 to 2 percent of your DNA probably comes from Neanderthals.
The Lion Man, a little statue with a lion's head on a human body, was carved from mammoth tusk about 40,000 years ago.
People were playing flutes made from bird bones about 40,000 years ago, in caves in what is now Germany.
Otzi the Iceman, frozen in the Alps for 5,300 years, has more than 60 tattoos, made by rubbing charcoal into tiny cuts.
When hikers found Otzi the Iceman in 1991, they thought he was a climber who had died recently. He was 5,300 years old.
Otzi the Iceman had an arrowhead stuck in his shoulder, and nobody noticed it until an X-ray ten years after he was found.
Dogs were our friends long before farming: they were tamed at least 15,000 years ago, before any crop or farm animal.
Nobody knows what hand sign Roman crowds used to spare or doom a gladiator. The famous thumbs down comes mostly from an 1872 painting.
A tiny human species, about one metre tall and nicknamed the hobbit, lived on an Indonesian island until about 50,000 years ago.
Footprints of children and adults at White Sands, New Mexico, show people were in North America over 20,000 years ago.
The famous fossil Lucy, 3.2 million years old, got her name from the Beatles song playing in the camp the night she was found.
Someone was making stone tools in Kenya 3.3 million years ago, before our own branch of the human family even existed.
Jericho had a stone tower about 8 metres tall around 8000 BC, roughly 5,000 years before the first pyramid.
In Catalhoyuk, a town of thousands in Turkey 9,000 years ago, there were no streets: people walked across the roofs and climbed in from above.
Some of Stonehenge's smaller stones were moved more than 200 km from the hills of Wales, 5,000 years ago.
The big flat Altar Stone at the heart of Stonehenge came all the way from northern Scotland, more than 700 km away.
Newgrange in Ireland is older than both Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza.
On the shortest day of the year, the rising sun shines down a passage into the heart of Newgrange in Ireland, as it has for about 5,000 years.
Skara Brae, a 5,000-year-old village in Scotland's Orkney islands, still has its beds and dressers, because they were made of stone.
Greek and Roman kids played knucklebones, tossing and catching little sheep ankle bones. The game survives today as jacks.
The oldest known bread was baked about 14,400 years ago in Jordan, by hunters and gatherers, thousands of years before farming.
People were making clay pots in China about 20,000 years ago, in the middle of the Ice Age.
The oldest known leather shoe, found in a cave in Armenia, is about 5,500 years old and was stuffed with grass.
Early humans in Zambia joined two logs with a notch about 476,000 years ago, before our own species even existed.
Human ancestors may have been sitting around fires about one million years ago, judging by ash in a South African cave.
What may be the oldest known zoo was in Egypt about 5,500 years ago, at Hierakonpolis, where elephants, hippos and baboons were kept.
Neanderthals made glue by heating birch bark, and used it to fix stone blades to handles about 200,000 years ago.
The oldest pet cat we know of was buried next to a person in Cyprus about 9,500 years ago, long before the Egyptians loved cats.
The Lascaux cave paintings in France, about 17,000 years old, were found in 1940 by four teenagers who crawled down a hole in the woods.
The Altamira cave paintings were found by an 8-year-old girl in 1879, and experts called them fakes for over 20 years.
About 15,000 years ago, people in Ukraine built their huts out of hundreds of mammoth bones.
Stone Age surgeons drilled holes in people's skulls, and the healed bone shows many patients survived for years.
The oldest known drilled teeth are about 9,000 years old: people in Pakistan bored into molars with tiny stone-tipped drills.
Almost every horse in the world today descends from horses tamed on the Russian steppe about 4,200 years ago.
The wheel came surprisingly late: around 3500 BC, thousands of years after people had farms, pottery and towns.
At the end of the last Ice Age the seas rose about 120 metres, drowning the coasts where many early people lived.
During the Ice Age you could walk from Siberia to Alaska, across land that is now under the sea.
People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, which meant crossing open sea by boat or raft.
Aboriginal Australian stories of coasts swallowed by the sea may be memories of real floods more than 7,000 years ago.
Before farming, the entire human population of Earth was probably just a few million people, fewer than live in many cities today.
Skeletons show many early farmers were shorter and had worse teeth than the hunter-gatherers who came before them.
The oldest known boat is a 10,000-year-old canoe dug out of a bog in the Netherlands.
About 11,000 years ago, people in England wore deer skulls with the antlers still attached, perhaps as headdresses.
The oldest known drawing is a crosshatch made with a red crayon on a stone in South Africa, about 73,000 years ago.
People were wearing shell bead necklaces in Morocco about 142,000 years ago, long before anyone painted a cave wall.
Silbury Hill in England is a man-made mound as tall as a 10-storey building, about 4,400 years old, and nobody knows what it was for.
The stone circle at Avebury in England is so huge that part of a village sits inside it.
A bronze disc from Germany, about 3,600 years old, shows the Sun, the Moon and the stars in gold. It is often called the oldest known picture of the sky.
A man buried near Stonehenge about 4,300 years ago grew up near the Alps, hundreds of miles away.
DNA from Cheddar Man, a Briton who lived 10,000 years ago, suggests he probably had dark skin and blue eyes.
A 5,700-year-old piece of chewed birch tar gum from Denmark held enough DNA to read the whole genome of the girl who chewed it.
A 1,800-year-old letter from a boy in Roman Egypt threatens his father: take me to Alexandria, or I will not eat or drink!
The oldest known wine was made in Georgia, between Europe and Asia, about 8,000 years ago, in big clay jars.
The oldest gold treasure in the world was buried in Bulgaria about 6,500 years ago, before the pyramids or Stonehenge.
Tollund Man, a 2,400-year-old body from a Danish bog, looked so fresh that the people who found him in 1950 called the police.
Stonehenge was built in stages over about 1,500 years, almost as long as the time from the fall of Rome to today.
Each of Stonehenge's giant stones weighs about as much as four elephants, and they were moved without wheels or metal tools.
The first sheep had hairy coats, not wool: fluffy woolly sheep came thousands of years after people first kept them.
English, Russian, Hindi and Persian all descend from one language spoken about 6,000 years ago, and not a single word of it was written down.
People were sewing clothes with bone needles at least 40,000 years ago, stitching animal skins together to survive the Ice Age.
The Sahara was green about 10,000 to 6,000 years ago, with lakes, hippos and crocodiles, and cattle herders lived there.
In the Egyptian desert, a cave has thousands-of-years-old paintings of people swimming, in one of the driest places on Earth.
Prehistoric Scots built round houses on man-made islands in lakes, and people kept building them, on and off, for thousands of years.
The ancient Egyptian word for cat was miu, which sounds just like a meow. The cat was probably named after its own voice.
Ice Age hunters in Europe painted their own hand outlines on cave walls by blowing paint around them.
Early humans walked out of Africa and reached China, Australia and Europe tens of thousands of years before anyone farmed.
The bow and arrow is at least 60,000 years old, judging by tiny stone points found in a South African cave.
The first writing, invented in Iraq around 3200 BC, was mostly used for bookkeeping: counting grain, beer and sheep.
One of the first named people in history may be Kushim, who signed a 5,000-year-old receipt for barley. He was basically an accountant.
There are 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle because ancient Mesopotamians counted in sixties.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest stories ever written, has a great flood, a giant boat and birds sent out to look for dry land.
The oldest known customer complaint is a clay tablet from about 1750 BC, in which a man named Nanni rages about being sold bad copper.
King Hammurabi's laws, about 3,800 years old, are carved on a black stone pillar taller than a person, now in the Louvre.
Under Hammurabi's laws, a surgeon's fee depended on who the patient was: a noble paid more than a commoner.
The earliest author known by name is a woman: Enheduanna, a priestess and princess who wrote hymns in Iraq around 2300 BC.
Sumerians drank beer through long straws, to get past the husks and bits of grain floating on top.
A 3,800-year-old hymn to Ninkasi, the Sumerian goddess of beer, doubles as a beer recipe.
The clay tablets in an Assyrian king's library survived because the palace burned down: the fire baked them hard as brick.
Babylon's Ishtar Gate, covered in glazed blue bricks with lions and dragons, has been rebuilt inside a museum in Berlin.
Nobody has ever found the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and some historians think they were really in a different city, Nineveh.
Uruk, in Iraq, may have had 40,000 people or more around 3000 BC, possibly the biggest city on Earth at the time.
The ancient Sumerian list of kings claims that one early king ruled for 28,800 years.
Mesopotamians signed documents by rolling a little carved stone cylinder across wet clay, like a personal rubber stamp.
The oldest recorded joke, from Sumer about 4,000 years ago, is a toilet joke. Some humour never changes.
Cuneiform, the wedge-shaped writing of ancient Iraq, was used for about 3,000 years, longer than the Latin alphabet has been used for English.
Many Assyrian winged bull statues have five legs, so they look right from both the front and the side.
Glassblowing was invented around the 1st century BC, and suddenly glass cups went from luxury to everyday object.
In 1857, four scholars translated the same ancient Assyrian text without talking to each other, to prove they could really read it. They mostly agreed.
A Babylonian map of the world from about 2,600 years ago shows the Earth as a flat disc surrounded by a ring of ocean.
An eclipse that Assyrian scribes noted in 763 BC lets historians pin exact dates on centuries of ancient history.
When George Smith read the Babylonian flood story on a tablet in 1872, he reportedly got so excited that he started taking his clothes off.
The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel from about 539 BC, records the Persian king Cyrus letting deported peoples go home and rebuild their temples.
Persian royal messengers, riding relays of fresh horses, could cross the empire in about a week. On foot it took three months.
The New York post office motto about snow, rain and gloom of night comes from Herodotus, describing Persian messengers 2,500 years ago.
Persian clay records show the empire paid women workers, and gave new mothers extra food rations.
Ancient Persians kept ice through the desert summer in giant domed buildings called yakhchals.
Ancient Persians dug underground canals to carry mountain water to desert towns, and some still flow after more than 2,500 years.
According to Herodotus, when a storm wrecked his bridge across the sea, the Persian king Xerxes had the water whipped 300 times.
Xerxes' army crossed from Asia into Europe on two bridges made of hundreds of boats tied together.
Herodotus said the Persian king's elite guard, the Immortals, always numbered exactly 10,000: anyone who fell was replaced at once.
Almost every alphabet in the West, Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic included, comes from the alphabet of the Phoenicians, about 3,000 years ago.
The first alphabet had no vowels at all, a bit like writing thnk y fr dnnr. The Greeks added them.
Royal purple dye came from sea snails, and it took thousands of snails to make a single gram, so it cost more than gold.
Phoenician sailors may have sailed around Africa 2,600 years ago. Herodotus doubted it because they said the Sun was on the wrong side, which is exactly what you'd see.
The word Bible comes from Byblos, an ancient city that sold papyrus, the paper of the ancient world.
The oldest peace treaty with both sides' copies surviving was signed by Egypt and the Hittites around 1259 BC. A replica hangs at the United Nations.
The Battle of Kadesh, in 1274 BC, involved about 5,000 chariots, probably the biggest chariot battle ever fought.
Pharaohs and foreign kings wrote letters to each other in Babylonian, the international language of diplomacy 3,400 years ago.
Around 1177 BC, many of the great kingdoms around the Mediterranean collapsed within a few decades, and historians still argue about why.
The oldest written song with its music, about 3,400 years old, was found on a clay tablet in Syria.
The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in 1947 by a young shepherd who threw a stone into a cave and heard a jar break.
The Dead Sea Scrolls contain copies of Bible books about a thousand years older than any copy known before them.
One of the Dead Sea Scrolls, written on copper, is a list of places where treasure was hidden. None of it has been found.
About 2,700 years ago, two teams dug a water tunnel under Jerusalem from opposite ends and met in the middle. A carving celebrates the moment.
The first coins were made in Lydia, in today's Turkey, around 600 BC, from a natural mix of gold and silver.
The saying rich as Croesus is about a real person: Croesus, king of Lydia around 560 BC, famous for his gold.
An oracle told King Croesus that if he attacked Persia, a great empire would fall. It did: his own.
A lyre with a golden bull's head, buried in Iraq about 4,500 years ago, is one of the oldest stringed instruments ever found.
The rules of the 4,500-year-old Royal Game of Ur were worked out from a clay tablet, so people can play it today.
The blue stone in the jewels of the ancient city of Ur came from Afghanistan, about 2,000 km away.
Plato may be a nickname meaning broad, perhaps for his wide shoulders. Ancient writers said he was a wrestler in his youth.
A Babylonian princess named Ennigaldi kept a collection of older relics with labels, about 2,500 years ago: possibly the first museum.
An Assyrian king built a stone aqueduct around 690 BC, centuries before the Romans built theirs.
Babylonian astronomers kept nightly diaries of the sky, the weather and food prices for about 600 years.
Our word magic comes from the Magi, the priests of ancient Persia, like the wise men of the Christmas story.
The word paradise comes from an old Persian word for a walled garden, the kind Persian kings loved to build.
A Persian king finished a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea about 2,500 years ago, an ancient ancestor of the Suez Canal.
The oldest known love poem, written in Iraq about 4,000 years ago, calls a king lion, dear to my heart, and his beauty honey sweet.
Clay tablets from an Assyrian king's library end with curses on anyone who steals them, an ancient version of a library warning.
An Assyrian king boasted that he could read and write, because most kings of his time couldn't.
The oldest known recipes, written about 3,750 years ago in Babylon, include several stews, one of them made with lamb.
The oldest known animation is painted around a 5,000-year-old bowl from Iran: a goat leaping to grab leaves from a tree.
A woman buried in Iran about 4,800 years ago had an artificial eye, made from a light material and decorated with gold lines.
Ancient Mesopotamian kings buried tablets in the foundations of temples, addressed to future kings who would someday dig them up.
A Babylonian king named Nabonidus loved digging up ancient ruins, and is sometimes called the first archaeologist.
The Behistun Inscription, carved high on a cliff in Iran in three languages, was the key to reading ancient Iraqi writing.
Mesopotamian students practised writing on round clay tablets, and some still have their teachers' examples copied clumsily beside them.
Persian kings drank only water from one special river, which travelled with them in silver jars, according to Herodotus.
Persepolis, the great palace of the Persian kings, was burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC. Ancient writers say the idea came up at a drunken party.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years, until an English cathedral spire beat it in the 1300s.
The Great Pyramid is made of about 2.3 million stone blocks, most heavier than a car.
The Great Pyramid's sides point north, south, east and west almost perfectly, off by less than a tenth of a degree.
The pyramid builders were not slaves: they lived in a town with bakeries and breweries and were buried in tombs of honour beside the pyramids.
The oldest known papyrus with writing on it is the logbook of a boat crew hauling stone for the Great Pyramid, 4,500 years ago.
The pyramid work gangs gave themselves team names, scrawled on the stones, like Friends of Khufu and Drunkards of Menkaure.
The Great Pyramid used to be covered in smooth, polished white stone that gleamed in the sun. Most was carted off to build medieval Cairo.
The Great Pyramid was already over 2,000 years old when the Greek historian Herodotus visited it as a tourist.
Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger made of iron that came from a meteorite: metal that had fallen from the sky.
Tutankhamun's tomb held about 130 walking sticks and canes, and he may have needed them: he probably had a bad foot.
Tutankhamun's tomb was packed with more than 5,000 objects, from golden chariots to boxes of food and his underwear.
Tutankhamun's gold mask weighs about 10 kg, as much as a small dog, and it is made of beaten gold.
Tutankhamun became pharaoh at about 9 years old, and died when he was only about 19.
In the famous story, Cleopatra was smuggled to Julius Caesar rolled up in a carpet. Plutarch actually says it was a sack for bedding.
Cleopatra was the first ruler in her family's 300 years in Egypt to bother learning the Egyptian language, according to Plutarch.
A papyrus from about 1,700 years ago has a recipe for toothpaste: salt, mint, dried iris flowers and pepper.
The ancient Egyptian calendar had 365 days, twelve months of 30 days plus five extra days celebrating the birthdays of gods.
We have 24 hours in a day because the ancient Egyptians split day and night into 12 hours each.
The first recorded strike in history was in Egypt about 1157 BC, when royal tomb builders put down tools because their pay was late.
Egyptian tomb builders kept records of why workers missed work, with excuses like brewing beer and being stung by a scorpion.
The first pyramid was a stack of six giant steps, designed by an architect named Imhotep who was later worshipped as a god.
Khufu's father built three big pyramids and moved more stone than any other pharaoh, including his son.
Egypt's Bent Pyramid changes angle halfway up, probably because the builders feared it would collapse.
The Great Sphinx was not built from blocks: it was carved straight out of the rock of the hill, and it is longer than a jumbo jet.
Napoleon's soldiers did not shoot the nose off the Great Sphinx: drawings show it was already missing long before they arrived.
One set of tunnels in Egypt holds about 8 million mummified animals, mostly dogs.
Ramesses II ruled Egypt for 66 years, lived to about 90 and had more than 100 children.
A tomb built for the sons of Ramesses II in the Valley of the Kings has more than 120 rooms.
Hatshepsut, one of Egypt's most successful pharaohs, was a woman, and her statues often show her wearing a false beard.
Pharaoh Hatshepsut sent ships to a faraway land called Punt and brought back living incense trees, shown on her temple walls.
After Hatshepsut died, someone chiselled her face and name off monuments, trying to erase her from history.
Pharaoh Akhenaten built a brand-new capital city in the desert and tried to make Egypt worship only the Sun disc.
The famous painted bust of Queen Nefertiti, about 3,350 years old, has only one eye; the other was never put in.
The Rosetta Stone, the key to reading hieroglyphs, is a rather dull decree about priests and taxes, written in three scripts.
When Champollion finally cracked hieroglyphs in 1822, he reportedly ran to his brother, shouted that he'd done it, and fainted.
Hieroglyphs were written for more than 3,000 years. The last known one was carved in 394 AD.
An Egyptian surgery manual about 3,600 years old describes 48 injuries with sensible, practical treatments, and almost no magic.
Egyptian doctors put honey on wounds, and it really does help fight infection: hospitals still use medical honey today.
An Egyptian pregnancy test had a woman wet bags of barley and wheat seeds: if they sprouted, she was pregnant. Modern tests found it often worked.
Egyptians played a board game called senet for thousands of years, and Tutankhamun was buried with several sets.
Cleopatra's Needles, the obelisks in London and New York, were carved about 1,400 years before Cleopatra was born.
An unfinished obelisk still lying in its quarry in Egypt would have weighed about 1,000 tonnes, but it cracked.
In the 1960s, the huge temples of Abu Simbel were cut into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground to save them from a new lake.
Twice a year, sunlight reaches deep into the temple of Abu Simbel to light up three statues, while a fourth, a god linked to the underworld, stays in shadow.
Egyptian eye makeup contained lead compounds that, scientists found, may have helped protect against eye infections.
Ancient Egyptian priests shaved their whole bodies every other day to stay clean, according to Herodotus.
Making an Egyptian mummy took about 70 days, most of it spent drying the body out under a natural salt.
Egyptian embalmers usually left the heart inside the mummy, because it would be weighed in the afterlife to judge the person.
Women in ancient Egypt could own property, sign contracts, run businesses and divorce their husbands.
Nubian kings from what is now Sudan conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs for nearly a century.
Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: over 200 of them, built by the kings and queens of Nubia.
A boy pharaoh about 4,300 years ago wrote an excited letter begging an explorer to bring a dancer back to court safely. The explorer carved it on his tomb.
Herodotus says that when a family cat died in Egypt, everyone in the house shaved off their eyebrows in mourning.
Egyptians watched for the bright star Sirius rising at dawn, because it meant the Nile flood was about to arrive.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world, stood for about 1,600 years before earthquakes toppled it.
At Alexandria, books found on arriving ships were taken and copied for the great library, and the owners often got the copies back.
The Library of Alexandria was not destroyed in one great fire: it faded away over centuries.
A Greek engineer in Egypt described a steam engine, a spinning ball powered by steam, about 2,000 years ago.
The first vending machine was invented in Egypt about 2,000 years ago: drop in a coin and it poured out a little holy water.
Euclid's geometry book, written in Alexandria about 2,300 years ago, was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.
Some Egyptian mummies from Roman times have painted portraits over their faces, so lifelike they look like modern paintings.
Ancient Egyptian bread had so much sand and grit in it that many mummies have badly worn-down teeth.
The Egyptian sign for a million was a little man with his arms thrown up in amazement.
A 4,500-year-old cedar boat over 40 metres long was found buried beside the Great Pyramid, in more than 1,200 pieces.
An Egyptian school text mocks every job except being a scribe, to convince boys to keep studying.
The second pyramid at Giza looks taller than the Great Pyramid, but only because it sits on higher ground.
A 4,400-year-old Egyptian tomb painting shows a trained baboon helping a policeman catch a thief.
Ancient Egyptians slept with their heads on headrests made of wood or stone instead of pillows.
Ancient Egyptian children played with dolls, balls, spinning tops and toy animals with moving jaws.
Ancient Romans visited Egypt as tourists and scratched graffiti on statues and in royal tombs, which can still be read today.
Egyptian workers were often paid in bread and beer: thick, nourishing and only mildly alcoholic.
The Nile flooded so reliably that the Egyptian year had three seasons: Flood, Growing and Harvest.
Egypt measured how high the Nile flood rose each year with special staircases, and used the result to set taxes.
In ancient Egypt, a cat could be mummified with as much care as a person, wrapped in linen and laid in a decorated coffin.
Ancient Egyptians wore wigs, and the rich had theirs scented and styled for parties.
Ancient Athenians believed a sacred snake guarded their Acropolis, and left it a honey cake every month, according to Herodotus.
At Egyptian banquets, guests may have worn cones of perfumed fat on their heads, as paintings show; one was found on a real burial in 2019.
When Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 3,000 years of pharaohs came to an end and Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.
A huge stone statue of Ramesses II stood in a busy Cairo square for over 50 years, until it was moved to a museum in 2006.
For the first 50 years of the ancient Olympics, there was only one event: a sprint of about 200 metres.
Ancient Olympic athletes competed completely naked, and the word gymnasium comes from the Greek word for naked.
Married women were banned from watching the ancient Olympics, but women had their own games at Olympia, held in honour of the goddess Hera.
A Spartan princess named Kyniska won the Olympic chariot race twice, around 396 and 392 BC. She owned the horses, so the victory was hers.
Ancient Olympic winners got only a wreath of olive leaves, but back home Athens rewarded its champions with free meals for life.
Archaeologists found 190 pottery votes against one Athenian politician written by just a few hands: someone had prepared them in advance.
Athenian juries had hundreds of members, often 501, chosen by a lottery machine so nobody could bribe them in advance.
In Athenian courts, speeches were timed with a water clock: when the water ran out, you had to stop talking.
Socrates never wrote a single word. Everything we know about him comes from his students.
Aristotle, one of the greatest thinkers in history, was the private tutor of the teenage Alexander the Great.
Alexander the Great conquered an empire stretching from Greece to India by the age of 30.
Alexander the Great founded around 20 cities named Alexandria, and one named after his horse.
Nobody knows where Alexander the Great is buried, even though his tomb was a famous tourist sight in Roman times.
The Antikythera mechanism, a 2,100-year-old Greek gadget full of bronze gears, could predict eclipses. Nothing as complex was built for over 1,000 years.
Hero of Alexandria designed temple doors that swung open by themselves when a fire was lit on the altar, about 2,000 years ago.
A Greek astronomer said the Earth goes around the Sun about 1,800 years before Copernicus, but almost nobody believed him.
Greek thinkers proposed that everything is made of tiny invisible particles called atoms about 2,400 years ago.
In the Middle Ages, a book of Archimedes' maths was scraped off and written over with prayers. Scientists recovered it with special imaging.
Archimedes worked out that pi is between 3.1408 and 3.1429, using shapes with 96 sides.
Pythagoras, of the famous triangle theorem, reportedly banned his followers from eating beans.
The Greek thinker Thales is said to have predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BC. It happened during a battle, and the armies were so shaken they made peace.
Hippocrates and his followers argued that illnesses had natural causes, not punishments from the gods.
The Parthenon survived 2,000 years mostly intact, then blew up in 1687 when a cannonball hit gunpowder stored inside.
Olympic cheats paid fines that bought bronze statues of Zeus, lined up on the way into the stadium with the cheats' names carved on them.
Spartan boys left home at age 7 to start military training, and men lived in barracks until they were about 30.
Sparta used heavy iron bars as money, to make getting rich difficult and stealing pointless.
Spartan women could own land, and by Aristotle's time they owned about two-fifths of Sparta.
At the Battle of Thermopylae, the famous 300 Spartans were joined by thousands of other Greek soldiers.
The original marathon runner, according to Herodotus, ran about 240 km from Athens to Sparta to ask for help in battle.
The ancient theatre at Epidaurus seats about 14,000 people, and plays are still performed there today.
The Trojan Horse does not appear in the Iliad: the poem ends before Troy falls. The story is told in later poems.
Troy was a real city, and its ruins in Turkey hold at least nine cities built on top of each other.
An ancient Greek script called Linear B was cracked in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect who did it as a hobby.
The Minoans of Crete had palaces with clay water pipes and drains about 3,700 years ago.
A Greek island town was buried by a volcano about 3,600 years ago, but the people seem to have escaped: almost no bodies have been found.
Minoan paintings show young people somersaulting over the backs of charging bulls.
The golden Mask of Agamemnon is about 300 years older than the king it was named after.
Ancient Greeks mixed their wine with water. Drinking it straight was considered barbaric.
Symposium, a word now used for academic meetings, originally meant a Greek drinking party.
At Greek parties, guests played a game called kottabos: flicking the last drops of their wine at a target.
The word idiot comes from the Greek for a private person who did not take part in public life.
The word school comes from the Greek word for free time, because only people with spare time could study.
The ancient Greeks believed a stone at Delphi marked the exact centre of the world.
Herodotus wrote about giant gold-digging ants in India. An explorer later suggested the story came from marmots digging up gold dust.
The French city of Marseille was founded by Greek sailors about 2,600 years ago.
Naples comes from the Greek Neapolis, which means new city. It is about 2,500 years old.
A Greek explorer named Pytheas sailed to Britain about 2,300 years ago and described the midnight sun and a frozen sea in the far north.
The philosopher Diogenes is said to have lived in a big clay storage jar in the middle of Athens.
When Alexander the Great asked Diogenes what he could do for him, the story goes, Diogenes told him to move out of his sunlight.
The oldest complete song that survives, with words and music, was carved on a gravestone in Turkey about 2,000 years ago.
After the Mycenaean palaces fell, the Greeks forgot how to write for about 400 years.
A Greek warship called a trireme was rowed by about 170 men sitting in three rows.
Athens built the navy that beat the Persians with money from a lucky silver strike in its own mines.
The word geography was invented by Eratosthenes, a Greek scholar in Egypt who also measured the size of the Earth.
The Greeks called foreigners barbarians because their languages sounded to Greek ears like bar-bar-bar.
A Greek thinker named Anaximander suggested about 2,600 years ago that the Earth floats in space, held up by nothing.
Aristotle pointed out that the Earth must be round, because its shadow on the Moon during an eclipse is always round.
Euclid proved about 2,300 years ago that prime numbers never run out, and his proof is still taught today.
When Philip of Macedon threatened that if he invaded Sparta he would destroy it, the Spartans reportedly replied with one word: If.
Before the Battle of Thermopylae, Persian scouts were amazed to see the Spartans calmly combing their hair.
The statue of Zeus at Olympia was about 12 metres tall, made of gold and ivory, and so big his head nearly touched the roof.
The Colossus of Rhodes stood for only about 54 years before an earthquake knocked it down, and the ruins lay there for about 800 years.
The Colossus of Rhodes almost certainly did not stand with its legs straddling the harbour.
The word mausoleum comes from Mausolus, a ruler whose giant tomb in Turkey was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
A man burned down the Temple of Artemis in 356 BC just to become famous, so the city banned anyone from saying his name.
Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the oldest one, the Great Pyramid, still stands.
Greek athletes rubbed themselves with olive oil and scraped it off afterwards with a curved metal tool, along with the sweat and dirt.
About 2,500 years ago, Greeks dug a 1-km tunnel through a mountain on Samos from both ends, and the two teams met almost exactly.
A house in Pompeii has a mosaic of a snarling dog at its door, with the words Cave canem: beware of the dog.
One of the oldest Greek inscriptions is a cheeky little poem scratched on a drinking cup about 2,700 years ago.
The Greeks used the same letters for numbers: alpha was 1, beta was 2, and so on.
Caligula had two giant ships built as floating palaces on a small lake near Rome. They were finally raised in the 1930s by draining the lake.
Athenian voters were paid for a day's attendance at the assembly, so poor citizens could afford to take part.
Greek doctors swore an oath named after Hippocrates, and a version of it is still taken by some new doctors today.
Fashionable Roman women wore blonde wigs made from the hair of captives from Germany.
Ancient Greek children played with yo-yos, and one appears painted on a vase about 2,500 years old.
Most historians agree Plato invented Atlantis as a story to make a point, but people have searched for it ever since.
The Greeks first called the Black Sea the unwelcoming sea, then renamed it the welcoming sea, perhaps hoping to change their luck.
The Olympic Games ran for over a thousand years before a Roman emperor ended them, probably around 393 AD.
Roman concrete in sea walls actually gets stronger over time, as seawater grows new crystals inside it.
The Pantheon in Rome, nearly 1,900 years old, still has the biggest dome in the world made of concrete without steel bars.
The Pantheon has an 8-metre-wide hole in the top of its dome. When it rains, the rain falls inside and drains away through holes in the floor.
Ancient Rome had about a million people. No European city got that big again until London around 1800.
Romans lived in apartment blocks up to six or seven storeys tall, and Emperor Augustus set a height limit of about 20 metres.
The Colosseum had a giant fabric sunshade over the crowd, rigged by sailors from the Roman navy.
The Colosseum had trapdoors and lifts in the floor, so animals and scenery could pop up in the middle of a show.
Gladiators did not always fight to the death: they were expensive to train, and many fights ended when one gave up.
Gladiators were nicknamed barley men because they ate mostly beans and grains, and they drank plant ash to strengthen their bones.
The Circus Maximus, Rome's chariot racing track, could hold about 150,000 fans, more than any football stadium today.
A Roman chariot racer named Diocles won so much prize money that one historian called him the best-paid athlete of all time.
Romans used urine to wash clothes, and Emperor Vespasian put a tax on collecting it from public toilets.
When his son complained about the urine tax, Vespasian held a coin to his nose and said money does not stink.
Roman public toilets had rows of seats side by side with no walls, and people chatted while they went.
Romans loved garum, a sauce made from fermented fish, and splashed it on almost everything, a bit like ketchup today.
Pompeii was probably buried in October 79 AD, not in August as long believed: a charcoal scribble found in 2018 points to autumn.
The walls of Pompeii are covered in graffiti: election slogans, ads, insults, love notes and people writing that they were there.
A carbonised loaf of bread from Herculaneum, buried by Vesuvius, still has the baker's stamp on it, almost 2,000 years later.
Scrolls burned to charcoal by Vesuvius are being read with X-rays and AI. The first word revealed, in 2023, was purple.
When pirates kidnapped a young Julius Caesar, he laughed at their ransom demand and told them to ask for more.
The year 46 BC lasted 445 days, because Julius Caesar stretched it to fix the calendar.
Caesar probably never said Et tu, Brute. That famous line comes from Shakespeare's play, written over 1,600 years later.
In Roman times, the Ides of March, March 15, was a deadline for paying off debts.
Augustus boasted that he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
Hadrian's Wall ran about 117 km across northern England, from coast to coast, with a small fort every Roman mile.
A birthday party invitation written by a Roman woman to her friend near Hadrian's Wall, about 1,900 years ago, still survives.
A letter to a Roman soldier stationed near Hadrian's Wall mentions a parcel with socks, sandals and two pairs of underpants.
The Romans built about 400,000 km of roads, enough to go around the Earth about ten times.
Romans grabbed lunch at fast-food counters called thermopolia, and Pompeii had dozens of them.
Romans fattened up dormice in special clay jars and ate them as a snack, sometimes dipped in honey.
Rich Romans ate their dinners lying down on couches, propped up on one elbow, usually three people to a couch.
A vomitorium was not a room for throwing up: it was a passage that let crowds pour out of a stadium.
Ancient Rome was fed by 11 aqueducts, and the longest carried fresh water from more than 90 km away.
The Roman aqueduct to Nimes in France drops only about 12 metres over its 50 km length, but the water still flowed all the way.
Rome's great sewer, the Cloaca Maxima, was started around 600 BC, and parts of it still carry water today.
Rich Romans had underfloor heating: hot air from a furnace flowed under raised floors and up through the walls.
Roman soldiers built a whole fortified camp, with walls and ditches, at the end of every day's march.
Hannibal crossed the snowy Alps with about 37 war elephants to attack Rome, and lost most of them soon after.
Cincinnatus was made dictator of Rome, won a war, then gave up his power after 16 days and went back to his farm.
Emperor Commodus fought as a gladiator in the arena himself, and paid himself a huge fee from the public purse for every show.
According to the historian Suetonius, Emperor Caligula planned to make his favourite horse a consul.
Nero did not fiddle while Rome burned: the fiddle hadn't been invented, and he was at his seaside villa when the fire started.
Emperor Claudius added three new letters to the Latin alphabet. They were dropped soon after he died.
The Romans had no lowercase letters: the small letters we use today only developed centuries later, in the Middle Ages.
The Romans had no symbol for zero, which made doing sums in Roman numerals a real headache.
In 69 AD, Rome had four different emperors in a single year, and three of them lost power within months.
In 193 AD, the emperor's bodyguards sold the Roman Empire at an auction. The winner lasted 66 days.
Emperor Diocletian retired to grow cabbages, and his palace in Croatia is still lived in: the old town of Split is built inside it.
The last Roman emperor in the west was a teenager named Romulus Augustulus, after Rome's legendary founder and its first emperor.
Rome's manhole covers still carry the letters SPQR, the motto of the ancient Roman state.
Our word money comes from Juno Moneta, a Roman goddess whose temple housed the mint where coins were made.
The word palace comes from the Palatine Hill in Rome, where the emperors lived in grand houses.
During the Roman festival of Saturnalia, people gave gifts, partied, and masters served dinner to their slaves.
A hill in Rome, Monte Testaccio, is made entirely of about 53 million broken olive oil jars.
A Roman bridge over the Danube, built about 105 AD, was more than a kilometre long, the longest arch bridge for over 1,000 years.
Trajan's Column in Rome is wrapped in a carved spiral strip about 190 metres long, showing more than 2,600 figures.
At the Roman baths in Bath, England, people threw in metal curse tablets asking the goddess to punish whoever stole their clothes.
The Lycurgus Cup, a Roman glass cup, looks green but glows red when lit from inside, thanks to tiny particles of gold and silver.
More than 100 small bronze twelve-sided objects from Roman times have been found, and nobody knows what they were for.
Romans sweetened wine with a syrup boiled in lead pots, which contained lead. Not great for them, but not the cause of Rome's fall.
Roman coins have been found as far away as Vietnam and southern India, carried along ancient trade routes.
The Roman writer Pliny complained that Romans wasted fortunes every year on luxuries from India, China and Arabia, like silk and pearls.
The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius kept a private diary of advice to himself. It became a famous book, Meditations, and it is a bestseller today.
In 195 BC, Roman women filled the streets to demand the end of a law limiting their gold and fancy clothes, and they won.
Augustus set up Rome's first public fire brigade, about 7,000 men who also patrolled the streets at night.
Crassus, the richest man in Rome, ran a private fire brigade that would buy burning houses cheaply before putting the fire out.
The Romans had a goddess of the sewers, called Cloacina, and a shrine to her stood in the Roman Forum.
In 410 AD the Visigoths sacked Rome, the first time in 800 years that an enemy had captured the city.
The Romans believed sacred geese once saved their city by honking to warn of a night attack by the Gauls.
In 9 AD, Germanic tribes destroyed three Roman legions in a forest, and Augustus is said to have cried out, Varus, give me back my legions!
When Queen Boudica's rebels burned Roman London in 60 AD, they left a layer of red ash that archaeologists still find under the city.
Romans thought trousers were for barbarians: proper Roman men wore tunics and togas.
The Romans had a goddess of door hinges, Cardea, and a two-faced god of doorways, Janus, who gave January its name.
Roman soldiers marched with about 30 kg of gear on their backs, and were nicknamed Marius's mules.
A Roman legionary could serve for 25 years before retiring with land or a cash bonus.
Romans used sponges on sticks in their toilets, probably shared, and rinsed them in a channel of running water.
The Pont du Gard, a Roman aqueduct bridge in France, is three stories of arches built without any mortar holding the stones together.
Spartan boys were encouraged to steal food to toughen them up, and were punished only if they got caught.
A Roman doctor's house in Rimini held about 150 surgical tools, including forceps and scalpels very like modern ones.
A Roman law let fathers sell their sons into slavery, but if he did it three times, the son was free of his father for good.
The Senate met in a building that still stands in the Roman Forum, because it was later turned into a church.
At its peak in 117 AD, the Roman Empire stretched from northern Britain all the way to the Persian Gulf.
Rome was supposedly founded on 21 April 753 BC, and Romans still celebrate the city's birthday on that date.
Most Romans ate with their fingers, a spoon and a knife. Dinner forks only caught on in Europe more than a thousand years later.
China's Terracotta Army has about 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, and no two faces look exactly alike.
The Terracotta Army was originally painted in bright colours, but the paint flakes off within minutes of hitting the air.
The Terracotta Army lay hidden for over 2,000 years until 1974, when farmers digging a well hit pieces of a clay soldier.
China's first emperor's tomb has never been opened. An ancient historian said it had rivers of mercury, and the soil above really is full of mercury.
China's first emperor made everyone use the same writing, coins and weights, and even the same width of cart axles.
China's first emperor was obsessed with living forever, and may have been poisoned by mercury pills meant to make him immortal.
Most of the Great Wall that tourists see today is about 600 years old, but the first walls went up over 2,600 years ago.
Paper was invented in China more than 2,100 years ago, and took over a thousand years to reach Europe.
The oldest Chinese writing was found on bones sold in medicine shops as dragon bones, until a scholar noticed the writing in 1899.
Chinese is the oldest writing system still in use: some characters are recognisable on bones from about 3,200 years ago.
The Romans loved Chinese silk but had no idea how it was made. Some Roman writers thought it was combed off the leaves of trees.
