In 132 AD, a Chinese inventor built an earthquake detector: a bronze jar where a dragon dropped a ball into a toad's mouth to show the direction of the quake.
The first Chinese compasses were spoons made of magnetic stone, used for fortune-telling rather than finding the way.
The wheelbarrow was invented in China about 2,000 years ago, more than a thousand years before it appeared in Europe.
Chinese workers were pouring cast iron about 2,500 years ago, over 1,500 years before Europeans could.
A Chinese census from 2 AD counted about 57 million people, one of the oldest headcounts in the world.
A Chinese noblewoman who died about 2,100 years ago was so well preserved that her skin was still soft and her joints could bend.
A silk book from a 2,100-year-old Chinese tomb shows drawings of 29 different kinds of comets.
The oldest known noodles, made from millet, were found in China in a bowl about 4,000 years old.
The oldest known tea was found in the tomb of a Chinese emperor who died in 141 BC.
A Chinese envoy sent west in 138 BC was captured and held for about 10 years, escaped, and carried on with his mission.
A Chinese emperor fought a war around 100 BC just to get the fast, strong horses of Central Asia, which he called heavenly horses.
Bronze masks with huge bulging eyes, about 3,000 years old, found at Sanxingdui in China, look like nothing else in the ancient world.
Fu Hao, a Chinese queen about 3,200 years ago, was also a general who led thousands of soldiers into battle.
A set of 65 bronze bells from a Chinese tomb, about 2,400 years old, can still be played: each bell rings two different notes.
China's first empire, the Qin dynasty, lasted only 15 years, yet the name China may come from it.
The oldest known decimal times table was written on bamboo strips in China about 2,300 years ago.
Around 480 AD, a Chinese mathematician calculated pi to seven decimal places, a record that stood for about 900 years.
Mohenjo-daro, a city in Pakistan about 4,500 years old, had straight streets, covered drains and bathrooms in many houses.
The writing of the Indus Valley civilization has never been deciphered, despite thousands of examples.
Indus Valley traders used stone weights that doubled in size: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on, like computer memory.
The Indus Valley cities had no grand palaces or giant temples, puzzling archaeologists to this day.
The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, about 4,500 years old, was waterproofed with natural tar.
Seals from the Indus Valley have been found in Iraq, showing trade across 2,000 km of sea and land about 4,000 years ago.
The Indus Valley civilization covered more land than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined.
The Indian emperor Ashoka was so horrified by a bloody war he won that he turned to Buddhism and carved messages of peace on pillars.
The lions on top of one of Emperor Ashoka's pillars are now India's national emblem.
Chess began in India about 1,500 years ago as a game called chaturanga, with pieces for elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers.
In 499 AD, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins on its axis, making the stars seem to move.
An ancient Indian medical book explains how to rebuild a nose using a flap of skin from the forehead or cheek.
An Indian king gave a Greek general 500 war elephants in exchange for land, about 2,300 years ago.
Over 3,000 years ago, Chinese kings asked oracle bones about everything, even whether a royal toothache was sent by an angry ancestor.
The biggest ancient tomb in Japan is a keyhole-shaped mound almost 500 metres long, with a larger footprint than the Great Pyramid.
Mummies with reddish hair and wool clothes, buried in western China about 4,000 years ago, turned out to descend from local Ice Age people.
Roman cavalry rode without stirrups. The oldest known stirrups appear in China in the 4th century AD.

Over 2,000 years ago, people in China piped natural gas through bamboo tubes and burned it to boil salt water into salt.
A 2,400-year-old flushing toilet was found in the ruins of a Chinese palace in 2023.
People in China were making a fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit about 9,000 years ago, the oldest known alcohol.
Flutes made from the wing bones of cranes in China about 9,000 years ago can still be played today.
Ban Zhao, a Chinese woman, finished writing an official history of China about 1,900 years ago, after her brother died.
A Chinese thinker described how light through a tiny hole makes an upside-down image, the principle of the camera, about 2,400 years ago.
Two Chinese royals were buried about 2,100 years ago in suits made of more than 2,000 jade pieces sewn together with gold wire.
The name Silk Road was invented in 1877 by a German geographer; ancient traders never called it that.
Chinese astronomers recorded Halley's Comet in 240 BC and a supernova in 185 AD, the oldest one ever written down.
Many Egyptian children had their heads shaved except for one long lock of hair on the side, called the sidelock of youth.
People in the Indus Valley were among the first to grow cotton and spin it into cloth, over 6,000 years ago.
The word sugar comes from Sanskrit: people in ancient India were the first to turn cane juice into crystals.
A Chinese irrigation system built around 256 BC still waters the farms of Sichuan today.
A canal built in China in 214 BC still holds water, and is one of the oldest canals in the world.
Confucius and Pythagoras were born only about 20 years apart, on opposite sides of Asia.
A Chinese record says an embassy from the Roman Empire reached the Han court in 166 AD. Rome and China barely knew each other.
In ancient China, chopsticks were first used for cooking and reaching into hot pots, not for eating.
The Art of War, written in China about 2,500 years ago, is still read by generals, coaches and business people.
Han dynasty emperors had a Music Bureau that collected folk songs from around China, partly to hear what ordinary people thought.
People in China were raising silkworms for silk at least 5,000 years ago, and kept the secret of silk for centuries.
The tomb of China's first emperor also held clay acrobats, musicians and life-size bronze ducks, swans and cranes, not just soldiers.
Silk was so precious in ancient China that it worked as money: officials and soldiers were sometimes paid in rolls of silk.
Ancient Chinese scholars wrote on strips of bamboo tied together with string, like a roll-up blind, and read them from top to bottom.
The Chinese have been playing a board game called Go for at least 2,500 years, and its rules have barely changed.
In ancient China, mirrors were made of polished bronze, and some were cast so that light bouncing off them showed a hidden picture.
A Chinese emperor in 213 BC ordered most books burned, keeping only practical ones like medicine and farming.
Ancient Chinese armies used crossbows with bronze triggers so standard that parts could be swapped between weapons.
People in Peru were building pyramids at Caral about 4,600 years ago, around the same time as the Great Pyramid of Giza.
The Olmecs of Mexico carved giant stone heads up to about 3 metres tall, and dragged the stone for many kilometres without wheels or pack animals.
The Olmecs were making bouncing rubber balls about 3,600 years ago, by mixing tree sap with the juice of a vine.
The name Olmec comes from an Aztec word meaning rubber people, after the rubber trees of their homeland.
The Maya invented the idea of zero on their own, one of only a few peoples in history to do so.
The Maya calendar did not predict the end of the world in 2012: a big cycle simply rolled over, like a car's odometer.
In 2018, lasers fired from planes revealed more than 60,000 hidden Maya houses, roads and buildings under the Guatemalan jungle.
People in Ecuador were using cacao, the plant chocolate comes from, about 5,300 years ago.
The Maya drank chocolate, and a 1,500-year-old jar found in a royal tomb still has the word for cacao painted on it.
Only four ancient Maya books survive. Spanish priests burned most of the others in the 1500s.
Teotihuacan in Mexico had about 100,000 people around 450 AD, more than most cities in Europe at the time.
The Aztecs found the ruins of Teotihuacan centuries after it was abandoned and named it the place where the gods were born. Its real name is unknown.
The Nazca Lines in Peru are giant drawings in the desert, best seen from the air. In 2024, AI helped find 303 new ones.
People in Chile were making mummies about 7,000 years ago, roughly 2,000 years before the Egyptians.
Potatoes were first farmed in the Andes about 8,000 years ago, and thousands of varieties still grow there.
At Poverty Point in Louisiana, about 3,500 years ago, hunter-gatherers moved enough earth to fill tens of thousands of dump trucks.
People were living at Monte Verde in southern Chile about 14,500 years ago, near the far end of the Americas.
Tiwanaku, a great city near Lake Titicaca, was built at about 3,800 metres high, higher than most ski resorts.
The oldest known ball court in the Americas, in Mexico, is about 3,650 years old.
La Danta, a Maya pyramid in Guatemala over 2,000 years old, is one of the largest pyramids in the world by volume.
A Moche lord buried in Peru around 1,750 years ago was found in 1987 with piles of golden jewellery, ear ornaments and a crown.
Llamas and alpacas were tamed in the Andes over 5,000 years ago, and they were the only big animals the Americas ever domesticated.
Ancient Americans never used wheels for transport, but some little clay animals made in Mexico over 1,000 years ago had wheels.
In the ancient Mexican ball game, players could not touch the heavy rubber ball with their hands: they hit it with their hips.
The Maya wrote with a script of hundreds of signs, and scholars only learned to read most of it in the late 20th century.
Chili peppers were being eaten in Mexico at least 6,000 years ago, thousands of years before they reached Asia.
A queen of Kush in Sudan fought the Roman army around 25 BC and won a peace treaty so good that Rome dropped its tax on her people.
A bronze head of Emperor Augustus was buried under the steps of a temple in Sudan, so that everyone entering would walk over him.
The kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia raised stone towers up to 33 metres tall, carved to look like multi-storey buildings.
Aksum, in Ethiopia, minted its own gold coins about 1,750 years ago, and its king was one of the first rulers to put a Christian cross on coins.
A Persian prophet in the 200s AD listed the four great kingdoms of the world: Rome, Persia, China and Aksum in Ethiopia.
The Nok people of Nigeria made striking clay heads more than 2,000 years ago, with carefully styled hair.
After Rome destroyed Carthage, the Roman Senate ordered a Carthaginian farming manual of 28 books translated into Latin.
Carthage had a round military harbour with sheds for about 220 warships, and an island headquarters in the middle.
The Garamantes, a people of the Sahara, built underground water channels and farmed in the desert about 2,000 years ago.
Ethiopia's script, first used in the ancient kingdom of Aksum, is still used to write Amharic today.
A Greek travel guide from about 2,000 years ago tells merchants where to sail and what to buy from Egypt to India and East Africa.
In some ancient Scythian cemeteries, about a third of the warriors buried with weapons were women, which may lie behind Greek tales of Amazons.
The oldest known carpet with a knotted pile is about 2,400 years old and was found frozen in a tomb in Siberia.
Julius Caesar wrote that young druids spent up to 20 years memorising their lore, because they refused to write it down.
A Celtic chief buried in Germany about 2,500 years ago had a bronze cauldron that once held about 500 litres of honey mead.
A Celtic woman buried in France around 500 BC had a bronze wine jar about as tall as a person, big enough to hold over 1,000 litres.
The White Horse of Uffington, a giant chalk drawing on an English hillside, is about 3,000 years old, and locals have scrubbed it clean for centuries.
The oldest known runestone, found in Norway, is about 2,000 years old, centuries before the Vikings.
Attila the Hun died on the night of his wedding in 453 AD, of a severe nosebleed.
About 3,000 years ago, the Lapita people sailed thousands of kilometres across the open Pacific to reach Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.
The oldest known dice, from a town in Iran about 4,500 years ago, look much like the dice we use today.
Sandals woven from tree bark about 10,000 years ago were found in a cave in Oregon, among the oldest shoes in the world.
The ancient Britons painted themselves blue before battle, according to Julius Caesar.
The Paracas people of Peru wove cloaks about 2,000 years ago with colours so well kept in the dry desert that they still look bright today.
One ancient Olympic event was a race in armour: runners sprinted wearing a helmet and carrying a heavy shield.
Julius Caesar noted that the Gauls counted time in nights, not days. English still does it in the word fortnight, fourteen nights.
Ancient people across Europe threw swords, jewellery and coins into rivers and lakes as offerings, and archaeologists still fish them out.
Ancient Romans and Greeks thought of butter as something barbarians ate. They cooked with olive oil.
Ancient Greeks and Romans knew sugar only as a rare medicine from India. To sweeten food, they used honey.
Tomatoes, potatoes, corn and chocolate were completely unknown in ancient Rome, Greece and Egypt: they all came from the Americas.
In ancient Rome, a man's first name was chosen from a list of only about a dozen common names, like Gaius, Marcus and Lucius.
Ancient Egyptians had a god of the household, Bes, who protected mothers and children and was shown as a dancing dwarf sticking out his tongue.
During the ancient Olympics, a sacred truce promised safe travel to athletes and fans, even through cities at war.
Ancient Egyptians believed the god Thoth invented writing, and their name for hieroglyphs meant the words of the gods.
Milo of Croton won six Olympic wrestling titles, and legend says he trained by carrying a calf every day until it grew into a bull.
Nobody in the ancient world wrote dates as BC or AD: a monk invented AD around 525 AD, and BC came even later.
Herodotus wrote that Egyptians did everything backwards from the Greeks: women went to market while men stayed home to weave.
A Roman noblewoman put earrings on her favourite pet eel, and a famous orator was said to have wept when his eel died.
Rich Egyptians in the city of Amarna had bathrooms, and one house even had a limestone toilet seat, about 3,350 years ago.
Roman children played with dolls with jointed arms and legs, some carved from ivory.
King Mithridates of Pontus was so afraid of being poisoned that he took tiny doses of poison every day to build up immunity, the stories say.
Ancient Romans sometimes wore a kind of bikini for sport: a mosaic in Sicily shows women exercising in two-piece outfits.
Some names of ancient Egyptian pet dogs survive, like Brave One, Reliable and Good Herdsman.
A Roman fort in England left behind thousands of shoes, from babies' booties to soldiers' boots.
Rome's Ponte Fabricio has carried people over the river Tiber since 62 BC, more than 2,000 years without a break.
Ancient Greek sailors believed the Mediterranean was surrounded by a giant river called Ocean that circled the whole world.
@bugs|Bugs
There are roughly 10 quintillion insects alive at any moment, which works out to over a billion insects for every human on Earth.
Scientists have named about one million insect species, and estimates suggest millions more are still waiting to be discovered.
Beetles are so varied that about one in every four kinds of animal scientists have ever named is a beetle.
Ants have been on Earth for well over 100 million years, appearing when dinosaurs still ruled the planet.
Scientists estimate about 20 quadrillion ants are alive right now, roughly 2.5 million ants for every person on Earth.
Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry; they use them to grow a fungus garden, and the fungus is their food.
Some tree-living ants that fall off a branch can steer their fall in midair and glide backwards to land on the trunk.
Army ants have no permanent home; each night the workers link their own bodies together to build a living nest called a bivouac.
Weaver ants stitch leaves together into nests using silk squeezed from their own larvae, held in their jaws like glue guns.
Fire ants can survive floods by linking legs and jaws into a floating raft that can stay afloat for days.
Honeypot ants have workers whose abdomens swell with nectar until they hang from the ceiling as living storage jars.
Bullet ants are named for their sting, which people describe as feeling like being shot, with pain lasting up to a day.
Trap-jaw ants snap their jaws shut at speeds over 100 km/h, one of the fastest movements in the animal kingdom.
Trap-jaw ants can bite the ground so hard that the snap launches them into the air, away from danger.
Some ants farm aphids, protecting them from predators and stroking them to collect the sugary honeydew they release.
The Sahara desert ant finds its way home by counting its steps and reading patterns of light in the sky like a built-in compass.
Slave-making ants raid other ant nests, steal the pupae, and raise them as workers for their own colony.
Ant queens of some species can live for nearly 30 years, an astonishing lifespan for an insect.
A supercolony of Argentine ants stretches roughly 6,000 km along the coast of southern Europe.
Some ants in Southeast Asia can explode on purpose, rupturing their bodies to spray sticky toxic goo on attackers.
American cockroaches run so fast that at top speed they rear up and sprint on their back legs alone.
Turtle ants have flat, shield-shaped heads that they use as living doors to plug the entrance of their nest.
A honey bee must visit around two million flowers to make a single pound of honey.
Honey bees tell each other where flowers are with a waggle dance that encodes both direction and distance.
A worker honey bee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its entire life.
Jumping spiders cannot move their big front eyes, so they swivel the retinas inside their heads instead to look around.
Honey almost never spoils, and archaeologists have found pots of honey thousands of years old in ancient Egyptian tombs.
A honey bee queen can lay up to around 2,000 eggs in a single day during peak season.
Honey bees can recognise human faces in lab experiments by learning patterns of features.
Male honey bees, called drones, have no stinger and die after mating with a queen.
In winter, honey bees huddle into a ball and shiver their flight muscles to keep the middle of the cluster nearly as warm as a human body.
Japanese honey bees can kill an attacking giant hornet by surrounding it in a ball and cooking it with their body heat.
Bees see ultraviolet light, and many flowers have hidden UV patterns that act like landing strips pointing to the nectar.
Bumblebees can pick up the faint electric field of a flower and use it to tell whether another bee just visited.
Some flowers only release pollen when shaken, so bumblebees grab on and vibrate until the pollen pours out like salt from a shaker.
Bumblebees given tiny balls kept rolling them around even with no reward, which scientists think may be a form of play.
Some stingless bees build their nest entrances with sticky resin to trap invading ants.
A honey bee colony can contain around 50,000 bees in summer, all daughters of a single queen except the drones.
Honey bees fan their wings at the hive entrance to evaporate water from nectar until it thickens into honey.
Termites in Africa build mounds taller than a giraffe, some reaching around 9 metres high.
Termite mounds work like giant lungs, with tunnels that help air flow and keep the nest at a steady temperature.
A termite queen can swell to many times the size of her workers, live for decades and, in some species, lay thousands of eggs a day.
Termites can live on wood only because tiny microbes in their guts break it down for them; without those helpers they would starve.
Unlike ant and bee colonies, a termite colony has a king as well as a queen, and he stays by her side for life.
In one termite species, old workers carry blue crystals in pouches on their backs and burst themselves open to spray toxic goo at invaders.
Magnetic termites in Australia build thin, wedge-shaped mounds lined up north to south, which helps control heat.
A field of termite mounds in Brazil covers an area roughly the size of Great Britain, and some mounds are about 4,000 years old.
The monarch butterfly migrates up to about 4,800 km between Canada and the mountains of central Mexico.
No single monarch makes the full round trip; it takes several generations to complete one annual migration cycle.
Butterflies taste with their feet, using sensors that tell them whether a leaf is good for their caterpillars.
The colored dust that rubs off a butterfly's wing is really thousands of tiny scales; underneath them, the wing is clear.
The blue morpho butterfly has no blue color in its wings; tiny ridges on its scales bend light so that only blue bounces back to your eyes.
Some butterflies drink tears from the eyes of turtles and crocodiles to get the salt they need.
Ladybugs are named after Our Lady, the Virgin Mary; in many parts of Europe the beetle was long known as Our Lady's bird.
Inside its chrysalis, a caterpillar dissolves much of its body into a soupy goo, then rebuilds itself as a butterfly.
Research suggests some moths can remember things they learned as caterpillars, even after metamorphosis.
A caterpillar can grow to around 1,000 times its hatching weight before it pupates.
Some caterpillars have more than 4,000 muscles, while a human body has around 600.
The glasswing butterfly has see-through wings that make it hard for predators to spot in flight.
The Atlas moth has wingtips that look like snake heads, a trick that may scare off predators.
Adult luna moths have no mouth and do not eat; they live only about a week to find a mate.
Male moths can detect a female's scent from several kilometres away using their feathery antennae.
The death's-head hawkmoth can squeak, and it sneaks into beehives to steal honey.
Some tiger moths fight back against hunting bats by making clicking sounds that jam the bats' echolocation.
Moths circle lamps not because they love light; they keep their backs to the brightest part of the sky, and a lamp tricks them into spinning.
The hummingbird hawk-moth hovers in front of flowers and sips nectar with a long tongue, looking just like a tiny bird.
Darwin saw an orchid with a nectar tube about 30 cm deep and predicted a moth with a tongue that long; it was found decades after he died.
Silk from a single silkworm cocoon can be unwound into one thread up to about 900 metres long.
Domesticated silkworm moths have been bred for so long they cannot fly and cannot survive in the wild.
Some caterpillars look like bird droppings so that predators simply ignore them.
The puss caterpillar looks like a fluffy wig, but its hairs hide venomous spines with an extremely painful sting.
Spicebush swallowtail caterpillars have fake eyespots that make them look like small snakes.
Rhinoceros beetles can carry around 30 times their own weight on their backs, like a person walking around with a car on top.
A dung beetle of one species was found to pull over 1,000 times its own body weight.
Some dung beetles navigate at night by following the glow of the Milky Way.
Dung beetles roll their dung balls in straight lines away from the pile so other beetles cannot steal them.
A summer honey bee worker lives only about five or six weeks, but bees born in autumn can survive through the whole winter.
A bombardier beetle defends itself by firing a spray as hot as boiling water from its rear, in rapid pulses like a tiny machine gun.
Firefly light is cold light: it gives off almost no heat, unlike an old-fashioned bulb, which wastes most of its energy as heat.
In some places in Southeast Asia, thousands of fireflies flash in perfect sync along riverbanks.
Some female fireflies copy the flash pattern of other species to lure males in and eat them.
Ladybugs can eat thousands of aphids during their lifetime, which makes gardeners love them.
When attacked, ladybugs ooze a smelly, bitter yellow liquid from their knees that makes birds think twice.
A goliath beetle grub can weigh about 100 grams, as much as a small apple, making it one of the heaviest insects ever weighed.
The titan beetle of the Amazon can grow over 16 cm long and has jaws strong enough to snap a pencil.
Diving beetles carry a bubble of air under their wing covers so they can breathe underwater.
The Namib desert beetle drinks fog: it tips its body into the misty wind and lets droplets roll down its back into its mouth.
Some fire beetles can sense the heat of a forest fire from many kilometres away and fly toward it to lay eggs in freshly burnt trees.
Only female mosquitoes bite; they need protein from blood to make their eggs, while males drink nectar.
Mosquitoes find you partly by tracking the carbon dioxide you breathe out, from several metres away.
Mosquitoes are the deadliest animals to humans, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths every year by spreading diseases such as malaria.
A mosquito's mouth is not one needle but six, including two saw-like blades and a tube for drinking.
Mosquitoes beat their wings around 500 to 800 times per second, which makes their high-pitched whine.
Some mosquito eggs can survive dry for months and hatch as soon as they are flooded with water.
The Hercules beetle can grow up to about 17 cm long, and more than half of that length can be the male's giant horn.
Flies see the world in slow motion compared to us, which is why swatting one is so hard.
A housefly cannot chew; it spits digestive juices onto food and sucks up the liquid.
Flies can take off backwards in a fraction of a second when they sense a swatter coming.
Flies have only two wings; their second pair shrank into tiny knobs that wobble like gyroscopes and keep them balanced in flight.
Hoverflies look like wasps with bold yellow and black stripes, but they have no sting at all.
A honey bee queen has a smooth stinger she can use again and again, but she saves it almost entirely for fighting rival queens.
The botfly lays eggs on a mosquito, which then carries them to a mammal where the larvae burrow into the skin.
About three quarters of the genes behind human diseases have a matching version in fruit flies, which is why these tiny flies fill science labs.
The first animals sent into space on purpose were fruit flies, in 1947, and they came back alive.
Blow flies can find a dead animal within minutes, and forensic scientists use them to estimate time of death.
Maggots of certain blowflies are used in hospitals to clean wounds, because they eat only dead tissue.
A male stalk-eyed fly has eyes on long stalks, and the fly with the widest eyes usually wins the females.
The petroleum fly is the only insect known to grow up inside pools of crude oil, feeding on bugs that get stuck in the goo.
Some midges beat their wings over 1,000 times per second, among the fastest wingbeats ever measured.
Dragonflies catch their prey in mid-air with a success rate that can top 90 percent.
A dragonfly can fly forwards, backwards, sideways, and hover, moving each of its four wings independently.
Dragonflies have nearly 360 degree vision, thanks to huge eyes made of up to about 30,000 lenses.
Ancient griffinflies, relatives of dragonflies, had wingspans of about 70 cm some 300 million years ago.
Dragonfly nymphs live underwater and shoot out a hinged lower jaw to grab tadpoles and small fish.
Dragonfly nymphs breathe through gills inside their rear ends, and by squirting water out hard they can jet forward.
The globe skimmer dragonfly makes a multi-generation migration of up to about 18,000 km across the Indian Ocean.
Some dragonflies can zip along at around 50 km/h, about as fast as a car driving through town.
Grasshoppers hear with ears on their bellies, just behind their back legs.
Katydids have their ears on their front legs, just below the knees, so they listen with their legs.
Crickets chirp by rubbing a scraper on one wing against a file of ridges on the other.
You can roughly estimate the temperature from how fast snowy tree crickets chirp, since they chirp faster when warm.
Desert locusts can switch from solitary insects to swarming ones when crowded, even changing color.
A large desert locust swarm can contain billions of locusts and eat as much food in a day as millions of people.
A single locust can eat roughly its own weight in plants every day.
Some male crickets dig burrows shaped like megaphones to make their songs louder.
Mole crickets have front legs like shovels and dig tunnels underground like tiny moles.
The giant weta of New Zealand can weigh more than a sparrow, making it one of the heaviest insects.
Cicadas drink so much watery tree sap that they pee in fast jets, and a tree full of them can make a light cicada rain.
Up close, some cicadas are about as loud as a motorcycle, making them among the noisiest insects on the planet.
Cicadas don't sing with their legs; they click drum-like plates on their sides in and out hundreds of times a second.
A cockroach can live for about a week without its head, until it dies of thirst.
Cockroaches can hold their breath for around 40 minutes, and they can survive being underwater for about that long.
American cockroaches can run about 50 body lengths per second.
Cockroaches existed long before the dinosaurs, with ancestors dating back over 300 million years.
A cockroach can squeeze through a crack as thin as two stacked coins by flattening its body to a quarter of its height.
The Madagascar hissing cockroach hisses by forcing air out through breathing holes on its body.
Praying mantises are the only insects known to see in 3D with stereo vision like ours.
A praying mantis can turn its head about 180 degrees to look over its shoulder.
Some praying mantises catch and eat hummingbirds, frogs and lizards, prey far bigger than you would expect.
The orchid mantis looks so much like a flower that insects fly right up to it to be eaten.
Stick insects are among the longest insects, with one Chinese species reaching about 64 cm with legs stretched out.
Many stick insect females can lay eggs that hatch without any males, producing all-female generations.
Some stick insect eggs look like seeds, so ants carry them into their nests where they stay safe.
The leaf insect looks so much like a leaf that its body even has fake veins and brown, bitten-looking edges.
Earwigs are caring mothers, guarding their eggs and licking them clean to protect them from mould.
The belief that earwigs crawl into people's ears to lay eggs in the brain is a myth.
A flea can jump over 100 times its own body length, launching with an acceleration far greater than a space shuttle's.
The claim that people swallow spiders in their sleep is a myth; spiders tend to avoid the vibrations of a breathing, snoring person.
Lice have lived on humans for so long that their DNA helps scientists date when people started wearing clothes.
Bed bugs can go for months without a single meal, patiently waiting for someone to climb into bed.
Bed bugs inject a numbing chemical when they bite, so most people sleep right through it.
Silverfish have been around for about 400 million years and can live for several years.
Springtails flip themselves through the air with a spring-loaded tail folded under their body.
Mayfly adults of many species live only a day or less, and some have no working mouthparts at all.
Mayfly nymphs can live underwater for a year or more before their short adult life.
Swarms of emerging mayflies along the Mississippi can be so dense they show up on weather radar.
Water striders walk on water thanks to thousands of tiny water-repellent hairs on their legs.
Backswimmers swim upside down and carry a bubble of air to breathe under the water.
The giant water bug can catch and eat fish, frogs and even small turtles.
In giant water bugs of some species, the female glues her eggs onto the male's back and he carries them until they hatch.
Caddisfly larvae build portable homes out of sand, pebbles or twigs, glued together with silk.
Artists have given caddisfly larvae gold flakes and gems, and the larvae built sparkling jewelled cases.
Antlions dig cone-shaped pits in sand and wait at the bottom with open jaws for ants to slide in.
Lacewing larvae carry the empty skins of their prey on their backs as camouflage.
Thrips are so tiny that many are under 1 mm long, yet they can ride the wind for hundreds of kilometres.
Aphids can be born already pregnant, with their own daughters developing inside them.
In ideal conditions, a single aphid could in theory produce billions of descendants in one season.
The spittlebug nymph hides inside a frothy blob of bubbles that it blows from its rear end.
The froghopper can leap about 70 cm into the air, over 100 times its own length, making it one of nature's champion jumpers.
Treehoppers have wildly shaped helmets that can look like thorns, ants or even bird droppings.
Some red food coloring is made from crushed cochineal bugs, tiny insects that live on cactus plants.
The shiny glaze on some candies and old wooden furniture, called shellac, is made from a goo produced by tiny lac bugs.
Whiteflies are not flies at all but tiny sap-sucking bugs related to aphids.
Termites are really a kind of social cockroach; their DNA places them right inside the cockroach family tree.
Weight for weight, some spider silk is stronger than steel and tougher than the material used in bulletproof vests.
Darwin's bark spider of Madagascar spins webs right across rivers, with anchor lines up to about 25 metres long.
Spider silk is a liquid inside the spider and only turns into a solid thread as it is pulled out of the body.
Many baby spiders travel by ballooning: they let out silk threads and float away on the breeze, sometimes kilometres up and hundreds of kilometres away.
A spider in your bathtub did not climb up the drain; it most likely fell in looking for water and could not climb the slippery sides.
Spiders may use the Earth's natural electric field to help lift off when they balloon, even on days with no wind.
The world's spiders eat an estimated 400 to 800 million tonnes of prey a year, more than all the meat and fish humans eat.
Spiders can't chew, so they pump digestive juices into their prey and slurp it up as a liquid.
Many orb-weaving spiders eat their old web every day and recycle the silk to build a new one.
Spiders have blue blood, because it carries oxygen using copper instead of iron.
Spiders stretch their legs out using fluid pressure, which is why a dead spider's legs curl up underneath it.
Most spiders have eight eyes, but many still see poorly and feel the world through vibrations in their web.
Jumping spiders have excellent eyesight and can leap many times their own body length to pounce on prey.
Jumping spiders tie a silk safety line to the ground before they jump, like a climber's rope.
Peacock spiders are only a few millimetres long, yet the males raise colorful fans and dance to impress females.
Portia jumping spiders plan routes to reach their prey, even taking detours where they lose sight of it for a while.
The goliath birdeater is the heaviest spider on Earth, about the size of a dinner plate with its legs spread.
Despite its name, the goliath birdeater rarely eats birds; it mostly eats insects, worms and frogs.
Goliath birdeaters can make a hissing sound by rubbing bristles on their legs together.
The giant huntsman spider of Laos has a leg span of about 30 cm, the widest of any spider known.
The diving bell spider lives underwater, breathing from a bubble of air it traps in a silk dome.
The bolas spider swings a single sticky ball on a thread that smells like a female moth, and catches the males that come.
The ogre-faced spider holds a net between its front legs and throws it over insects walking past at night.
Ogre-faced spiders have two huge eyes that see so well in the dark that they outperform those of cats and owls.
Spitting spiders catch prey by spraying it with a zigzag of venomous glue from their fangs.
Pelican spiders have such long necks and jaws that they look like tiny birds, and they hunt only other spiders.
Some jumping spiders look and walk exactly like ants, waving their front legs in the air to fake antennae.
One jumping spider from Central America is mostly vegetarian, eating little food bundles that grow on acacia plants.
Some spiders look just like bird droppings, which keeps hungry birds from giving them a second glance.
The Cyclocosmia trapdoor spider has a flat, hard rear end that it uses to plug its burrow like a cork.
In some social spiders, thousands of spiders share one giant web and hunt together to catch big insects.
Wolf spider mothers carry dozens of babies on their backs until the spiderlings are ready to leave.
In some spider species, the mother lets her babies eat her alive as their very first meal.
Shine a flashlight across a lawn at night and you may see wolf spider eyes glowing back like tiny diamonds.
Male nursery web spiders bring females a gift of food wrapped in silk, so they are less likely to be eaten.
Female black widows sometimes eat the male after mating, but in many cases the male gets away unharmed.
Mirror spiders have silvery patches on their backs that can shrink and grow when they are disturbed.
A spider can make up to seven different kinds of silk, each for a job like trapping, wrapping, or swaddling eggs.
Orb-weaving spiders can build a whole new web in under an hour.
Spiders live on every continent except Antarctica, and over 50,000 species have been named.
Spiders have lived on Earth for more than 300 million years, long before the first dinosaurs.
Some salt-marsh wolf spiders survive more than a day underwater during floods by slipping into a coma, then wake up once they dry out.
Scorpions glow bright blue-green under ultraviolet light, and scientists still are not sure why.
Scorpions can be frozen overnight and then walk away when they thaw out in the sun.
Some scorpions can survive a whole year without eating a single meal.
Scorpions give birth to live babies, which climb onto their mother's back and ride there until they grow.
Scorpions have been around for over 430 million years, and their basic body shape has hardly changed since.
Millions of years ago, giant sea scorpions, distant cousins of today's scorpions, grew longer than a grown man.
The vinegaroon, a whip scorpion, sprays an acid that smells strongly of vinegar when it feels threatened.

Daddy longlegs, or harvestmen, are not spiders: they have no silk, no venom, and a single rounded body.

Ticks cannot jump or fly; they climb onto grass, hold out their front legs, and wait to grab anything walking past.
A female tick can swell to about 100 times her starting weight while feeding on blood.
A tick's saliva contains a painkiller, which is why people often do not notice one feeding for days.

A mosquito can drink about two to three times its own weight in blood in a single meal.
Most adults have tiny mites living in the pores of their faces; they crawl out at night to mate, then slip back in before morning.

Some mites spend their whole lives on the feathers of birds, and a few kinds even live inside the hollow quills.

Earthworms have no lungs; they breathe through their skin, which is why they must stay moist to survive.

The giant Gippsland earthworm of Australia can grow longer than a person is tall, and you can sometimes hear it gurgle underground.
A single hectare of healthy farmland can be home to over a million earthworms.
Earthworms swallow soil as they tunnel, and over a year they can turn over tonnes of earth in a single field.
In worm grunting, people rub a wooden stake to make the ground buzz, and hundreds of earthworms wriggle up to the surface.
Earthworms grip the soil with tiny bristles along their bodies, which is why a robin has to tug so hard.
Nobody is fully sure why earthworms crawl out after rain; it may be easier for them to travel across wet ground.
Many earthworms in Canada and the northern US are newcomers from Europe; the Ice Age glaciers wiped out the native ones.
Every earthworm is both male and female at once, but it still needs a partner to make baby worms.
Doctors still use leeches after some surgeries to keep blood flowing in reattached fingers and ears.
A medical leech can drink several times its own weight in blood in one meal and then go months without eating.

Tiny roundworms frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 46,000 years were thawed out and came back to life.

A parasite can turn a snail's eye stalks into pulsing, striped tubes that look like caterpillars, so birds eat them.

A snail's tongue is covered in thousands of tiny teeth arranged in rows, like a rough file for scraping food.
A snail cannot leave its shell, because the shell is part of its body and grows along with it.

Cone snails, sea snails with beautiful shells, fire a venomous harpoon fast enough to stun fish.
Limpets, small sea snails, have teeth made of one of the strongest natural materials ever tested.
Tardigrades, or water bears, are smaller than a grain of salt but have eight stubby legs with claws.

Tardigrades live almost everywhere, from mountaintops and rainforests to the deep sea and the moss on your roof.

Despite their name, centipedes never have exactly 100 legs, because they always have an odd number of pairs.
In 2021, scientists found the first millipede with over 1,000 legs, living deep underground in an Australian mine.
The giant Amazonian centipede can grow about 30 cm long and catches bats in caves by hanging from the ceiling.
A centipede's front legs have become venomous fangs, so it bites with its legs.

Light is so fast that a modern computer chip ticks billions of times a second, and light only gets about 10 cm per tick.
Light slows down by a quarter when it enters water, and by about a third when it passes through glass.
In 1999, scientists slowed a beam of light down to about 17 meters per second, slower than a bicycle.
Scientists have stopped light completely inside a special crystal, held it for about a minute, and then let it go again.
White light is not a color of its own: it is every color of the rainbow mixed together, as Isaac Newton showed with a prism.
The sky is blue because the air scatters blue sunlight around much more than red, so blue reaches your eyes from every direction.
Sunsets are red and orange because the light has crossed so much air near the horizon that most of the blue got scattered away.
Clouds look white because their droplets are big enough to scatter every color of light equally.
Every rainbow is actually a full circle: the ground hides the bottom half, but from a plane you can sometimes see the whole ring.
No two people ever see exactly the same rainbow, because each rainbow depends on exactly where your eyes are.
The sky between the two arcs of a double rainbow is darker than the rest of the sky, and it has a name: Alexander's dark band.
A rainbow is always on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun, centered right on the shadow of your own head.
Pink-purple magenta is not in the rainbow at all: your brain makes it up when your eyes get red and blue light at the same time.
Every color you have ever seen is your brain mixing signals from just three kinds of color sensors in your eyes.
Your phone screen has no yellow pixels at all: it fakes yellow by lighting red and green dots side by side.
Radio waves, microwaves, X-rays and visible light are all the same thing: light, just with different wave sizes.
Some radio waves are longer than a football field, while gamma rays can be smaller than the core of an atom.
Your body glows all the time in infrared light, which is why a thermal camera can see you in total darkness.
Your TV remote shines an invisible light, and many phone cameras can see it flashing when you press a button.
Many flowers have bullseye patterns that only show up in ultraviolet light, which bees can see and we cannot.
A mirror does not really swap left and right: it swaps front and back, and your brain reads that as a left-right flip.
Snow is made of clear ice, but it looks white because its countless crystal faces bounce all the colors back at you.
Sunlight actually pushes on you: a very gentle shove, too weak to feel, but strong enough to steer spacecraft.
In 2010, a Japanese spacecraft called IKAROS unfolded a huge thin sail and flew through space pushed only by sunlight.
Thunder rumbles instead of cracking once, because sound from different parts of a long lightning bolt reaches you at different times.
Most of the internet travels as flashes of light through glass threads, including cables lying across the ocean floor.
The glass in internet cables is so clear that light can travel about 15 kilometers through it and still keep half its brightness.
A diamond sparkles because it bends light so strongly that light bounces around inside before escaping toward your eyes.
A straw in a glass of water looks broken because light changes direction as it leaves the water.
The shimmering water on a hot road is not water at all: it is a picture of the sky, bent upward by hot air near the ground.
Polarized sunglasses work because glare bouncing off water and roads is mostly light vibrating side to side, which the lenses block.
A laser beam shot at the Moon spreads out so much that it is several kilometers wide when it arrives.
You can measure the speed of light with a microwave oven and a chocolate bar: take out the turntable, heat it, and measure the gap between melted spots.
Crunch a wintergreen candy in a dark room and it throws off tiny blue-green sparks of light, made as the sugar crystals crack apart.
Lasers can cool atoms to a millionth of a degree above absolute zero, colder than anywhere known in nature.
Peeling sticky tape in a vacuum gives off X-rays, strong enough that scientists used it to take an X-ray picture of a finger.
A green laser pointer fires roughly ten million billion tiny particles of light every second.
Human eyes adapted to the dark can react to just a handful of particles of light, and may even notice a single one.
Tap a mug of fresh hot chocolate with a spoon and the note rises as you go, because tiny air bubbles slow the sound down, then escape.
Fireflies make light with a chemical reaction that gives off very little heat, so it is often called cold light.
An LED bulb uses about 75 percent less electricity than an old-style bulb to make the same amount of light.
The color of something glowing hot tells you its temperature: red hot is the coolest, then yellow, then white hot.
Old orange street lamps make light of almost a single color, which is why cars under them all look the same dull shade.
The swirling colors on a soap bubble come from light bouncing off both sides of a film thinner than a wave of light.
A peacock's feathers have no blue or green pigment at all: tiny structures in them bend light to create the colors.
Almost no animals make blue pigment: blue birds and butterflies get their color from tiny structures that play tricks with light.
It makes almost no difference which side of aluminum foil touches your food. The shiny and dull sides are just a leftover from how it is rolled at the factory.
Your pupils can grow so much in the dark that they let in more than 10 times as much light as in bright sun.
The lens in your eye projects the world upside down onto the back of your eye, and your brain flips it right side up.
A black car gets hotter in the sun than a white one because black soaks up almost all the light instead of bouncing it away.
The tiny tracks on a CD split white light into rainbows, the same way a prism does.
White paper reflects almost as much light as a mirror does. The difference is that paper scatters it in every direction, so it shows no picture.
Water is actually very slightly blue on its own, which is part of why deep pools and glaciers look blue.
Wet sand and wet clothes look darker because water lets more light sink in and get absorbed, instead of bouncing straight back off the surface.
You will never see a rainbow from the ground when the Sun is higher than about 42 degrees, which is why rainbows show up in the morning and late afternoon.
Fresh snow can reflect up to about 80 percent of the Sun's ultraviolet rays, so skiers can get sunburned under the chin and nose.
The sky scatters violet light even more than blue, but it looks blue because sunlight has less violet in it and our eyes are less sensitive to violet.
Nuclear reactors in pools of water glow an eerie blue, because tiny particles there outrun light in water and make a light boom.
An LED works in reverse too: shine a bright light on one and it makes a tiny electric current, like a miniature solar panel.
Atoms are almost entirely empty space: if an atom were a football stadium, its core would be about the size of a pea.
If you removed all the empty space from the atoms in every human on Earth, everyone would fit inside a sugar cube.
Liquid oxygen is magnetic: pour it between the poles of a strong magnet and it hangs there as a pale blue bridge.
You never really touch anything: the electrons in your hand push away the electrons in the object before atoms ever meet.
There are more atoms in a glass of water than there are glasses of water in all the oceans on Earth.
A single grain of sand contains more atoms than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the world.
Every breath you take probably contains at least one molecule of air from Julius Caesar's last breath.
Atoms are so small that several hundred thousand of them lined up side by side would fit across the width of a human hair.
Almost every atom in your body has been around for billions of years, long before Earth existed.
Fridge magnets stick on only one side, because they are made of stripes of alternating poles arranged so the pull is strong on the back and weak on the front.
Your body replaces most of its atoms over the years, so very little of you is made of the same stuff you were made of as a baby.
An electron has never been seen to have any size at all: as far as experiments can tell, it is a perfect point.
A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron, so almost all the weight of an atom sits in its tiny core.
Most of the mass of a proton does not come from the particles inside it, but from the energy of the forces holding them together.
Quantum particles can tunnel through walls they should not be able to cross, and the Sun only shines because of it.
Your phone's memory chips rely on electrons doing something impossible in everyday life: passing straight through a barrier.
Earth's magnetic field has weakened by about 9 percent over the last 200 years, though that does not mean a flip is coming soon.
Fire single electrons one by one at two narrow slits and they build up a striped pattern, as if each one went through both slits.
If you watch which slit each electron goes through, the striped pattern vanishes, and they act like ordinary little balls.
Einstein called quantum entanglement spooky action at a distance, and experiments have since shown it is real.
Two entangled particles stay linked so that measuring one instantly tells you about the other, even on opposite sides of Earth.
Entanglement cannot be used to send messages faster than light, no matter how far apart the particles are.
In 2017, a Chinese satellite shared entangled particles of light between ground stations more than 1,200 km apart.
The more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can know about how fast it is moving, and that is a law of nature.
Even at absolute zero, atoms never stop jiggling completely, because quantum physics forbids perfect stillness.
Schrodinger's cat, alive and dead at the same time, was invented to show how absurd quantum rules look when applied to cats.
Quantum physics is the most precisely tested theory in history: one prediction matches experiment to better than one part in a billion.
Every electron in the universe is completely identical to every other one; there is no way to tell two apart.
A physicist once joked that all electrons look the same because there is only one electron, zigzagging back and forth through time.
Every particle has an antimatter twin, and when matter meets antimatter they wipe each other out in a flash of energy.
A banana gives off a tiny bit of antimatter: its natural potassium releases a positron, an anti-electron, every so often.
Antimatter is the most expensive substance ever made: one gram would cost trillions of dollars to produce.
Scientists think the Big Bang made almost equal amounts of matter and antimatter, and nobody knows for sure why matter won.
Hospitals use antimatter every day: PET scans work by spotting the bursts of energy made when anti-electrons meet ordinary electrons inside the body.
You are slightly radioactive too: thousands of atoms inside your body break apart every second.
A neutrino could pass through a wall of lead a light-year thick and still have a good chance of coming out the other side.
In 2017 scientists found a big hidden space inside the Great Pyramid of Giza, using particles from space called muons that pass through stone.
The IceCube detector is a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice wired with thousands of light sensors, waiting for rare flashes from ghostly particles called neutrinos.
Particles made by cosmic rays high in the sky should die before reaching the ground, but their fast clocks run slow, so they make it.
Many smoke detectors contain a speck of radioactive americium, which lets a tiny current flow through the air until smoke blocks it.
Carbon dating works because living things take in a little radioactive carbon, and after they die half of it vanishes every 5,730 years.
Uranium in rocks decays so slowly that half of it takes about 4.5 billion years to disappear, roughly the age of the Earth.
The heat inside the Earth comes partly from radioactive atoms decaying deep below your feet.
In 1938, scientists discovered that uranium atoms could be split, releasing enormous energy, and the nuclear age began.
Splitting every atom in a kilogram of the right kind of uranium would release as much energy as burning about 3,000 tonnes of coal.
Two billion years ago, a uranium deposit in Gabon started running as a natural nuclear reactor, all by itself.
In a nuclear power plant, splitting atoms just boils water; the steam spins a turbine like in a coal plant.
Gram for gram, the Sun's core makes less heat than your body does. It is so hot only because it is enormous and holds its heat in.
A collision between two protons in the Large Hadron Collider carries about the energy of a flying mosquito, packed into a space a trillion times smaller.
Fusion reactors on Earth must heat their fuel to over 100 million degrees C, several times hotter than the Sun's core.
In 2022, a US lab got more energy out of a fusion reaction than its lasers put in, a first in history.
Particle accelerators smash protons together at more than 99.999999 percent of the speed of light.
The Large Hadron Collider's tunnel is a ring about 27 km around, buried up to 175 meters under France and Switzerland.
The magnets of the Large Hadron Collider are kept colder than outer space, at about minus 271 degrees C.
A proton in the Large Hadron Collider laps the 27 km ring about 11,000 times every second.
The Higgs boson, predicted in 1964, was finally found in 2012 after the biggest machine ever built went looking for it.
The particles inside protons, called quarks, have never been seen alone: pull two apart and the energy makes new quarks instead.
The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 at CERN, a physics lab, so that scientists around the world could share their results more easily.
Quarks come in six kinds with odd names: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top.
The word quark was taken from a line in James Joyce's novel Finnegans Wake: Three quarks for Muster Mark!
The top quark is the heaviest known elementary particle, about as heavy as an entire gold atom.
Some particles live for less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second before falling apart.
A free neutron, outside an atom, lasts only about 15 minutes on average before it falls apart.
Protons may last forever: experiments show they survive at least a trillion trillion times the current age of the universe.
Old uranium glass, made with a pinch of uranium for color, glows bright green under a black light and can make a Geiger counter click.
In 1989, IBM scientists spelled out their company name using 35 individual atoms.
In 2013, IBM made a stop-motion movie called A Boy and His Atom, using single molecules as the pixels.
Scientists have made atoms so cold they merge into a single quantum blob, a strange state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.
Watch hands once glowed in the dark thanks to radioactive radium paint, until the harm done to the women who painted them became clear in the 1920s.
Every time you use a laser, a computer chip or an MRI scan, you rely on quantum physics.
Silly Putty bounces like a rubber ball, slowly flows into a puddle if you leave it alone, and shatters if you hit it hard with a hammer.
Your head is aging a tiny bit faster than your feet, because time runs faster the farther you are from Earth's center.
Scientists have measured time running differently between two clocks just 33 centimeters apart in height.
If GPS ignored Einstein's relativity, your map position would drift by about 10 kilometers every single day.
Scott Kelly spent nearly a year on the space station, so he came back a few milliseconds younger than he would have been.
In 1971, scientists flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners and found they disagreed with clocks left on the ground, just as Einstein predicted.
If you could travel near the speed of light for a while and come back, you could find that decades had passed on Earth.
There is no universal now: two events that happen at the same time for you can happen at different times for someone moving past.
At the speed of light, time would stand still: from light's point of view, its trip across the universe takes no time at all.
E = mc2 means mass is packed with energy: a single gram of anything holds more energy than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.
A hot cup of coffee weighs a tiny bit more than the same cup when cold, because energy has mass.
Einstein published four world-changing papers in 1905 while working as a clerk in a patent office.
Einstein won his Nobel Prize not for relativity, but for explaining how light knocks electrons out of metal.
Einstein's theory says gravity is not a pull at all: massive things bend space and time, and other objects follow the curves.
Earth actually spins once every 23 hours and 56 minutes. The extra 4 minutes in our 24-hour day come from moving along our orbit around the Sun.
Light itself bends around the Sun, and measuring that during a 1919 eclipse made Einstein world-famous overnight.
Gravity is by far the weakest force: a small fridge magnet beats the gravity of the entire Earth when it holds up a paperclip.
The electric force between two protons is about a trillion trillion trillion times stronger than the gravity between them.
When you jump, you push the whole Earth away from you a tiny bit. It moves far less than the width of an atom, but it does move.
A bullet dropped from your hand and one fired straight sideways from a gun at the same height hit the ground at the same time.
The bottom of a rolling car tire is momentarily standing still on the road, while the top is moving forward twice as fast as the car.
Drop a stretched-out Slinky and its bottom end hangs still in midair for a split second, because it does not yet know the top has been let go.
Spin an egg and tap it to a stop: a raw egg starts turning again by itself because the liquid inside is still swirling, but a boiled egg stays still.
Toast really does tend to land butter side down: falling from table height, it only has time to make about half a turn.
A person who weighs 100 kg at the North Pole would weigh about half a kilogram less at the equator, thanks to Earth's spin and its bulging middle.
Gravity on Earth is not the same everywhere: it varies slightly with mountains, rocks underground and even ocean depths.
If you dropped a ball into a tunnel straight through the Earth, it would fall for about 42 minutes and pop out the other side.
In theory, a straight tunnel through the Earth between any two cities, not just through the center, would take about the same 42 minutes.
At the center of the Earth, you would be weightless, because the planet would pull on you equally from every side.
Every object attracts every other object: you are gently pulling on the Moon right now, and it pulls on you.
Two people standing a meter apart attract each other with a force about as tiny as the weight of a grain of salt.
Henry Cavendish weighed the Earth in 1798 using lead balls and a thin wire at his home, and got it almost right.
The whole Earth weighs about 6 thousand billion billion tonnes, roughly 80 times as much as the Moon.
A person in stiletto heels can press on a floor harder than an elephant does, because all their weight lands on a tiny heel instead of a huge foot.
Lying on a bed of nails is safer than it looks: with hundreds of points sharing your weight, no single nail pushes hard enough to pierce the skin.
There are two high tides a day because the Earth is stretched in two directions: toward the Moon and away from it.
Suction cups do not suck. The air around them pushes them against the wall, which is why they would not stick at all in space.
In 1654 a German mayor pumped the air out of two metal half-spheres, and teams of horses could not pull them apart.
A hair dryer pointed upward can hold a ping pong ball floating in its airstream, and the ball stays put even if you tilt the dryer a little.
Skydivers stop speeding up after about 12 seconds, at around 200 km per hour, because air pushes back as hard as gravity pulls.
A cat falling from a great height reaches top speed sooner than a human, around 100 km per hour, and can spread out like a parachute.
An ant can fall from any height and walk away, because air resistance keeps its top speed very low.
A raindrop falls at only about 30 km per hour, because air resistance stops it from going any faster.
A penny dropped from a skyscraper would not kill anyone: it tumbles and only reaches around 40 to 80 km per hour.
Galileo is said to have dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but historians doubt he ever did.
Isaac Newton developed his ideas on gravity while staying home during a plague outbreak in 1665 and 1666.
Newton's apple tree still lives at his childhood home in England, and cuttings from it grow around the world.
Newton also spent years searching for a way to turn other metals into gold, and wrote over a million words about it.
In 2012 skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from about 39 kilometers up and broke the speed of sound with nothing but his body and a pressure suit.
A spinning coin wobbles faster and faster as it settles, ending in a sudden rattle. A desk toy called Euler's disk keeps this up for over a minute.
Car side windows are made of toughened glass that shatters into small blunt cubes on purpose, instead of long dangerous shards.
Gravity travels at exactly the speed of light: if the Sun vanished, Earth would keep orbiting for about 8 minutes.
A Prince Rupert's drop is a glass tadpole whose head survives hammer blows, yet snapping its thin tail makes the whole thing burst into powder.
When a gravitational wave passes through you, it stretches and squeezes your body by far less than the width of an atom.
Your weight on a scale changes in an elevator: it reads heavier as the elevator starts up and lighter as it starts down.
In a falling elevator you would float, because you and the elevator would fall together, just like astronauts in orbit.
When you watch the Sun touch the horizon at sunset, it has actually already dipped below it. The air bends its light up to your eyes.
Memory metal can be crumpled up, then dipped in hot water, and it springs back to the exact shape it was made in.
On a spinning space station, artificial gravity could be made just by spinning: the floor would push on your feet like gravity.
Fighter pilots can feel up to 9 times their own weight in tight turns, enough to make blood drain from their brains.
Your weight is just the floor pushing back on you: a scale measures that push, not the pull of gravity itself.
Everything falls at the same rate in a vacuum, a rule tested in space so precisely that any difference would be under one part in a million billion.
Earth spins at about 1,670 km per hour at the equator, yet you feel nothing, because everything moves smoothly with you.
Aerogel is so light it is almost all air, yet a small block can hold up a brick and shield a flower from a blowtorch flame.
Gold can be hammered so thin that light shines through it, and the light that gets through looks green.
A pendulum about 1 meter long takes almost exactly one second for each swing, which is why old clocks tick once a second.
A Foucault pendulum slowly changes the direction of its swing over the day, proving that the Earth is turning underneath it.
Clocks on the Moon run slightly faster than clocks on Earth, gaining about 56 millionths of a second every day.
Static electricity from shuffling across a carpet can reach several thousand volts, yet barely hurts because the current is so brief.
A single hurricane can release heat energy hundreds of times greater than all the electricity humans generate in the same time.
A single lightning bolt is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, around 30,000 degrees C.
A lightning bolt is only about as wide as a thumb, yet it can stretch for kilometers across the sky.
Count the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder, and every 3 seconds means the strike is about 1 kilometer away.
Lightning flashes somewhere on Earth about 40 to 50 times every second, adding up to over a billion flashes a year.
The Empire State Building is a lightning magnet: it gets struck about 20 to 25 times every year.
As of 2025, the longest lightning flash on record stretched about 829 km, from eastern Texas to near Kansas City, during a storm in 2017.
A car protects you from lightning not because of its rubber tires, but because its metal body steers the current around you.
Birds can sit safely on a power line because both their feet are at the same voltage, so no current flows through them.
It is current, not voltage, that hurts you: a tiny current of about a tenth of an amp through the heart can be deadly.
Electricity in a wire does not race along: the electrons themselves drift slower than a snail, often less than a millimeter a second.
Every time you turn on a light, electrons in the wire mostly jiggle back and forth, 50 or 60 times a second, going nowhere.
Your body runs on electricity: nerve signals are tiny electrical pulses that zip along at up to about 120 meters per second.
Your heart makes its own electricity, which is why a machine can record your heartbeat from wires stuck to your skin.
A single bolt of lightning carries enough energy to power a home for days to weeks, but it is gone in a split second.
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod in the 1750s, and the same simple idea still protects buildings today.
Many stage and theme park ghosts use a trick over 150 years old called Pepper's ghost: a hidden, brightly lit figure reflected in a sheet of glass.
Some metals, cooled enough, become superconductors: a current set going in a ring of one can flow for years with no battery.
A chilled superconductor can lock a magnet in midair above it, so the magnet hovers and stays put even when you tilt it.
Superconducting magnets in MRI scanners are tens of thousands of times stronger than Earth's magnetic field.
MRI scanners are so strong that a metal chair or oxygen tank can be yanked across the room and into the machine.
Earth is a giant magnet: its magnetic field comes from churning molten iron in the outer core, thousands of kilometers below.
In 2006 scientists built a working invisibility cloak, but it only hid a small copper cylinder from microwaves, not from human eyes.
Compass needles point to Earth's magnetic north pole, which wanders by tens of kilometers a year and is not the same as the true North Pole.
The north pole of a compass is attracted to Earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic, which means that pole is actually a magnetic south pole.
Some birds, sea turtles and salmon seem to sense Earth's magnetic field and use it like a built-in compass.
Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the charged particles streaming from the Sun, steering some toward the poles to make auroras.
A magnet will never have just one pole: cut a bar magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south.
Heat a magnet enough and it stops being a magnet; for iron, that happens at about 770 degrees C.
Frogs can float in midair inside very strong magnets, because the water in their bodies is gently pushed away by magnetic fields.
The physicist who levitated a frog with magnets won both a joke Ig Nobel Prize and, later, a real Nobel Prize.
Strong neodymium magnets can be strong enough to crush fingers between them or erase credit cards.
A spinning magnet near a coil of wire makes electricity: most of the world's power comes from that simple trick.
Michael Faraday, who discovered how to make electricity from magnets, had little formal schooling and started as a bookbinder's apprentice.
A mirage called Fata Morgana can make distant ships appear to hover above the sea, and may explain old legends of ghost ships.
People who lose the lens of their eye can see a little ultraviolet light. The painter Claude Monet may have, after his cataract surgery.
Your microwave oven heats food by making water molecules twist back and forth billions of times a second.
The holes in a microwave oven's door are too small for the microwaves to get through, but light passes easily, so you can watch.
Putting a grape in a microwave can create a tiny ball of glowing plasma, because the grape traps microwaves like an antenna.
Rubbing a balloon on your hair moves electrons from your hair to the balloon, so the balloon can stick to a wall.
A van de Graaff generator can build up hundreds of thousands of volts, enough to make a person's hair stand straight up.
A fully charged phone battery holds less energy than a single small square of chocolate.
Gram for gram, gasoline stores about 50 times more energy than a lithium-ion battery.
Lightning is not just from clouds to ground: most lightning flashes stay inside or between clouds and never touch the Earth.
Benjamin Franklin's kite was probably never hit by lightning. It collected charge from the stormy air; a direct strike would likely have killed him.
Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla fought a war over electricity in the 1880s and 1890s, and Tesla's alternating current won.
You can make a battery from a lemon, a copper coin and a zinc nail, though it takes many lemons to light a small bulb.
Space is completely silent: with no air to carry vibrations, even a huge explosion would make no sound at all.
Sound travels about 4 times faster in water than in air, and more than 15 times faster through steel.
Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometers of ocean, because sound travels so well through water.
Put your ear to a long metal railing while someone taps the far end, and you will hear the tap twice: through the metal, then the air.
A sonic boom is not made just once: a supersonic plane drags a continuous boom behind it along its whole path.
The crack of a whip is a tiny sonic boom: its tip moves faster than the speed of sound.
Helium makes your voice sound squeaky not by changing your vocal cords, but because sound travels faster in helium.
On a quiet night, sound can carry surprisingly far, because cooler air near the ground bends sound back down toward you.
The loudest sound in recorded history was probably the 1883 Krakatoa eruption, heard nearly 5,000 kilometers away.
Every 10 decibels sounds about twice as loud to us, but actually means ten times more sound energy.
A rock concert can be a trillion times more intense than the faintest sound a human can hear.
Some anechoic chambers are so quiet that people can hear their own heartbeat, blood flow and joints creaking.
Elephants talk to each other with rumbles too deep for humans to hear, which can travel several kilometers.
Bats and dolphins see with sound: they listen for echoes of their own calls to find food in the dark.
Dogs can hear sounds about twice as high-pitched as humans can, which is why dog whistles seem silent to us.
As people age, they lose the ability to hear high notes, so some sounds only teenagers can still hear.
The sound of the ocean in a seashell is just the noise around you, echoing and amplified inside the shell.
An ambulance siren sounds higher as it comes toward you and lower as it drives away, because its sound waves get squashed and stretched.
Opera singers really can shatter a wine glass with their voice, by matching the exact note the glass rings at.
Soldiers break step when crossing bridges, because marching in rhythm can make a bridge sway dangerously.
Noise-cancelling headphones fight sound with sound: they play a mirror-image wave that cancels out the noise.
Ultrasound lets doctors see babies before birth by bouncing sound too high-pitched for us to hear off the body.
The bass in music travels through walls much better than high notes, which is why you hear only the thumping from next door.
A guitar string would be almost silent on its own: the wooden body vibrates along with it and makes the sound loud.
When an orchestra tunes up, the note they all match is a vibration of exactly 440 times every second.
Snow muffles sound because fluffy fresh snow is full of air pockets that soak up sound like foam.
Your ears can detect vibrations smaller than the width of an atom at the eardrum.
Hot water and cold water sound different when poured, and many people can tell which is which just by listening.
Einstein never failed math. He had mastered calculus by about age 15; the myth may come from a Swiss school flipping its grading scale.
Scientists have created temperatures of trillions of degrees by smashing heavy atoms together at nearly the speed of light.
After Einstein died in 1955, the doctor who did his autopsy took his brain without permission and kept it for decades.
At room temperature, the air molecules hitting your face are zipping around at about 500 meters per second.
Outer space is not cold in the way you might think: with no air, heat leaves your body very slowly, mainly by glowing invisibly in infrared.
Physicist Richard Feynman amused himself during World War II by cracking colleagues' locked filing cabinets at Los Alamos and leaving cheeky notes inside.
Physicist Niels Bohr played in goal for a top Danish football club, and his brother Harald won an Olympic silver medal in football in 1908.
Water is densest at about 4 degrees C, so the bottom of a frozen lake stays around 4 degrees C all winter.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water, an odd effect called the Mpemba effect that scientists still debate.
Water boils at about 70 degrees C on top of Mount Everest, which makes cooking pasta there frustrating.
Pressure cookers cook faster because higher pressure lets water get hotter than 100 degrees C before it boils.
Water can boil and freeze at the same time, at a special combination of temperature and pressure called the triple point.
Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because metal pulls heat out of your hand much faster.
Blowing on hot soup cools it by sweeping away the warm, moist air, helping more water evaporate and carry heat off.
Sweating cools you because evaporating water carries a lot of heat away from your skin.
A drop of water on a very hot pan skitters around instead of boiling away, floating on a cushion of its own steam.
Liquid nitrogen is about minus 196 degrees C, cold enough to make a flower shatter like glass.
Helium cooled close to absolute zero becomes a superfluid that can climb up and over the walls of its container.
Three of Galileo's fingers and a tooth are on display in a museum in Florence, removed from his body almost a century after he died.
Skates do not glide because the blade's pressure melts the ice, as often taught: that effect is far too small, and ice has a slippery surface layer anyway.
Popcorn pops at around 180 degrees C, when steam trapped inside each kernel reaches about 9 times normal air pressure and bursts the shell.
Thermal expansion means the Eiffel Tower grows about 15 centimeters taller on hot summer days.
Railway tracks used to have small gaps between rails, the cause of the classic clickety-clack sound of trains.
Boil a cup of water and the steam it makes would fill about 1,600 cups, which is how steam engines got their push.
A burn from steam is worse than from boiling water at the same temperature, because steam releases extra heat as it turns back to water.
Thermos flasks keep drinks hot or cold with a vacuum between two walls, since heat cannot easily cross empty space.
A fridge does not make cold: it pumps heat out and dumps it into your kitchen, so leaving its door open actually warms the room.
Lise Meitner helped discover how to split the atom but was left out of the Nobel Prize. Element 109, meitnerium, is named after her.
A spinning ice skater speeds up when pulling in her arms, because spinning things keep their total spin when they change shape.
A cat can turn over in midair and land on its feet without pushing off anything, by twisting the front and back of its body separately.
Bicycles stay upright mostly because riders constantly steer into a fall, not just because of spinning wheels.
A moving bicycle can even balance itself without a rider, thanks to the way its front wheel steers into any lean.
A tablecloth can be yanked out from under dishes because, if pulled fast enough, friction has too little time to drag them along.
Friction is why you can walk: on a perfectly frictionless floor, you could not take a single step forward.
Two phone books with their pages interleaved are almost impossible to pull apart, even with cars pulling in opposite directions.
A curveball curves because its spin drags air around one side, pushing the ball sideways in flight.
Golf balls have dimples because the dimples let air hug the ball longer, cutting drag so it flies about twice as far.
A thrown spiral football flies more steadily than a wobbly one because spinning objects resist being tipped over.
Physicist Andre Geim once listed his hamster, H.A.M.S. ter Tisha, as a co-author on a scientific paper.
If you threw a baseball while standing on frictionless ice, you would slide backward a little as the ball flew forward.
A water strider walks on water because surface tension makes the water's surface act like a stretchy skin.
A steel paperclip can float on water if you lay it down gently, held up only by surface tension.
