Water climbs up thin tubes and paper towels all by itself, pulled upward by its attraction to the surfaces.
Tall trees lift water over 100 meters up to their leaves without a pump, pulled up by evaporation from the leaves.
A steel ship floats because its hollow shape pushes aside its own weight in water long before the hull is under.
Archimedes is said to have shouted Eureka in his bath when he realized how floating and water displacement work.
You float more easily in the Dead Sea because its very salty water is much denser than fresh water.
The air in a room weighs more than you might think: in an average living room, it can weigh as much as a person.
The air pressing on you weighs about 1 kilogram on every square centimeter of your body, but you feel nothing because it pushes from all sides.
Air pressure can crush a steel drum: heat a little water inside, seal it, let it cool, and it collapses with a bang.
A straw could never lift water more than about 10 meters high, no matter how hard you suck, because air pressure only pushes that far.
Your ears pop on a plane because the air pressure outside changes faster than the air trapped behind your eardrums.
Airplane cabins are pressurized only to the air pressure of a mountain about 2,000 meters high, so packets of chips puff up.
Airplane wings fly by pushing air downward: the wing deflects a huge amount of air down, and the air pushes the plane up.
The common school story about air above a wing needing to catch up with air below it is wrong; it actually gets there first.
A big jet's wings can lift more than 400 tonnes, about the weight of 60 elephants, by moving air around.
A hummingbird beats its wings up to about 80 times a second, so fast they hum.
A bee's wings beat about 200 times a second, which is what makes its buzzing sound.
A shower curtain billows in toward you, and scientists argued for years over why; a swirling vortex of air in the shower is a leading explanation.
When two trucks pass each other closely on a highway, they get pulled toward each other by the fast air between them.
The Earth wobbles like a slow spinning top, tracing a circle with its axis once every 26,000 years.
Every object that falls from rest drops about 5 meters in its first second, whether it is a pebble or a piano, if air does not matter.
Falling with no air to slow you down, you would pass the speed of sound after only about 35 seconds.
A car crash at 50 km per hour is like falling from roughly the third or fourth floor of a building.
Doubling a car's speed quadruples its energy, which is why crashes at high speed are so much more dangerous.
Seatbelts and airbags save lives by stretching out the time of a crash, which makes the force on your body much smaller.
An egg dropped onto a pillow survives because the pillow slows it down over a longer distance, softening the blow.
A boomerang comes back because its spinning wings produce lift that slowly turns it in a big circle.
In 2009 Stephen Hawking threw a party for time travelers and sent out the invitations only after it was over. Nobody came.
A hollow ball rolls down a slope more slowly than a solid ball of the same size, because more of its energy goes into spinning.
An astronaut on the space station can push a fully loaded cargo ship by hand, but it takes a long time to get it moving.
In space, a wrench thrown away would keep going forever in a straight line, unless something pulled on it.
A swing goes higher when you pump your legs at just the right moments, which is a kind of resonance.
Diamonds are the hardest natural material, but you can still shatter one with a hammer, because hard is not the same as tough.
Clap in front of the great pyramid at Chichen Itza in Mexico and the echo off its stairs comes back as a chirp, a bit like a bird call.
A sheet of graphene as thin as plastic wrap could, in theory, hold up an elephant balanced on a pencil.
Flawless glass fibers can be stronger than steel when pulled; tiny cracks are what make it break so easily.
Concrete is very strong when squeezed but weak when stretched, which is why buildings hide steel rods inside it.
A single strand of human hair can hold about 100 grams, so a full head of hair could in theory support a couple of elephants.
Most of the visible matter in the universe is not solid, liquid or gas, but plasma, the glowing fourth state of matter found in stars.
A plasma ball's tendrils reach for your finger because your body gives the electricity an easier path to the ground.
Glass is a solid, not a slow liquid: old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because the glass flowed.
Snow can vanish on a cold sunny day without melting, turning straight from ice into water vapor.
People can run across a pool of cornstarch mixed with water, because the mixture firms up under each fast footstep.
Ketchup gets runnier when you shake it, which is why a firm tap on the bottle gets it flowing.
Pitch, a tar-like substance, looks solid but flows: in an experiment running in Australia since 1927, fewer than a dozen drops have fallen.
Gallium is a metal that melts in your hand, because it turns liquid at about 30 degrees C.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, which is why old thermometers used it.
Hot air rises because it is less dense: a hot air balloon floats on the same principle as a boat floats on water.
In St Paul's Cathedral in London, a whisper against the wall of the Whispering Gallery can be heard clearly on the far side, over 30 meters away.
The calories on a food label measure energy: one food calorie could heat a liter of water by 1 degree C.
A single peanut holds enough energy to bring a small cup of water close to boiling if burned completely.
Your body gives off about as much heat as a 100-watt light bulb when you are resting.
Your brain uses about 20 watts, less than many light bulbs, to do everything you think and feel.
On old phone lines, s and f sounded alike, because the lines carried only a narrow band of pitches and cut off the high hiss that tells them apart.
The energy in coal and oil is ancient sunlight, captured by plants and tiny sea creatures millions of years ago.
The Sun delivers more energy to Earth in about an hour and a half than all of humanity uses in a year.
Every machine wastes some energy as heat, which is why a perpetual motion machine can never work.
Hydroelectric dams turn the energy of falling water into electricity, and the water fell there thanks to sunlight lifting it as vapor.
China's Three Gorges Dam, the biggest power station on Earth, can make as much electricity as about 20 large nuclear reactors.
Wind turbine blades can be longer than a football field is wide, and their tips can move at over 300 km per hour.
You can estimate the temperature from a cricket: count its chirps in 14 seconds and add 40 to get roughly the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.
A champagne cork can fly out at around 40 kilometers per hour, pushed by gas at more than twice the pressure in a car tire.
Mixing is easy and unmixing is hard: stir milk into coffee and no amount of stirring will separate it again.
Disorder always tends to grow, which may be why we remember the past and not the future.
An ice cube in warm water never gets colder while the water gets hotter; heat only flows from hot to cold by itself.
A heat pump works even in freezing weather, squeezing heat out of cold air, and can deliver three or four times more heat than the electricity it uses.
A super ball bounces higher than a tennis ball because it loses far less energy as heat when it squashes.
Tapping the top of a shaken soda can does not stop it foaming over, a 2014 study of 1,000 cans found.
A meteor glows mainly because it squashes the air in front of it so hard that the air heats up, not just from rubbing.
A spacecraft returning from space hits the air so fast that its heat shield faces temperatures over 1,500 degrees C.
Car brakes turn the energy of motion into heat, and racing car brakes can glow red hot after a hard stop.
Some electric cars recapture energy when braking, turning the car's motion back into battery charge.
A battery does not store electricity: it stores chemicals that make electricity when they react.
A single AA battery has roughly enough energy to lift a person about 15 meters, if all of it could be used.
Gold is yellow because of Einstein's relativity: its electrons move so fast that it absorbs blue light; otherwise gold would look silvery.
Relativity also helps explain why mercury is liquid at room temperature while its neighbors on the periodic table are solid.
Most of the voltage of a car's lead-acid battery comes from relativistic effects on lead's fast-moving electrons, a 2011 study found.
To a proton racing around the Large Hadron Collider, the 27 km ring would look squashed down to just a few meters long.
The meter is defined by light: it is the distance light travels in exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second.
The best atomic clocks are so precise they would not lose a second in the entire age of the universe.
One second is officially the time it takes a cesium atom to vibrate a little over 9 billion times.
Earth's spin is so irregular that official clocks have added a leap second 27 times since 1972, but the world plans to stop adding them by 2035.
Light's speed was first measured in the 1670s, by noticing that Jupiter's moons seemed to run late when Jupiter was farther away.
There is no such thing as brown light: brown is just dim orange or red, seen next to brighter colors.
Adding salt to pasta water barely changes its boiling point: a normal pinch raises it by much less than 1 degree C.
Newton gave the rainbow seven colors, including indigo, partly to match the seven notes of a musical scale.
To see your whole body in a mirror, the mirror only needs to be half your height, no matter how far away you stand.
Two mirrors facing each other create an endless tunnel of reflections that grows greener and darker, because glass absorbs a little each bounce.
The back of a shiny spoon shows you right side up, while the inside shows you upside down.
During a partial solar eclipse, the gaps between tree leaves act like tiny pinhole cameras and cast hundreds of crescent Suns on the ground.
A tiny hole in a wall of a dark room projects an upside-down picture of the outside world onto the opposite wall.
You can start a fire with a lens made of clear ice, carved to focus sunlight onto a single spot.
Shadows on snow look blue because they are lit only by the blue sky, not by the direct sunlight.
Red eye in flash photos is the camera flash lighting up the blood-rich back of your eye and bouncing straight back.
Cats' eyes glow in the dark because a mirror-like layer behind their retina bounces light back through it a second time.
Tonic water glows bright blue under a black light, because the quinine in it turns invisible ultraviolet into visible light.
Your body actually gives off visible light, but it is about 1,000 times too faint for your eyes to see.
Vikings may have used sunstones, crystals that reveal where the Sun is through clouds by sensing polarized light.
Bees and ants can navigate by the patterns of polarized light in the sky, even when the Sun is hidden.
A rainbow can appear at night: moonbows are made by moonlight and usually look white to us, because our night vision sees little color.
Fogbows are rainbows made by tiny fog droplets, and they are almost completely white.
A bright ring around the Sun or Moon, called a halo, is made by sunlight bending through millions of tiny ice crystals high in the sky.
At the very last moment of a sunset, the top of the Sun can flash bright green for a second or two.
Raindrops larger than about 5 millimeters across usually break apart as they fall, so huge raindrops are very rare.
Distant mountains look bluish because the air between you and them scatters blue light toward your eyes.
Ocean waves do not carry the water along: the water mostly moves in circles while the wave's energy travels on.
If water could not be squeezed at all, sea level would be about 30 meters higher, because the ocean is slightly compressed by its own weight.
At the bottom of the deepest ocean, the water pushes on you as hard as a car balanced on every fingernail-sized spot.
Every 10 meters of depth in the sea adds as much pressure as the entire atmosphere above you.
In a glass of stout beer, bubbles can sink instead of rise, carried down the sides of the glass by the flowing liquid.
Mentos make diet soda erupt because their rough surfaces give dissolved gas millions of places to form bubbles all at once.
Salt on icy roads works because salty water has to get much colder than fresh water before it can freeze.
You can make ice cream in a bag by shaking it in ice and salt, because salt lets the ice get colder than its normal freezing point.
Water heated in a microwave in a smooth cup can pass 100 degrees C without boiling, then erupt violently when disturbed.
A kettle is noisiest just before it boils: steam bubbles form on the bottom and collapse with tiny bangs in the cooler water above.
Sandcastles need water: tiny bridges of water between the grains hold them together, but too much water makes them collapse.
Stretch a rubber band quickly against your lips and it feels warm; let it shrink back and it feels cool.
Sand in an hourglass flows at the same rate whether the top is full or nearly empty, unlike water in a bottle.
Shake a bag of mixed nuts and the biggest ones, like Brazil nuts, end up on top, a puzzle physicists still study.
Bend dry spaghetti and it almost always snaps into three or more pieces. In 2018 scientists found that twisting it hard first lets it break cleanly in two.
Clicking the metal disc in a reusable hand warmer makes the liquid inside crystallize all at once, giving off heat as it turns solid.
Stir a cup of tea and the leaves gather in the middle at the bottom, not at the edges, a puzzle explained by Einstein in 1926.
Water does not drain clockwise in one hemisphere and counterclockwise in the other: the Earth's spin is far too weak to decide in a sink.
Cereal floating in milk clumps together and sticks to the bowl's edge, because each piece bends the milk's surface around it.
Coffee spills dry with a dark ring at the edge because the liquid flows outward as it evaporates, carrying the coffee bits with it.
Soap bubbles are round because surface tension pulls the film into the shape with the least surface area for the air inside.
A balloon dipped in liquid nitrogen shrivels flat, then puffs back up to full size as it warms, because the cold shrinks the air inside.
On a clear day at noon, sunlight delivers about 1,000 watts to every square meter of ground, roughly the power of a microwave oven.
A domino can knock over one about 1.5 times bigger than itself, so a chain of about 29 growing dominoes could topple one as tall as the Empire State Building.
Some nuclear submarines never refuel: one load of fuel lasts the boat's whole working life of more than 30 years.
Humans can sit in a sauna at 100 degrees C, but water at 100 degrees C scalds instantly, because air carries heat away so slowly.
People can walk over hot coals without being burned because the coals are covered in ash and do not pass heat into feet quickly.
Your tongue can stick to frozen metal because the metal pulls heat away so fast that the moisture on your tongue freezes instantly.
Lightning can make trees explode, by instantly boiling the water inside them into steam.
Thunderstorms can fire out beams of antimatter into space, which satellites have detected from orbit.
The hum of power lines and transformers is alternating current shaking metal 100 or 120 times a second.
Some bacteria grow chains of tiny magnets inside themselves and use them like compass needles to swim in the right direction.
Earth's magnetic field at the surface is about 100 times weaker than a typical fridge magnet.
The word magnet comes from Magnesia, a region of ancient Greece where naturally magnetic stones were found.
Wi-Fi often uses almost the same radio frequency as microwave ovens, which is why a running microwave can slow down some connections.
Nobody can predict when a single radioactive atom will decay: it is truly random, yet billions together decay on a perfect schedule.
Even in empty space, two metal plates placed very close together get pushed toward each other by the restless quantum jitter of empty space.
Sound waves can levitate small objects: scientists hold droplets and tiny beads in midair using powerful sound.
Sound can make light: tiny bubbles squeezed by strong sound waves can collapse so violently that they flash.
Sound zips through diamond at about 12 km per second, roughly 35 times faster than through air.
Your singing really does sound better in the shower, because hard walls bounce the sound around and make your voice richer.
Chalk squeaks on a blackboard and violins sing for the same reason: something sticks, slips, sticks and slips, very fast.
Fresh snow squeaks under your boots only when it is very cold, roughly minus 10 degrees C or below.
Thunder usually cannot be heard more than about 15 to 25 kilometers away from the lightning that made it.
You weigh about 0.3 percent less on top of Mount Everest than at sea level, because you are farther from Earth's center.
Your body is made of roughly 7 billion billion billion atoms, far more than the number of stars in the whole observable universe.
A modern phone chip holds well over 10 billion tiny switches, each much smaller than a typical virus.
A wool sweater keeps you warm mostly because it traps still air, which is very bad at carrying heat.
The inside of an igloo can be tens of degrees warmer than the air outside, warmed by nothing more than body heat and snow's insulation.
The center of the Earth is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, over 5,000 degrees C.
High enough above Earth, about 19 km up, air pressure is so low that water would boil at body temperature.
A baseball pitched at about 150 km per hour reaches the batter in roughly 0.4 seconds, barely longer than a blink.
A knuckleball dances unpredictably because it barely spins, so tiny changes in the air around its seams push it around.
The faster you go around a bend, the harder you get pushed toward the outside, and doubling your speed makes that push four times stronger.
Roller coaster loops are not circles but teardrop shapes, so riders are not crushed by too much force at the bottom.
On a roller coaster, the moment you feel your stomach float is the moment you are briefly in free fall.
Spinning a bucket of water fast over your head keeps the water in, because the bucket keeps pulling it into a circle.
Squeezed hard enough, ice can take nearly 20 different forms, and some of them may exist only deep inside icy moons and planets.
Some kinds of ice found under huge pressure stay solid even when they are hot enough to burn you.
A soap film can stretch across a wire frame in shapes that solve hard math problems, finding the smallest possible surface.
A cup of hot tea cools faster if you add the milk later rather than right away, because hotter things lose heat faster.
A car on a sunny day can heat up to over 60 degrees C inside, because sunlight gets in through the glass and the heat gets trapped.
Clear nights are colder than cloudy nights, because clouds act like a blanket that sends heat back down to the ground.
Frost can form on a car roof even when the air is above freezing, because the roof loses heat to the clear night sky.
Black asphalt in summer can get 20 degrees C or more hotter than the air around it.
A thunderstorm can hold as much energy as several atomic bombs, released as rain, wind and lightning.
A Faraday cage can block a phone signal: wrap a phone in enough metal foil and it may lose all its bars.
Static shocks are worse in winter because cold, dry air lets electric charge build up on your body instead of leaking away.
An average airliner is struck by lightning about once a year, and they are built so the current flows harmlessly along the outside.
A spark from a light switch, a static zap and a lightning bolt are all the same thing at different sizes.
@art|Art & music
The Mona Lisa is not painted on canvas but on a wooden board, and it is only about the size of a small poster.
In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with the Mona Lisa and kept it hidden in his Paris room for over two years.
When the Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911, crowds lined up at the Louvre just to stare at the empty wall where it had hung.
Pablo Picasso was questioned by police as a possible suspect when the Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911. He was innocent.
Leonardo's Last Supper started flaking within decades because he tried an experimental paint on a dry wall instead of wet plaster.
Leonardo da Vinci wrote most of his notes backwards, in mirror writing that runs from right to left.
Michelangelo did not paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling lying down. He stood on a scaffold for four years, craning his neck upward.
Michelangelo wrote a funny poem complaining that painting the Sistine ceiling bent his spine like a bow and pushed his beard toward the sky.
Michelangelo was only 24 when he finished the Pieta, and it is the only work he ever signed.
According to Vasari, Michelangelo carved his name on the Pieta after overhearing visitors credit it to another sculptor.
Michelangelo carved his David from a giant marble block that other sculptors had started on, given up, and left lying around for decades.
Michelangelo's David is about 5 meters tall, nearly three times the height of a real man.
Van Gogh made about 2,100 artworks, almost all of them in the last ten years of his short life.
Van Gogh only started painting seriously at about 27 and died at 37, so his whole career lasted roughly ten years.
Van Gogh painted his famous sunflowers to decorate the bedroom of his friend Paul Gauguin, who was coming to stay.
A tiny pencil note on The Scream says "Could only have been painted by a madman." In 2021 experts confirmed Munch wrote it himself.
Two different versions of The Scream were stolen in separate heists, in 1994 and 2004, and both were found again.
The thieves who stole The Scream in 1994 left a note thanking the museum for its poor security.
In 1990 two thieves dressed as police officers talked their way into a Boston museum and took 13 artworks. The case is still unsolved.
Boston's Gardner Museum still displays the empty frames of its stolen paintings, because the founder's will forbids rearranging anything.
Rembrandt's Night Watch is not set at night. Old darkened varnish only made it look that way, and the name stuck.
In 1715 Rembrandt's Night Watch was trimmed on all four sides just so it would fit on a wall, cutting off two people.
The Girl with a Pearl Earring was probably not a real person: Vermeer likely painted an imaginary face as a study.
Forger Han van Meegeren sold a fake Vermeer to Nazi leader Hermann Goering, then painted another fake in front of witnesses to prove it.
Ultramarine blue paint was made by grinding up a gemstone from Afghanistan, and in Renaissance Europe it could cost more than gold.
Renaissance contracts sometimes spelled out how much of the costly blue paint an artist had to use, usually for the Virgin Mary's robe.
Mummy brown was a real paint made from ground-up Egyptian mummies, and artists bought it in tubes into the 20th century.
Painter Edward Burne-Jones reportedly held a funeral in his garden for his tube of mummy brown after learning what it was made of.
A glowing paint called Indian yellow was said to be made from the urine of cows fed only on mango leaves.
A popular green of the 1800s was made with arsenic, and it was used in wallpaper, ball gowns and even sweets.
In 1856 an 18-year-old student trying to make a malaria medicine accidentally made mauve, the first mass-produced artificial dye. It set off a purple craze.
Hokusai's Great Wave is a print, not a painting, so thousands of copies were made from the same carved wooden blocks.
Hokusai used more than 30 different names during his career and is said to have moved house about 93 times.
Before 1841, painters mixed their own paint and stored it in pig bladders. Then an American painter invented the squeezable paint tube.
The word Impressionism started as an insult: a critic mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise in 1874.
Claude Monet painted about 250 pictures of water lilies, all from a pond he designed and dug in his own garden.
Cataracts made colors look muddy to Monet in his 70s, and his paintings from those years turned strongly red and brown.
Georges Seurat built one of his most famous paintings entirely out of tiny dots of color, and it took him about two years.
More than half of everything Edgar Degas made shows dancers.
Paul Gauguin was a stockbroker before he quit and became a full-time painter in his mid-thirties.
Henri Rousseau painted wild jungles but never left France. He got his ideas from Paris zoos, botanical gardens and books.
Pablo Picasso's full name has about 20 parts, honoring a long list of saints and relatives.
Pablo Picasso made an estimated 50,000 artworks in his life, roughly two a day for seventy years.
Picasso's Guernica is nearly 8 meters wide and 3.5 meters tall, yet he painted it in about five weeks.
Picasso refused to let Guernica go to Spain until democracy returned. It arrived in 1981, after both he and Franco had died.
Salvador Dali said his famous melting clocks were inspired by Camembert cheese going soft in the sun.
Dali's painting of melting clocks is tiny, about the size of a sheet of paper.
Salvador Dali designed the Chupa Chups lollipop logo in 1969, and it is still on the wrappers today.
Frida Kahlo began painting while stuck in bed after a bus accident at 18. Her mother fixed a mirror above the bed so she could paint herself.
The serious farm couple in American Gothic were modeled by the painter's sister and his dentist.
The famous painting known as Whistler's Mother is officially called Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1.
Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait hides a tiny round mirror that reflects two extra people, possibly including the painter.
Instead of a normal signature, Jan van Eyck wrote on the wall of one painting: Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.
A panel of Belgium's famous Ghent Altarpiece was stolen in 1934 and has never been found. A copy hangs in its place.
In Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, one man has sheet music painted on his backside, and people have played the tune.
The painter Caravaggio killed a man in a fight in 1606 and spent the rest of his life on the run.
Velazquez painted himself into his masterpiece Las Meninas, standing at a giant canvas and staring right back at you.
Francisco Goya painted his creepiest pictures straight onto the walls of his own house. They were later peeled off and moved to a museum.
Andy Warhol painted 32 soup cans because Campbell's sold exactly 32 flavors in 1962.
Andy Warhol made a film that is over five hours of his friend sleeping.
Artist Anish Kapoor won the exclusive right to use one of the blackest materials ever made. Another artist replied by selling the pinkest pink, to anyone but Kapoor.
X-rays revealed that Malevich's famous Black Square, painted in 1915, hides two earlier colorful paintings underneath.
In 1917 Marcel Duchamp entered a store-bought urinal into an art show, called it Fountain, and changed art forever.
Duchamp's original Fountain was lost. The ones in museums are copies he approved decades later.
Rene Magritte painted a pipe with the words "This is not a pipe" underneath, because it is only a picture of one.
Gustav Klimt's The Kiss shimmers because it contains real gold leaf.
In 2018 a Banksy painting shredded itself inside its frame seconds after selling at auction for about 1.4 million dollars.
The half-shredded Banksy, renamed Love is in the Bin, sold again in 2021 for about 25 million dollars, far more than before.
In 2017 a Leonardo da Vinci painting of Christ sold for about 450 million dollars, the most ever paid for a painting at auction.
The Statue of Liberty's hidden iron skeleton was designed by Gustave Eiffel, the man behind the Eiffel Tower.
About 90 percent of Mount Rushmore was carved with dynamite.
Ancient Greek marble statues were once painted in bright colors. The pure white look we admire today is just the paint worn away.
Rodin's The Thinker was first meant to sit on top of a giant door called The Gates of Hell, as the poet Dante.
Rodin worked on The Gates of Hell for about 37 years and it was still unfinished when he died.
Rodin's first life-size statue looked so real that critics accused him of making a mold from a living man.
Easter Island's famous stone heads are not just heads. Many have full bodies buried underground.
Louise Bourgeois built a giant spider sculpture as tall as a three-story house, as a loving tribute to her mother.
Chicago's shiny Bean sculpture is made of 168 steel plates welded together so smoothly you cannot see a single seam.
Rio's Christ the Redeemer statue is covered in thousands of small triangular stone tiles, and lightning hits it several times a year.
China's Leshan Giant Buddha, carved into a cliff, is about 71 meters tall and took around 90 years to finish.
The famous Bayeux Tapestry is not actually a tapestry. It is a 70-meter-long embroidery, as long as a passenger jet.
The Bayeux Tapestry, made over 900 years ago, includes a picture of Halley's Comet streaking across the sky.
A painting of a pig on an Indonesian cave wall is at least 45,000 years old, one of the oldest known pictures of an animal.
Prehistoric people made hand stencils by blowing paint around a hand pressed to the rock, like Stone Age spray paint.
The oldest known musical instruments are flutes made from bird bones and mammoth ivory, about 40,000 years old.
A 40,000-year-old statue of a man with a lion's head, carved from mammoth ivory, is one of the oldest known sculptures.
Egyptian blue, a paint made about 5,000 years ago, glows under infrared light, so scientists can spot faded traces of it on old statues.
A red dye called carmine comes from crushed insects, and it took around 70,000 of them to make a pound.
Only about 35 paintings by Vermeer are known today, so few that all of them could fit in a single room.
Bright red vermilion paint was made from a mercury ore, so painters were handling poison.
Some of the bright yellows in Van Gogh's paintings are slowly turning brown as the paint reacts to light.
The first box of Crayola crayons, sold in 1903, had eight colors and cost a nickel.
In 2017 Crayola retired a yellow called Dandelion and replaced it with a new blue named Bluetiful.
In 2009 a chemist in Oregon accidentally created a brand new blue pigment, the first one discovered in about 200 years.
A hundred years ago some baby advice said pink was for boys and blue was for girls.
In 2003 a thief climbed scaffolding into a Vienna museum and stole a golden salt cellar. It turned up three years later, buried in a forest.
In 2010 a lone thief nicknamed Spider-Man stole five paintings, including a Picasso and a Matisse, from a Paris museum in one night.
A Frenchman stole about 200 artworks from small museums and kept them in his bedroom. After his arrest, his mother destroyed many of them.
In 2025 thieves used a furniture lift to reach a Louvre window and stole French crown jewels in about seven minutes, in broad daylight.
Mozart wrote his first symphony when he was about 8 years old.
Mozart composed more than 600 works before he died at just 35.
At 14, Mozart reportedly heard a secret piece of church music in the Vatican once and wrote the whole thing down from memory.
Beethoven kept composing after he went almost completely deaf, including his famous Ninth Symphony.
At the premiere of his Ninth Symphony, the deaf Beethoven had to be turned around to see the audience cheering.
Johann Sebastian Bach had 20 children, though only about half of them lived to grow up.
Beethoven was so fussy about his coffee that, according to his secretary, he counted out exactly 60 beans for every cup.
Vivaldi was a priest, nicknamed the Red Priest because of his red hair.
Vivaldi taught music at a Venice orphanage for girls whose orchestra became famous across Europe.
Handel wrote his huge oratorio Messiah, over two hours of music, in about 24 days.
Chopin's heart is in a church in Warsaw, while the rest of him is buried in Paris.
Pianist Franz Liszt was so adored that fans fought over his broken piano strings and cigar stubs. People called it Lisztomania.
Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture has real cannon fire written into the music.
A piano piece by Erik Satie hints it should be repeated 840 times in a row. One 1963 performance took over 18 hours.
John Cage's most famous piece, 4'33", is four and a half minutes of the musicians playing nothing at all.
A performance of a John Cage organ piece in a German church started in 2001 and is planned to end in the year 2640.
Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring was so shocking at its 1913 Paris premiere that the audience nearly rioted.
A grand piano's strings pull on its frame with a combined force of roughly 20 tons, about the weight of three elephants.
Antonio Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments, and roughly 650 of them still exist.
In blind tests, many top violinists could not tell a Stradivarius from a good modern violin, and often preferred the new one.
In 2011 a Stradivarius violin sold for about 15.9 million dollars, with the money going to help Japan after its tsunami.
Didgeridoos are traditionally made from tree trunks that termites have hollowed out from the inside.
Didgeridoo players can play without stopping by breathing in through the nose while squeezing air out of their cheeks.
The theremin is played without being touched: the player waves their hands in the air near two metal antennas.
The bagpipes probably began in the ancient Middle East, not Scotland.
As a child, saxophone inventor Adolphe Sax reportedly fell three floors, swallowed a pin and was burned by gunpowder. Neighbors called him little Sax the ghost.
A pipe organ in Atlantic City has more than 33,000 pipes, some taller than a house and some smaller than a pencil.
A violin bow is strung with about 150 to 200 hairs from a horse's tail.
The ukulele was created in Hawaii from small guitars brought by Portuguese immigrants, and its name roughly means jumping flea.
The steel drum was invented in Trinidad and Tobago in the 20th century by hammering old oil barrels into musical instruments.
In Indonesia, musicians never step over the instruments of a gamelan orchestra, out of respect.
Many of a sitar's strings are never plucked at all. They just hum along on their own when the other strings are played.
Fans stole composer Joseph Haydn's skull days after his burial in 1809. It was only reunited with the rest of him in 1954.
Japan's shakuhachi bamboo flute was once played by wandering Zen monks as a form of meditation.
Mongolian throat singers can sing two or more notes at the same time.
Benjamin Franklin invented a musical instrument made of spinning glass bowls, and Mozart and Beethoven wrote music for it.
Trumpets from King Tutankhamun's tomb were played on BBC radio in 1939, sounding again after more than 3,000 years.
The oldest complete song with its music is carved on a Greek tombstone about 2,000 years old, and it can still be sung today.
Do-re-mi comes from a Latin hymn: around 1025 a monk took the first syllable of each line. Do was first called ut, and was changed because ut is hard to sing.
Beethoven's Fur Elise may not be for an Elise at all. Some experts think his messy handwriting really said Therese, a woman he once hoped to marry.
During World War II the BBC opened broadcasts with Beethoven's Fifth, because da-da-da-DUM is V for Victory in Morse code.
Ravel's Bolero repeats the same tune for about 15 minutes, only getting louder and adding instruments.
Mahler's Symphony No. 8 is nicknamed the Symphony of a Thousand because its first performance used over 1,000 musicians and singers.
Violinist Paganini played so wildly well that rumors said he had sold his soul to the devil.
Paganini could play an entire piece on just one violin string, a party trick that amazed audiences across Europe.
Schubert wrote more than 600 songs, sometimes several in a single day, and he died at just 31.
Schubert's Unfinished Symphony was kept by a friend for more than 40 years before anyone performed it.
The Beatles recorded most of their first album in a single day in 1963.
Paul McCartney woke up with the melody of Yesterday in his head, and its working title was Scrambled Eggs.
Yesterday by the Beatles has been recorded by other artists more than 1,600 times.
The Beatles played their last concert on the roof of their London office in 1969, until police came to shut it down.
Michael Jackson's Thriller is estimated to have sold about 70 million copies, more than any other album.
Michael Jackson patented special shoes that hooked into the stage so he could lean forward impossibly far without falling.
Michael Jackson first did the moonwalk on TV in 1983, and it became an instant legend.
Queen's Bohemian Rhapsody is almost six minutes long with no chorus, yet it topped the UK charts for nine weeks.
Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara on the island of Zanzibar, off the coast of Africa.
Elvis Presley never performed overseas. His only concerts outside the United States were in three Canadian cities in 1957.
Elvis Presley was naturally fair-haired. His famous jet-black hair was dyed.
Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, the ABC song and Baa Baa Black Sheep all share the same old French melody.
Mozart wrote a set of 12 variations on the tune we know as Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.
The guitar riff of the Rolling Stones' Satisfaction came to Keith Richards in his sleep, and he recorded it half awake.
In 2016 Bob Dylan became the first musician to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Jimi Hendrix was left-handed and often played a right-handed guitar flipped upside down.
About 400,000 people turned up to the Woodstock festival in 1969, far more than anyone expected.
Phil Collins played both Live Aid concerts in one day in 1985, in London and Philadelphia, by flying across the ocean on Concorde.
The first music video MTV ever played, in 1981, was Video Killed the Radio Star.
Celine Dion is Canadian, but she won Eurovision in 1988 singing for Switzerland.
All I Want for Christmas Is You came out in 1994 but only reached number one in the US in 2019, 25 years later.
Whitney Houston's huge hit I Will Always Love You was written by Dolly Parton, who says she wrote it on the same day as Jolene.
Until a 2015 court ruling, a music company claimed the Happy Birthday song was under copyright, earning around 2 million dollars a year from it.
Elvis wanted to record I Will Always Love You, but Dolly Parton said no when his manager demanded half the song's rights.
Prince played all 27 instruments on his first album, which he made as a teenager.
The Rolling Stones' famous tongue logo was designed by an art student who was paid about 50 pounds.
Stevie Wonder signed his first record deal at just 11 years old.
Of all the Beach Boys, only drummer Dennis Wilson actually surfed.
The first song played in space was Jingle Bells, on a harmonica smuggled aboard a NASA flight in 1965.
Auto-Tune was invented by an engineer who used to study sound waves to help oil companies find oil underground.
Cher's 1998 hit Believe was the first big song to use Auto-Tune as an obvious robotic voice effect.
Ella Fitzgerald entered a talent contest at Harlem's Apollo Theater planning to dance, got cold feet, sang instead and won.
Louis Armstrong learned to play the cornet in a home for troubled boys in New Orleans.
In 2000 ABBA reportedly turned down an offer of about one billion dollars to reunite for a tour.
In 2020 BTS became the first Korean act to reach number one on the US singles chart, with Dynamite.
George Harrison of the Beatles took sitar lessons from Indian master Ravi Shankar, bringing the sitar into pop songs.
Fela Kuti invented Afrobeat in Nigeria by mixing West African highlife music with jazz and American funk.
Egyptian singer Umm Kulthum's monthly concerts could last for hours, with single songs running over an hour, and the whole Arab world tuned in.
The Lumiere brothers showed the first films to a paying audience in a Paris cafe basement in December 1895.
The story that early audiences ran screaming from a filmed train arriving at a station is most likely a legend.
In 1902 a former stage magician made A Trip to the Moon, the film where a rocket lands right in the Moon's eye.
The Jazz Singer of 1927 is famous as the first talking feature film, yet it has only about two minutes of spoken dialogue.
Before Snow White came out in 1937, people in Hollywood called it Disney's Folly, sure a full-length cartoon would flop.
The oldest surviving animated feature film, from 1926, was made entirely with paper cutout silhouettes by Lotte Reiniger.
Toy Story was the first feature film made completely on computers, and some of its frames took up to 30 hours to create.
For almost 20 years, Mickey Mouse's squeaky voice was performed by Walt Disney himself.
Walt Disney almost named his famous mouse Mortimer, but his wife reportedly talked him into Mickey.
Mickey Mouse's first sound cartoon, Steamboat Willie from 1928, became free for anyone to use in the US in 2024.
A four-second crowd scene in Studio Ghibli's The Wind Rises reportedly took one animator over a year to draw.
The blood in the famous shower scene of Hitchcock's Psycho was actually chocolate syrup.
The shower scene in Psycho lasts about three minutes on screen but took a whole week to film.
In the book, Dorothy's magic shoes are silver. The film made them ruby red to show off its new color technology.
A pair of ruby slippers from The Wizard of Oz was stolen from a museum in 2005. The FBI found them 13 years later.
The first Tin Man in The Wizard of Oz ended up in hospital because of his aluminum powder makeup, and was replaced.
The snow falling on the poppy field in The Wizard of Oz was made of asbestos.
Jaws' mechanical shark kept breaking down, so Spielberg showed it less, which made the movie much scarier.
The hum of a lightsaber came from an old film projector mixed with buzz picked up from a TV set.
Chewbacca's voice was built from recordings of bears, walruses, lions and other animals.
Darth Vader was played on set by a bodybuilder, but his deep voice belongs to actor James Earl Jones.
Darth Vader's breathing was recorded through a scuba diving regulator.
The Wilhelm scream, a sound effect recorded for a 1951 western, has been reused in hundreds of movies, including Star Wars.
India makes more films every year than any other country, well over 1,000.
In 2020 the South Korean film Parasite became the first movie not in English to win the Oscar for Best Picture.
During World War II, Oscar statuettes were made of painted plaster because metal was needed for the war.
Walt Disney won 22 competitive Oscars, more than any other person in history.
Comic actor Harold Lloyd did his famous dangling-from-a-clock stunts after losing a thumb and finger in an accident with a prop bomb.
In one Buster Keaton film, the whole front of a house falls on him, and he survives only because he is standing exactly where an open window lands.
Sulley in Monsters, Inc. has about 2.3 million individual hairs, and Pixar had to write new software just to animate them.
Most of Toy Story 2 was accidentally deleted from Pixar's computers. It was saved by a backup on an employee's home computer.
Pixar hides the code A113, the number of a classroom at the art school where many of its animators studied, in its movies.
Disney animators kept two live fawns at the studio to study how deer move while making Bambi.
The Simpsons family members are named after creator Matt Groening's own family, including his parents Homer and Margaret.
Mel Blanc voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, and his gravestone reads That's All Folks.
Superman's creators sold the rights to the character for 130 dollars in 1938.
The comic where Superman first appeared cost 10 cents in 1938. In 2024 a copy sold for about 6 million dollars.
Spider-Man first appeared in the very last issue of a comic series that was about to be canceled.
Charles Schulz drew nearly 18,000 Peanuts comic strips over 50 years, almost all of them by himself.
The final Peanuts comic strip was printed the morning after Charles Schulz died in 2000.
In the first Godzilla film, an actor stomped through tiny model cities inside a heavy rubber suit weighing about 100 kilograms.
Godzilla's roar was made by rubbing a leather glove coated in sticky resin along the strings of a double bass.
The King Kong of 1933 was a puppet only about 46 centimeters tall, moved a tiny bit at a time and filmed frame by frame.
Jurassic Park's T. rex roar mixed the sounds of a baby elephant, a tiger and an alligator.
In Jurassic Park, the raptors talking to each other is actually the sound of tortoises.
E.T.'s voice was mostly performed by a woman named Pat Welsh, whose raspy voice came from years of smoking.
Marty McFly in Back to the Future was first played by a different actor, who was replaced by Michael J. Fox after weeks of filming.
The movie Boyhood was filmed a few days at a time over 12 years, so you watch its young star actually grow up.
To film the bullet-dodging scene in The Matrix, about 120 still cameras were fired one after another around the actor.
The falling green code in The Matrix is made of Japanese characters scanned from the designer's wife's sushi cookbooks.
Christopher Lee was the only Lord of the Rings actor who had actually met author J.R.R. Tolkien.
Andy Serkis said Gollum's gulping voice was inspired by his cat coughing up a hairball.
Charlie Chaplin's body was stolen from his grave in 1978 and held for ransom. Police recovered it about 11 weeks later.
Alfred Hitchcock appeared in tiny cameo roles in about 39 of his own films.
In Lifeboat, set entirely on a small boat, Hitchcock made his cameo as the before-and-after photos in a newspaper diet ad.
Orson Welles was only 25 when he made Citizen Kane, often ranked the greatest film ever.
The Hollywood sign first read Hollywoodland. It was put up in 1923 as an advertisement for a housing development.
Each letter of the Hollywood sign is about as tall as a four-story building.
The Bollywood film Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge has played at the same Mumbai cinema since 1995, with only brief breaks, the longest run in Indian film history.
A two-hour movie at the standard 24 frames per second flashes about 172,800 separate pictures at you.
Movie trailers are called trailers because they used to be shown after the main film, not before.
Popcorn became the movie snack during the Great Depression, when it was one of the few treats people could still afford.
The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King won all 11 Oscars it was nominated for.
Katharine Hepburn won four Best Actress Oscars, more than any other performer.
Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai was remade as the cowboy film The Magnificent Seven.
George Lucas borrowed ideas for Star Wars from a Japanese samurai film, The Hidden Fortress.
Aardman animators making Wallace and Gromit often finish only about three seconds of film in a whole day.
For Coraline, the puppets had thousands of tiny 3D-printed faces that were swapped by hand to change expressions.
Horse hooves in old movies and radio shows were often just two coconut shells clopped together.
Sound effect artists often break celery and twist vegetables to make the sound of breaking bones in films.
The terrifying Jaws theme is built on just two notes played back and forth.
John Williams has more than 50 Oscar nominations, more than any other living person.
Italian composer Ennio Morricone wrote music for over 400 films and TV shows.
The Doctor Who theme was one of the first electronic TV themes, built in 1963 by Delia Derbyshire cutting and splicing tape by hand.
Kermit the Frog's first version was made from Jim Henson's mother's old coat and a ping pong ball cut in half for eyes.
Caroll Spinney played Big Bird on Sesame Street for nearly 50 years, peering out through a tiny monitor strapped to his chest.
Winnie-the-Pooh was named after a real black bear called Winnipeg who lived at London Zoo.
The real teddy bear toys that inspired Winnie-the-Pooh are on display at the New York Public Library.
The idea for Paddington Bear came from a lonely teddy bear its author spotted on a shop shelf on Christmas Eve.
Tom and Jerry cartoons won seven Oscars, even though the cat and mouse almost never say a word.
Shakespeare is the first known writer to use hundreds of English words, including lonely, bedroom and eyeball.
Not a single handwritten script of a Shakespeare play survives, except possibly a few pages of a play he co-wrote.
About half of Shakespeare's plays would be lost forever if two of his actor friends had not collected them in a book after he died.
Shakespeare spelled his own name in different ways in his six surviving signatures, and never the way we spell it today.
Shakespeare's will mentions his wife just once, to leave her his second-best bed.
Shakespeare's Globe Theatre burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a play set fire to the thatched roof. Nobody died.
The Tale of Genji, written by a Japanese noblewoman over 1,000 years ago, is often called the world's first novel.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, written on clay tablets in ancient Iraq, is one of the oldest stories in the world, around 4,000 years old.
Miguel de Cervantes, author of Don Quixote, was captured by pirates and held prisoner in Algiers for five years.
Cervantes lost the use of his left hand in a great sea battle in 1571, and was proud of it for the rest of his life.
Shakespeare and Cervantes, the two giants of English and Spanish writing, died within days of each other in 1616.
Charles Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks and paid to publish it himself.
Mary Shelley began Frankenstein at 18 in a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron, in 1816, the Year Without a Summer, when a volcano's ash made Europe cold and stormy.
Sherlock Holmes author Arthur Conan Doyle believed in fairies. He backed photos of them that two girls admitted, decades later, were paper cutouts.
Bram Stoker wrote Dracula, set in Transylvania, without ever visiting Transylvania.
Arthur Conan Doyle got so tired of Sherlock Holmes that he killed him off, then brought him back years later after readers protested.
Agatha Christie is the best-selling novelist of all time, with an estimated 2 billion books sold.
Agatha Christie's play The Mousetrap has run in London since 1952, longer than any other play in history.
Agatha Christie learned about poisons working in a hospital pharmacy during World War I, and used them in her mysteries.
The first Harry Potter book was rejected by about 12 publishers before one finally said yes.
The Harry Potter books have sold more than 500 million copies, enough to give one to every person in the European Union.
Dr. Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham using only 50 different words, to win a bet with his publisher.
The Cat in the Hat uses only about 236 different words, because it was written to help children learn to read.
Lewis Carroll made up Alice in Wonderland for a real girl named Alice, telling the story aloud during a boat trip.
Roald Dahl was a fighter pilot in World War II before he wrote children's books.
As a schoolboy, Roald Dahl tested new chocolate bars sent by a chocolate company, which later inspired Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
Ernest Hemingway survived two plane crashes in two days in Africa, and some newspapers printed his obituary.
Fyodor Dostoevsky was standing in front of a firing squad in 1849 when a last-second message from the tsar spared his life.
Dostoevsky wrote a whole novel in 26 days to meet a deadline by dictating it to a young stenographer. A few months later he married her.
Jane Austen's novels came out without her name on them. The first one said only By a Lady.
The Bronte sisters first published their novels under the men's names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.
George Eliot, author of Middlemarch, was really a woman named Mary Ann Evans.
Edgar Allan Poe wrote what is often called the first detective story, in 1841, decades before Sherlock Holmes.
The Baltimore Ravens football team is named after Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven.
Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, but fewer than a dozen were published while she was alive.
Franz Kafka asked his best friend to burn all his writing after he died. The friend refused, and published it instead.
J.R.R. Tolkien invented the Elvish languages first and said his stories were partly written to give them a world to live in.
Tolkien scribbled the first line of The Hobbit on a blank page of a student's exam paper he was marking.
George Orwell was a pen name. The author of 1984 was really Eric Blair, and borrowed his new surname from an English river.
Mark Twain's pen name comes from a riverboat call meaning the water is two fathoms deep, safe for a steamboat.
Mark Twain was born when Halley's Comet appeared in 1835, predicted he would go out with it, and died the day after it returned in 1910.
Copenhagen's Little Mermaid statue has had its head cut off by vandals twice.
In the original Grimm fairy tale, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off parts of their own feet to squeeze into the slipper.
Aladdin and Ali Baba were not in the old Arabic manuscripts of the Thousand and One Nights. A French translator added them in the 1700s.
In the original Pinocchio story, the puppet dies halfway through. Readers begged for more, so the author brought him back.
J.M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to a London children's hospital, which still earns money from it today.
Moby-Dick sold only about 3,000 copies while Herman Melville was alive.
When F. Scott Fitzgerald died, The Great Gatsby was a flop. During World War II about 150,000 free copies went to soldiers and revived it.
In Search of Lost Time by Marcel Proust is roughly 1.2 million words long, about the length of the whole Harry Potter series.
Georges Perec wrote a 300-page novel in French without a single letter e, and its English translation also avoids the e.
Gabriel Garcia Marquez could only afford to mail half of his famous novel to the publisher at first. His wife pawned household items to send the rest.
Hemingway wrote about 47 different endings for A Farewell to Arms. Asked what had stumped him, he said: Getting the words right.
Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of two countries, India and Bangladesh.
The Little Prince has been translated into more than 500 languages, more than almost any book besides religious texts.
The author of The Little Prince, a pilot, vanished on a flight over the Mediterranean in 1944. His silver bracelet was found by a fisherman in 1998.
Dante's Divine Comedy helped turn the dialect of Florence into the Italian spoken today.
To make himself finish The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, Victor Hugo reportedly locked away his clothes so he could not go out.
L. Frank Baum said he named the Land of Oz after the label on a drawer of his filing cabinet: O-Z.
The Very Hungry Caterpillar was first going to be about a bookworm named Willi, until Eric Carle's editor suggested a caterpillar.
Ian Fleming named James Bond after a real bird expert whose book on Caribbean birds sat on his shelf.
James Bond's creator Ian Fleming also wrote Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang, the children's story about a flying car.
Shakespeare's Juliet is not yet 14 years old, younger than almost every actress who has played her.
Beatrix Potter's publishers turned down Peter Rabbit, so she printed the first copies herself in 1901.
Bill Gates bought a notebook of Leonardo da Vinci's scientific writings in 1994 for about 30 million dollars.
Walt Whitman spent nearly 40 years rewriting his only book of poetry, which grew from 12 poems to almost 400.
Jack Kerouac typed On the Road on one continuous roll of taped-together paper about 36 meters long.
Stephen King threw his first novel, Carrie, in the trash. His wife fished it out and told him to finish it.
Students at Cambridge were not allowed dogs, so the poet Lord Byron reportedly kept a pet bear instead.
Leo Tolstoy was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature several times but never won it.
Leo Tolstoy's wife copied out the huge drafts of War and Peace by hand, several times over.
Victor Hugo's funeral in Paris in 1885 drew an estimated two million people into the streets.
Hans Christian Andersen was afraid of being buried alive and sometimes left a note saying he only seemed dead.
Herman Melville based Moby-Dick partly on the true story of a whaling ship sunk by an angry sperm whale in 1820.
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the first draft of Jekyll and Hyde in about three days, then burned it and rewrote it.
Robert Louis Stevenson drew the treasure map first, and Treasure Island grew out of it.
Basho's tiny haiku about a frog jumping into an old pond is so famous that one book collected more than 100 English translations of it.
Daniel Defoe was nearly 60 when he published Robinson Crusoe, his very first novel.
Roald Dahl invented more than 250 new words, like snozzcumber and whizzpopper, and some are now in the Oxford English Dictionary.
The ancient Greek theatre at Epidaurus seats about 14,000 people, and actors there could be heard in the back row without any microphone.
In ancient Greek theatre, every role, including all the women, was played by men wearing masks.
In Shakespeare's day, Juliet, Lady Macbeth and every other female role were played by boys.
Theatres leave a single ghost light burning on the empty stage all night, so nobody falls into the orchestra pit in the dark.
Many actors refuse to say the word Macbeth inside a theatre, calling it the Scottish Play to avoid bad luck.
Actors wish each other break a leg instead of good luck, because saying good luck is believed to jinx a show.
The Phantom of the Opera ran on Broadway for 35 years before it finally closed in 2023.
Lin-Manuel Miranda performed a song from Hamilton at the White House in 2009, six years before the musical opened.
Japanese Kabuki theatre was started around 1603 by a woman, but women were soon banned from it, and men have played every role since.
In Japanese Bunraku puppet theatre, it takes three people to work a single puppet, and they stay visible on stage.
The Oberammergau Passion Play in Germany has been staged about every 10 years since 1634, keeping a promise villagers made during a plague.
Wagner's Ring Cycle is four operas long and lasts about 15 hours, usually spread over several nights.
Wagner had his own opera house built in Bayreuth, with the orchestra hidden in a pit under the stage.
The architect of the Sydney Opera House quit in 1966 before it was finished, and never saw the completed building in person.
King Louis XIV loved ballet and danced in it himself. He got the nickname Sun King after playing the sun god Apollo at 14.
Ballet steps have French names because King Louis XIV founded the first royal dance academy in 1661.
A professional ballet dancer can wear out a pair of pointe shoes in a single performance.
Swan Lake flopped when it premiered in 1877. It only became a classic after a new production in 1895, after Tchaikovsky's death.
Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker made the celesta famous, a keyboard that sounds like tinkling bells, used for the Sugar Plum Fairy.
The tango was born in the working-class neighborhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s.
In 1518 hundreds of people in Strasbourg danced uncontrollably in the streets for days, and nobody is sure why.
Gene Kelly reportedly filmed the famous Singin' in the Rain dance while sick with a fever.
In Indian classical dance, hand gestures called mudras can stand for a deer, a lotus, a bee and hundreds of other ideas.
The haka is a traditional Maori challenge dance, famously performed by New Zealand's rugby team before international matches.
Breakdancing, born at Bronx block parties in the 1970s, became an Olympic sport at the Paris 2024 Games.
Ballerina Anna Pavlova performed her four-minute solo The Dying Swan an estimated 4,000 times.
The story goes that Fred Astaire's first screen test report said: Can't act. Slightly bald. Also dances.
Around 1900, Isadora Duncan shocked audiences by dancing barefoot in a loose tunic instead of a corset and ballet shoes.
The first known photograph of a person was an accident: a man getting his boots shined on a Paris street in 1838 stayed still long enough to appear.
Victorian mothers sometimes hid under a cloth behind their babies to hold them still for photos. They are known as hidden mother photos.
The first color photograph was made in 1861 by a physicist. It shows a tartan ribbon.
Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975. It weighed about as much as a bowling ball, took 23 seconds per photo, and Kodak shelved it to protect its film sales.
The famous photo of workers eating lunch on a steel beam high above New York was a staged publicity shot in 1932, but they really were 69 floors up.
The girl in the famous Afghan Girl photo was found and identified 17 years after her picture was taken.
Dorothea Lange took her famous Migrant Mother photo in about ten minutes, with just six shots.
The Kodak Brownie camera went on sale in 1900 for one dollar, putting photography in ordinary hands for the first time.
Edwin Land invented the instant Polaroid camera after his 3-year-old daughter asked why she couldn't see a photo right away.
In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a galloping horse and proved that all four hooves leave the ground at once.
The famous photo of Albert Einstein sticking out his tongue was taken on his 72nd birthday, when he was tired of smiling for photographers.
In 1839 Robert Cornelius took one of the first photos of a human face, a self-portrait, by sitting still for several minutes.
Victorians often looked stern in photos partly because they had to hold still for long exposures, and wide grins were seen as foolish.
The Coca-Cola bottle was designed in 1915 so you could recognize it by touch in the dark, or even when smashed on the ground.
The London Underground map is easy to read because its designer ignored real distances and drew the lines like an electrical circuit.
The I Love NY logo was sketched by designer Milton Glaser in the back of a taxi, and he did the work for free.
The Nike swoosh was designed in 1971 by a student who was paid just 35 dollars.
The FedEx logo hides a white arrow in the space between the E and the x. Once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
Comic Sans was created in 1994 for the speech bubbles of a cartoon dog in a Microsoft program, but was finished too late to be used there.
The Helvetica font was first called Neue Haas Grotesk; it was renamed after the Latin name for Switzerland, where it was born.
The Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for only 20 years. It was saved partly because it made a great radio antenna.
The Eiffel Tower is repainted by hand about every seven years, using around 60 tons of paint.
Famous writers and artists signed a protest against the Eiffel Tower before it was built, calling it a monstrous eyesore.
A LEGO brick made in 1958 still clicks perfectly onto one made today.
Antoni Gaudi worked on the Sagrada Familia for 43 years and is buried in its crypt.
Gaudi was hit by a tram in 1926, and because of his shabby clothes, people mistook him for a beggar and were slow to help.
The Taj Mahal took about 20 years and some 20,000 workers to build.
The Louvre's glass pyramid has 673 panes of glass, despite a popular rumor that it has exactly 666.
The Louvre was originally a fortress built around 1190 to protect Paris. You can still see its old foundations in the basement.
The Mona Lisa sits behind bulletproof glass, and over the years it has been attacked with acid, a rock, a teacup, cake and soup.
The Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg keeps dozens of cats to protect its art from mice, a tradition going back centuries.
The Guggenheim Museum in New York is one long spiral ramp: you look at the art while walking slowly downhill.
The Bauhaus, one of the most influential design schools ever, lasted only 14 years before it closed under Nazi pressure in 1933.
The Parthenon has almost no straight lines. Its columns bulge and lean slightly so that from a distance they look perfectly straight.
Around 1415, Brunelleschi showed people perspective using a painted panel with a peephole and a mirror.
Lorenzo Ghiberti spent about 27 years making a pair of bronze doors for Florence's Baptistery. Michelangelo called them the Gates of Paradise.
Notre-Dame's great rose windows survived the 2019 fire that brought down its spire.
Notre-Dame Cathedral reopened in December 2024, about five years after the fire.
Chartres Cathedral in France still has most of its stained glass from the 1200s.
Borobudur temple in Indonesia is decorated with over 2,600 carved stone panels and more than 500 Buddha statues.
Portugal covers whole buildings in painted ceramic tiles called azulejos, turning streets into giant picture books.
Delft Blue pottery began as a Dutch attempt to copy Chinese porcelain that Europeans could not make themselves.
For centuries Europeans could not work out how to make porcelain. The secret was finally cracked in Germany around 1708 by an alchemist held captive to make gold.
Venice's Murano glassmakers were forbidden to leave the republic, so they could not share their secret techniques.
Leonardo da Vinci planned a giant bronze horse for Milan, but the metal saved for it was turned into cannons. A version was finally built in 1999.
Raphael painted himself into his masterpiece The School of Athens, peeking out at you from the right edge.
Albrecht Durer made his famous 1515 picture of a rhinoceros without ever seeing one, giving it armor plates and an extra horn on its back.
Bruegel's painting Netherlandish Proverbs crams more than 100 old sayings into one busy village scene.
Rubens was not only a star painter but also a diplomat who helped make peace between England and Spain.
Rembrandt painted, drew or etched himself about 80 times, from a cocky young man to a wrinkled old one.
Rembrandt went bankrupt in 1656 and had to sell his house and his whole art collection.
J.M.W. Turner left about 30,000 sketches and watercolors to the British nation when he died.
For his painting of a famous 1816 shipwreck, Gericault interviewed survivors and built a model of the raft in his studio.
Manet's painting Olympia caused such an uproar in 1865 that guards were posted to protect it from angry visitors.
In 1863 so many paintings were rejected by the official Paris exhibition that Napoleon III set up a show of the rejects, letting the public judge.
Edvard Munch sometimes left his paintings outside in rain and snow for months, calling it a horse cure that would toughen them up.
Van Gogh's brother Theo, who supported him all his life, died only about six months after Vincent.
Toulouse-Lautrec's legs stopped growing after he broke both thigh bones as a teenager, probably because of a rare bone condition.
Alphonse Mucha became famous overnight in 1894 with a poster for the star actress Sarah Bernhardt.
Near the end of his life, Henri Matisse could no longer stand to paint, so he made art by cutting shapes out of painted paper with scissors.
A Matisse hung upside down at New York's Museum of Modern Art for 47 days in 1961. In 2022 experts said a Mondrian had probably hung upside down for 75 years.
Van Gogh painted The Starry Night during the day, from memory, showing the view from his room at an asylum in southern France.
Wassily Kandinsky said he could hear colors and see sounds, and he named some paintings like pieces of music.
Swedish artist Hilma af Klint painted abstract art years before Kandinsky, but asked that it stay hidden until 20 years after her death.
Edward Hopper's famous diner painting Nighthawks shows no way into the diner. There is no visible door.
Norman Rockwell painted 323 covers for the Saturday Evening Post magazine.
Roy Lichtenstein painted giant comic-strip scenes, even copying the tiny dots of cheap comic book printing.
Keith Haring drew thousands of chalk pictures on empty black advertising boards in the New York subway, often dodging police.
In 2017 a skull painting by Jean-Michel Basquiat sold for about 110 million dollars. He had started out as a graffiti artist.
TV painter Bob Ross was a master sergeant in the US Air Force before he became the calmest man on television.
Bob Ross got his famous perm to save money on haircuts. He came to dislike it, but kept it because it was his trademark.
Bob Ross made 403 episodes of his painting show, usually finishing a whole landscape in under half an hour.
Winston Churchill painted more than 500 pictures, and took up painting in his 40s.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the entire German parliament building in silver fabric in 1995.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude paid for their giant wrapping projects themselves, by selling their sketches and models.
Ai Weiwei filled a hall at London's Tate Modern with about 100 million porcelain sunflower seeds, each one painted by hand.
Artist Yayoi Kusama, famous for her polka dots, has chosen to live in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital since 1977 and walks to her studio nearby.
Damien Hirst's famous shark in a tank of preserving fluid began to rot, and had to be replaced with a new shark.
In 2024 a banana duct-taped to a wall, an artwork by Maurizio Cattelan, sold at auction for about 6.2 million dollars. The buyer ate it.
In 2010 Marina Abramovic sat silently in a chair at a New York museum for over 700 hours while visitors took turns sitting across from her.
Medieval monks often doodled knights fighting giant snails in the margins of their books, and historians still argue about why.
The Book of Kells, a dazzling Irish manuscript over 1,200 years old, is written on calfskin from an estimated 185 calves.
The Japanese art of kintsugi repairs broken pottery with gold-dusted lacquer, making the cracks the most beautiful part.
Diego Rivera's mural in New York's Rockefeller Center was destroyed in 1934 because he refused to paint over a portrait of Lenin.
Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera lived in two separate houses side by side, joined by a little bridge on the roof.
Only about 50 Faberge eggs were made for the Russian royal family, and several are still missing.
A US scrap metal dealer nearly melted down a golden egg he bought for about 14,000 dollars. It turned out to be a lost Faberge egg worth millions.
In 1962 the Mona Lisa was given an insurance value of 100 million dollars for a trip to the US, one of the highest ever.
A German forger fooled art experts for decades, until a tiny trace of modern white paint in a supposed 1914 painting gave him away.
Scans show a hidden portrait of a man under Picasso's painting The Blue Room. Young and broke, he often painted over old canvases.
Picasso's sad Blue Period began after the death of his close friend in 1901.
Picasso's first word is said to have been piz, short for lapiz, the Spanish word for pencil.
Cubism got its name when a critic sneered that Braque's paintings turned everything into little cubes.
The Fauves got their name when a critic called the painters wild beasts because of their crazy bright colors.
The Dada art movement's name is said to have been picked at random from a dictionary. In French, dada means hobby horse.
Surrealist artists played a game where each person draws part of a figure on folded paper without seeing what the others drew.
Japanese woodblock prints became a craze in 1800s Europe and inspired Monet, Van Gogh and Degas.
Monet collected more than 200 Japanese prints, and they still hang in his house at Giverny.
Van Gogh copied Japanese prints in oil paint, adding Japanese characters he could not read as decoration.
Hiroshige's famous series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo actually contains 118 prints.
China's most famous piece of calligraphy, written in 353, is lost. Legend says the emperor who loved it was buried with it.
A Chinese scroll painted about 900 years ago is over 5 meters long and shows more than 800 people going about their day.
India's Ajanta Caves, full of Buddhist paintings up to 2,000 years old, were rediscovered in 1819 by a British officer hunting a tiger.
The Maori see their carved meeting houses as the body of an ancestor: the ridge beam is the spine and the rafters are the ribs.
Navajo healers make detailed sand paintings for ceremonies, then destroy them when the ritual ends.
Tibetan monks spend days building a sand mandala grain by grain, then sweep it away to show that nothing lasts.
Some giant stone heads carved by the ancient Olmec of Mexico weigh over 20 tons, and were moved for kilometers without wheels or draft animals.
A hummingbird drawn in the Peruvian desert by the Nazca people is about 93 meters long, and it is best seen from the air.
In 2024 researchers using AI discovered about 300 new Nazca desert drawings in just six months.
The Day of the Dead skeleton lady, La Catrina, began around 1910 as a joke print mocking Mexicans who copied European fashions.
Picasso was strongly inspired by African masks he saw in Paris when he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907.
In Ghana's kente cloth, each color has a meaning: gold for wealth, green for growth, blue for peace.
Indonesian batik is made by drawing designs with hot wax so the dye cannot reach those parts of the cloth.
The Benin Bronzes, thousands of sculptures taken by British troops in 1897, are now slowly being returned to Nigeria.
An Aztec feathered headdress made with hundreds of shimmering quetzal tail feathers survives in a museum in Vienna.
The Lewis Chessmen, carved from walrus ivory about 850 years ago, were found on a Scottish island in 1831.
The Sutton Hoo helmet was found crushed into hundreds of fragments and had to be pieced back together like a puzzle.
Folding 1,000 paper cranes is said to grant a wish, and a Japanese girl named Sadako made the cranes a worldwide symbol of peace.
J.M.W. Turner said he had sailors tie him to a ship's mast for four hours in a snowstorm so he could paint it. Some historians doubt the story.
Tutankhamun's famous gold mask weighs about 10 kilograms, as much as a large watermelon.
When Howard Carter first peered into Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 and was asked if he could see anything, he answered: Yes, wonderful things.
Ancient Egyptian artists drew people with the face in profile but the eye and shoulders facing forward, following the same rules for nearly 3,000 years.
Ancient Egyptian painters used grids to keep the bodies of people they drew in perfect proportion.
Medieval painters made important people bigger than everyone else, no matter how far away they were standing.
Donatello's bronze David is thought to be the first freestanding nude statue made in Europe since ancient times.
Bernini carved marble so skillfully that in Apollo and Daphne, the stone leaves and fingers look thin enough to see light through.
Sculptor Camille Claudel was as gifted as Rodin, her teacher, but spent her last 30 years locked away in an asylum.
When Degas first showed his statue Little Dancer Aged Fourteen in 1881, it wore a real fabric tutu and real hair.
Alexander Calder invented the mobile, the hanging sculpture that moves, and Marcel Duchamp gave it its name.
Alexander Calder built a tiny circus out of wire and performed shows with it himself, playing every role.
In 1926 US customs refused to treat Brancusi's sculpture Bird in Space as art and taxed it as a kitchen utensil. A court overturned that in 1928.
Picasso refused to be paid for the giant sculpture he designed for Chicago, giving it to the city as a gift.
Robert Indiana never copyrighted his famous LOVE design, so it was copied everywhere and he made little money from it.
Brussels' tiny Manneken Pis statue has a wardrobe of over 1,000 costumes and gets dressed up several times a month.
The steel wings of England's Angel of the North sculpture stretch about 54 meters, almost as wide as a jumbo jet's wings.
@prehistoric|Prehistoric
T. rex lived closer in time to you than to Stegosaurus. Over 80 million years separate those two dinosaurs; only 66 million separate T. rex from us.
Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built. A small herd survived on an Arctic island until about 4,000 years ago.
If Earth's history were squeezed into one day, modern humans would show up in only the last 6 seconds before midnight.
If Earth's history were one calendar year, dinosaurs would arrive around December 13 and vanish on December 26.
Sharks are older than trees. Shark-like fish were swimming about 450 million years ago, long before the first forests grew.
Dinosaurs ruled the land for about 165 million years. Our species has been around for about 300,000.
A chicken is more closely related to T. rex than T. rex was to Stegosaurus or Triceratops.
Birds are dinosaurs, and there are about 11,000 kinds of them, so more species of dinosaur are alive today than species of mammal.
Crocodiles are more closely related to birds than to lizards or snakes, which makes a crocodile a distant cousin of a chicken.
The smallest dinosaur ever known is alive today: the bee hummingbird of Cuba, which weighs about as much as a paperclip or two.
Birds evolved from the "lizard-hipped" dinosaurs, not from the group scientists named "bird-hipped". Oops.
Iguanodon's thumb spike was first stuck on its nose, because nobody knew where the odd cone-shaped bone belonged.
On New Year's Eve 1853, scientists held a dinner party inside a life-size model of an Iguanodon in London.
Scientists name about 50 new dinosaur species every year, roughly one a week, so most known dinosaurs are recent finds.
Dinosaurs lived on every continent, including Antarctica, which was much warmer back then.
Antarctica had a meat-eating dinosaur with a curly crest on its head, nicknamed Elvisaurus for its hairdo.
T. rex had the strongest bite of any known land animal, strong enough to crush bone like a car crusher.
A teenage T. rex could gain about 2 kilograms a day during its growth spurt, like putting on a bag of sugar every day.
T. rex lived fast and died young: even the oldest known skeletons, like Sue, were only about 30 years old.
Scientists estimate about 2.5 billion T. rex lived in total over the species' 2 to 3 million years.
Some T. rex teeth were about the size of a banana, root included, and their edges were serrated like steak knives.
Sue, one of the biggest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, sold at auction in 1997 for about 8.4 million dollars.
A Stegosaurus skeleton nicknamed Apex sold for 44.6 million dollars in 2024, more than any T. rex.
T. rex had a huge smell center in its brain, so scientists think it could sniff out food from far away.
Computer models suggest an adult T. rex could not really run: at high speed its leg bones would have been overloaded.
T. rex's arms were only about a meter long on a body around 12 meters long, but they were packed with muscle.
Sue the T. rex had holes in her jaw that scientists think came from a parasite that still infects pigeons today.
Spinosaurus was longer than T. rex, about 14 meters, and many scientists think it hunted fish in rivers.
The original Spinosaurus bones were destroyed when bombs hit a museum in Munich during World War II.
Spinosaurus had heavy, dense bones like a penguin's, which some scientists think helped it dive.
