A dinosaur from Brazil was named Irritator because fossil dealers had faked parts of its skull with plaster.
Carnotaurus had bull-like horns over its eyes and arms so tiny they make T. rex's look big.
Real Dilophosaurus had no neck frill and did not spit venom. Jurassic Park made that up.
The real Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey. The movie raptors were modeled on its much bigger cousin, Deinonychus.
Velociraptor arm bones have little bumps where big feathers attached, just like on a bird's wing.
Scientists found a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops fossilized mid-fight, probably buried when a sand dune collapsed on them.
Utahraptor, a cousin of Velociraptor, was about 6 meters long with a hooked toe claw longer than your hand.
Microraptor had feathered wings on its arms and its legs, so it flew with four wings.
Microraptor's feathers were glossy black with a rainbow sheen, like a crow's, as pigment grains in its fossil show.
Scientists can tell the color of some dinosaurs from tiny pigment grains still preserved in fossil feathers.
A small dinosaur called Sinosauropteryx had a ginger and white striped tail, like a raccoon's.
Psittacosaurus was dark on top and pale underneath, the same camouflage trick sharks and deer use today.
In 2016, scientists found a feathered dinosaur tail trapped in a lump of amber about 99 million years old.
Oviraptor's name means "egg thief", but it was actually sitting on its own eggs to protect them.
Some dinosaurs laid blue-green eggs, like a robin's, a color once thought to be a bird-only invention.
Dinosaur eggs took about 3 to 6 months to hatch, far longer than bird eggs, as tooth growth lines in embryos show.
Even the biggest dinosaurs, weighing as much as ten elephants, hatched from eggs no bigger than a soccer ball.
A small dinosaur called Mei long was fossilized asleep with its head tucked under its arm, exactly like a sleeping duck.
Argentinosaurus may have weighed about 70 tonnes, more than ten African elephants put together.
Giant long-necked dinosaurs had air pockets inside their bones, like birds, which made their huge skeletons lighter.
Long-necked dinosaurs never chewed. They raked in leaves and swallowed them whole.
Nigersaurus had about 500 teeth in a mouth shaped like a vacuum cleaner head, and it grew a new tooth roughly every two weeks.
Mamenchisaurus had a neck about 15 meters long, as long as a city bus and then some.
Brontosaurus was declared fake in 1903, lumped in with Apatosaurus, then brought back as a real dinosaur in 2015.
Stegosaurus weighed several tonnes but had one of the smallest brains for its size of any dinosaur.
The spiky tail of Stegosaurus is called a thagomizer, a joke word from a Far Side cartoon that scientists adopted.
An Allosaurus backbone has a hole that exactly fits a Stegosaurus tail spike, proof of a real prehistoric fight.
Some horned dinosaurs had skulls over 2.5 meters long, longer than a tall man lying down.
Duck-billed dinosaurs could have about 1,000 teeth in their mouths at once, constantly replacing worn ones.
Parasaurolophus had a long hollow head crest that scientists think worked like a trombone for deep, booming calls.
A mummified duck-billed dinosaur showed it had a soft fleshy comb on its head, like a rooster.
An armored dinosaur was named Zuul after the monster in Ghostbusters. Its full name means "Zuul, destroyer of shins".
An armored dinosaur dug up in a Canadian mine in 2011 is so well preserved it looks like a stone statue of itself.
Scientists even found that armored dinosaur's last meal, mostly ferns, still in its stomach after 110 million years.
Pachycephalosaurus had a domed skull up to about 25 centimeters thick, roughly the length of a school ruler.
Therizinosaurus had claws longer than a man's arm from elbow to fingertip, yet it probably ate plants.
For almost 50 years, Deinocheirus was known only from two giant arms. Later finds revealed a humpbacked, duck-billed giant.
One Deinocheirus was found with over 1,400 stones in its belly, swallowed to help grind up food.
A small dinosaur called Shuvuuia had owl-like ears and eyes, so scientists think it hunted in the dark.
Yi qi was a pigeon-sized dinosaur with bat-like wings made of skin. Its name means strange wing.
Limusaurus had teeth as a baby and lost them all as it grew up, ending with a toothless beak.
Mussaurus means "mouse lizard" because it was named from tiny babies. The adults were about 6 meters long.
Archaeopteryx, the famous half-bird half-dinosaur, was found just two years after Darwin published his theory of evolution.
Archaeopteryx had feathered wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail.
Pterosaurs were not dinosaurs, but their cousins, and they were the first animals with backbones to fly.
A pterosaur's whole wing hung from one enormously long finger, its fourth, like a kite on a single pole.
Quetzalcoatlus had wings about 10 meters across, as wide as a small plane, and stood as tall as a giraffe.
Scientists think giant pterosaurs took off by pushing up from the ground with their arms, like pole vaulters.
Pterosaurs were covered in fuzz, a bit like a bat or a fluffy chick, which probably helped keep them warm.
One pterosaur, Pterodaustro, had about 1,000 bristle-like teeth to sieve food from water, like a flamingo.
The smallest known pterosaurs were about the size of a sparrow, small enough to sit in your hand.
Baby pterosaurs could probably fly almost as soon as they hatched, scientists think.
Fossil footprints show pterosaurs walked on all fours, with their wings folded up beside them.
Some pterosaurs had head crests several times taller than their skulls, like a sail on their heads.
Ichthyosaurs looked just like dolphins, but they were reptiles. Nature invented the same shape twice.
Ichthyosaurs gave birth to live babies in the sea, and some fossil mothers were caught mid-birth.
One ichthyosaur had eyes about 26 centimeters wide, the size of a dinner plate, perhaps for seeing in deep, dark water.
Bones found on an English beach suggest an ichthyosaur about 25 meters long, nearly the size of a blue whale.
Mary Anning was about 12 when she and her brother found the first ichthyosaur skeleton recognized by science.
Elasmosaurus had a neck about 7 meters long, made of 72 bones. A giraffe's long neck has just 7.
When Elasmosaurus was first rebuilt in 1868, the scientist put its head on the end of its tail.
Mosasaurs, giant sea predators of the dinosaur age, were actually huge lizards related to snakes and monitor lizards.
When French troops seized a famous mosasaur skull in 1795, legend says they paid 600 bottles of wine to the men who found it.
A Tylosaurus fossil was found with a whole other sea reptile, a plesiosaur, inside its stomach.
Liopleurodon was about 6 to 7 meters long, nowhere near the 25-meter monster shown on TV.
Tanystropheus had a neck about 3 meters long, half the length of its whole body, probably for snatching fish.
Archelon, a sea turtle from the dinosaur age, was about 4.6 meters long, bigger than a small car.
Dunkleosteus was an armored fish with no teeth. Instead, it had self-sharpening bony blades.
Helicoprion had a spiral of teeth like a circular saw in its jaw. It was not a shark, but a ratfish relative.
Megalodon's teeth were up to about 18 centimeters long, as long as your hand, and people still find them on beaches.
Megalodon never met a dinosaur. It appeared about 40 million years after they were gone.
A giant sperm whale relative called Livyatan had teeth about 36 centimeters long, the biggest bite teeth of any known animal.
Sharks' skeletons are soft cartilage, so most fossil sharks are known only from their teeth.
People once thought fossil shark teeth were dragon tongues turned to stone. They were called tongue stones.
Sea scorpions about 400 million years ago grew up to 2.5 meters long, longer than a grown man.
Arthropleura, a millipede relative from about 300 million years ago, grew longer than a man is tall.
A dragonfly relative called Meganeuropsis had wings about 70 centimeters across, as wide as a pigeon's.
Scientists think giant insects of the coal-swamp era thrived because the air had much more oxygen than today.
Yutyrannus, a 9-meter cousin of T. rex, was covered in long feathery filaments, like a giant shaggy bird.
Some coal-age trees over 30 meters tall were giant relatives of tiny club mosses that you can hold in your hand.
Dimetrodon, the sail-backed beast sold with toy dinosaurs, was not a dinosaur. It is actually closer to us mammals.
Dimetrodon died out about 40 million years before the first dinosaur appeared, so it never saw a single one.
Before the dinosaurs, saber-toothed predators called gorgonopsians ruled the land, and they were mammal relatives.
Lystrosaurus, a pig-sized plant-eater, survived the worst extinction in history and then spread almost everywhere.
Fossils of the same small freshwater reptile found in both Brazil and Africa helped prove the continents were once joined.
Some ancient relatives of crocodiles walked on two legs and looked almost exactly like ostrich-shaped dinosaurs.
SuperCroc, Sarcosuchus, was about 9 meters long and roughly as heavy as an elephant.
Deinosuchus, a giant alligator relative about 10 meters long, left bite marks on dinosaur bones.
Some ancient crocodile relatives ate only plants, and others lived in the open sea with flippers and tail fins.
Trilobites lasted about 270 million years, longer than the dinosaurs. They vanished before the first dinosaur hatched.
Trilobites had eyes made of crystal: their lenses were the same mineral as limestone.
Scientists have named more than 20,000 kinds of trilobite, more than all the species of birds alive today.
Some ammonites, coiled-shell relatives of squid, grew shells nearly 2 meters across, like a giant cartwheel.
In Whitby, England, people carved snake heads onto ammonite fossils and sold them as snakes turned to stone by a saint.
The pointy fossils of belemnites, extinct squid relatives, were once believed to be thunderbolts fallen from the sky.
A sea creature, an ammonite, was found trapped in tree amber about 99 million years old, probably washed up on a beach.
The nautilus belongs to a group of shelled animals that has been swimming the seas for about 500 million years.
Horseshoe crabs have been around for about 445 million years, and they are closer to spiders than to crabs.
The coelacanth was thought to have died out with the dinosaurs, until a fisherman caught a living one in 1938.
The tuatara of New Zealand is the last survivor of a reptile family that thrived alongside the first dinosaurs.
Ginkgo trees belong to a family more than 200 million years old. Dinosaurs walked past their ancestors.
The dawn redwood was described from fossils, then found growing alive in a Chinese village a few years later.
Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck and wrists, was found after scientists picked the right age of rock and went looking for it.
The first four-legged animals had more than five fingers. One had eight on each hand.
The bones in your hand can be traced back to the fin of a fish that lived over 375 million years ago.
Three tiny bones in your ear were once part of the jaw of your reptile-like ancestors.
Some scientists think hiccups are a leftover reflex from ancestors that breathed with both gills and lungs.
In the Cambrian explosion, about 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appeared in a geological blink.
Anomalocaris, a Cambrian top predator, had spiky grabbing arms and a round mouth like a pineapple slice.
Opabinia had five eyes and a long nozzle with a claw, and the audience laughed when it was first shown in 1972.
Hallucigenia was first drawn upside down and back to front: its spikes were mistaken for legs and its head for its tail.
An Edmontosaurus tail bone has a broken-off T. rex tooth stuck in it, and the bone healed around it: the plant-eater got away.
The first dinosaur, Megalosaurus, was named in 1824, nearly 20 years before anyone had invented the word dinosaur.
Some of the oldest shells known, about 550 million years old, have small holes drilled in them, maybe by the first predators.
Dickinsonia looked like a flat oval bathmat, yet chemicals in its fossils prove it was an animal, about 558 million years old.
One of the first fossils of very early animal life was spotted in 1957 by a 15-year-old schoolboy. A schoolgirl had seen it a year earlier, but nobody believed her.
Stromatolites, rocks built by microbes, are some of the oldest signs of life, about 3.5 billion years old. They still grow in Australia.
For about 3 billion years, nearly all life on Earth was too small to see without a microscope.
The oxygen we breathe began building up about 2.4 billion years ago, made by tiny ocean bacteria.
Scientists think Earth froze over almost completely, from pole to equator, at least twice before animals appeared.
The oldest known bits of Earth are tiny crystals from Australia, about 4.4 billion years old.
There have been five great mass extinctions. The worst, about 252 million years ago, wiped out roughly 8 or 9 in every 10 sea species.
The Great Dying, the worst extinction ever, was probably caused by volcanic eruptions in Siberia that lasted for many thousands of years.
After the Great Dying, tropical seas may have reached about 40 degrees C, as hot as a hot tub.
The Great Dying, 252 million years ago, is the only known mass extinction that hit insects hard.
Life took about 10 million years to fully bounce back from the Great Dying, the worst extinction ever.
The asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs was about 10 kilometers wide, roughly the height of Mount Everest plus a bit.
The dinosaur-killing asteroid left a crater about 180 kilometers wide, now buried under Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula.
The crater of the dinosaur-killing asteroid was not linked to their extinction until 1991, after oil geologists had mapped it.
In 1980, a father-and-son team found a strange metal-rich layer of clay worldwide and proposed an asteroid killed the dinosaurs.
Fossil fish suggest the dinosaur-killing asteroid struck in spring, in the Northern Hemisphere.
At one fossil site in North Dakota, fish died with tiny glass beads from the asteroid impact stuck in their gills.
The dinosaur-killing asteroid hit rocks full of sulfur, which scientists think filled the sky with haze and froze the planet.
Scientists think almost no land animal bigger than a medium-sized dog survived the asteroid 66 million years ago.
Right after the asteroid, ferns took over much of the land, leaving a burst of fern spores in the rocks.
Within about 700,000 years after the asteroid, mammals went from rat-sized survivors to animals the size of a big dog.
About three quarters of all species on Earth died out when the asteroid hit, not just the dinosaurs.
About 445 million years ago, an ice age wiped out roughly 85 percent of all sea species.
Dinosaurs only took over after another mass extinction, about 201 million years ago, wiped out their crocodile-like rivals.
More than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived are now extinct, so extinction is the rule, not the exception.
Many scientists warn that species are now vanishing hundreds of times faster than the natural rate.
Maiasaura means good mother lizard: its nesting grounds show parents looked after their babies until they could leave the nest.
Giant pterosaurs like Quetzalcoatlus probably hunted on the ground, stalking small animals like enormous storks.
Neanderthals in Germany hunted straight-tusked elephants weighing up to about 13 tonnes, and one could feed a whole group for weeks.
The petrified logs in Arizona's Petrified Forest are about 225 million years old, and the wood has turned into rainbow-colored quartz.
In Australia, some dinosaur and early mammal fossils are made of opal, the shimmering gemstone.
Some dinosaur bones are slightly radioactive, because uranium from groundwater soaked into them over millions of years.
The Venus of Willendorf, a little stone figure about 30,000 years old found in Austria, was carved from a stone that probably came from northern Italy.
A fossil poop thought to be from a T. rex, found in Canada, was about 44 centimeters long and full of crushed bone.
In Bolivia, thousands of dinosaur footprints climb a steep cliff. The ground was flat when they walked; it was tilted up later.
In 2005, a scientist found soft, stretchy tissue inside a 68-million-year-old T. rex leg bone.
No dinosaur DNA has ever been found. DNA falls apart far too fast to last 66 million years, so Jurassic Park is safe.
The oldest DNA ever read is about 2 million years old, from Greenland, where mastodons once roamed a forest.
Scientists have read DNA over a million years old from mammoth teeth frozen in Siberia.
Amber has trapped frogs, lizards, spiders and even a baby bird from about 99 million years ago.
At the Messel Pit in Germany, some 47-million-year-old beetles still shine with their original metallic colors.
A 47-million-year-old horse from Germany was found with her unborn foal still inside her.
In China, volcanic ash buried whole forests about 125 million years ago, preserving feathers, fur and even last meals.
In Nebraska, dozens of rhinos lie where they died about 12 million years ago, buried by ash from a volcano in Idaho.
The La Brea Tar Pits, still bubbling in the middle of Los Angeles, have produced millions of ice age fossils.
More than 2,000 saber-toothed cats have been pulled out of the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.
Only one human skeleton has been found in the La Brea Tar Pits: a woman who died about 10,000 years ago.
Dire wolves were real, not a TV invention: these heavy-jawed wolves, bigger than gray wolves, hunted in the Americas until about 13,000 years ago.
Walking along England's Jurassic Coast, you pass rocks that cover about 185 million years of Earth history.
The Himalayas began rising about 50 million years ago, when India, drifting north like a raft, crashed into Asia.
In Egypt's desert lies the Valley of the Whales, full of fossil whale skeletons from when the area was sea.
Ice age cave artists worked by the light of little stone lamps that burned animal fat.
About 5.6 million years ago, the Mediterranean Sea almost dried up, leaving salt layers over a kilometer thick.
Hippos once lived where London is now. Their bones were found under Trafalgar Square.

When T. rex lived, a day was about half an hour shorter, because Earth spun faster back then.

Basilosaurus means "king lizard", because it was first mistaken for a sea reptile. It was a whale.
Elephant shrews, tiny long-nosed animals from Africa, are more closely related to elephants than to real shrews.

Mammoths had small ears and short tails, which helped them lose less heat in the freezing cold.

At White Sands in New Mexico, human footprints step right inside the tracks of a giant ground sloth, as if someone was following it.
Farming has existed for only about the last 4 percent of our species' history. Before that, everyone was a hunter-gatherer.
Hawaii's Big Island is younger than the human family: it rose out of the sea within the last million years.
Niagara Falls is young: it formed only about 12,000 years ago, as ice age glaciers melted away.
Plesiosaurs could not be hiding in Loch Ness: the loch was buried under solid ice until about 10,000 years ago.
Many dinosaurs were probably warm-blooded, or close to it, and grew fast like birds rather than slowly like lizards.
Gomphotherium, an early elephant relative, had four tusks: two in its upper jaw and two in its lower jaw.
Mammals were gliding between trees like flying squirrels about 160 million years ago, while dinosaurs walked below.
Dung beetles were already at work 75 million years ago: fossil dinosaur dung from Montana is riddled with their tunnels.
Stegosaurus plates were not attached to its skeleton. They sat in the skin, and scientists think they were mostly for show.
Dinosaur bones have growth rings, like trees, so scientists can count how old an animal was when it died.
In 1878, coal miners in Belgium found about 38 Iguanodon skeletons deep underground.
Fossils of an Antarctic dinosaur were found near the top of a mountain, about 4,000 meters up.
Some giant pterosaurs had hollow bones with walls only about a millimeter thick, light but strong.
Trilobites could roll up into a ball for protection, just like a woodlouse does.
Some trilobites had a trident-like prong sticking out of their heads, which scientists think was used to fight rivals.
The eyes of Anomalocaris, a Cambrian hunter, had about 16,000 lenses each, like a dragonfly's.
When oxygen first built up, it rusted iron dissolved in the oceans, leaving striped red rocks we still mine for iron today.
All the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, so you could have walked from Brazil to Africa.
About 50 million years ago, crocodiles, turtles and hippo-like mammals lived in the Canadian Arctic, near the North Pole.
Fossil teeth suggest baby megalodons grew up in warm, shallow nursery waters, as some sharks do today.
A 2023 study suggests megalodon was partly warm-blooded, keeping its body warmer than the water around it.
One of the oldest known primates, from about 55 million years ago, was about the size of a mouse and could sit in a teaspoon.
Scientists think monkeys reached South America from Africa about 35 million years ago by floating across the ocean on rafts of plants.
The American lion, which lived in North America during the ice age, was bigger than today's African lions.
Cheetah-like cats once lived in North America, and scientists think they are why pronghorn antelope still run so fast.
Dung left by giant ground sloths over 10,000 years ago still sits in some dry caves in the American Southwest.
Footprints on a beach in England, about 850,000 years old, the oldest human prints outside Africa, were washed away by the tide within weeks of being found.
A shell from Java engraved with a zigzag about half a million years ago is the oldest known doodle, made by Homo erectus, not our species.
About 14,000 years ago, someone in Italy had a cavity scraped clean with a sharp stone, the oldest known dentistry.
Scientists can tell one T. rex was a female carrying eggs, because her bones had a special calcium layer, like the bones of egg-laying hens.
Fossils show whale nostrils moving step by step from the tip of the snout to the top of the head, becoming a blowhole.
Most of the dinosaurs in Jurassic Park, including T. rex, Velociraptor and Triceratops, actually lived in the Cretaceous.
A small ice age horse found frozen in Siberia was so well preserved that its hair, skin and hooves were intact.
Bullockornis, a giant flightless bird from Australia about 2.5 meters tall and related to ducks, is nicknamed the demon duck of doom.
Tasmanian tigers once lived all over mainland Australia, and Aboriginal rock paintings show them, but they vanished there about 3,000 years ago.
Cave bears were so common that some European caves hold the remains of thousands of them.
The coelacanth's fins have bones like little arms, and it is more closely related to you than to a tuna.
Ice age hunters in Europe used spear-throwers, carved from antler, to launch spears much farther than by hand.
@plants|Plants
A grove of about 47,000 aspen trunks in Utah, called Pando, is one single living thing joined by its roots, weighing an estimated 6,000 tonnes.
Part of the lovely smell after rain comes from oils that plants give off during dry spells, which soak into rocks and soil until rain sets them free.
As of 2024, the tallest known tree is a California redwood named Hyperion, about 116 meters tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty on its pedestal.
The location of Hyperion, the world's tallest known tree, is kept secret, and hikers who go looking for it can be fined.
A giant sequoia called General Sherman holds enough wood to fill about half an Olympic swimming pool, the most of any single tree.
A bristlecone pine in California called Methuselah is over 4,800 years old, so it was already a young tree when the Great Pyramid of Giza was built.
In 1964 a student cut down a bristlecone pine to count its rings and found he had just killed a tree nearly 5,000 years old.
A spruce in Sweden called Old Tjikko has a trunk that is fairly young, but its roots have been regrowing new trunks for about 9,500 years.
Giant sequoia bark can be almost a meter thick and feels spongy, which helps it shrug off forest fires.
Some pine cones stay glued shut with resin for years and only pop open in the heat of a wildfire, sowing seeds on freshly burned ground.
A big oak tree can breathe out roughly 150,000 liters of water through its leaves in a single year, enough to fill a small swimming pool.
Trees grow taller only at their tips, so a nail hammered into a trunk stays at the same height for the rest of the tree's life.
The Amazon rainforest makes much of its own rain: water breathed out by trees forms clouds that rain down on more trees further west.
There are roughly 3 trillion trees on Earth, about 400 for every person alive, so you could say you each own a small forest.
Scientists estimate the number of trees on Earth has fallen by almost half since humans started farming.
A banyan tree drops roots from its branches that grow into new trunks, so a single tree can end up looking like a whole forest.
The Great Banyan in Kolkata, India, covers more ground than two soccer fields, and it still thrives even though its original trunk was removed in 1925.
African baobab trees can store huge amounts of water in their swollen trunks, by some estimates up to about 100,000 liters.
Some African baobabs have been alive for over 2,000 years, and many of the very oldest ones suddenly died between 2005 and 2017.
Australia's mountain ash and Borneo's yellow meranti are the tallest flowering plants on Earth, with living trees about 100 meters tall.
The rainbow eucalyptus sheds its bark in strips, leaving a trunk streaked with green, blue, purple, orange and red, as if someone painted it.
The sandbox tree's seed pods explode with a bang like a gunshot, flinging seeds at about 250 kilometers per hour.
Ginkgo trees have barely changed in about 200 million years, so dinosaurs walked past trees that look almost exactly like the ones on city streets today.
Several ginkgo trees about a kilometer from the Hiroshima atomic blast in 1945 survived, and they are still alive today.
The Wollemi pine was known only from fossils until 1994, when a park ranger stumbled on fewer than 100 living trees hidden in a gorge near Sydney.
During Australia's 2019-2020 bushfires, firefighters ran a secret mission with sprinklers and water bombers to save the last wild Wollemi pines.
In some forests, the tops of neighboring trees refuse to touch, leaving thin glowing gaps in the canopy known as crown shyness.
The middle of a big tree trunk is dead wood, which is why a tree can be completely hollow inside and still grow perfectly well.
Bamboo is a grass, and some kinds can grow almost a meter in a single day, fast enough to notice if you watched closely.
Some bamboo species flower only once every 100 years or so, and all the plants of that kind flower together around the world, then die.
When a bamboo forest in northeast India flowers all at once, the flood of seeds causes rat populations to explode and eat farmers' crops.
A coconut can float across an ocean for months and still sprout into a palm tree when it washes up on a beach.
The coco de mer palm of the Seychelles makes the biggest seed of any plant, weighing up to about 17 kilograms, as heavy as a toddler.
The talipot palm waits up to about 80 years to flower, then grows a giant spray of millions of flowers, sets seed, and dies.
The raffia palm has the longest leaves of any plant, up to about 25 meters, around twice the length of a city bus.
Aspen leaves flutter in the faintest breeze because their stems are flat, like a ribbon, instead of round.
Mangrove trees live in salty seawater, filtering most of the salt out at their roots or sweating it out through their leaves.
Some mangroves breathe through hundreds of little pencil-shaped roots that stick straight up out of the mud like snorkels.
Red mangrove seeds sprout while still hanging on the parent tree, then drop off as ready-made baby trees.
Strangler figs start life high in another tree's branches and send roots down around it, often squeezing their host to death.
By matching patterns of thick and thin tree rings, scientists have built a calendar that counts back year by year for over 12,000 years.
Cork comes from the bark of the cork oak, which can be peeled off every nine years or so without harming the tree.
Lignum vitae wood is so heavy that it sinks in water, and it was once used for the propeller shaft bearings of ships and even a nuclear submarine.
Standing under a manchineel tree in the rain can blister your skin, because the rain washes its burning sap down from the leaves.
The Australian gympie-gympie tree has stinging hairs so painful that the pain can come back for weeks or even months after a single brush.
A tree's roots usually spread out two to three times wider than its branches, but most of them stay in the top meter of soil.
The deepest roots ever found belong to a wild fig in a South African cave, reaching about 120 meters down, as deep as a 40-story building is tall.
A cypress tree in Mexico called the Arbol del Tule has a trunk so thick that it takes about 30 people holding hands to circle it.
Eucalyptus trees survive bushfires by sprouting from buds hidden under their bark, turning blackened trunks green again within weeks.
Yellow and orange autumn colors are in leaves all summer long, just hidden under the green until the green fades away in fall.
The bright red of autumn leaves is different: trees make that red pigment fresh in fall, rather than revealing it.
Larches are cone-bearing trees that break the evergreen rule: their needles turn gold and fall off every autumn.
The dawn redwood was known only from fossils and thought extinct for millions of years until living trees were found in China in the 1940s.
The loneliest tree on Earth once stood in the Sahara about 400 km from any other tree, until a truck driver knocked it down in 1973.
It takes about 40 liters of maple sap to boil down into a single liter of maple syrup.
A bristlecone pine can survive by letting most of its trunk die, keeping just one thin strip of living bark connecting its roots to a few branches.
A major cancer drug, Taxol, was first found in the bark of the Pacific yew tree.
Quinine, the first good treatment for malaria, came from the bark of a South American tree, and it's still what makes tonic water taste bitter.
Bullhorn acacias give ants free housing in their hollow thorns and free food from their leaves, and the ants fiercely attack anything that nibbles the tree.
The whistling thorn acacia in Africa actually whistles when wind blows across holes that ants chewed in its swollen thorns.
Black walnut trees leak a chemical from their roots that stunts or kills many plants trying to grow nearby, like tomatoes.
A fig is not a simple fruit but a hollow pouch lined with hundreds of tiny flowers, which become the crunchy bits inside.
Most fig species can only be pollinated by their own species of tiny wasp, which crawls inside the fig through a hole smaller than a pinhead.
Cotton is a close cousin of okra and hibiscus, and its creamy flowers look a lot like theirs.
In the 1600s, a scientist grew a willow from 2 kg to over 76 kg while its pot of soil lost only about 57 grams, showing trees aren't made from soil.
Water climbs to the top of a 100-meter tree without any pump, pulled up as water evaporates from the leaves, like sipping through a very long straw.
Scientists think no tree can grow much taller than about 130 meters, because water can't be pulled any higher.
Coast redwoods drink fog: they soak up water through their needles from the mist that rolls in off the Pacific.
Up in the redwood canopy, 100 meters above the ground, soil collects on branches and grows ferns, bushes and even small trees.
When a redwood falls, new trunks often sprout from its roots in a circle around it, called a fairy ring.
Giant sequoias can live for more than 3,000 years, outliving the entire Roman Empire several times over.
A bonsai pine that survived the Hiroshima bombing, about 3 km from the blast, is now about 400 years old and lives at a museum in Washington, DC.
A sacred fig in Sri Lanka was planted in 288 BC and is still growing, the oldest human-planted tree with a known planting date.
In 2021, Kyoto's cherry trees hit full bloom earlier than in any year of a record that goes back over 1,200 years.
A Joshua tree is not a tree but a giant yucca, and only tiny yucca moths can pollinate its flowers.
Apple seeds contain a chemical that releases cyanide when chewed, but you would have to crunch through a huge pile of them to be harmed.
Chewing gum was originally made from chicle, the milky sap of a Central American tree called sapodilla.
Aspen trees have greenish bark that can make a little food from sunlight, even in winter after their leaves have fallen.
Paper birch bark peels off in waterproof sheets, and people in North America used it to build canoes.
Quaking aspen roots can survive a forest fire underground and send up thousands of new shoots right afterward.
The cannonball tree grows big round fruits right on its trunk, and they can crash to the ground with a loud bang when they fall.
The corpse flower can grow a bloom about 3 meters tall that smells like rotting meat, to lure the beetles and flies that pollinate it.
A corpse flower heats its central spike to about human body temperature, helping its rotten-meat stink drift further through the jungle.
A corpse flower can take seven to ten years to bloom for the first time, and then the bloom lasts only a day or two.
Rafflesia makes the biggest single flower on Earth, up to about a meter across and heavier than a bowling ball, and it smells like a dead animal.
Rafflesia has no leaves, stems or roots at all: it lives hidden inside a jungle vine and only shows itself when it blooms.
Rafflesia has stolen dozens of genes from the vine it lives inside, a rare case of a plant taking DNA from its host.
Sacred lotus flowers keep themselves warm, at around 30 to 35 C, even on chilly nights, like a cozy room for visiting beetles.
A lotus seed from a dry lakebed in China sprouted after sitting dormant for about 1,300 years.
In 2005 scientists sprouted a 2,000-year-old date palm seed from the ancient fortress of Masada in Israel, and it grew into a healthy palm tree.
Russian scientists grew flowers from fruit buried 32,000 years ago by an Ice Age squirrel in the Siberian permafrost.
In parts of Europe, male bees try to mate with bee orchids, whose flowers look and smell like female bees, and fly off carrying pollen.
Vanilla is the second most expensive spice in the world after saffron, and its pods are cured for months to develop their smell.
Nectarines and peaches are the same species: a nectarine is simply a peach with one gene change that gives it smooth skin.
Vanilla comes from an orchid, and outside Mexico almost every vanilla flower must be pollinated by hand, often with a little stick.
The trick for hand-pollinating vanilla was invented in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on the island of Reunion.
Saffron is the dried threads of a purple crocus flower, and it takes around 150,000 flowers to make one kilogram.
There are about 28,000 kinds of orchids, roughly four times as many as there are kinds of mammals.
Orchid seeds are as fine as dust, with millions in one pod, and they carry so little food that they can only sprout with help from a fungus.
The grapefruit is a young fruit: it began as an accidental cross between a pomelo and a sweet orange in Barbados in the 1700s.
Grapefruit juice can make some medicines far stronger than intended, because it blocks a gut enzyme that normally breaks them down.
Every known Wood's cycad is a clone of one male plant found in South Africa in 1895; no female has ever been found in the wild.
The philosopher Socrates was put to death in 399 BC with a drink of poison hemlock, a wild cousin of carrots and parsley.
In a 2019 study, evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of hearing the buzz of a passing bee.
Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west every day, but grown-up flowers stop and face east forever, which warms them up for morning bees.
A sunflower head is not one flower but up to about 2,000 tiny flowers packed together, and each one can make a seed.
The seeds on a sunflower head sit in two sets of spirals, and their counts are usually neighboring numbers in the Fibonacci sequence, like 34 and 55.
Deadly nightshade is also called belladonna, beautiful lady, because women once used its juice to make their pupils look big and dark.
Bats pollinate hundreds of plants, including bananas, agaves and baobabs, which open pale, smelly flowers at night just for them.
In Madagascar, lemurs pollinate the traveller's palm, poking their noses into its tough flowers and coming out dusted with pollen.
Hummingbird flowers are often red and have almost no smell, because birds see red well but barely smell anything.
The smallest flowering plant, Wolffia, floats on ponds and is smaller than a grain of rice; a handful can hold thousands of whole plants.
Wolffia can double its numbers in about a day and a half, among the fastest growth of any plant.
The dead horse arum smells like rotting meat and even warms itself up to trick blowflies into crawling inside.
Some arum flowers trap flies overnight in a slippery chamber, then let them go the next morning covered in pollen.
Night-blooming cereus, a cactus, often opens its huge white flowers for just one night a year, and they wilt by morning.
Flowering plants appeared relatively late in Earth's history, and their sudden rise was so puzzling that Darwin called it an abominable mystery.
A shrub found only on the Pacific island of New Caledonia, Amborella, is the last survivor of the oldest branch of flowering plants.
Hydrangeas can change color with the soil: acidic soil turns them blue, and limey soil turns them pink.
Roses are close cousins of apples, pears, cherries, plums, almonds and strawberries, all members of the rose family.
Tomatoes were grown in Europe for years mainly as decorations, because many people suspected they were poisonous like their nightshade cousins.
George Washington Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts, but he did not invent peanut butter; people were making it before him.
Some flowers change color once they've been pollinated, like a sign saying the nectar is gone, so bees don't waste their time.
Snapdragon flowers are shaped like a closed mouth that only opens for bees heavy enough to push the lips apart.
The bucket orchid makes bees tumble into a little pool of liquid, and the only way out is a tunnel that sticks pollen on their backs.
Australian trigger plants hide a spring-loaded arm in each flower that whacks visiting insects with pollen in a split second.
Bunchberry dogwood flowers burst open in less than half a thousandth of a second, faster than a blink.
Mulberry flowers fling their pollen at over half the speed of sound, one of the fastest movements in the living world.
Tiny shrimp-like creatures carry pollen between seagrass flowers at night, a 2016 study found, like bees of the sea.
Every strand of corn silk is connected to one kernel, and that kernel only grows if a pollen grain lands on its silk.
A single ragweed plant can release about a billion grains of pollen, which is why it causes so much hay fever.
Pollen is so different from plant to plant that detectives use it like a fingerprint to work out where a suspect or object has been.
The outer shell of pollen is one of the toughest natural materials known, and it can survive in rocks for millions of years.
One South African flower smells exactly like honeybees being eaten by spiders, to lure flies that like to steal from spider kills.
A dandelion seed flies with a parachute that creates a little ring of swirling air above it, a kind of flight nobody had seen until 2018.
A dandelion head is not one flower but over a hundred tiny ones, each making its own seed with a parachute.
In medieval England, peppercorns were so valuable that people sometimes paid their rent with them.
Truly blue pigments are rare in flowers; most blue petals are made with red pigments tweaked by acidity and metals.
There is no naturally blue rose, and the gene-engineered blue rose unveiled in Japan in 2004 actually looks lavender.
When a bird lands on a bird of paradise flower, its weight pops the flower open and coats the bird's feet with pollen.
The botanist Linnaeus imagined a flower clock: a garden of species that open and close at different hours so you could tell the time.
The Queen of the Andes takes up to about 80 years to flower, then shoots up a spike about 10 meters tall with thousands of blossoms and dies.
Jack-in-the-pulpit plants can switch sex: small, young plants are male, and they become female once they are big enough to make seeds.
Ginkgo trees are either male or female, and the female trees drop seeds that smell like rancid butter or vomit.
Date palms are male or female, and people have been hand-pollinating them by climbing up the trees for thousands of years.
Only female holly bushes grow red berries, and only if a male holly is growing somewhere nearby.
Avocado flowers change sex: each one opens as female one day, closes, and reopens as male the next.
The agave, or century plant, can wait decades to bloom, then sends up a flower stalk several meters tall in a few months, and dies.
Most of the yams sold in US supermarkets are really sweet potatoes; true yams are a different plant from Africa and Asia.
A huge water lily in the Amazon has floating leaves up to about 3 meters across, strong enough to hold a small child if the weight is spread out.
Giant Amazon water lily flowers open white on the first night, trap beetles inside, then reopen pink on the second night to let them go.
To a botanist, bananas, grapes, tomatoes, eggplants and avocados are all berries, but strawberries and raspberries are not.
The little seeds on the outside of a strawberry are actually tiny fruits, each one holding a single real seed inside.
Peanuts aren't nuts but beans, and after the flower is pollinated, its stalk bends down and pushes the baby peanut into the soil to grow.
An almond isn't a true nut: it's the seed inside the pit of a fruit closely related to peaches, plums and cherries.
Each cashew nut hangs from the bottom of a juicy fruit called the cashew apple, which many countries eat or turn into juice.
Cashew shells contain an itchy oil related to the one in poison ivy, which is why cashews are never sold in their shells.
Mangoes are cousins of poison ivy, and some people get an itchy rash from touching mango skin.
A pineapple is made of many fruits fused together: every scaly bump on its skin grew from its own separate flower.
A pineapple plant takes about two years to grow a single pineapple, and each plant makes just one fruit at a time.
Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so while you eat it, it is gently digesting your tongue a little.
Bananas are slightly radioactive because of the potassium they contain, though you'd need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
A banana plant isn't a tree but a giant herb, and its trunk is made of leaves rolled up tightly around each other.
Almost every banana in Western supermarkets is a Cavendish, and they are all clones of one another, so a single disease could threaten them all.
The banana most people ate before the 1950s, the Gros Michel, was wiped off farms around the world by a fungus living in the soil.
Wild bananas are packed with hard seeds as big as peppercorns; the little black specks in a supermarket banana are what's left of them.
Bananas curve because they start growing downward, then bend up toward the sun as they get bigger.
Pumpkins, cucumbers, peppers, pea pods and zucchini are all fruits to a botanist, because they grow from flowers and hold seeds.
In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled that tomatoes count as vegetables for tax purposes, even though botanists call them fruits.
Broccoli, cabbage, kale, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are all the same plant species, just bred by farmers to look completely different.
Every head of broccoli is a bunch of tiny flower buds that haven't opened yet; leave it too long and it bursts into yellow flowers.
Carrots used to be mostly purple and yellow, and the orange carrot only became common after Dutch farmers bred it a few hundred years ago.
Rhubarb stalks make great pie, but its big leaves are poisonous, packed with the same acid found in some cleaning products.
Potatoes and tomatoes are such close relatives that a potato plant can grow little green fruits that look like tiny tomatoes.
Gardeners can join a tomato plant onto a potato plant to make one plant that grows tomatoes on top and potatoes underneath.
Sweet potatoes aren't closely related to potatoes at all; they belong to the morning glory family.
Apples float in water because about a quarter of an apple is air, which is what makes bobbing for apples possible.
Plant an apple seed and you get a brand new kind of apple, so every tree of a favorite variety is grown from a cutting of another one.
Every Granny Smith apple tree in the world descends from a single seedling found in an Australian garden in the 1860s.
Every navel orange tree descends from one odd tree in Brazil in the 1800s, and none of them have seeds, so they are all grown from cuttings.
Oranges, lemons and limes are mostly hybrids, and almost all of them trace back to just a few wild ancestors like the pomelo and the mandarin.
Avocados may have evolved to be swallowed whole by giant ground sloths and other huge animals that have been extinct for over 10,000 years.
Avocados only ripen after they're picked, so farmers can leave them hanging on the tree for months as a kind of living storage.
Birds can't feel the burn of chili peppers, so they happily eat them and spread the seeds, while mammals that would crush the seeds stay away.
The burning heat of a chili pepper is mostly in the white pith around the seeds, not in the seeds themselves.
Cinnamon is the rolled-up inner bark of a tree, peeled off in thin layers and left to dry and curl.
Cloves are flower buds, picked before they open and dried in the sun until they turn brown and hard.
Black pepper, white pepper and green peppercorns all come from the same climbing vine, just picked and treated differently.
Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit: nutmeg is the seed, and mace is the bright red lace wrapped around it.
Coffee beans are the seeds of a red cherry-like fruit; each cherry usually holds two beans facing each other.
Plants use caffeine as a bug killer, and some flowers put a little in their nectar, which helps bees remember to come back.
Chocolate comes from seeds in pods that grow straight out of the trunk of the cacao tree, as if someone glued footballs onto it.
An ear of corn almost always has an even number of rows of kernels, usually around 16.
Gregor Mendel worked out the basic rules of how traits are inherited by growing and studying about 28,000 pea plants.
Bread wheat has about five times as much DNA as a human, because it's a mix of three different ancient grasses.
Corn was bred thousands of years ago from teosinte, a wild grass whose ears had only about a dozen rock-hard kernels.
Rice is the main food for more than half of all the people on Earth, all from the seeds of one kind of swamp grass.
Quinoa isn't a grain at all: it's the seed of a plant related to spinach and beets.
Most of the green wasabi served outside Japan is actually horseradish and mustard dyed green, because real wasabi is hard to grow.
The durian fruit smells so strong that it's banned on Singapore's trains and buses.
Miracle fruit contains a protein that makes sour things taste sweet for up to an hour, so lemons taste like lemonade.
Jackfruit is the largest fruit that grows on trees, reaching up to about 50 kilograms, heavier than many 10-year-olds.
Kiwifruit used to be called Chinese gooseberry, until New Zealand exporters renamed it after their national bird in 1959.
Ripe cranberries bounce and float because they have little air pockets inside, which is why farmers flood the fields to harvest them.
A watermelon is about 92 percent water, so a big one is mostly a ball of juice wrapped in a rind.
Brazil nuts grow about 10 to 25 at a time inside a hard pod the size of a grapefruit, which can fall 50 meters from the treetop.
Agoutis, which look like giant guinea pigs, are almost the only animals that can gnaw open Brazil nut pods, and they bury the nuts that later sprout.
Brazil nut trees hardly ever produce nuts on plantations, because they need wild forest bees and those bees need wild forest orchids.
Olives straight off the tree are so bitter that they're basically inedible; they have to be cured for weeks first.
Some olive trees around the Mediterranean are thought to be over 2,000 years old and still produce olives.
Onions make you cry because cutting them releases a gas that stings your eyes, and they flood with tears to wash it away.
Garlic barely smells until you crush it; crushing mixes two chemicals that were kept apart in separate parts of each cell.
Most European grapevines grow on American roots, because a tiny bug from America nearly destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s.
Green, yellow and red bell peppers usually come from the same kind of plant; the green ones are just picked before they ripen.
The squirting cucumber shoots its seeds out in a jet of slimy juice when ripe, spraying them several meters away.
Touch a ripe seed pod of an impatiens flower and it explodes, curling up like a spring and flinging its seeds away.
Witch hazel seed pods squeeze their seeds until they shoot out like bullets, landing up to about 10 meters away.
Maple seeds spin like helicopter blades, and the spinning makes a little whirlwind on top that keeps them in the air longer.
Mistletoe seeds are so sticky that birds wipe them off their beaks onto branches, which is just where the mistletoe needs to grow.
A tropical vine called Alsomitra has winged seeds that glide like paper airplanes, and they inspired some early airplane designs.
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, dug into an Arctic mountain in Norway, holds over a million seed samples as a backup for the world's crops.
The first seeds ever taken back out of the Svalbard Seed Vault, in 2015, replaced crop seeds lost in Syria's civil war.
In 1879 a scientist buried bottles of seeds in Michigan, and some of the seeds still sprouted when dug up more than 140 years later.
Some seeds won't sprout until they smell smoke, waiting in the soil for a fire to clear space for them.
In some years, oak trees across a whole region make a huge crop of acorns all at once, producing more than squirrels and deer can possibly eat.
A single jay can bury thousands of acorns every autumn, and the ones it forgets grow into new oak forests.
Many seeds come with a little fatty snack attached, so ants carry them home, eat the snack, and throw the seed into their rich compost.
Some African trees depend on elephants to eat their fruit and spread the seeds in big piles of dung.
A vine in Chile called Boquila can change the shape of its leaves to copy whatever plant it's climbing on, and scientists still debate how.
Some passionflower vines grow little yellow bumps that look like butterfly eggs, so butterflies think the leaf is taken and lay elsewhere.
