@words|Words
The word "nice" used to mean foolish. It comes from a Latin word for not knowing anything.
A thousand years ago, calling someone "silly" was a compliment: it meant blessed or happy.
"Muscle" comes from the Latin for little mouse, because a flexing muscle looks like a mouse moving under your skin.
"Disaster" literally means a bad star, from the old belief that bad luck came from stars and planets being in the wrong place.
A "clue" was originally a ball of thread, like the one a Greek hero unrolled to find his way out of the Minotaur's maze.
The word "robot" comes from the Czech word for forced labour, and was first used in a 1920 play about artificial workers.
"Quarantine" comes from the Italian for forty days, how long ships had to wait offshore in Venice during the plague.
Chocolate, tomato, avocado and chili are all words English got from the language of the Aztecs.
"Shampoo" comes from a Hindi word meaning to press or knead. In English it first meant a massage, not hair washing.
"Pajamas" comes from Persian words meaning leg clothing. British people in India brought the loose trousers home as nightwear.
"Jungle" comes from a Hindi word that originally meant dry wasteland, the very opposite of a rainforest.
Ketchup probably started as a fermented fish sauce from southern China. The tomato came much later.
"Tycoon" comes from a Japanese title meaning great lord, which foreigners used for the shogun.
"Tsunami" is Japanese for harbour wave, because the giant waves seemed to appear out of nowhere in harbours.
"Karaoke" means empty orchestra in Japanese: the band is there, but the singer is missing until you step up.
"Emoji" has nothing to do with "emotion". It is Japanese for picture plus character, and the similarity is pure coincidence.
"Alcohol" comes from an Arabic word for the fine black powder used as eyeliner, which we still call kohl.
"Algebra" comes from an Arabic book title meaning the reunion of broken parts, the way you'd set a broken bone.
The word "algorithm" is the mangled name of al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician who lived over 1,000 years ago.
"Zero" and "cipher" are twins: both come from the same Arabic word, sifr, meaning empty.
"Checkmate" comes from the Persian "shah mat", usually translated as the king is helpless.
"Magazine" comes from an Arabic word for storehouse. That's why a gun's magazine is where the bullets are stored.
"Berserk" comes from Viking warriors called berserkers, probably meaning bear shirts, who fought in a wild frenzy.
"Window" comes from the Viking words for wind eye: originally just a hole in the roof to let the smoke out.
For the Vikings, the word "sky" simply meant cloud. English already had a word for the sky: "heaven".
English borrowed "they", "them" and "their" from the Vikings. Languages almost never borrow words as basic as pronouns.
"Bead" comes from the Old English word for prayer, because beads on a string were used to count prayers.
"Goodbye" is a squashed-down version of "God be with ye", worn smooth by centuries of people saying it in a hurry.
"Hello" only became a normal greeting in the late 1800s, helped by the telephone. Thomas Edison pushed it for answering calls.
"Bedlam" was the nickname of a London hospital for the mentally ill, the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem.
"Maudlin", meaning tearfully sentimental, comes from Mary Magdalene, who was almost always painted weeping.
"Tawdry" comes from St Audrey's lace, the cheap neckwear sold at fairs held in her honour.
"Boycott" was a real man: Captain Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent whose whole town refused to deal with him in 1880.
The leotard is named after Jules Leotard, the French acrobat who invented the flying trapeze act in the 1850s.
Silhouettes are named after Etienne de Silhouette, a French finance minister so penny-pinching that anything cheap and bare was mocked with his name.
"Nicotine" is named after Jean Nicot, a French ambassador who sent tobacco to Paris in 1560 as a medicine.
The guillotine is named after a doctor who argued for it as a more humane method. He didn't invent it.
"Shrapnel" was a person: Henry Shrapnel, a British officer who invented a shell packed with musket balls.
"Mesmerize" comes from Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century doctor who claimed he could heal people with invisible magnetic forces.
Braille is named after Louis Braille, who was blinded at 3 in an accident in his father's workshop and invented his reading system at 15.
"Malaria" comes from the Italian for bad air. People blamed the disease on swamp smells long before they suspected mosquitoes.
"Influenza" is Italian for influence: people once believed epidemics were caused by the influence of the stars.
"Panic" comes from Pan, the Greek god of the wild, whose sudden shouts in the forest were said to terrify travellers.
Every bowl of breakfast cereal is named after Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain.
"Volcano" comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire, whose blacksmith forge was imagined deep under a mountain.
"Echo" was a nymph in Greek myth, cursed so she could only ever repeat the last words other people said.
"Tantalize" comes from Tantalus, punished in Greek myth with fruit and water that always moved just out of reach.
A "mentor" is named after Mentor, the old friend in The Odyssey whose shape a goddess borrowed to give advice.
In Old English, "cloud" meant a rock or a hill. It probably came to mean clouds because they looked like heaps of rock in the sky.
In medieval English, "girl" meant any young child, boy or girl.
"Meat" once meant any food at all. That's why old-fashioned sweets were called "sweetmeats".
"Deer" once meant any animal. Shakespeare wrote about "mice and rats, and such small deer".
"Starve" once simply meant to die, from any cause, not just hunger.
"Wife" originally just meant woman, which is why a midwife can be married or not.
"Naughty" originally meant having naught, in other words being poor.
"Awful" originally meant full of awe, so something awful was actually inspiring and impressive.
"Terrific" originally meant terrifying. Only in the late 1800s did it flip to mean wonderful.
In the 1500s, "bully" was a term of endearment meaning sweetheart.
"Lady" probably comes from an Old English word meaning bread kneader, and "lord" from one meaning loaf guardian.
A "companion" is literally someone you share bread with, from Latin "com" (with) and "panis" (bread).
"Daisy" comes from "day's eye", because the flower opens at sunrise and closes at night.
"Dandelion" comes from the French for lion's tooth, after the plant's jagged leaves.
"Hippopotamus" means river horse in Greek, even though hippos are more closely related to whales than horses.
"Porcupine" comes from old French words meaning thorny pig, though a porcupine is actually a rodent.
"Aardvark" is Afrikaans for earth pig, a fitting name for an animal that digs for ants all night.
"Orangutan" comes from Malay words meaning person of the forest.
The story that "kangaroo" means "I don't understand" is a myth. It comes from "gangurru", a real word in an Aboriginal language.
"Dinosaur" means terrible lizard. The word was invented in 1842, long after people had started digging up their bones.
"Octopi" is based on a mix-up: octopus comes from Greek, not Latin, so it was never meant to end in i. The usual plural is "octopuses".
The word "scientist" was only invented in the 1830s. Before that, people like Newton were called natural philosophers.
"Serendipity" was invented in 1754 by a writer inspired by a fairy tale called The Three Princes of Serendip.
The word "nerd" first appeared in a Dr. Seuss book in 1950, as the name of an imaginary zoo animal.
Lewis Carroll invented the word "chortle" in 1871, probably by mashing together chuckle and snort.
John Milton made up the word "pandemonium" in 1667 as the name of the capital city of Hell. It means "all the demons".
"Utopia" is a pun: in Greek it can mean "good place" or "no place", hinting that the perfect society doesn't exist.
The word "cyberspace" was invented by a science fiction writer in 1982, years before most people had heard of the internet.
The word "meme" was invented in 1976 by biologist Richard Dawkins, decades before cat pictures took it over.
The number googol, a 1 followed by 100 zeros, was named by a 9-year-old boy. Google's name is a twist on it.
The word "gas" was simply made up by a Flemish chemist in the 1600s, probably inspired by the Greek word "chaos".
"Vaccine" comes from the Latin for cow, because the first smallpox vaccine was made from a cow disease called cowpox.
The pupil of your eye comes from the Latin for little doll, after the tiny reflection of yourself you see in someone's eye.
"Sinister" is simply the Latin word for left. Left-handedness was long seen as unlucky.
"Dexterity" comes from the Latin word for right, so being dexterous literally means being right-handed.
"Ambidextrous" literally means right-handed on both sides, as if you had two right hands.
"Candidate" comes from the Latin for dressed in white, because Romans running for office wore chalk-whitened togas.
"Calculate" comes from the Latin for small pebble, because Romans did their sums by moving stones around.
"Kidnap" was originally a slang word for stealing children: "kid" plus "nap", an old word for snatch.
The "mare" in nightmare has nothing to do with horses. It was a goblin believed to sit on sleepers' chests.
The "were" in werewolf is an old English word for man, so a werewolf is literally a man-wolf.
"Mortgage" comes from old French words meaning death pledge, because the deal dies when you pay it off, or when you fail to.
"Bankrupt" comes from the Italian for broken bench, after the benches where moneylenders did business.
"Clock" comes from the medieval Latin word for bell, because the first clocks rang the hours instead of showing them.
"Planet" comes from the Greek word for wanderer, because planets drift across the sky while the stars stay put.
"Comet" comes from the Greek for long-haired, because a comet's tail looked like flowing hair.
"Galaxy" comes from the Greek word for milk, which is why our galaxy is the Milky Way.
"Lunatic" comes from luna, the Latin word for moon, from the old belief that the full moon could drive people mad.
September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth month, because the Roman year began in March.
July is named after Julius Caesar and August after the emperor Augustus. Before that they were just called fifth and sixth month.
Four English weekdays are named after Norse gods: Tuesday after Tiw, Wednesday after Woden, Thursday after Thor and Friday after Frigg.
Saying "aks" instead of "ask" is not a modern mistake. It is over 1,000 years old, and Chaucer wrote it that way in the 1300s.
"Bird" used to be "brid". Over time the r and the i simply swapped places.
An "apron" used to be "a napron", and an "adder" was "a nadder". People misheard where the n belonged, and it jumped to the little word in front.
"Whisky" comes from the Gaelic "uisce beatha", water of life. The French "eau de vie" and Scandinavian "aquavit" mean the same thing.
A "nickname" used to be "an ekename", meaning an extra name. This time the n jumped the other way.
"Pea" exists by mistake. The original word was "pease", but people thought it sounded plural and invented a singular.
"Cherry" was originally "cherise". English speakers thought the s sound made it plural and chopped it off.
The "helicopter" splits as "helico" (spiral) and "pter" (wing), so the "copter" in it is just a happy accident.
The burger is named after the German city of Hamburg. "Burger" was snipped off later, as if "ham" were the first part.
"Alligator" comes from the Spanish "el lagarto": the lizard.
Before the fruit arrived, English had no word for orange. People called the colour yellow-red.
The colour pink is named after pink flowers, not the other way round.
To "escape" literally means to get out of your cape, leaving whoever grabbed you holding only your cloak.
"Crimson" comes from the Arabic name of a tiny insect that was crushed to make red dye.
"Khaki" means dust-coloured in Hindi and Urdu, because the uniform was designed to blend into dusty ground.
"Idiot" comes from a Greek word for a private person: someone who didn't take part in public life.
"School" comes from the Greek word for leisure, because only people with free time could afford to study.
"Symposium" comes from Greek words meaning drinking together. Ancient Greek symposiums were dinner parties.
"Enthusiasm" comes from the Greek for having a god inside you.
"Tragedy" literally means goat song in Greek, and nobody is quite sure why.
The part of your brain that stores memories is called the hippocampus, Greek for seahorse, because of its curly shape.
"Vanilla" comes from the Spanish for little pod, after the long bean the flavour comes from.
The cappuccino is named after Capuchin friars, whose brown hooded robes matched the colour of coffee with milk.
"Biscuit" literally means twice cooked, because hard biscuits were baked twice so they would last on long sea voyages.
Spaghetti means little strings, vermicelli means little worms, linguine means little tongues and orecchiette means little ears.
"Sushi" doesn't mean raw fish. It refers to the vinegared rice; raw fish on its own is sashimi.
Japanese "arigato" sounds a lot like Portuguese "obrigado", but it's pure coincidence: both mean thank you.
The Japanese word for bread, "pan", came from Portuguese traders who arrived in Japan in the 1500s.
The Spanish word "ojala", meaning I hope, comes from an Arabic phrase meaning if God wills.
Thousands of Spanish words come from Arabic, left over from nearly 800 years of Moorish rule in Spain.
Jeans are named after the Italian city of Genoa, and denim after the French town of Nimes: "serge de Nimes".
Muslin is named after Mosul in Iraq, calico after Calicut in India, and cashmere after Kashmir.
The bikini was named in 1946 after Bikini Atoll, where the US had just tested atomic bombs. It was meant to be explosive.
The tuxedo is named after Tuxedo Park, a wealthy town in New York where it became fashionable.
The word "spa" comes from Spa, a small town in Belgium famous for its healing springs.
The turkey bird is named after the country by mistake. Turks call it "hindi", meaning from India, and the French call it "dinde", from India too.
Grapefruit got its name because it grows in bunches on the tree, like giant grapes.
The Canary Islands are named after dogs, not birds: the Latin "canis". The canary birds were named after the islands.
Brazil is named after a tree. Brazilwood, prized for its red dye, gave the whole country its name.
Argentina's name comes from the Latin word for silver, because explorers hoped to find silver mountains there.
Venezuela means little Venice. Explorers saw villages built on stilts over the water and thought of the Italian city.
Australia's name simply comes from Latin for southern, because Europeans had long imagined a great southern land.
Pakistan's name was invented in 1933 by a student who built it from the names of regions in the area.
Canada probably gets its name from "kanata", an Iroquoian word for village.
Chicago's name comes from a Native American word for a wild onion that grew along the river there.
"Welsh" comes from an Old English word meaning foreigner, which is a bit rich since the Welsh were there first.
The "wal" in walnut comes from the same Old English word for foreign: the walnut was the foreign nut.
Germany is called Deutschland in German, Allemagne in French, Niemcy in Polish and Saksa in Finnish.
"Dollar" comes from the "thaler", a silver coin minted in a valley in Bohemia in the 1500s.
"Coach" comes from Kocs, a small village in Hungary where a fast new kind of carriage was built.
"Kindergarten" means children's garden. The German educator who coined it imagined children growing like plants.
The tulip is named after the Turkish word for turban, because the flower looked like one.
"Juggernaut" comes from Jagannath, a Hindu god whose enormous temple carts are pulled through the streets of Puri in India.
"Loot" comes from the Hindi word "lut", meaning plunder, picked up by British soldiers in India.
"Cheetah" comes from a Hindi word meaning spotted, which is exactly what you notice first about one.
"Avatar" comes from a Sanskrit word for a god coming down to Earth in a new body. Video games borrowed the idea.
"Yoga" and "yoke" are distant cousins, both from an ancient root meaning to join together.
"Honcho", as in head honcho, comes from Japanese. American soldiers picked it up in Korea and Japan in the 1950s.
"Kowtow" comes from Chinese words meaning to knock your head, from bowing so low your forehead touched the ground.
Having a "yen" for something comes from a Chinese word for craving.
To "shanghai" someone once meant to kidnap them onto a ship, often bound for the Chinese port of Shanghai.
"Gung ho" comes from a Chinese phrase meaning work together, adopted as a motto by a US Marine unit in World War II.
The words "barbecue", "hammock", "hurricane" and "canoe" all come from the Taino people of the Caribbean.
Moose, raccoon, skunk and chipmunk are all words borrowed from Native American languages.
In Inuit languages, "igloo" means any house, not just one made of snow.
"Taboo" comes from the Tongan word "tapu", brought to English by Captain Cook in the 1770s.
A tattoo on your skin comes from a Polynesian word, but a military tattoo comes from a Dutch call to shut the taps in bars.
"Boss", "cookie", "yacht" and "coleslaw" all come from Dutch. Coleslaw literally means cabbage salad.
An "easel" comes from the Dutch word for donkey, because both are made to carry a load.
"Santa Claus" comes from Sinterklaas, the Dutch name for Saint Nicholas.
"Landscape" started as a Dutch painting term. English borrowed it for pictures of scenery before using it for scenery itself.
"Coffee" travelled from Arabic "qahwa" to Turkish "kahve" to Italian "caffe" before reaching English.
About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today, and roughly 40 percent of them are endangered.
Papua New Guinea has around 840 languages, more than any other country, spread across mountains and valleys that kept communities apart.
Over half of all people on Earth speak one of just a couple of dozen languages, while thousands of others have only a few speakers.
Basque, spoken in Spain and France, is a language isolate: it has no known relatives anywhere on Earth.
Rotokas, a language of Papua New Guinea, gets by with just 12 letters, one of the smallest alphabets in the world.
The Hawaiian alphabet has only 13 letters: five vowels, seven consonants and a glottal stop mark.
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr in Australia don't use left and right. They'd say there's an ant on your north leg.
In Mandarin, "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold, depending only on the tone of your voice.
A Chinese linguist wrote a whole poem about a poet eating lions using only the syllable "shi" in different tones.
Japanese has a sound word for silence: "shiin", often written in comics when a room goes totally quiet.
Japanese is written with three systems at once, two alphabets of syllables plus thousands of Chinese characters, often in one sentence.
The shapes of some Korean letters are drawings of the mouth and tongue making that sound.
South Korea has a national holiday just for its alphabet: Hangul Day, every October 9.
Sequoyah, who could not read any language, invented a writing system for Cherokee. Within a few years most Cherokee could read.
Esperanto was invented in 1887 by an eye doctor who hoped a shared, easy language would bring world peace.
Klingon from Star Trek is a fully working language, with a dictionary, a grammar and translations of Shakespeare.
The Dothraki language in Game of Thrones was built from scratch by a linguist, with thousands of words, and some fans have learned to speak it.
Hebrew was not anyone's everyday language for centuries, until it was revived in the late 1800s. Today millions speak it at home.
Latin is still an official language of Vatican City, where cash machines have offered instructions in Latin.
Bolivia's constitution recognises 37 official languages: Spanish plus 36 Indigenous languages.
Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh, spoken by a small minority in the mountains.
The last native speaker of Manx, from the Isle of Man, died in 1974. Today children are learning it again in school.
Ubykh, from the Caucasus, had about 80 consonants and only two or three vowels. Its last fluent speaker died in 1992.
The language of the Miami people of Ohio and Indiana had no speakers left by the 1960s, and was brought back from old notes.
The Wampanoag language had no speakers for over a century until a linguist revived it, and her daughter became a native speaker.
In the 1980s, fewer than 50 children spoke Hawaiian. Language nest preschools brought it back from the brink.
Malagasy, spoken in Madagascar off Africa, is most closely related to languages from Borneo, over 7,000 km away.
One language family, Austronesian, stretches from Madagascar to Easter Island, more than halfway around the world.
Finnish and Hungarian are related, even though Finland and Hungary are nowhere near each other.
Maltese is the only Semitic language, the family of Arabic and Hebrew, that is written in the Latin alphabet.
Romani, the language of the Roma people of Europe, began in India over 1,000 years ago.
Yiddish is basically a Germanic language, but it is written in the Hebrew alphabet.
English's closest living relative is Frisian, spoken on the coast of the Netherlands and Germany.
An old rhyme says "bread, butter and green cheese" is good English and good Frisian, because it sounds almost the same in both.
"Pants" comes from Pantalone, a skinny old man in Italian comedy plays who wore tight trousers.
In 1786 a British judge in India noticed Sanskrit was strangely like Latin and Greek: father was pitar, pater and pater. They had a long-lost common ancestor.
Navajo is related to languages spoken thousands of kilometres north in Alaska and Canada.
Tok Pisin, an official language of Papua New Guinea, grew out of English, and its name comes from "talk pidgin".
Afrikaans grew out of the Dutch spoken by settlers in South Africa, and Dutch speakers can still mostly read it.
Some languages have two words for "we": one that includes the person you're talking to, and one that doesn't.
In Finnish, Turkish and Hungarian, the same word means he and she. You can't tell from the pronoun.
Sweden added a gender-neutral pronoun, "hen", to its official dictionary in 2015.
English speakers have used "they" for a single person since the 1300s.
In German, the word for girl, "Maedchen", is grammatically neither male nor female, but neuter, because of its ending.
Old English had grammatical gender: the sun was female, the moon was male, and the word for woman was neuter.
In Turkish and Quechua, the grammar shows whether you saw something happen yourself or only heard about it.
Some Australian Aboriginal languages had a special "mother-in-law language" you had to switch to when your in-laws were nearby.
Slovenian and Arabic have special word forms for exactly two of something, besides singular and plural.
Mandarin verbs never change form. "I eat", "he ate" and "they will eat" all use the same word for eat.
Japanese has many words for "I", and choosing one tells people a lot about your age, gender and how formal you're being.
"Children" is a double plural: the old plural was "childer", and people stuck another plural ending on top, the same -en as in oxen.
"Treacle" first meant a medicine against snake bites, from a Greek word for wild beasts. Only later did it become sticky syrup.
"Kine" was once the plural of cow, the same way "mice" is the plural of mouse.
People once said "the news are": "news" was treated as a plural, as in new things.
English speakers say "big old red car", never "red old big car", following an adjective order rule almost nobody was taught.
We say tick-tock, zig-zag, ping-pong and flip-flop, but never tock-tick or flop-flip. The order is an unwritten rule.
The rule against splitting infinitives, as in "to boldly go", was invented by 1800s grammarians with no real basis in English.
The rule against ending a sentence with a preposition goes back to the poet John Dryden in 1672, copying Latin.
Double negatives were normal in Chaucer's day. He once stacked four negatives into a single sentence.
The letters "ough" can be said at least eight ways in English: though, through, rough, cough, bough, thought, hiccough and borough.
The b in "debt" was never pronounced. Renaissance scholars added it to show off the Latin root, "debitum".
"Island" has a silent s because scholars wrongly linked it to "isle". The two words aren't related at all.
"Could" has an l because people copied "would" and "should". Unlike them, "could" never had an l sound.
The k in "knight" used to be pronounced, just like in its German cousin "Knecht".
Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowels shifted dramatically, which is a big reason spelling and sound don't match.
"Colonel" is spelled the Italian way but pronounced "kernel" from an old French version of the word.
Noah Webster gave Americans "color", "center" and "defense". He also tried "tung" for tongue, which didn't catch on.
Samuel Johnson's 1755 dictionary defined oats as a grain given to horses in England but which in Scotland supports the people.
Samuel Johnson defined a "lexicographer", a dictionary writer like himself, as "a harmless drudge".
The Oxford English Dictionary took about 70 years to finish. The first full edition was completed in 1928.
One of the busiest volunteers for the Oxford English Dictionary sent in his work from a hospital for the criminally insane.
For years, a 1934 Webster's dictionary contained "dord", a word that never existed. It came from a misread note card.
Dictionaries sometimes include fake words as traps for copycats. "Esquivalience" was one.
"OK" started in 1839 as a newspaper joke: an abbreviation of "oll korrect", a silly misspelling of all correct.
"OK" spread thanks to President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed Old Kinderhook, whose 1840 supporters formed "OK Clubs".
The verb "run" has around 645 meanings in the Oxford English Dictionary, more than any other word. It took the record from "set".
"Sarcasm" comes from a Greek word meaning to tear flesh like a dog, so a sarcastic remark is literally a bite.
"Cleave" can mean to split apart or to cling together. Words that are their own opposites are called contronyms.
To "dust" can mean adding dust, like on a cake, or removing it, like from a shelf.
"Sanction" can mean to approve something or to punish it, so a sanctioned party could be allowed or punished.
"Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo" is a real, grammatical English sentence.
"The old man the boat" is a correct sentence. "Old" is the noun and "man" is the verb, as in sailors who man a ship.
The earliest known "OMG" is in a 1917 letter to Winston Churchill, from a British admiral who spelled it out: Oh! My God!
"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" uses every letter of the alphabet. Typists used it to test their machines.
"Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow" uses every letter of the alphabet in just 29 letters.
"Tattarrattat" is the longest palindrome in the Oxford English Dictionary. James Joyce invented it for a knock on the door.
The Finnish word "saippuakivikauppias", a soapstone seller, is a palindrome 19 letters long.
"Stressed" spelled backwards is "desserts", which might explain a lot about comfort eating.
The letter A began about 3,500 years ago as a picture of an ox's head. Turn an A upside down and you can still see the horns.
The letter O started out over 3,000 years ago as a drawing of an eye, and it still looks like one.
"Alphabet" is just the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, stuck together.
Almost every alphabet used in Europe and the Middle East descends from one invented around 3,000 years ago by the Phoenicians.
Writing was invented independently at least three times: in Mesopotamia, in China and in Central America.
Cuneiform, the oldest writing, was made by pressing a cut reed into wet clay, leaving wedge-shaped marks.
The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in three scripts, which let scholars finally crack Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822.
The last known inscription in Egyptian hieroglyphs was carved in 394 AD. After that, nobody could read them for 1,400 years.
Egyptian hieroglyphs could be written left to right or right to left. You read toward the faces of the animals and people.
Linear A, a script used on ancient Crete about 3,500 years ago, still hasn't been deciphered by anyone.
The script of the Indus Valley, one of the world's first cities, still can't be read by anyone.
The rongorongo script of Easter Island has never been deciphered, and only a couple of dozen carved objects survive.
Early Greek was sometimes written boustrophedon, "as the ox ploughs": one line left to right, the next right to left.
Ancient Romans usually wrote without spaces between words, and often without punctuation either.
Irish monks in the early Middle Ages popularised putting spaces between words, to help them read Latin.
We say "uppercase" and "lowercase" because printers kept capital letters in the upper case, or box, of type.
Lowercase letters as we know them grew out of a neat handwriting style promoted by Charlemagne's scribes around 800 AD.
The letters J, U and W were latecomers. For centuries, I and J were the same letter, and so were U and V.
W is called "double u" in English but "double v" in French, and it looks like two Vs stuck together.
The "Ye" in "Ye Olde Shoppe" was always pronounced "the". The Y was standing in for an old letter, thorn.
English once had extra letters, including thorn and eth for the "th" sound. Icelandic still uses both.
The & sign is a squashed "et", Latin for and. Its name comes from children reciting the alphabet, which ended "and per se and".
The dot on top of a lowercase i or j has its own name. It is called a tittle, and almost nobody knows it.
The @ sign is called "snail" in Italian, "monkey tail" in Dutch and "elephant's trunk" in Danish and Swedish.
The # sign has an official-sounding name, "octothorpe", invented by engineers at Bell Labs in the 1960s.
The semicolon was introduced by a Venetian printer in 1494. The same printer later invented italic type.
The comma comes from a Greek word meaning a piece cut off: it marks where a sentence gets chopped into bits.
The ancient Greeks marked pauses with dots at different heights; our full stop comes from the lowest one.
The interrobang, a question mark and exclamation mark merged into one, was invented in 1962 by an advertising man.
The abbreviation "lb" for pound comes from libra, the Latin word for scales, which is also where the pound sign comes from.
"Xmas" isn't modern. The X is the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christ in Greek, and it's been used for centuries.
"Mayday" comes from the French "m'aidez", meaning help me. A British radio officer chose it in 1923.
In Morse code, E is a single dot because it's the most common letter in English.
Julius Caesar wrote secret messages by shifting every letter three places along the alphabet.
Cockney rhyming slang hides words: "apples and pears" means stairs, and "dog and bone" means phone.
French slang called verlan flips syllables backwards. The name itself is "l'envers", meaning the reverse, reversed.
Oxford Dictionaries' Word of the Year for 2015 wasn't a word at all. It was the "face with tears of joy" emoji.
The 1935 word "pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis", a lung disease, was invented just to be the longest word.
"Uncopyrightable" is one of the longest English words that doesn't repeat a single letter.
"Strengths" packs nine letters into a single syllable, with only one vowel among them.
"Rhythms" is the longest common English word without the vowels a, e, i, o or u.
"Facetious" and "abstemious" contain all five vowels, in alphabetical order.
"Queueing" is one of very few English words with five vowels in a row: u, e, u, e, i.
"Typewriter" can be typed using only the top row of letters on a keyboard.
"Stewardesses" is one of the longest words you can type with only your left hand.
"Dreamt" is the only common English word ending in the letters "mt".
A Welsh village has a 58-letter name, created in the 1800s partly to attract tourists to its train station.
The full ceremonial name of Bangkok is over 160 letters long when written in English letters.
German built one law name 63 letters long, about checking beef labels. The law was scrapped in 2013, taking the word with it.
In Turkish you can stack endings onto one word until it means a whole sentence, sometimes over 70 letters long.
In some Inuit languages, a single long word can say what English needs a whole sentence for.
The Yaghan word "mamihlapinatapai" describes a look between two people who each wish the other would make the first move.
German has a word, "Kummerspeck", literally grief bacon, for weight gained from comfort eating.
Japanese has a word, "tsundoku", for buying books and letting them pile up unread.
Japanese has a word, "komorebi", for sunlight filtering through the leaves of trees.
Spanish has a word, "sobremesa", for the time spent chatting around the table after a meal is over.
Russian has a word, "pochemuchka", for a person, often a child, who asks too many questions.
Brazilian Portuguese has a word, "cafune", for tenderly running your fingers through someone's hair.
Swedish has a word, "mangata", for the road-like path of moonlight reflected on water.
The German "Ohrwurm", ear worm, gave English the word "earworm" for a song stuck in your head.
The idea of a "skyscraper" was copied word for word: French says sky-scratcher and German says cloud-scraper.
"Flea market" is a word-for-word copy of the French "marche aux puces", market of fleas.
"Brainwashing" is a direct translation of a Chinese phrase, which entered English during the Korean War.
Languages that got tea by sea call it something like "tea", while those that got it overland call it "chai" or "cha".
English has borrowed words from hundreds of languages, but its 100 most common words are almost all native English.
After 1066, English farmers kept cows, pigs and sheep, but the French-speaking nobles ate beef, pork and mutton.
English law courts used a mix called "Law French" for centuries, and it was only banned by Parliament in the 1730s.
Old English, the language of Beowulf, is so different that modern English speakers need a translation to read it.
The first book printed in English, around 1473, wasn't printed in England but in Bruges, in what is now Belgium.
Around 1490, the printer William Caxton told of a woman who couldn't understand a traveller asking for "eggs": she called them "eyren".
"OK" may be the most widely understood word on Earth, used in languages all over the world.
"Huh?" means roughly the same thing and sounds almost the same in languages all over the world, a 2013 study found.
American Sign Language and British Sign Language are so different that their users can't understand each other.
American Sign Language is more closely related to French Sign Language than to British Sign Language, thanks to a French teacher.
On Martha's Vineyard, so many people were born deaf that for centuries hearing and deaf islanders all used sign language.
There are around 300 different sign languages in the world, each with its own grammar and vocabulary.
Sign languages have accents and regional dialects, just like spoken languages.
In American Sign Language, raising your eyebrows turns a statement into a yes-or-no question. Faces are part of the grammar.
British Sign Language spells words using two hands, while American Sign Language uses just one.
Signers have "tip of the fingers" moments, the sign language version of having a word on the tip of your tongue.
Plains Indian Sign Language let dozens of Native American nations with different spoken languages talk to each other.
Monks who took vows of silence developed their own sign systems so they could still ask for bread or salt at meals.
When toddlers say "goed" or "mouses", it's a good sign: they've worked out a grammar rule and are applying it everywhere.
"Mama" and "papa" sound alike in so many languages because "m", "p" and "a" are among the easiest sounds for babies to make.
Twins sometimes invent a private language that only the two of them understand, which linguists call cryptophasia.
Children raised with two languages may mix them in one sentence, but they aren't confused: they know which is which.
A 2016 study estimated the average 20-year-old American knows about 42,000 dictionary words.
Studies show women and men both speak about 16,000 words a day on average, busting the myth that women talk far more.
If you watch lips saying "ga" while hearing "ba", your brain hears "da". It's called the McGurk effect.
Shown a spiky shape and a rounded one, people almost everywhere call the spiky one "kiki" and the round one "bouba".
The most common word in a language is used about twice as often as the second most common, and three times the third.
"The" is the most common word in English, making up roughly one word in every 15 you read.
The "tip of the tongue" feeling, knowing a word but not finding it, happens to people in almost every language studied.
"Hoist with his own petard" comes from Hamlet. A petard was a small bomb, so it means being blown up by your own trap.
A "wild-goose chase" was originally a kind of horse race in which riders had to follow the leader, like geese in flight.
Shakespeare first called jealousy "the green-eyed monster" in Othello.
Nobody knows where "raining cats and dogs" comes from. The story about animals sliding off thatched roofs is a myth.
"Saved by the bell" comes from boxing, not from people buried alive with bells attached to their coffins.
"Passing the buck" comes from poker, where a marker called the buck showed whose turn it was to deal.
A "red herring" was popularised by a writer in 1807 who told of using a smelly smoked fish to throw hounds off a scent.
"Stealing someone's thunder" goes back to a 1700s playwright whose new thunder sound effect was used by a rival theatre.
"Gaslighting" comes from a 1938 play in which a husband makes his wife doubt her sanity, partly by dimming the gas lights.
"Catch-22" comes from Joseph Heller's 1961 novel, about a rule that makes escape impossible no matter what you do.
"Hobson's choice", meaning no real choice, comes from a 1600s Cambridge stable owner who made customers take the horse by the door.
"Crocodile tears" comes from an ancient belief that crocodiles weep while eating their victims.
"Long in the tooth" comes from horses, whose gums shrink with age so their teeth look longer.
A "nest egg" was originally a fake egg left in a hen's nest to encourage her to keep laying.
A cricket "hat trick" comes from 1858, when a bowler who took three wickets with three balls was given a hat.
A "deadline" was originally a line around a US Civil War prison camp. Prisoners who crossed it could be shot.
"Freelance" was coined by Walter Scott in his 1820 novel Ivanhoe for a medieval knight who fought for whoever paid.
"Jump the shark" comes from a 1977 episode of the TV show Happy Days in which a character waterskis over a shark.
"Cut to the chase" comes from early films, where the chase scene was the most exciting part.
Long before computers, a "computer" was a person, often a woman, whose job was doing calculations by hand.
"Wiki" comes from the Hawaiian word for quick. The inventor got the idea from a shuttle bus at Honolulu airport.
"Laser", "radar" and "scuba" started life as abbreviations, but they became so normal that people forgot they were.
"Taser" comes from the title of a children's adventure book: Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle, with an A added.
A "byte" was deliberately misspelled with a y so it wouldn't be confused with "bit".
"Smith" is the most common surname in English because so many villages had a blacksmith.
"Mc" and "Mac" in names mean son of, and the Irish "O'" means descendant of. "Fitz" means son of in Norman French.
In Iceland, last names are usually built from a parent's first name, so a family can have several surnames. The phone book lists first names.
The name Wendy was very rare until J.M. Barrie used it in Peter Pan in 1904.
The name Vanessa was invented by the writer Jonathan Swift in the 1700s as a nickname for a friend.
The name Lorna was invented for the 1869 novel Lorna Doone, and it became popular because readers loved the heroine.
"Mr" comes from "master" and "Mrs" from "mistress", which once meant the woman in charge of a household.
"Ms" was suggested in 1901 by a US newspaper as a polite title that doesn't reveal whether a woman is married.
Peggy is a nickname for Margaret, Polly for Mary, and Bob for Robert, often created by rhyming on the shorter forms.
Jack started out as a nickname for John, which is why so many Johns end up called Jack.
In 1996, Swedish parents tried to name their son a 43-character jumble of letters, pronounced "Albin". A court said no.
UNESCO's International Mother Language Day, February 21, honours students killed in 1952 defending the Bengali language.
Hawaiian became an official language of the state of Hawaii in 1978, alongside English, after nearly dying out.
In 1928 Turkey switched from the Arabic alphabet to Latin letters in a matter of months, and the president toured the country teaching it.
Vietnamese is written with Latin letters thanks to missionaries in the 1600s, before that it used Chinese-style characters.
China simplified thousands of its characters in the 1950s, but Taiwan and Hong Kong still use the traditional forms.
Knowing about 3,000 Chinese characters is enough to read a newspaper, but big dictionaries list over 50,000.
One Chinese character, used for a kind of noodle, takes more than 50 brush strokes to write.
The Armenian alphabet was invented by a monk in about 405 AD and is still used today, with very few changes.
The Cyrillic alphabet is named after Saint Cyril, though it was most likely created by his students after his death.
Serbian is written in two alphabets, Cyrillic and Latin, and Serbs read both.
Thai is written without spaces between words. Spaces mark the ends of phrases or sentences instead.
The Khmer alphabet of Cambodia has 74 letters, the largest alphabet in the world according to Guinness World Records.
A modern script for West African languages, N'Ko, was invented in 1949 by a man determined to prove Africans could write their own.
The Vai people of Liberia had their own writing system, invented in the 1830s by a man who said it came to him in a dream.
Canadian Inuit write with symbols first designed for the Cree language by a missionary in 1840.
Samuel Pepys wrote his famous diary in shorthand, which is partly why it stayed private for over 100 years.
Cicero's secretary invented a shorthand in ancient Rome. One of its symbols, a 7-like sign for "and", still appears on Irish road signs.
"Salary" comes from the Latin word for salt. The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt has never been proven.
"Glamour" is a Scottish twist on "grammar". Book learning once seemed so mysterious that the word came to mean a magic spell.
"Trivia" comes from the Latin for a place where three roads meet, the sort of spot where people swapped small talk.
"Sarcophagus" means flesh-eating in Greek, from a stone that was believed to make bodies vanish quickly.
"Ostracize" comes from ancient Athens, where citizens voted to banish someone by scratching his name on bits of broken pottery.
January is named after Janus, the Roman god with two faces, one looking back at the old year and one forward to the new.
Military tanks got their name as a disguise: during World War I the British called them water tanks to keep them secret.
"Sideburns" is a jumbled version of Burnside, a US Civil War general famous for his enormous side whiskers.
The teddy bear is named after President Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a captured bear on a hunting trip in 1902.
Nachos are named after Ignacio "Nacho" Anaya, a Mexican waiter who threw them together for hungry customers in 1943.
The Caesar salad has nothing to do with Julius Caesar. It is named after Caesar Cardini, an Italian restaurant owner in Mexico.
Peach Melba and Melba toast are named after Nellie Melba, an Australian opera star of the 1890s.
The pavlova dessert is named after Anna Pavlova, a Russian ballerina, and Australia and New Zealand both claim to have invented it.
The Ferris wheel is named after George Ferris, who built a giant one for the 1893 world's fair in Chicago.
The Jacuzzi is named after a family of Italian immigrant brothers in California who first made pumps for farms.
"Maverick" comes from Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher who didn't brand his calves, so unbranded cattle were called mavericks.
The raincoat called a mackintosh is named after Charles Macintosh, a Scottish chemist who invented waterproof fabric in the 1820s.
"Chauvinism" is named after Nicolas Chauvin, a French soldier fanatically loyal to Napoleon, who may never have existed.
To "bowdlerize" a book means to censor it, after Thomas Bowdler, who published a family-friendly Shakespeare in 1807.
Spoonerisms, like "you have tasted the whole worm", are named after an Oxford professor. Most of his famous slips were probably invented.
A malapropism, mixing up similar words, is named after Mrs Malaprop, a comic character in a 1775 play who did it constantly.
"Gargantuan" comes from Gargantua, a giant with a colossal appetite in a 1500s French novel.
"Yahoo" was invented by Jonathan Swift in Gulliver's Travels as the name of a race of brutish human-like creatures.
"Gobbledygook" was coined in 1944 by a Texas congressman who said wordy officials sounded like gobbling turkeys.
"Blurb" comes from a 1907 joke book cover featuring a made-up young woman called Miss Belinda Blurb.
In 1924 a contest offered $200 for a new word to shame people who ignored alcohol bans. The winner was "scofflaw".
"Smog", a blend of smoke and fog, was coined in the early 1900s to describe the air in London.
"Brunch" was coined in 1890s Britain as student slang for a meal halfway between breakfast and lunch.
The earliest known use of "selfie" is from an Australian online forum in 2002. By 2013 it was the Word of the Year.
A "fathom" was the length of a man's outstretched arms, which is why sailors measured water depth with it.
"Mile" comes from the Latin for a thousand paces, which is how Roman soldiers measured distance.
"Inch" and "ounce" are the same word in disguise: both come from the Latin "uncia", meaning a twelfth part.
"Pencil" comes from the Latin for little tail, because the first pencils were fine brushes. Penicillin shares that root.
"Pen" comes from the Latin word for feather, because people wrote with quills for over a thousand years.
The Bible is named after Byblos, an ancient port that exported papyrus, the paper of the ancient world.
"Library" comes from the Latin word for the inner bark of trees, which people once wrote on.
"Breakfast" literally means breaking the fast you've kept all night while you slept.
"Dinner" comes from an old French word meaning to break your fast. So, originally, dinner meant breakfast.
"Supper" comes from the French "souper", to have soup, because the evening meal was often just that.
"Nostril" was originally "nose thirl", meaning nose hole. "Thrill" comes from the same word, which once meant to pierce.
The ladybird, or ladybug, is named after "Our Lady", the Virgin Mary.
"Caterpillar" probably comes from old French words meaning hairy cat.
"Earwig" comes from an old belief that the insect crawls into sleeping people's ears.
"Chameleon" comes from Greek words meaning ground lion, a grand name for a lizard that mostly sits still on branches.
The dodo's name probably comes from a Portuguese word for fool, because the bird showed no fear of sailors.
"Gorilla" comes from a Greek account of an expedition 2,500 years ago that met hairy wild people in Africa.
"Platypus" is Greek for flat foot, a fair description of an animal that seems built from spare parts.
Group names like "a murder of crows" mostly come from 15th-century books of hunting terms, and many were jokes never really used.
The verb "to be" is a mash-up of three different ancient verbs, which is why "am", "was" and "be" look nothing alike.
"Went" was stolen from a different verb, "wend", and became the past tense of "go".
English lost its separate plural "you", so people invented "y'all", "youse" and "you guys" to fill the gap.
In Shakespeare's time, calling a stranger "thou" could be an insult, because "thou" was for close friends, children and servants.
Early Quakers called everyone "thee" and "thou", even judges and kings, to show that all people were equal.
Many languages, like Vietnamese, use one word for both blue and green. Linguists call it "grue".
Russian has two basic words for blue, one for light and one for dark. Studies found Russian speakers tell the shades apart faster.
If a language has only three colour words, they are almost always black, white and red, a 1969 study found.
Ancient Greek poems describe the sea as "wine-dark", and nobody is quite sure what colour Homer meant.
In Japan, green traffic lights are often called blue, because the old word "ao" covered both colours.
The Danish word for 50, "halvtreds", is a shortened form of an old phrase meaning two and a half times twenty.
"Million" comes from the Italian for a big thousand, a word medieval Italians coined because Latin had no single word for it.
In Britain, "billion" meant a million million until 1974, when the government switched to the American meaning of a thousand million.
In World War I, Choctaw soldiers sent US Army messages in their own language, a generation before the famous Navajo code talkers.
Thomas Jefferson invented a wheel-shaped cipher machine, and a similar design was still used by the US Army more than a century later.
The phonetic alphabet spells "Alfa" and "Juliett" oddly so that speakers of every language pronounce them correctly.
In Aesop's fable, a lion keeps all the food for himself after a hunt, which is where "the lion's share" comes from.
"Sour grapes" comes from Aesop's fable of a fox who decides the grapes he can't reach were probably sour anyway.
A "Pyrrhic victory" comes from King Pyrrhus, who won a battle so costly he said another such win would ruin him.
"Crossing the Rubicon" refers to Julius Caesar marching his army across a small Italian river in 49 BC, which meant war.
"The writing on the wall" comes from a Bible story in which a mysterious hand writes a king's doom on his palace wall.
"Scapegoat" was coined in 1530 by William Tyndale, translating a Bible ritual in which a goat carried away the people's sins.
"A flash in the pan" comes from old muskets, where the gunpowder in the pan could flash without firing the shot.
"Lock, stock and barrel" means the whole thing because those are the three main parts of an old gun.
"Hair of the dog" comes from an old belief that you could cure a dog bite by putting some of that dog's hair on the wound.
"Curiosity killed the cat" started out as "care killed the cat", where care meant worry, in a 1598 play.
"The proof is in the pudding" is a shortened version of "the proof of the pudding is in the eating", which makes more sense.
The earliest known uses of "the whole nine yards" are about "the whole six yards", which makes most origin stories impossible.
"Posh" doesn't stand for "port out, starboard home". That story showed up decades after the word.
"Etaoin shrdlu" sometimes appeared by mistake in old newspapers: it was what typesetters got by running a finger down the keys.
Placeholder text "Lorem ipsum" is scrambled Latin from a passage by Cicero about the pursuit of pain.
A popular story says a Dublin theatre owner invented the word "quiz" for a bet in 1791. It's a myth: the word was in print years earlier.
"Avon" is an old Celtic word for river, so the River Avon is really the River River.
"Sahara" is Arabic for desert, so the Sahara Desert is really the Desert Desert.
Any English town ending in "-by", like Whitby or Derby, was probably once a Viking settlement: "by" meant farm or village.
English towns ending in "-chester" or "-caster", like Manchester and Lancaster, were built on old Roman forts.
A New Mexico town renamed itself "Truth or Consequences" in 1950, after a radio quiz show.
America is named after Amerigo Vespucci, an Italian explorer who realised it was a new continent, not Asia.
The Pacific Ocean was named by Magellan, who found it peaceful after a rough passage around South America.
About four in ten Vietnamese people share the surname Nguyen.
Around one in five South Koreans has the surname Kim, so in a room of 20 people you can expect about four Kims.
Japanese doesn't distinguish the sounds l and r, which is why the two can be tricky for Japanese learners of English.
In a Turkish village called Kuskoy, people whistle Turkish across the mountains. Locals call it "bird language".
West African talking drums can "speak" by copying the rising and falling tones of languages like Yoruba.
Xhosa and Zulu in southern Africa include click sounds as ordinary consonants, made by snapping the tongue off the roof of the mouth.
The "th" sounds in English are rare among the world's languages, which is why so many learners find them so tricky.
A famous 1861 patient could only say one word, "tan". His brain led doctors to discover the brain's main speech area.
Say any word over and over and it starts to sound meaningless. Psychologists call it semantic satiation.
Fast-sounding languages like Spanish pack less meaning into each syllable, so all languages share information at about the same speed.
Cornish was declared extinct, but enough people revived it that in 2010 UNESCO changed its status to critically endangered.
Many languages start words with the "ng" sound, as in the Vietnamese name Nguyen, even though English only allows it at the end.
For decades, children at Native American boarding schools were punished for speaking their own languages.
UNESCO has warned that around half of the world's languages could disappear by the end of this century.
Thousands of the world's languages have never been written down, so when the last speaker dies, the language can vanish without a trace.

In the Belgian town of Baarle-Hertog, the Dutch border runs through houses, and your country depends on where your front door is.
Russia is so wide that when people in its far west eat breakfast, people on its Pacific coast are already having dinner.
France has more time zones than any other country, about 12, thanks to its islands scattered from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean.
China is as wide as five time zones, yet the whole country sets its clocks to a single time: Beijing's.
Nepal's clocks run 5 hours and 45 minutes ahead of world time, one of the few time zones that is off by a quarter of an hour.
Nepal has the only national flag that is not a rectangle: it is two triangles stacked on top of each other.
Switzerland and Vatican City are the only two countries with square flags.
Australia is wider than the Moon: the mainland is about 4,000 kilometres across, the Moon about 3,500.
Alaska is the most northern, most western and, oddly, most eastern US state, because its islands cross the 180 degree line.
Vatican City, the smallest country on Earth, covers just 0.44 square kilometres, about the size of 60 soccer fields.
Lesotho is a country completely surrounded by South Africa, and even its lowest point is higher than 1,000 metres.
Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are so far inland that you have to cross two countries to reach the sea.
Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, but because the Earth bulges, Ecuador's Chimborazo is the spot farthest from the centre of the Earth.
Venezuela's Angel Falls is so tall, about 979 metres, that much of its water turns to mist before it reaches the bottom.
Not a single bridge crosses the Amazon River anywhere along its entire length.
The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, with spots over 200 metres deep, deep enough to hide a skyscraper.
Indonesia is made of more than 17,000 islands spread over a distance wider than the United States.
By one official count, Sweden has about 267,000 islands, possibly more than any other country on Earth.
Finland is called the land of a thousand lakes, but it actually has nearly 188,000 of them.
By most counts, Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
About 80 percent of Greenland is covered by ice, and the ice is so heavy it has pushed the middle of the island below sea level.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth: a desert is about how little rain or snow falls, not how hot it is.
Istanbul sits on two continents: a strait splits the city between Europe and Asia, and people commute between them by ferry.
Bolivia has two capitals: the constitution names Sucre, but the government actually works from La Paz.
La Paz, Bolivia, sits about 3,600 metres up, making it the highest seat of government in the world.
South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria for the government, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the courts.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world, well over 150 letters when written in English.
A hill in New Zealand has an 85-letter Maori name, often called the longest place name in the English-speaking world.
Canberra was built as Australia's capital because Sydney and Melbourne could not agree which of them should get the job.
Brasilia was built almost from nothing in the late 1950s, and from above its plan looks like an airplane.
Myanmar's new capital, Naypyidaw, has highways up to 20 lanes wide that are often almost empty.
Chile is about 4,300 kilometres long but on average only about 175 kilometres wide, like a ribbon down a continent.
The Gambia is a thin strip of land along a river, almost entirely wrapped inside Senegal.
Tristan da Cunha has no airport: its roughly 240 residents live about six days by boat from South Africa.
Pitcairn Island, settled by the mutineers of the ship Bounty, has fewer than 50 people living on it.
In 2011 Samoa skipped December 30 entirely, hopping across the date line to match the calendars of Australia and New Zealand.
Kiribati is the only country in all four hemispheres, because its islands straddle both the equator and the 180 degree line.
Two Diomede Islands, one Russian and one American, are under 4 kilometres apart but nearly a full day apart in time.
The border between the US and Canada is the longest land border between two countries in the world.
The Haskell Library sits on the US-Canada border, and a black line on its floor shows where one country ends.
Point Roberts is a little US town you can only reach by land by driving through Canada.
Spain has a town, Llivia, that sits entirely inside France, linked to Spain by a single road.
Pheasant Island, in a river between France and Spain, changes countries every six months.
The Caribbean island of Saint Martin is split between France and the Netherlands, and you can cross the border without stopping.
Borneo is the only island in the world split among three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei.
Brunei is split into two separate pieces, with a strip of Malaysia in between.
Russia's Kaliningrad is cut off from the rest of Russia, squeezed between Poland and Lithuania.
Russia and China each share a land border with 14 different countries, more than any other nation.
Mongolia is the emptiest country on Earth, with only about two people for every square kilometre.
About a quarter of Mongolians still live as herders, moving with their animals and living in round felt tents called gers.
Bhutan measures its success with Gross National Happiness, not just with money.
Bhutan's forests soak up more carbon dioxide than the whole country gives off.
Iceland has no army at all, yet it was one of the countries that founded NATO in 1949.
Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and spent the money on schools and hospitals instead.
In Iceland's Silfra crack, divers swim between two continents' tectonic plates and can nearly touch both at once.
Icelanders are listed in the phone book by first name, because their last names just say whose son or daughter they are.
Iceland has an official naming committee that must approve any new baby name not already on its list.
About two-thirds of Canadians live within 100 kilometres of the US border.
The Canadian city of Windsor lies directly south of Detroit in the United States.
Reno, Nevada, is farther west than Los Angeles, California, even though Nevada sits east of California on the map.
Because Panama bends, a ship crossing the Panama Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travels from west to east.
Venice is built on more than 100 small islands joined together by around 400 bridges.
Amsterdam has more than 1,500 bridges, several times as many as Venice.
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, kept dry by dikes and pumps.
Amsterdam's main airport sits about 3 metres below sea level, on the bottom of a lake that was drained.
Mexico City was built on an old lake bed and parts of it have sunk by around 10 metres in the last century.
At the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, you can watch the sun set from the ground, ride up the tower and watch it set again.
Mount Everest grows about 4 millimetres a year, because India is still crashing slowly into the rest of Asia.
The border between Nepal and China runs right across the top of Mount Everest.
Lake Titicaca, between Peru and Bolivia, is the highest lake in the world big enough for large boats, about 3,800 metres up.
The Uros people live on floating islands on Lake Titicaca that they build by stacking bundles of reeds.
The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth, so big that five countries line its shores.
The Aral Sea was once one of the four biggest lakes in the world, and today much of its old bed is desert with stranded ships.
The Danube flows through 10 countries, more than any other river, and through four capital cities.
Every rainy season, Cambodia's Tonle Sap River changes direction and flows backward, swelling its lake to several times its size.
Victoria Falls is about 1.7 kilometres wide, and locals call it Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders.
Niagara Falls has crept about 11 kilometres upstream over the last 12,000 years by wearing away its own cliff.
Iguazu Falls, between Argentina and Brazil, is made of about 275 separate waterfalls.
The Okavango in Botswana is a river that never reaches the sea: it spreads out and vanishes into the Kalahari Desert.
The world's shortest scheduled flight, between the Scottish islands of Westray and Papa Westray, lasts about 90 seconds, sometimes less.
Fortune cookies are almost unknown in China: they were popularized in the United States, likely from a Japanese cracker.
Tempura came to Japan from Portuguese missionaries and traders in the 1500s.
Japan's beloved curry rice arrived through the British navy, which had picked up curry in India.
The croissant is based on the Austrian kipferl, a crescent pastry that Viennese bakers brought to Paris.
Coffee was first brewed as a drink in Yemen, where Sufi monks used it to stay awake for night prayers.
The word mocha comes from Mokha, a port in Yemen that once shipped much of the world's coffee.
Finland drinks more coffee per person than any other country, around 12 kilograms of beans a year each.
Turkey drinks more tea per person than any other country, even more than Britain.
In Japan, slurping noodles loudly is polite: it shows you are enjoying them and helps cool them down.
Chopsticks are used in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam, but in Thailand most meals are eaten with a spoon and fork.
In Ethiopia, injera, a spongy sourdough flatbread, is the plate, the spoon and part of the meal all at once.
Gursha is an Ethiopian custom of hand-feeding a friend a mouthful of food as a sign of love and respect.
Pizza Margherita is said to be named after Queen Margherita, with its colors matching the Italian flag.
Hawaiian pizza, with ham and pineapple, was invented in Canada by a Greek immigrant in the 1960s.

In Greece, people celebrate their name day, the feast of the saint they are named after, often more than birthdays.
In Spain, many people have two surnames, one from their father and one from their mother.
Spain's Canary Islands are much closer to Africa than to mainland Spain.
For decades, cars in Gibraltar drove straight across the airport runway, stopping whenever a plane came in.
Gibraltar is home to the only wild monkeys in Europe, Barbary macaques.
Portugal and England have the oldest alliance in the world still in force, dating back to 1373.
Portugal's University of Coimbra library keeps a colony of bats that eat the insects that would damage its old books.
France is the most visited country in the world, welcoming roughly 100 million foreign tourists a year.
Paris has a sister city agreement with only one city in the world: Rome.
Under the streets of Paris, catacombs hold the bones of about 6 million people.
The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 centimetres taller on hot days as the iron expands.
Germany has over 1,500 kinds of sausage and more than 3,000 kinds of bread.
Germany's autobahn has long stretches with no speed limit at all, only a recommended speed.
In Germany, Sunday is a legal day of rest: most shops close, and noisy chores like mowing the lawn can be banned.
Mount Roraima, a flat-topped mountain where Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana meet, inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World.
By law, Switzerland has enough nuclear fallout shelter places for its entire population.
Switzerland's Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world, about 57 kilometres.
In Switzerland, it is illegal to keep just one guinea pig, because they are social animals and need company.
Austria's Hallstatt is so admired that China built a full-size copy of the village.
In the Netherlands, there are more bicycles than people, about 23 million bikes for about 18 million residents.
In the Dutch village of Giethoorn, there are almost no roads: people get around by boat on canals.
Belgium went 541 days without an elected government in 2010 and 2011, and life carried on.
In the UK, the monarch has two birthdays: a real one and an official one celebrated in summer.
Scotland's national animal is the unicorn, a symbol of purity and power in Scottish heraldry.
In London, black cab drivers must memorize about 25,000 streets for a test called The Knowledge.
The necktie comes from scarves worn by Croatian soldiers in the 1600s, and the French word cravate comes from Croat.
Slovenia is more than half covered by forest, and it is home to hundreds of brown bears.
Dubrovnik's city walls are almost 2 kilometres long and still surround the old town completely.
Bulgaria produces much of the world's rose oil, from a valley where roses are picked by hand at dawn.
Romania's Bran Castle is marketed as Dracula's castle, though the real Vlad the Impaler likely barely stayed there.
In Romania, the Merry Cemetery has bright blue wooden crosses painted with funny poems about the people buried there.
Poland's Wieliczka salt mine has a whole underground chapel carved out of salt, including the chandeliers.
Budapest sits on more than 100 natural hot springs, and people play chess in its outdoor thermal baths.
Ukraine's capital Kyiv has one of the deepest metro stations in the world, Arsenalna, about 105 metres underground.
The Russian city of Norilsk is the northernmost city with over 100,000 people, and it has no road to the rest of Russia.
In Yakutsk, Siberia, people keep their cars running all day in winter, because a stopped engine may not start again.
Canada's Nunavut is bigger than Mexico but home to only about 40,000 people.
In Churchill, Canada, residents leave their cars unlocked so anyone can escape a wandering polar bear.
Churchill, Canada, has a polar bear jail, where bears that wander into town are held until they can be flown away.
Canada's Quebec stores maple syrup in a strategic reserve, and thieves once stole about 2,700 tonnes of it.
The Quebec town of Saint-Louis-du-Ha! Ha! is thought to be the only place in the world with two exclamation marks in its name.
Alaska has more coastline than all the other US states combined.
The US city of Juneau, Alaska's capital, cannot be reached by road: only by plane or boat.
Chichen Itza's pyramid was built so that at the spring and autumn equinoxes, a shadow serpent slides down its steps.
Belize's Great Blue Hole is a near-perfectly round underwater sinkhole about 300 metres wide.
Cuba's streets are famous for American cars from the 1950s, kept running for decades with homemade parts.
Haiti was the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people who won their freedom, in 1804.
Barbados is the birthplace of rum, by most accounts, and its Mount Gay distillery dates back to 1703.
Colombia has more bird species than any other country, around 1,900.
In Colombia's Cano Cristales, a river turns red, yellow, green and blue each year thanks to a water plant.
Bogota closes over 100 kilometres of roads to cars every Sunday so people can cycle, skate and walk.
In 2008 Ecuador became the first country to give nature its own rights in its constitution.
Argentina has its own legendary time for dinner: many families eat at 10 pm or later.
Buenos Aires has one of the widest avenues in the world, 9 de Julio, about 140 metres across.
Brazil has the largest Japanese population outside Japan, about 2 million people.
Sao Paulo has one of the world's largest helicopter fleets, as rich residents fly over the traffic.
Suriname is the most forested country on Earth, with over 90 percent of its land covered in trees.
In Guyana, Kaieteur Falls is about four times taller than Niagara and drops in a single plunge.
@chemistry|Chemistry
Gallium is a metal that melts at about 30 degrees C, so a spoon made of it would melt in your hand or droop in a cup of hot tea.
Every atom of gold on Earth was forged in violent cosmic events like colliding dead stars, long before the Sun even existed.
Helium was discovered on the Sun in 1868, by studying sunlight, nearly 30 years before anyone found it on Earth.
Only two elements are liquid at room temperature: the metal mercury and a smelly red-brown liquid called bromine.
Osmium is the densest natural element: a lump the size of a soccer ball would weigh over 120 kilograms.
Astatine is so rare that scientists think less than a gram of it exists in the whole Earth's crust at any moment.
Diamond and the grey stuff in your pencil are both pure carbon; only the way the atoms are stacked is different.
Helium is the only element that can never be frozen solid at normal pressure, no matter how cold you make it.
Pure cesium is so reactive that it explodes when it touches water, and it can catch fire just from contact with air.
Cesium melts at about 28 degrees C, so a chunk of it would turn liquid on a hot summer afternoon.
Fluorine is the most reactive element known: it attacks almost everything, and even water can burst into flame in it.
Sodium is so soft you can slice it with a butter knife, revealing a shiny silver surface that goes dull within seconds.
About 99 percent of your body's mass comes from just six elements: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus.
By weight, your body is roughly two-thirds oxygen, and most of it is locked up in the water inside you.
Hydrogen is the most common atom in your body: about 6 out of every 10 atoms in you are hydrogen.
Your body holds roughly 16 kilograms of carbon, enough to make thousands of pencil leads.
An adult body contains about 4 grams of iron, roughly enough to make one small nail.
Bismuth is technically radioactive, but it decays so slowly that its half-life is a billion times longer than the age of the universe.
Bismuth crystals grow in rainbow-colored staircase shapes; the colors come from a super thin layer of rust on the surface.
Technetium was the first element made by humans, in 1937, and its name comes from the Greek word for artificial.
Only a handful of atoms of oganesson, the heaviest element ever made, have ever been detected, and each fell apart in about a millisecond.
Radon, a radioactive gas, seeps out of ordinary rocks and soil and can build up in basements, so many homes test for it.
Real neon only glows red-orange; most of the other colors in so-called neon signs come from other gases or coated glass.
Argon makes up nearly 1 percent of every breath you take, more than 20 times the amount of carbon dioxide in air.
Air is about 78 percent nitrogen, a gas so lazy that you breathe it in and out all day without using any of it.
The helium in party balloons was made by radioactive rocks deep underground over millions of years and caught in gas wells.
Helium is so light that once it escapes a balloon it can drift up and leak out of Earth's atmosphere into space for good.
Lithium is the lightest metal: it is so light that it floats on water and even on cooking oil.
A layer of rare iridium found in rocks around the world helped prove that a giant asteroid hit Earth when the dinosaurs died out.
Einsteinium was first discovered in the fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952, and kept secret for years.
Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by a man boiling down huge amounts of urine because he hoped to find gold.
White phosphorus glows in the dark as it slowly reacts with air, which is how the element got a name meaning light-bearer.
Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his 1869 periodic table and correctly predicted elements nobody had discovered yet.
Four elements are named after one tiny Swedish village, Ytterby, whose mine turned up a stream of new elements.
Polonium was named by Marie Curie after her homeland, Poland, at a time when Poland did not exist as a country.
Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive more than a century later and are stored in lead-lined boxes.
The letters J and Q do not appear in any element symbol on the entire periodic table.
Most rocks and beach sand are made mainly of just two elements: oxygen and silicon, the stuff of computer chips.
Aluminium is the most common metal in Earth's crust, yet in the 1800s it was so hard to extract that it cost more than gold.
Napoleon III reportedly served his most honored guests with aluminium cutlery while ordinary guests had to make do with gold.
The tip of the Washington Monument is a small aluminium pyramid, chosen in 1884 when the metal was a costly showpiece.
Helium turns liquid only at about minus 269 degrees C, just 4 degrees above the coldest temperature possible.
Carbon can form millions of different compounds, from sugar to plastic to DNA, more variety than almost any other element.
Iron is the most common element in planet Earth by weight, because the core at the center is mostly iron.
Uranium, neptunium and plutonium sit side by side on the periodic table and were named after Uranus, Neptune and Pluto, in the same order.
Chlorine gas is yellow-green, and its name comes from the Greek word chloros, meaning pale green.
Gently warmed iodine crystals give off a striking violet vapor, and much of the solid can turn straight into gas without melting first.
Bromine gets its name from the Greek word for stench, because its fumes smell so sharp and nasty.
Pure sulfur is a yellow solid with hardly any smell; the rotten egg odor people blame on it comes from a sulfur gas.
Gold is so soft and stretchy that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about one square meter in size.
Gold leaf can be beaten so thin that light shines through it, glowing a surprising blue-green color.
A tonne of old phones holds far more gold than a tonne of gold ore, which is why recycling electronics is nicknamed urban mining.
Titanium is about as strong as many steels but around 45 percent lighter, which is why planes and hip implants use it.
Bone can grow right onto titanium, which is why it is used to anchor artificial teeth and joints inside the body.
Magnesium burns with a blinding white light so bright that early photographers used it as a camera flash.
Burning magnesium cannot be put out with water, because the hot metal steals oxygen from the water and keeps burning.
Neodymium magnets are so strong that two of them snapping together can pinch skin badly or shatter the magnets.
Your phone contains dozens of different elements, including rare earth metals that help it buzz, play sound and light the screen.
Rare earth elements are not actually rare; they are just hardly ever found in rich, easy-to-mine clumps.
Cobalt and nickel are named after goblins and demons that German miners blamed for ores that looked rich but gave no copper.
The sparks from a lighter come from a metal mix rich in cerium that throws off tiny burning shavings when scraped.
Element 113 was the first element discovered in Asia; Japanese scientists named it nihonium, after Nihon, their word for Japan.
Francium is so unstable that no one has ever seen a visible lump of it: any sample would destroy itself with its own heat.
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes; if ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and fish would be in trouble.
Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes, enough force to burst pipes and split solid rock.
Boiling water thrown into very cold air, around minus 30 degrees C, can burst into a cloud of snow as the droplets freeze in mid-air.
Pure water barely conducts electricity; it is the dissolved salts and minerals in everyday water that let current flow.
A single drop of water contains roughly 1.5 sextillion molecules, more than all the grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches combined.
Water molecules are so sticky to each other that a carefully placed paper clip can float on top of a glass of water.
Water can stay liquid well below 0 degrees C if it is very pure and still; a tap on the bottle can make it freeze in seconds.
Ice can be slippery even far below freezing, and scientists are still debating exactly why its surface is so slick.
Scientists have identified around 20 different kinds of ice, most of which only form under enormous pressures.
The water you drink has been cycling around Earth for billions of years, and some of it may be older than the Sun.
Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases that can burn or feed a fire, yet together they make water, which puts fires out.
Heavy water, made with a heavier kind of hydrogen, looks just like normal water, but its ice cubes sink in ordinary water.
At the top of Mount Everest, water boils at only about 70 degrees C, too cool to make a decent cup of tea.
In a pressure cooker, water boils at around 120 degrees C, which is why food cooks so much faster inside one.
Snowflakes are not white because of their ice, which is clear; they look white because their many surfaces scatter all colors of light.
A large lake or ocean looks blue partly because water itself is very faintly blue: it absorbs a little red light.
Hot water can hold far less dissolved gas than cold water, which is why a warm soda goes flat so much faster.
Ice cubes look cloudy in the middle because dissolved air gets pushed inward as the water freezes from the outside in.
