Seawater is salty enough that about 35 grams of salt are dissolved in every liter, roughly two tablespoons.
Vodka does not freeze in a home freezer, because its alcohol pushes its freezing point down to about minus 27 degrees C.
Salt on icy roads works by lowering the freezing point of water, but below about minus 10 degrees C it barely helps.
Spreading salt on ice makes it colder: the melting soaks up heat, which is how old-fashioned ice cream makers work.
Cooking an egg is chemistry you cannot undo: heat unravels its proteins, and they tangle into a solid web.
The browning of toast, steak and roasted coffee is called the Maillard reaction, and it creates hundreds of new flavor molecules.
Caramel is what happens when sugar is heated until its molecules break apart and rebuild into hundreds of new compounds.
Chilling an onion before cutting it slows down the tear-causing gas, so you cry less.
Baking soda makes cakes rise by releasing bubbles of carbon dioxide when it meets acid and heat.
Bread rises because yeast eats sugar and burps out carbon dioxide, which gets trapped in the stretchy dough.
Part of the tingly bite of sparkling water is a sour taste: dissolved carbon dioxide turns into a weak acid on your tongue.
People can detect geosmin, the earthy smell of rain, in water at a few parts per trillion: like a teaspoon in hundreds of Olympic pools.
Freshly cut grass smells the way it does because the injured plant releases chemicals as a kind of distress signal.
Apples and avocados turn brown after cutting because enzymes react with oxygen in the air, a bit like rust on metal.
A squeeze of lemon juice keeps cut apples from browning, because the acid slows down the enzymes that cause it.
Chili peppers feel hot because capsaicin tricks the same nerve sensors in your mouth that detect real heat.
Water does little to calm chili burn, because capsaicin does not dissolve in water; milk and fatty foods work much better.
Birds can eat the hottest chili peppers without feeling a thing, because their heat sensors do not react to capsaicin.
Mint feels cold because menthol switches on the same nerve sensors in your mouth that respond to real cold.
Pop Rocks crackle because each candy piece holds tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide sealed in at high pressure, which burst as the candy melts.
Coffee contains over a thousand different aroma chemicals, and scientists are still working out which matter most.
Decaf coffee is often made by washing beans with carbon dioxide squeezed so hard it acts like a liquid.
Honey almost never spoils: it is so sugary and slightly acidic that germs cannot survive in it.
The sweetener aspartame was discovered in 1965 when a chemist licked his finger to pick up a piece of paper and tasted something sweet.
Table salt is made of sodium, a metal that explodes in water, and chlorine, a poisonous gas.
Sourdough gets its tang from bacteria that make lactic and acetic acids, the same acids found in yogurt and vinegar.
Cheese, yogurt, soy sauce, chocolate and bread all rely on microbes doing chemistry before they reach your plate.
Chocolate melts at around body temperature, which is why it stays solid in the box but melts the moment it touches your tongue.
Chocolate can set in six different crystal forms, and only one of them gives a glossy, snappy bar that melts nicely.
The white film on old chocolate is usually just fat or sugar that crept to the surface, not mold, and is safe to eat.
Dogs should never eat chocolate, because they break down a chemical in it called theobromine far more slowly than people do.
A can of diet soda floats in water while a can of regular soda sinks, because all the sugar dissolved in the regular one makes it heavier.
Ice cream stays soft partly because of the air whipped into it: some brands are nearly half air by volume.
Pickles are preserved by acid, which stops most germs from growing; people have pickled food for thousands of years.
An old egg floats while a fresh one sinks, because moisture slowly escapes through the shell and the air pocket inside grows.
Sugar in jam preserves fruit the same way salt preserves meat: it sucks water out of microbes so they cannot grow.
Black tea turns lighter in color when you squeeze in lemon, because the acid changes some of its natural brown pigments.
Red cabbage juice works as a color-changing acid test: it turns pink in vinegar and green or yellow in baking soda water.
Blueberries can turn greenish in baking because their purple pigment changes color when the batter is not acidic enough.
An overcooked hard-boiled egg gets a greenish ring around its yolk, made where iron from the yolk meets sulfur from the white.
Not everyone can smell the odd scent asparagus gives to urine; the ability depends on a person's genes.
Garlic breath can linger for a day, because a smelly sulfur compound enters your blood and leaves through your lungs.
Cut garlic only gets its strong smell after crushing, when an enzyme turns a scentless chemical into allicin.
Raw kidney beans contain a natural toxin, which is why they must be boiled thoroughly before eating.
Rhubarb leaves contain oxalic acid, which is why people eat the stalks and throw the leaves away.
Nutmeg in large amounts can make people sick, thanks to a chemical called myristicin in the spice.
Bitter almonds contain a substance that the body can turn into cyanide, which is why the sweet kind is what we eat.
Microwaves heat food mainly by making water molecules in it spin back and forth billions of times a second.
Spinach is not the iron powerhouse cartoons suggest: much of its iron is locked up by oxalic acid, so your body absorbs little of it.
Stale bread can be refreshed briefly in a hot oven, which melts the hardened starch crystals back into softness.
Fridges make bread go stale faster, because cool temperatures speed up the starch crystallization.
Searing meat does not seal in juices, but it does create the browned flavor chemicals that make it taste so good.
Salt makes food taste less bitter, which is why a pinch of it can make coffee or grapefruit taste smoother.
You can dissolve about 2 kilograms of sugar in just 1 liter of room-temperature water, and more than twice that in boiling water.
Rock candy is made by letting sugar crystals slowly grow on a string from a super-sweet syrup over about a week.
Cotton candy is just melted sugar flung out through tiny holes, where it cools instantly into fine glassy threads.
Milk is white because its tiny fat droplets and protein clumps scatter all colors of light equally.
Skim milk looks slightly blue because it has fewer fat droplets, so the smaller protein clumps scatter blue light more.
Lactose-free milk tastes sweeter than regular milk, because the milk sugar has been split into two smaller, sweeter sugars.
Egg whites whip into foam because beating unravels their proteins, which then link up around tiny air bubbles.
A copper bowl helps egg whites whip into a stiffer foam, because copper bonds to the proteins and steadies them.
Mayonnaise is oil and water held together by egg yolk, which contains natural molecules that grab both at once.
Soap works because each soap molecule has one end that loves water and another that loves grease, pulling dirt away.
Firework colors come from metals: strontium glows red, barium green, copper blue and sodium a bright yellow.
Blue is the hardest firework color to make, because the copper compounds that glow blue break down if the flame gets too hot.
A candle flame is blue at the bottom and yellow at the top; the yellow glow comes from tiny specks of hot soot.
In space, a candle flame forms a round blue ball, because without gravity hot air does not rise to stretch it upward.
Rusting is a very slow form of burning: iron combines with oxygen, releasing heat too gradually for you to feel.
Hand warmers get hot by rusting iron powder on purpose, speeding up the reaction so fast that you can feel the heat.
A candle's wick barely burns: the flame feeds on melted wax drawn up the wick and turned into vapor by the heat.
Wood itself does not really burn as a solid: heat breaks it down into gases first, and it is those gases that catch fire.
Flour floating in the air as a fine dust can explode, which is why flour mills and grain silos have strict safety rules.
Glow sticks shine because two chemicals mix when you bend the stick, releasing energy as light instead of heat.
Putting a glow stick in the freezer slows its chemical reaction, so it glows dimmer but lasts much longer.
Fireflies make light with almost no wasted heat, using a chemical reaction far more efficient than an old light bulb.
Crime scene investigators spray luminol, which glows blue when it reacts with the iron in traces of blood, even after cleaning.
Copper slowly turns green in the weather: the Statue of Liberty was originally shiny reddish-brown like a new penny.
Silver tarnishes black because it reacts with tiny traces of sulfur in the air, from things like eggs, rubber and pollution.
Tarnished silver can be cleaned in a hot bath of baking soda and aluminium foil, which pulls the sulfur onto the aluminium.
Stainless steel stays shiny because of chromium, which forms an invisible layer that heals itself if scratched.
Aluminium does not rust away like iron because it instantly coats itself in a tough, invisible layer of oxide.
Gold never rusts or tarnishes, which is why gold objects pulled from ancient shipwrecks still shine like new.
Thermite, a famously fierce metal mixture, burns at over 2,000 degrees C and is used to weld railway tracks together.
Some metals can be welded together cold in the vacuum of space, because there is no air to coat their surfaces.
Mercury dissolves gold and silver like sugar in tea, forming soft pastes called amalgams.
Gallium can soak into aluminium and make it as brittle as a cracker, which is why airlines restrict carrying it.
Rubber got its English name in 1770, when chemist Joseph Priestley noticed a lump of it could rub out pencil marks.
Pure gold is so soft you can dent it with your teeth, which is why most jewelry gold is mixed with other metals.
Gold leaf on fancy desserts is safe to eat, because gold is so unreactive that it passes straight through your body untouched.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,400 degrees C, which is why it could glow white-hot inside old light bulbs.
Memory metal, an alloy of nickel and titanium, can be bent out of shape and then springs back when warmed.
Mercury is so dense that a bowling ball or a heavy steel cannonball would float on it.
A bottle of mercury the size of a 2-liter soda bottle would weigh about 27 kilograms.
Mercury was once used to make felt hats, and the poisoning it caused among hat makers may have inspired the phrase mad as a hatter.
Lead was added to petrol for decades to stop engines knocking; it spread lead pollution across the whole planet.
Early matches were made with white phosphorus, which caused a terrible bone disease in match factory workers called phossy jaw.
Safety matches split the dangerous chemistry in two: some on the match head and red phosphorus on the strip of the box.
Gunpowder was invented in China, probably by alchemists searching for an elixir of eternal life.
Alfred Nobel made his fortune from dynamite, which he invented to make nitroglycerin safer to handle; he then created the Nobel Prizes.
Nitroglycerin, the explosive in dynamite, is also used as a heart medicine to widen blood vessels and ease chest pain.
Airbags inflate in about 30 milliseconds, faster than a blink, by a chemical reaction that suddenly releases nitrogen gas.
The Space Shuttle's main engines burned hydrogen and oxygen, so their exhaust was mostly just hot water vapor.
A sparkler can burn at over 1,000 degrees C, hot enough to melt some metals, which is why sparklers cause so many burns.
Old orange street lamps used glowing sodium vapor and gave off almost pure yellow light, which made everything look colorless.
Self-heating cans warm food by mixing water with quicklime, a reaction that gives off a lot of heat.
Instant cold packs work by dissolving a salt in water, a reaction that soaks up heat and makes the pack icy.
Plaster of Paris gets warm as it sets, because water is locking into its crystals and releasing heat.
Concrete keeps getting stronger for years after it is poured, as water slowly reacts with the cement.
Roman concrete in harbor walls has survived 2,000 years of seawater, partly because seawater helps grow new minerals inside it.
Concrete is the most used human-made material on Earth, and only water is used more by people.
Old church windows are often thicker at the bottom, but not because glass slowly flows: they were made uneven and set in heavy side down.
Obsidian is natural volcanic glass, and its edges can be sharper than a steel scalpel; some surgeons have used obsidian blades.
Tough phone screen glass is soaked in a hot salt bath that swaps small atoms in its surface for bigger ones, squeezing it tight.
Bulletproof glass is not one sheet but layers of glass and plastic that spread the force of a bullet out.
Soda cans have a thin plastic lining inside; without it, the acidic drink would slowly eat into the aluminium.
Recycling an aluminium can saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make a new one from ore.
A recycled aluminium can can be back on a store shelf as a new can in about two months.
The fizz in sparkling wine is carbon dioxide made by yeast inside the sealed bottle, which builds up pressure greater than a car tire.
A bottle of champagne releases around a million bubbles if poured into a glass, according to scientists who study them.
Bubbles in champagne mostly start at tiny fibers of cellulose stuck to the glass, often from the towel that dried it.
Bleach and ammonia must never be mixed, because together they release toxic gases.
The smell of a swimming pool is not chlorine itself; it is mostly chemicals formed when chlorine reacts with sweat and urine.
Bleach does not really wash stains away: it breaks apart the colored molecules so they stop absorbing light and become invisible.
Ozone, the gas that protects us from UV rays high in the sky, is a pollutant that hurts your lungs at ground level.
The strongest known acid, fluoroantimonic acid, eats through glass, so chemists have to store it in containers lined with Teflon.
The fresh smell after a thunderstorm is partly ozone, made when lightning splits oxygen molecules in the air.
Every lightning strike splits nitrogen in the air and helps turn it into natural fertilizer that falls with the rain.
About half of the nitrogen atoms in your body were probably pulled out of the air by a factory making fertilizer.
Thieves steal catalytic converters from cars because they hold platinum, palladium and rhodium, metals that at times cost more than gold.
Without enzymes, some reactions in your body would take millions of years; with them, they happen in a split second.
Elephant toothpaste is a classic science show trick: soap traps oxygen from breaking hydrogen peroxide into a giant foam.
Hydrogen peroxide fizzes on a cut because an enzyme in your blood and cells breaks it into water and oxygen bubbles.
Iron in your blood is what makes it red; some animals like octopuses have copper-based blood that is blue.
Crushed cochineal insects have been used for centuries to make a red food dye, still found in some sweets and drinks.
The artificial sweetener saccharin was discovered in 1879 when a chemist forgot to wash his hands and noticed his dinner tasted sweet.
Super glue was discovered by accident while scientists were trying to make clear plastic gun sights; it stuck to everything.
Super glue sets almost instantly because tiny traces of water on surfaces, even humidity in the air, trigger it to harden.
WD-40 stands for Water Displacement, 40th formula: the chemists who created it in 1953 only got it right on their 40th try.
Nylon, the first fully synthetic fiber, was first sold in 1938 as toothbrush bristles, before it became famous as stockings.
Nylon stockings were so popular that when they went on sale in 1940, millions of pairs sold in days, and riots later broke out over shortages.
Kevlar, the fiber in bulletproof vests, was invented by chemist Stephanie Kwolek in 1965 and is five times stronger than steel by weight.
Nitrogen triiodide is so touchy that, once dry, the touch of a feather makes it explode with a loud snap and a puff of purple smoke.
People have run across pools filled with cornstarch and water, because the mix firms up under the sudden force of each step.
Spanish miners in South America once threw platinum away as a worthless nuisance mixed in with their gold; now it is a precious metal.
Post-it Notes came from a failed attempt to make a super strong glue; the weak, reusable glue found its use years later.
Coca-Cola's early recipe contained a small amount of cocaine from coca leaves; it was removed in the early 1900s.
Aspirin comes from a chemical in willow bark, which people chewed for pain relief for thousands of years.
The first anesthetics used in surgery in the 1840s, ether and later chloroform, turned operations from screaming agony into sleep.
Laughing gas, nitrous oxide, was a party amusement in the 1800s before dentists realized it could block pain.
Insulin was first given to a diabetic boy in 1922, turning a death sentence into a manageable condition almost overnight.
Quinine, the bitter taste in tonic water, was used for centuries to treat malaria, and it makes tonic water glow under UV light.
Highlighter ink, white shirts and some teeth glow under black light because they absorb invisible UV light and give off visible light.
Ripe bananas glow faintly blue under ultraviolet light, thanks to chemicals made as their green chlorophyll breaks down.
Before modern bleach, people whitened fabric by laying it out on grass in the sun for weeks.
Some ancient Romans reportedly used urine as a mouthwash, because the ammonia in stale urine helps clean teeth.
Soap has been made for at least 4,000 years, by boiling fats with wood ash, which contains a natural alkali.
Blue jeans come out of the dye bath yellow-green and turn blue before your eyes as the dye reacts with oxygen in the air.
Orange cheddar is not naturally orange: it is dyed with annatto, a seed extract, a habit that began to mimic cheese from rich summer milk.
The vivid green paint once used in Victorian wallpaper contained arsenic, and damp rooms could release toxic fumes.
Ultramarine, a deep blue made from the stone lapis lazuli, was once more expensive than gold, so painters saved it for special robes.
A new blue pigment called YInMn blue was discovered by accident in 2009, the first new inorganic blue in about two centuries.
Vantablack absorbs about 99.96 percent of light, so a crumpled object coated in it looks like a flat black hole.
Carrots were bred to be orange; the orange comes from beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A.
The red in autumn maple leaves is newly made each fall, a pigment that may act like sunscreen for the dying leaf.
Hydrangea flowers can be blue or pink depending on the soil: acidic soil lets them take up aluminium, which turns them blue.
The color of most blue flowers comes from the same family of pigments that makes red cabbage and blueberries colorful.
Lobsters turn red when cooked because heat breaks apart a protein that keeps their red pigment looking blue-grey.
Your blood is always red, never blue; veins only look blue because of how skin absorbs and scatters light.
Gold specks too small to see look ruby red, not gold, which is how glassmakers have made ruby-red glass for centuries.
Rubies and sapphires are the same mineral; a pinch of chromium makes a ruby red, while iron and titanium make sapphire blue.
Emeralds get their green from tiny traces of chromium or vanadium; without them, the same crystal would be colorless.
Diamonds can be blue because of tiny traces of boron, like the famous Hope Diamond.
Diamonds are not forever in air: heat one to around 700 to 900 degrees C and it can slowly burn away to carbon dioxide.
Scientists can now grow real diamonds in a lab in a few weeks, chemically identical to diamonds dug out of the ground.
In theory, diamond slowly turns into graphite at everyday temperatures, but so slowly that no one will ever see a diamond change.
Diamond conducts heat better than copper, which is why a real diamond feels cold when you touch it to your lip.
Vitamin B12 has an atom of the metal cobalt at its heart, making it the only vitamin built around a metal.
Graphene was first isolated in 2004 using sticky tape to peel layers off pencil-like graphite, and it won a Nobel Prize.
Graphene is often said to be about 200 times stronger than steel, yet a sheet of it one meter square would weigh less than a milligram.
Soccer-ball shaped molecules made of 60 carbon atoms, called buckyballs, were discovered in 1985 and later found in space.
Buckyballs are named after Buckminster Fuller, an architect who built domes with the same pattern as their atoms.
Pencil lead has never contained lead; it is graphite and clay, named back when people thought graphite was a kind of lead.
The 'tin' in tin cans is mostly steel with a very thin coating of tin, or often no tin at all today.
Tin foil is now almost always aluminium foil; real tin foil left food tasting faintly of tin.
US pennies made since 1982 are about 97.5 percent zinc under a thin copper skin, and in 2025 the US stopped making pennies altogether.
Rub a dull copper coin with ketchup and it turns shiny within minutes, as the vinegar and salt in it strip away the dark coating.
The grooves on the edges of some coins were added to stop people from shaving off precious metal.
The Olympic gold medal is mostly silver, coated with at least 6 grams of real gold.
Two of the chemicals that make rotting meat smell so awful are really named putrescine and cadaverine.
The smell added to natural gas is so strong that people can notice it at less than one part per billion in air.
Skunk spray gets its awful stink from sulfur compounds called thiols, close cousins of the smell added to cooking gas.
In 1889 a chemistry experiment in Freiburg, Germany, released a smell so foul that people across part of the town fainted or were sick.
At high levels hydrogen sulfide is deadly, and it is extra dangerous because it soon numbs your sense of smell.
The bitterest chemical known, denatonium, is added to some antifreeze and nail-biting polish so that people spit them out at once.
Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it sticks to your blood about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does.
Durian, the stinkiest fruit, owes its smell of onions and old socks to dozens of different sulfur compounds.
The new car smell is a cocktail of chemicals drifting out of the plastics, glues and fabrics inside the car.
Old books can smell faintly of vanilla because aging paper releases vanillin, the same molecule that flavors vanilla.
Most vanilla flavoring is made in factories, sometimes from wood pulp leftovers, because real vanilla is so costly.
A tiny change to a molecule can change its smell completely: one form of carvone smells of spearmint and its mirror image of caraway.
Your nose can tell apart a huge number of smells; one study estimated over a trillion, though that number has been disputed.
Sweat itself has almost no smell; body odor comes from bacteria on your skin breaking it down into smelly chemicals.
Morning breath comes mainly from sulfur gases made by bacteria in your mouth while saliva flow slows during sleep.
Farts are mostly odorless gases; the smell comes from tiny traces of sulfur compounds, often less than 1 percent.
Your stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve some metals, but a thick layer of mucus keeps it from digesting your stomach.
Your stomach lining replaces itself every few days, partly to keep up with the acid inside.
Thaumatin, a protein from a West African fruit, is about 2,000 times sweeter than sugar, so a tiny pinch goes a very long way.
Fluoride in toothpaste strengthens teeth by swapping into the enamel's crystals and making them tougher against acid.
Pure capsaicin, the fire in chili peppers, is so strong that it would still taste hot mixed into a million times its weight of sugar water.
Your body makes its own vitamin D from sunshine: UV light hitting your skin triggers the chemical reaction.
Humans, guinea pigs and some bats are among the few animals that cannot make their own vitamin C.
Sailors on long voyages got scurvy because they lacked vitamin C; British sailors were nicknamed limeys for the citrus they carried.
Your body is constantly replacing its atoms: most of the atoms in you now were not part of you a few years ago.
A glass of water holds more molecules than there are glasses of water in all the world's oceans.
A human hair is roughly half a million atoms wide, which shows just how unimaginably small atoms are.
The full chemical name of titin, a giant protein in your muscles, would run to about 190,000 letters and take hours to read aloud.
The hydrogen in your body was made in the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago.
Most of the carbon, oxygen and nitrogen in your body were made inside stars that exploded long before the Sun formed.
Iron is where stars hit a dead end: fusing it uses up energy instead of releasing it, so its build-up helps trigger giant stars to explode.
A huge cloud of alcohol floats in space near the center of the Milky Way, with enough to fill billions upon billions of glasses.
As of 2024, more than 300 different molecules had been detected in space, including a simple sugar and other building blocks of life.
It may rain diamonds deep inside Neptune and Uranus, where crushing pressure squeezes carbon into crystals.
Venus is covered in clouds of sulfuric acid, and its surface is hot enough to melt lead.
The Moon's dust smells like spent gunpowder, according to Apollo astronauts who tracked it into their cabin.
Glenn Seaborg was the first person to have an element named after him while still alive: seaborgium, named in 1997.
In 1980, scientists turned a tiny amount of bismuth into gold using a particle accelerator, at a cost far greater than the gold itself.
Your own body is mildly radioactive too: thousands of potassium and carbon atoms inside you decay every second.
The original 7 Up soft drink contained lithium, the same element later used in mood medicine, until it was taken out in 1948.
Carbon dating can only date things up to about 50,000 years old; after that, too little radioactive carbon is left to measure.
Brazil nuts are among the most radioactive foods, because their trees soak up radium from the soil.
Uranium glass, popular in the early 1900s, glows bright green under UV light because it contains a little uranium.
Radium paint was once used on glowing watch dials, and many workers who licked their brushes to a fine point later fell ill.
A lump of plutonium feels warm to the touch, heated from inside by its own radioactive decay.
NASA's deep space probes like Voyager are powered by the heat of decaying plutonium, still working decades after launch.
Oxygen did not exist in Earth's air for its first 2 billion years; tiny ocean microbes slowly filled the sky with it.
When microbes first filled the air with oxygen, it was poison to most life on Earth at the time.
About half of the oxygen you breathe was made by tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton.
The air in a 1 liter bottle weighs about a gram, and the air in a typical living room weighs as much as an adult person.
Air presses on your body with a force of well over 10 tonnes, but you never feel it because it pushes from every side, inside and out.
Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, and it never melts into a liquid: it turns straight into a gas at minus 78 degrees C.
Dry ice turns straight into gas, so a chunk sealed inside a bottle can build up enough pressure to burst it violently.
The fog from dry ice in water is not carbon dioxide; it is tiny droplets of water condensed by the bitterly cold gas.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water, a strange puzzle called the Mpemba effect that scientists still argue about.
The same vapor cushion lets a water droplet dance on a very hot pan instead of boiling away at once.
Cooks use liquid nitrogen to make ice cream in seconds; freezing so fast keeps the ice crystals tiny and the texture smooth.
Sulfur hexafluoride is so heavy that it makes your voice sound deep, and you can float a foil boat on an invisible pool of it.
Krypton is a real gas, discovered in 1898, decades before Superman's home planet borrowed its name.
Old-style light bulbs were filled with argon or nitrogen, because in ordinary air the glowing filament would burn up almost at once.
Laughing gas, nitrous oxide, is also used to make whipped cream fluffy and to give racing cars a burst of power.
Methane from cow burps is a major source of greenhouse gas; one cow can belch out roughly 100 kilograms of methane a year.
Methane is about 80 times stronger at trapping heat than carbon dioxide over its first 20 years in the air.
Fire spreads terrifyingly fast in pure oxygen; a fire in a capsule filled with it killed the three Apollo 1 astronauts during a 1967 test.
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, but on Earth it is almost all locked up in water.
Hydrogen burns with an almost invisible pale blue flame, which makes hydrogen fires hard to see in daylight.
The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen because the US would not sell Germany enough helium.
Aerogel is so light it is often called frozen smoke: it is mostly air, yet a small block can hold up a brick.
NASA used aerogel to catch comet dust in space, trapping the speeding grains like flies in a blanket of frozen smoke.
Mussels stick to wet rocks with a natural glue so strong that scientists are copying it to make surgical glues.
Geckos climb walls with no glue at all: billions of tiny hairs on their feet cling to surfaces with weak electric attractions.
Fireflies, glowing mushrooms and deep sea fish all make cold light the same basic way, using chemicals called luciferins.
Ants spray formic acid to defend themselves, and the acid's name comes from formica, the Latin word for ant.
Nettles sting because their tiny brittle hairs act like needles, injecting irritating chemicals such as histamine into your skin.
Bees and wasps both sting, but their venoms are different chemical mixtures, so old remedies of vinegar or baking soda do little.
Cats go wild for catnip because of nepetalactone, a chemical in the plant that may also help keep mosquitoes away.
Plants talk in chemicals: some attacked by caterpillars release scents that call in wasps to eat the caterpillars.
A giant sequoia gets almost all of its huge mass from thin air: the carbon comes from carbon dioxide, not the soil.
Chlorophyll, the green pigment in plants, has a structure remarkably similar to the heme that makes your blood red.
Cyanide is found naturally in small amounts in cassava, a staple food for many people, which must be carefully prepared.
The bitter taste is a warning system: many poisonous plant chemicals taste bitter, and humans evolved to dislike them.
Artificial sweetener sucralose is about 600 times sweeter than sugar, so a tiny pinch replaces a whole spoonful.
Table salt is a rock, the mineral halite, and it is one of the very few rocks that people sprinkle straight onto their food.
Salt was so valuable in ancient times that it was traded like money and used to pay workers in some places.
The Dead Sea is so salty, almost ten times saltier than the ocean, that people float on it effortlessly without swimming.
Himalayan pink salt gets its rosy color from tiny traces of iron and other minerals, but it is still almost all ordinary salt.
Sea salt and table salt are chemically almost the same; most of the difference is the size of the crystals.
A pinch of baking soda in the cooking water keeps green vegetables bright green, but it also turns them mushy.
Adding iodine to salt is one of the cheapest health measures in history and helped raise children's IQ in many countries.
Wasabi's burn shoots up your nose instead of staying on your tongue, because its fiery chemical floats off as a vapor.
Brown sugar is mostly white sugar with a bit of molasses added back, which also keeps it soft and moist.
Caffeine is a natural insecticide that plants make to paralyze and kill insects that try to eat them.
Caffeine blocks a chemical in your brain that builds up while you are awake and makes you feel sleepy.
A cup of coffee usually has more caffeine than a cup of tea, but tea leaves contain more caffeine than coffee beans by weight.
Dark roast coffee does not have more caffeine than light roast; the longer roasting actually breaks a little of it down.
Green tea and black tea come from the same plant; black tea is made by letting the leaves react with air before drying.
Mixing baking soda and vinegar mostly cancels them out: once the fizz is over, you are left with little more than salty water.
Vinegar dissolves kettle scale because the acid reacts with the chalky crust, the same mineral that makes up chalk and seashells.
An egg soaked in vinegar for a day or two loses its shell, leaving a bouncy, rubbery egg held together by its skin.
A chicken bone soaked in vinegar for a few days becomes so bendy you can tie it in a knot, because the acid removes its minerals.
The streaks that run down the inside of a wine glass, called legs or tears, come from alcohol evaporating faster than water, not from quality.
The white cliffs of Dover are made of the skeletons of trillions of tiny sea creatures that lived millions of years ago.
Stalactites in caves grow as dripping water leaves behind minerals, often only about a centimeter every century or so.
Acid rain slowly dissolves marble statues and limestone buildings, wearing away details carved centuries ago.
Lemon juice is more acidic than most sodas, and stomach acid is more acidic than both.
The acid scale works in steps of ten, so lemon juice is roughly a hundred times more acidic than tomato juice.
Lime juice on your skin in strong sunlight can cause painful burns and dark blotches, because chemicals in it react to UV light.
Biting aluminium foil with a metal filling can give a sharp zap of pain, because the foil, filling and saliva make a tiny battery.
Lead's symbol Pb comes from plumbum, its Latin name, which also gave us the word plumber: Roman water pipes were made of lead.
The inventors of the lithium-ion battery won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; John Goodenough, at 97, became the oldest Nobel winner ever.
Steel wool burns with showers of sparks, and simply touching it to both ends of a 9-volt battery can set it alight.
Rust needs both water and oxygen; iron in a dry desert or a sealed airless jar can last for centuries.
The Iron Pillar of Delhi has stood for about 1,600 years with very little rust, thanks to a protective layer formed by its phosphorus.
Bend a bar of pure tin and it gives off a faint crackling sound, called tin cry, as the crystals inside it slip past each other.
Ships have blocks of zinc bolted to their hulls that slowly dissolve in seawater instead of the steel.
Gold is so unreactive that it is found in nature as pure nuggets, which is why it was one of the first metals people used.
The largest gold nugget ever found, the Welcome Stranger in Australia in 1869, weighed about 70 kilograms.
Silver kills bacteria, which is why it is used in some bandages and why people once dropped silver coins into milk to keep it fresh.
Drinking silver for years can turn skin permanently blue-grey, a rare condition called argyria.
Copper pipes can turn blonde hair greenish, because copper in the water binds to the hair, not because of the pool chlorine itself.
Left in the cold for a long time, pure tin can slowly crumble into grey powder, a decay known as tin pest.
Early refrigerators used toxic gases like ammonia, and leaks killed people, which pushed inventors to find safer coolants.
Fritz Haber, who won a Nobel Prize for making fertilizer from air, spent years in the 1920s trying to pay Germany's war debts with gold from seawater, and failed.
A single chlorine atom released from old spray cans can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules high in the sky.
Thomas Midgley invented both leaded petrol and ozone-destroying fridge gases, two of the most harmful inventions in history.
Jello wobbles because gelatin proteins form a tangled net that traps water, making a solid that is mostly liquid.
Fresh pineapple can stop Jello from setting, because an enzyme in it chops up the gelatin proteins; canned pineapple is fine.
Meat tenderizer powder is often made from papaya or pineapple enzymes that break down tough proteins.
A spoonful of soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth, all busy doing chemistry.
Compost heaps can reach about 60 degrees C or more in the middle, heated entirely by microbes breaking down waste.
Large haystacks can catch fire by themselves when microbes inside generate enough heat.
Oily rags left in a pile can burst into flames on their own as the oil reacts with air and the heat builds up.
Perfumes change over the day: the light molecules you smell first evaporate within minutes, while heavy base notes can linger for hours.
Oil paintings can take decades to fully harden, as the oil keeps reacting with the air long after it feels dry.
Antoine Lavoisier, the father of modern chemistry, was executed by guillotine during the French Revolution in 1794.
Green patches on potatoes are harmless chlorophyll, but they are a warning sign of a bitter natural poison called solanine building up too.
Lavoisier named both oxygen and hydrogen; hydrogen means water-maker, because burning it produces water.
Several chemists were badly hurt or killed trying to isolate fluorine; Henri Moissan finally did it in 1886 and later won a Nobel Prize.
Humphry Davy was so delighted when he first made potassium that he reportedly danced around his lab in excitement.
Robert Bunsen did not invent the Bunsen burner alone, but he used its clean flame to discover two new elements, cesium and rubidium.
Cesium was named after the Latin for sky blue, because of the bright blue lines it shows when its light is split into colors.
Robert Bunsen, of the Bunsen burner, lost the sight in one eye when an arsenic compound he was studying exploded.
Carl Scheele discovered oxygen, chlorine and several other substances, and may have been killed by his habit of tasting chemicals.
Linus Pauling won two unshared Nobel Prizes, one for chemistry and one for peace, a feat no one else has matched.
In the 1920s some people drank radium water as a health tonic, until a famous fan of it died of radium poisoning in 1932.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photo of DNA, Photo 51, gave crucial clues to its double helix shape.
Your DNA, if stretched out from all your cells and laid end to end, would reach to the Sun and back many times.
DNA is surprisingly tough: scientists have read genetic material from mammoth remains more than a million years old.
The whole recipe for a human is written with just four chemical letters in DNA, repeated about 3 billion times per set.
Perfumes often contain musk molecules that once came from deer glands but are now almost all made in labs.
The smell of banana sweets comes mostly from one simple chemical, isoamyl acetate, which honeybees also release as an alarm signal.
Some transition glasses darken in sunlight because molecules in the lens change shape when hit by UV light, then relax indoors.
Self-cleaning glass has a thin coating that uses sunlight to break down dirt, which the rain then washes away.
Hair turns grey partly because cells start making hydrogen peroxide, which bleaches hair from the inside.
Permanent waves work by breaking the sulfur bridges in hair and rebuilding them while the hair is wrapped around curlers.
Burning hair smells so bad because it is full of sulfur-rich protein, which releases smelly gases in a flame.
Polystyrene foam cups are about 95 percent air, which is why they are so light and keep drinks warm.
Teflon is so slippery that almost nothing sticks to it, which raised the question of how it sticks to the pan; the pan is roughened first.
Plastic bags were invented in Sweden in the 1960s, partly in the hope of saving trees used to make paper bags.
A plastic bottle can take hundreds of years to break down, crumbling into ever smaller pieces called microplastics.
Microplastics have been found almost everywhere scientists look, from deep ocean trenches to fresh Arctic snow.
Chocolate and peanut butter help remove gum from hair, because the oils loosen the gum's grip.
Squeezing orange peel next to a balloon can pop it, because an oil in the peel called limonene dissolves the rubber.
In early ancient Egypt silver was rarer than gold, and for a time it was valued more highly.
Glass was being made in Mesopotamia about 4,500 years ago, starting with tiny beads before cups and windows.
Pyrex-type glass can take sudden heat because added boron makes it expand much less than ordinary glass.
Fiber optic glass is so clear that light can travel through many kilometers of it, while window glass turns green in just a meter or so.
Thick window glass looks green at the edge because of tiny traces of iron in the sand used to make it.
Mirrors were once backed with tin and mercury; today a thin layer of silver or aluminium does the reflecting.
Lead crystal glass sparkles more because the lead bends light more strongly, but it is no longer advised for storing drinks.
Smelling salts work by releasing ammonia, which stings the inside of your nose so much that it makes you take a sudden breath.
Glow-in-the-dark stickers soak up light and release it slowly for hours; the brightest ones use a powder called strontium aluminate.
The Nobel Prize winning blue LED was so hard to make that it took until the 1990s, decades after red and green ones.
Sapphire crystal used on some watch faces is lab-grown and so hard that only diamond can easily scratch it.
Rust is not a single substance but a messy mix of iron compounds, which is why it can be orange, red, brown or black.
Iron in breakfast cereal is real metal powder; crush fortified cereal in water and a strong magnet can pick out tiny flakes.
Cast iron pans add small amounts of iron to food, especially to acidic dishes like tomato sauce cooked for a long time.
Tear gas is not really a gas: it is usually a fine powder or mist of tiny droplets that stings the eyes, nose and throat.
Activated charcoal has so many tiny holes that a single gram can have a surface area larger than a tennis court.
Silica gel packets in shoe boxes are not poisonous; they are just very porous sand-like beads that soak up moisture.
Baby diapers can absorb hundreds of times their weight in water, thanks to a powder that swells into a jelly.
Instant snow for decorations uses the same super-absorbent powder as diapers, swelling into fluffy flakes with water.
A popular slime toy is just glue and a borax solution, which links long glue molecules together like a net.
Reusable click hand warmers hold a supercooled liquid; snapping the metal disc inside makes it crystallize at once and give off heat.
Newspapers yellow quickly in sunlight because the cheap wood pulp contains lignin, which reacts with light and air.
Old photographs were developed with silver: the dark parts of a black-and-white photo are tiny grains of silver metal.
Photography once used so much silver that film companies were among the world's biggest users of the metal.
Invisible ink made from lemon juice appears when gently heated, because the juice browns faster than the paper around it.
The fizz of a bath bomb is the same reaction as baking soda meeting vinegar, using a dry powdered acid instead.
Sodium bicarbonate, plain baking soda, can be used to put out small grease fires because heat makes it release carbon dioxide.
Never throw water on a pan of burning oil: the water sinks, flashes into steam and blasts burning oil everywhere.
Toasted marshmallows brown thanks to sugar caramelizing on the outside while the inside turns into molten foam.
Instant noodles are often fried before drying, which leaves tiny holes that let them soften in just a few minutes.
Freeze-dried food is frozen and then put in a vacuum, where ice turns straight into vapor, leaving food light and crisp.
The tiny white crystals sometimes found in wine are harmless tartrate crystals, sometimes called wine diamonds.
Aged cheeses like parmesan have crunchy white crystals, which are clumps of an amino acid, not salt.
@inventions|Inventions
The microwave oven was invented after engineer Percy Spencer stood next to a radar part and noticed the candy bar in his pocket had melted.
The first microwave oven, sold in 1947, stood almost as tall as a man and weighed about as much as a grand piano.
Post-it Notes began as a failure: a 3M chemist made a glue so weak it barely stuck, and it sat unused for years until a colleague needed bookmarks that would not fall out.
Velcro was inspired by the prickly burrs that kept sticking to a Swiss engineer's dog after walks in the Alps.
Teflon, the non-stick coating on frying pans, was discovered by accident in 1938 when a chemist opened a gas tank and found slippery white powder instead.
Superglue was discovered by accident during World War II and thrown aside as useless, because it stuck to absolutely everything it touched.
Play-Doh was first sold as a putty for cleaning soot off wallpaper, and only became a children's toy when coal fires went out of fashion.
The Slinky was invented after a naval engineer watched a spring fall off a shelf and keep "walking" across the floor.
Bubble wrap was originally invented as a trendy textured wallpaper. Nobody bought it for walls, so it ended up protecting packages instead.
One of the first implantable pacemakers exists because inventor Wilson Greatbatch grabbed the wrong part, and his circuit started pulsing like a heartbeat.
The very first medical X-ray photo, taken in 1895, showed the bones of the inventor's wife's hand, wedding ring and all. She reportedly said she had seen her own death.
Corn flakes were discovered when the Kellogg brothers left a batch of cooked grain sitting out, then rolled it anyway and got flakes.
The safety pin was invented in 1849 by a man who sold the patent for 400 dollars just to pay off a 15-dollar debt.
The word zipper was first a brand name for rubber boots with zip fasteners, sold by tire maker B.F. Goodrich in the 1920s.
Before rubber erasers, people rubbed out pencil mistakes with balls of soft bread.
One of the first mass-produced toothbrushes was invented in an English prison around 1770, using a bone from dinner and some bristles.
The queen's godson Sir John Harington built a flushing toilet for Queen Elizabeth I in 1596, about 300 years before flush toilets became common.
Packaged toilet paper was first sold in the United States in 1857, and each sheet was printed with the inventor's name.
The Band-Aid was invented in 1920 by a man whose wife kept cutting her fingers in the kitchen, so he stuck gauze to tape for her.
Kleenex tissues were first sold as a way to wipe off cold cream makeup. Customers started blowing their noses on them instead.
Escalator was once a brand name owned by the Otis elevator company, but it became such a common word that Otis lost the trademark in 1950.
To prove elevators were safe, Elisha Otis rode a platform high above a crowd in 1854 and had the only rope cut. His safety brake caught him.
When the shopping cart was invented in 1937, shoppers refused to use it, so the inventor hired people to push carts around his store as if they loved them.
The first product ever scanned with a barcode at a store checkout was a pack of chewing gum, in Ohio in 1974.
The barcode was inspired by Morse code: its inventor drew dots and dashes in the sand on a beach, then stretched them down into thin and thick lines.
The world's first traffic light was installed in London in 1868. It ran on gas, and within weeks it exploded and injured the policeman operating it.
The first parking meters were installed in Oklahoma City in 1935, and angry drivers tried to have them banned.
Windshield wipers were invented by a woman, Mary Anderson, after she watched a streetcar driver struggle to see through the snow in 1902.
Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin invented the modern three-point seat belt in 1959, and Volvo gave the design away free so every carmaker could use it.
The first long car trip in history was taken in 1888 by Bertha Benz, who drove about 100 kilometers without telling her husband and bought fuel at a pharmacy.
Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut the time to build a car chassis from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
The Model T was not always black. Early ones came in colors like red, green and grey, and black was the only choice just from 1914 to 1925.
The first person caught speeding was fined in England in 1896, for driving at about 8 miles per hour in a 2 mile per hour zone.
Around the year 1900, roughly a third of cars on American roads were electric, quieter and cleaner than the gasoline ones.
The first car to break 100 kilometers per hour, in 1899, was an electric car shaped like a torpedo.
The air-filled tire was patented in 1845, then forgotten for over 40 years until a Scottish vet reinvented it for his son's tricycle.
The first bicycle, built in 1817, had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet.
The first train passenger killed in a railway accident was a member of Parliament, struck by a locomotive at the line's grand opening in 1830.
The time zones we use today exist because of trains: railways needed one shared time so passengers would stop missing them.
On a single day in 1883, American railroads reset their clocks to new time zones, and many towns had to live through noon twice.
Japan's bullet trains have run since 1964 and carried billions of passengers without a single passenger death from a crash or derailment.
A French high-speed train hit about 575 kilometers per hour in 2007, roughly twice the speed a jumbo jet needs to take off.
A Japanese magnetic levitation train reached about 603 kilometers per hour in 2015, floating above its track without touching it.
The steam locomotive Mallard hit 126 miles per hour in 1938, and no steam engine has officially gone faster since.
The Union Pacific Big Boy steam locomotives weighed about 1.2 million pounds, roughly as much as three blue whales.
The Channel Tunnel was dug from both England and France at once, and the two sides met under the sea less than 40 centimeters out of line.
The Brooklyn Bridge was finished by Emily Roebling, who learned engineering to carry messages after her husband, the chief engineer, fell too ill to leave his room.
The Golden Gate Bridge's famous orange color was first just the primer paint. The architect liked it, and the U.S. Navy's idea of black and yellow stripes was dropped.
A safety net under the Golden Gate Bridge during construction caught 19 workers, who called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club.
The Eiffel Tower was the tallest structure humans had ever built for 41 years, until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930.
The Statue of Liberty's copper skin is only about as thick as two pennies stacked together.
The Empire State Building went up in about 410 days, with workers adding as many as four floors in a single week.
The spire on top of the Empire State Building was designed as a parking spot for airships, but the winds made docking far too dangerous.
If Hoover Dam's concrete had been poured in one go, it would have taken about 125 years to cool. Builders ran cold water pipes through it instead.
Hoover Dam holds enough concrete to pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York.
In 1928 a man swam the whole Panama Canal and was charged a toll by his weight: 36 cents.
In 2021 one giant container ship, the Ever Given, got stuck sideways in the Suez Canal for six days, blocking a route that carries about 12 percent of world trade.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, has no locks at all, because the Mediterranean and Red Sea are almost at the same level.
The Wright brothers' first flight in 1903 lasted 12 seconds and covered about 37 meters, shorter than the wingspan of a jumbo jet.
Only 66 years passed between the Wright brothers' first 12-second flight and humans walking on the Moon.
Neil Armstrong carried a scrap of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 airplane with him to the Moon.
Before building the first airplane, the Wright brothers made their living fixing and selling bicycles.
The world's first scheduled airline, in Florida in 1914, carried one passenger at a time across a bay in about 23 minutes.
On Concorde, you could leave London and land in New York earlier, by the clock, than when you took off.
Concorde flew so fast that air friction heated its skin and stretched the whole plane several inches longer in flight.
Airplane black box flight recorders are not black at all. They are painted bright orange so searchers can find them in wreckage.
A Boeing 747 is made of roughly 6 million parts, and about half of them are fasteners like rivets and bolts.
The heaviest plane ever built, the Antonov An-225, was one of a kind: only one was finished, and it was destroyed in 2022.
Airplane windows have rounded corners because early jetliners with square windows suffered cracks that started at the corners.
That tiny hole in an airplane window is on purpose: it lets air pressure even out between the window panes so the outer pane takes the strain.
At cruising height, airplane food tastes blander, because dry, low-pressure cabin air dulls our sense of salty and sweet.
The first passengers in a hot air balloon, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. All three survived.
Humans first flew in 1783, in a paper-and-cloth hot air balloon over Paris, 120 years before the first airplane.
The jet engine was invented twice at almost the same time, by Frank Whittle in England and Hans von Ohain in Germany, who knew nothing of each other's work.
Passenger jet tires are filled with nitrogen instead of plain air, partly because it is less likely to feed a fire if a tire overheats.
Shipping containers changed the world: in 1956 they cut the cost of loading a ship from almost 6 dollars a tonne to about 16 cents.
As of 2024, the biggest container ships carry about 24,000 containers, which would make a line about 140 kilometers long.
The longest ship ever built, the supertanker Seawise Giant, was longer than the Empire State Building is tall.
A lighthouse lens invented in 1822 by Augustin Fresnel uses rings of glass to make one lamp visible from more than 30 kilometers away.
The hovercraft was first tested by its inventor using two tin cans, one inside the other, and an air blower.
In 1959, just weeks after it was shown to the public, a hovercraft crossed the English Channel.
Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge grew about a meter longer during construction when the 1995 Kobe earthquake moved its towers apart.
The tallest tower of France's Millau Viaduct bridge rises about 343 meters, taller than the Eiffel Tower.
As of 2024, the world's longest bridge is a railway viaduct in China that runs about 164 kilometers, well over an hour's drive at highway speed.
In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted in the wind like a ribbon until it collapsed. The only death was a dog named Tubby.
In 1968, London Bridge was sold to an American businessman, taken apart stone by stone and rebuilt in the Arizona desert.
In 1952 a London bus driver found Tower Bridge opening beneath him and jumped his double-decker across the gap.
Roman concrete contains tiny lumps of lime that can react with rainwater and seal cracks, one reason Roman harbors have survived about 2,000 years.
The Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye. Even from low orbit, astronauts say it is very hard to spot.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years.
The Great Pyramid is built from roughly 2.3 million stone blocks, many heavier than a car.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa started tilting before it was finished. Builders spent about 200 years on it and made the upper floors slightly curved to compensate.
Engineers between 1990 and 2001 pulled the Leaning Tower of Pisa back by about 40 centimeters, without making it stand straight.
The Sydney Opera House roof is covered in about a million tiles, and the building came in 10 years late and over 14 times its budget.
Inside Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a giant steel ball weighing about 660 tonnes, which sways to cancel out the building's motion in typhoons.
The first skyscraper, built in Chicago in 1885, had only 10 floors. Its secret was a steel and iron frame instead of thick walls.
When the first tunnel under a river opened in London in 1843, about 50,000 people paid a penny to walk through it on day one.
Thomas Edison's first power station, opened in New York in 1882, started out lighting about 400 lamps for just 82 customers.
The word volt comes from Alessandro Volta, who built the first true battery in 1800 out of stacked metal discs and salty cardboard.
The first practical solar cell was shown off in 1954, powering a toy Ferris wheel and a radio.
The first electricity from nuclear power, in Idaho in 1951, lit up just four light bulbs.
In 1878 an English country house called Cragside became the first home lit by electricity from water power.
Thomas Edison's team tested thousands of materials for light bulb filaments. One that worked well was carbonized bamboo, which glowed for over 1,000 hours.
Edison did not invent the light bulb alone. In England, Joseph Swan had a working bulb too, and the two later joined forces in a company called Ediswan.
A light bulb in a California fire station has been glowing almost nonstop since 1901.
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod, bifocal glasses and a better wood stove, and never patented any of them.
Until 2019, the world's official kilogram was a single metal cylinder locked in a vault near Paris. Every scale on Earth traced back to it.
The official kilogram cylinder in Paris slowly drifted away from its copies by about the weight of an eyelash, which is why scientists replaced it.
The pendulum clock, invented in 1656, made clocks about 60 times more accurate almost overnight, from minutes of error a day to seconds.
In 1761 John Harrison's sea clock lost only about 5 seconds on an 81-day voyage to Jamaica, solving how sailors could tell where they were.
Clock hands go clockwise because they copied sundials, whose shadows sweep that way in the Northern Hemisphere.
Many clock faces show the number 4 as IIII instead of IV, a tradition clockmakers have kept for centuries.
Big Ben's clock is fine-tuned with old pennies: adding one to its pendulum makes the clock gain about two-fifths of a second a day.
The quartz crystal in a watch vibrates exactly 32,768 times every second, and the watch counts those wiggles to keep time.
Anders Celsius's original scale was upside down: water boiled at 0 and froze at 100. It was flipped after his death.
In medieval England, an inch was legally defined as three grains of barley laid end to end.
James Watt invented the word horsepower to sell his steam engines, by comparing them to the horses they would replace.
James Watt did not invent the steam engine. He made an existing one far more efficient by adding a separate chamber to cool the steam.
About 2,000 years ago, Hero of Alexandria built a spinning steam engine, plus a coin-operated machine that dispensed holy water.
Leonardo da Vinci sketched designs for a flying machine with a spiral rotor, more than 400 years before the first working helicopter.
The single-rotor helicopter design still used today first flew in 1939, built by Igor Sikorsky, who had dreamed of it since reading Jules Verne as a boy.
The tin can was invented around 1810, but a proper can opener did not appear until about 45 years later. Until then people used a hammer and chisel.
France offered a big cash prize for a way to keep army food from spoiling. The winner, in 1810, sealed food in glass jars and boiled them.
Eyeglasses were invented in Italy around 1286, which means people have been wearing glasses for more than 700 years.
The lawn mower was invented in 1830 by an Englishman inspired by a machine that trimmed the fuzz off cloth in a textile mill.
One of the first vacuum cleaners, in 1901, was so big it was pulled by horses and parked outside, with long hoses fed in through the windows.
The dishwasher was invented in 1886 by a wealthy woman, Josephine Cochrane, who was fed up with her servants chipping her fine china.
Before refrigerators, ice was cut from frozen lakes in New England and shipped in sawdust as far as India.
Air conditioning was invented in 1902 not for people but for a printing plant, where humid air made the paper wrinkle.
The first words ever spoken by telephone, in 1876, were Alexander Graham Bell calling his assistant from the next room: Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.
The oldest known recording of a human voice was made in 1860, but it could not be played back until scientists turned it into sound in 2008.
Thomas Edison's first sound recording, made in 1877, was him reciting Mary Had a Little Lamb.
In 1901 Guglielmo Marconi received the first radio signal sent across the Atlantic: three short beeps, the letter S in Morse code.
Philo Farnsworth said the idea for electronic television came to him at 14, while plowing a potato field in straight rows, line by line.
The first photo of a human being, from 1838, shows a man getting his shoes shined on a Paris street. Everyone else moved too fast to show up.
Early Kodak owners mailed the entire camera back to the factory, which developed the photos and returned it loaded with fresh film.
The lighter was invented before the match: a hydrogen-powered lighter appeared in 1823, a few years before the friction match.
The ballpoint pen was invented by a Hungarian journalist who noticed that newspaper ink dried fast and wanted a pen that would not smudge.
A Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible arrangements, and its own inventor needed about a month to solve it the first time.
The Frisbee got its name from the Frisbie Pie Company, whose empty pie tins college students loved tossing to each other.
Monopoly is based on an earlier game invented by Lizzie Magie in 1904, which was meant to show how unfair land monopolies are.
Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago. It reached Europe more than 1,000 years later.
Only about 49 copies of the Gutenberg Bible, one of the first books printed in Europe, are known to survive today.
The potter's wheel came before the wheel on carts: people were spinning clay for centuries before they thought to roll on wheels.
One of the oldest wooden wheels ever found was dug out of a marsh in Slovenia and is about 5,000 years old.
Ancient Mexican cultures made little wheeled toy animals but never used wheels for carts, partly because they had no animals to pull them.
Duct tape was invented in World War II by a factory worker, Vesta Stoudt, who wanted a waterproof tape that soldiers could tear by hand.
WD-40 gets its name from its lab notebook: Water Displacement, 40th formula. The first 39 tries did not work.
Bubble gum is pink because, when an accountant invented it in 1928, pink was the only food coloring he had on hand.
Sliced bread first went on sale in 1928. The U.S. government briefly banned it in 1943 to save wartime resources, and people were furious.
The cash register was invented by a saloon owner in 1879 to stop his bartenders from pocketing money.
The first cash machine opened in London in 1967. Its inventor shortened the PIN to four digits because his wife said six was too many to remember.
The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by a doctor too embarrassed to press his ear to a patient's chest, so he rolled up a sheet of paper instead.
Blue jeans got their copper rivets in 1873 because a tailor's customer kept ripping the pockets of his work trousers.
One of the earliest plastics was developed partly to replace ivory in billiard balls, as elephants were being hunted to make them.
When nylon stockings came back after World War II, shoppers lined up by the thousands and fights broke out in what were called nylon riots.
The chocolate chip cookie was created around 1938 by Ruth Wakefield of the Toll House Inn, who reportedly let Nestle use her recipe for a lifetime supply of chocolate.
In the 1750s, so few men carried umbrellas in London that Jonas Hanway, one of the first to do so, was jeered in the street.
The Popsicle was invented by 11-year-old Frank Epperson, who, by his own account, left a cup of soda with a stirring stick outside on a freezing night in 1905.
Gunpowder was discovered by Chinese alchemists who were trying to make a potion for living forever.
People in China were flying kites more than 2,000 years ago, and some were used to send signals or measure distances.
The Swiss Army knife was first made in 1891 for Swiss soldiers, mainly so they could open canned food and fix their gear.
The first flat-pack furniture idea at IKEA came when an employee took the legs off a table so it would fit in a car.
The paper bag with a flat bottom, the kind used in grocery stores, was invented by Margaret Knight, who built a machine to fold them in the 1860s.
Earmuffs were invented by 15-year-old Chester Greenwood of Maine, whose ears kept freezing when he went ice skating.
The thermos flask began in 1892 as a lab tool for keeping chemicals extremely cold. A German company later sold it for keeping drinks hot.
The first electric toaster that popped toast up by itself was invented in 1919 by a factory worker tired of burnt toast in the canteen.
Cotton candy was co-invented by a dentist, William Morrison, and sold as Fairy Floss at the 1904 World's Fair, where it was a huge hit.
Hourglasses were used on ships to measure speed: sailors timed how fast a knotted rope ran out, which is why ship speed is still measured in knots.
The traffic cone was invented in the 1940s by Charles Scanlon, a road painter in Los Angeles.
Cat's eyes road reflectors were patented in 1934 by Percy Shaw, who said the idea came when his headlights lit up the eyes of a cat on a dark road.
The world's first speed camera was invented by a Dutch rally driver, of all people, in the 1950s.
When car radios appeared around 1930, some U.S. states considered banning them, fearing drivers would be dangerously distracted.
Cars did not come with turn signals for decades: drivers stuck their arms out the window to show where they were turning.
The first gasoline car, patented by Karl Benz in 1886, had only three wheels and topped out around 16 kilometers per hour.
Cruise control was invented by Ralph Teetor, a blind engineer who got fed up with his lawyer speeding up and slowing down as he talked while driving.
The first stop signs, in 1915 Detroit, were white with black letters. They only turned red in the United States in 1954.
Ferdinand Porsche built a hybrid car, with a gas engine charging electric motors in the wheels, back in 1900.
Car tires were originally whitish. They turned black when makers added carbon black, a soot that makes rubber much tougher.
Penny-farthing bicycles had giant front wheels because the pedals were fixed straight to the wheel, so a bigger wheel meant more speed per pedal turn.
In 1896 Susan B. Anthony said the bicycle had done more to free women than anything else in the world.
The starry ceiling of New York's Grand Central Terminal is painted backwards, with the constellations shown as if seen from outside the sky.
Swiss railway clocks pause their second hand for about a second and a half at the top of every minute, waiting for a signal to set every clock in sync.
Japanese train staff point at signals and say them out loud, a habit one study found cuts mistakes by up to 85 percent.
San Francisco's cable cars are among the only moving National Historic Landmarks in the United States.
In 1950 a young circus elephant named Tuffi jumped out of Germany's hanging Wuppertal monorail into the river below and survived with barely a scratch.
Charles Lindbergh flew across the Atlantic alone in 1927 with no front window: a fuel tank blocked the view, so he looked out the sides or used a periscope.
In 1914 Lawrence Sperry showed off the first autopilot in Paris by flying past the crowd with his hands in the air while his mechanic walked on the wing.
In 1990 an SR-71 Blackbird spy plane flew from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C. in about 64 minutes.
The SR-71 Blackbird leaked fuel while parked, because its panels only sealed tightly once air friction heated and expanded the metal in flight.
Between 2015 and 2016 a plane called Solar Impulse 2 flew all the way around the world on sunshine alone.
In 1983 an Air Canada jet ran out of fuel mid-flight because of a mix-up between pounds and kilograms. The pilots glided it to a safe landing.
In a strength test, a Boeing 787's wings were bent upward about 7.6 meters at the tips without breaking.
The Boeing 747 has its famous hump because it was designed to carry cargo through a nose that swings open, so the cockpit had to sit up top.
Runway numbers are compass directions with the last digit dropped, so runway 27 points west, at 270 degrees.
The Hindenburg airship was nearly as long as the Titanic, and its passenger lounge had a lightweight aluminum piano.
The Swedish warship Vasa sank in 1628 less than a mile into its first voyage, because it was too top-heavy. Today it sits in a museum, about 98 percent original.
The steamship Great Eastern, launched in 1858, was so huge that it was the only ship big enough to lay the first lasting cable across the Atlantic.
Samuel Morse was a famous painter before he invented the telegraph, driven partly by grief after news of his wife's death reached him too late.
The canal lock with two gates, still used on canals worldwide, was invented in China around the year 984.
Scotland's Falkirk Wheel lifts boats 24 meters by rotating, and each turn uses about as much energy as boiling eight kettles.
Each ship that crosses the Panama Canal uses about 200 million liters of fresh water to fill and empty the locks.
Barcelona's Sagrada Familia has been under construction since 1882, and it only got an official building permit in 2019.
The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is about 828 meters tall, roughly two and a half Eiffel Towers stacked up.
People at the top of the Burj Khalifa see the sun set a few minutes later than people at its base.
The Roman Colosseum had a giant retractable awning to shade the crowd, worked by teams of sailors pulling ropes.
The Roman aqueduct that fed the city of Nimes drops only about 12 meters over 50 kilometers, a slope far too gentle to see with your eyes.
Inca builders fitted stones so tightly without any mortar that, centuries later, you still cannot slide a knife blade between many of them.
From 1696, England taxed houses by the number of windows, so many owners bricked theirs up. You can still see the blocked windows on old buildings.
In 2013 a curved glass skyscraper in London focused sunlight onto the street so strongly that it melted parts of a parked car.
As of 2024, the longest wind turbine blades are over 100 meters long, longer than a jumbo jet's wingspan.
Enough sunlight hits Earth in about an hour and a half to power all of humanity for a whole year.
A uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip holds about as much energy as a tonne of coal.
Japan's electricity runs at two different frequencies, because in the 1890s Tokyo bought German generators and Osaka bought American ones.
In 1880 Wabash, Indiana, became one of the first towns lit by electric street lights, and people traveled from far away to see the night glow.
The lead-acid battery in most gasoline cars was invented in 1859, before the car itself.
Alessandro Volta designed his first battery after studying electric fish, and he called it an artificial electric organ.
At the 1900 Paris World's Fair, Rudolf Diesel's engine was shown running on peanut oil.
In 1086 a royal survey counted about 5,600 water mills in England, roughly one for every few hundred people.
Norway gets around 90 percent of its electricity from flowing water, thanks to its steep mountains and rainy weather.
Iceland heats roughly 9 out of 10 homes with hot water piped up from deep underground.
A giant solar furnace in the French Pyrenees uses about 10,000 mirrors to focus sunlight hot enough to melt steel.
Until 1911, France refused to use Greenwich Mean Time and used Paris time instead, which ran about nine minutes ahead.
Wristwatches were once seen as jewelry for women. Men switched from pocket watches largely because soldiers in World War I needed their hands free.
A clock in Copenhagen has a gear that takes about 25,753 years to turn just once.
In a mountain in Texas, engineers are building a giant clock designed to keep ticking for 10,000 years.
Cat litter was invented in 1947 when Edward Lowe gave a neighbor some absorbent clay instead of sand for her cat box, and it worked far better.
Since 1959, the inch has officially been defined using the metric system: it is exactly 2.54 centimeters.
During the French Revolution, France tried decimal time: 10 hours in a day, 100 minutes in an hour and 100 seconds in a minute. It was dropped within two years.
Stone tools about 3.3 million years old have been found in Kenya, older than the first members of our own human genus.
Phillips head screws spread because car factories loved them: the screwdriver centers itself, which suited fast assembly lines.
Roman builders lifted heavy stones with cranes powered by workers walking inside giant wheels, like hamsters in a hamster wheel.
The wheelbarrow was used in China by around the year 200, about a thousand years before it showed up in Europe.
The telescope was invented by Dutch eyeglass makers in 1608. Galileo heard about it and built a better one himself within about a year.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made microscopes with a single tiny lens no bigger than a lentil, yet they magnified things around 200 times.
Garrett Morgan, the son of formerly enslaved parents, patented a traffic signal in 1923 that added a warning position between stop and go.
In 1911 Ray Harroun won the first Indianapolis 500 using a rearview mirror, one of the earliest uses of one on a car.
Nikola Tesla said the idea for his famous electric motor came to him on a walk in a Budapest park, and he sketched it in the dirt with a stick.
Thomas Edison earned 1,093 U.S. patents. His very first was an electric vote counter for lawmakers, and none of them wanted it.
In 1890 Edison sold a talking doll with a tiny record player inside. Its scratchy voice frightened children and it flopped within weeks.
Hollywood star Hedy Lamarr co-patented a way to hop between radio frequencies in 1942, an idea later linked to modern wireless technology.
The disposable diaper cover was invented in 1946 by a mother, Marion Donovan, who cut up her shower curtain to make it.
Liquid Paper correction fluid was invented by a secretary, Bette Nesmith Graham, whose son later became a member of the band The Monkees.
The paper coffee filter was invented in 1908 by Melitta Bentz, who punched holes in a brass pot and lined it with paper from her son's school notebook.
The painter Renoir reportedly said that without paint in tubes, invented in 1841, there would have been no Impressionism, since artists could finally paint outdoors.
The first patent for a pencil with an eraser on the end was granted in 1858, then later thrown out for being two old ideas glued together.
About 25 million plastic hula hoops were sold in just four months in 1958, when the craze swept the United States.
Silly Putty was an accident from a World War II search for fake rubber. The goo bounced and stretched but was useless for tires.
Mr. Potato Head was the first toy ever advertised on television. The first kits came with no potato, so kids used real vegetables.
The trampoline was invented by a teenage gymnast in the 1930s, inspired by the safety nets under circus trapeze artists.
The Ferris wheel was built for Chicago's 1893 World's Fair to outdo the Eiffel Tower, and each of its cars could hold 60 people.
Roller coasters grew out of Russian ice slides from the 1600s, giant wooden ramps covered in ice that riders sped down on sleds.
The first escalator, in 1896, was a ride at Coney Island, where people lined up just to try the moving staircase.
When London's Harrods installed an escalator in 1898, staff waited at the top offering brandy and smelling salts to shaken customers.
The first moving walkway carried visitors along a pier at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.
The Aqua-Lung, which made modern scuba diving possible, was invented in 1943 by Jacques Cousteau and an engineer, using a part from a car's gas system.
SOS does not stand for Save Our Souls. It was chosen because three dots, three dashes and three dots are easy to send and hard to mistake.
The first fax machine was patented in 1843, more than 30 years before the telephone was invented.
Alexander Graham Bell and rival inventor Elisha Gray filed papers for the telephone at the patent office on the very same day in 1876.
The first handheld cell phone call was made in 1973. The phone weighed over a kilogram and took 10 hours to charge for about 30 minutes of talking.
Some of the first good headphones were handmade at a kitchen table in Utah by Nathaniel Baldwin, who sold them to the U.S. Navy.
The piano was invented around 1700 and named pianoforte, Italian for soft-loud, because unlike the harpsichord it could play both.
The saxophone was invented in the 1840s by Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax, who named it after himself.
Counting all its branches, the Great Wall of China stretches about 21,000 kilometers, more than half the way around the Earth.
China's Grand Canal runs about 1,800 kilometers, and parts of it were dug about 2,500 years ago.
After the Great Stink of 1858, when the River Thames reeked of sewage, London built new sewers so big that they still work today.
London's sewer engineer Joseph Bazalgette made his pipes about twice as wide as needed, saying they would only get one chance to do it right.
Japan's Kansai Airport sits on a man-made island in the sea, and the island has been slowly sinking since it opened in 1994.
Dubai has imported sand to build skyscrapers, because desert sand grains are worn too smooth and round to make strong concrete.
In 1930 an eight-story office building in Indianapolis was slowly rotated 90 degrees while about 600 people kept working inside.
In the 1850s and 1860s, Chicago jacked up whole brick buildings by several feet to fit new sewers underneath, while people kept shopping inside.
Tunnel boring machines are traditionally given women's names, a custom linked to Saint Barbara, patron saint of miners and tunnelers.
A stone bridge in Greece, built about 3,300 years ago, is still used by people walking across it today.
The world's first iron bridge, built in England in 1779, was put together with joints copied from woodworking, because no one had built in iron before.
Villagers in India's Meghalaya grow living bridges by guiding fig tree roots across rivers, and some of them last for centuries.
Every year villagers in Peru rebuild a 30-meter Inca rope bridge by hand, twisting it from grass the way their ancestors did 500 years ago.
