The bridge between Denmark and Sweden dives into the sea and turns into a tunnel halfway across, so ships and planes are not blocked.
The Great Pyramid lines up with true north to within a tiny fraction of a degree, built about 4,500 years ago without a compass.
The wooden roof frame of Notre-Dame in Paris was nicknamed the forest, because it took about 1,300 oak trees to build.
Japan's tall wooden pagodas survive earthquakes thanks to a central pillar that sways separately from the floors. Tokyo Skytree copied the idea.
Venice stands on millions of wooden posts driven into the mud. Kept away from air underwater, the wood has lasted for centuries.
Amsterdam's Royal Palace, built in the 1600s, still rests on 13,659 wooden posts driven deep into the soggy ground.
The ancient Romans built about 80,000 kilometers of paved roads, and some of them are still driven on today.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders, stood about 100 meters tall and guided ships for more than 1,000 years.
Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle looks taller than it is: its upper parts are built smaller, a trick called forced perspective.
Rome's Trevi Fountain is still fed by an aqueduct the Romans opened in the year 19 BC.
The tallest wooden building in the world, as of 2024, is an apartment tower in Milwaukee about 87 meters tall.
The CN Tower in Toronto is hit by lightning roughly 75 times a year, and it is built to take every strike safely.
The Statue of Liberty's torch has been closed to visitors since 1916, after an explosion nearby damaged the arm.
Mount Rushmore's carving took 14 years, and about 90 percent of it was done with dynamite rather than chisels.
When the White House got electric lights in 1891, President Benjamin Harrison and his wife were reportedly so nervous about the switches that staff turned them on and off.
By treaty, up to three quarters of Niagara's water is diverted to power plants at night, when fewer tourists are watching the falls.
In 1808 Richard Trevithick charged people a shilling to ride behind his steam locomotive on a circular track in London, calling it Catch Me Who Can.
Old-style light bulbs turned only about 5 to 10 percent of their electricity into light. The rest became heat, which is how the Easy-Bake Oven baked cakes with a bulb.
When the first neon signs came to the United States in 1923, at a Los Angeles car dealership, people reportedly stopped in the street to stare.
Albert Einstein co-invented a refrigerator with no moving parts in 1926, after reading about a family killed by gas leaking from their fridge.
The first nuclear reactor was built in 1942 in a squash court under the stands of a football field at the University of Chicago.
An acre was once roughly how much land a team of oxen could plow in one day, usually a long, thin strip of field.
Horses are still measured in hands, an old unit equal to 4 inches, the width of a man's hand.
British shoe sizes go up in steps of one barleycorn, an old unit equal to a third of an inch.
Daniel Fahrenheit set zero on his scale using a freezing mix of ice, water and salt, the coldest thing he could reliably make in his lab.
In 1794 a French scientist sailing to deliver a standard kilogram to Thomas Jefferson was captured by pirates, and the kilogram never arrived.
Mount Everest was first measured in 1856 by surveyors who never went near it, using angles taken from more than 100 kilometers away.
Since 1833, a red ball has dropped down a pole at Greenwich at exactly 1 p.m. almost every day, so ships on the Thames could set their clocks.
The New Year's Eve ball drop in Times Square was inspired by time balls, which harbors used to signal the exact time to sailors.
The first sandpaper was made in China around the 1200s by gluing crushed shells, seeds and sand onto paper.
Masking tape was invented in 1925 after an engineer saw car painters cursing because their two-tone paint jobs kept peeling.
Nails were once so valuable that in 1645 Virginia passed a law to stop settlers burning down old houses just to collect the nails.
The oldest known fishhooks, made from sea snail shells, are about 23,000 years old and were found in a cave in Japan.
The oldest known boat is a dugout canoe from the Netherlands that is roughly 10,000 years old.
Ancient Egyptians used wooden pin locks about 4,000 years ago that work on the same basic idea as the lock on your front door.
The wire coat hanger was invented in 1903 by a factory worker whose coworkers complained there were never enough hooks.
Some of the first home hair dryers in the early 1900s were vacuum cleaners: ads suggested attaching the hose to the blowing end.
King Gillette's disposable razor blades were a flop at first. In 1903, his first year of sales, he sold just 51 razors.
The pressure cooker was invented in 1679 by Denis Papin, who also built one of the first safety valves to stop it from bursting.
In 1831 angry tailors in Paris smashed the first sewing machine factory, fearing the machines would take their jobs.
The spinning jenny, invented in the 1760s, let a single worker spin eight threads at once instead of one.
King Philip II of Spain had one of the first known wheelchairs built for him in 1595, complete with a footrest.
Early medical thermometers were about 30 centimeters long and took around 20 minutes to give a reading.
The first fire hydrants were holes drilled into wooden water pipes, then plugged up afterwards, which is why they are still called fire plugs.
The firefighter's pole was invented in Chicago in 1878, when a firefighter found sliding down was much faster than taking the stairs.
The mathematician Blaise Pascal started one of the world's first public bus services in Paris in 1662, using horse-drawn carriages.
The word taxi comes from taximeter, the device invented in the 1890s to measure the distance and the fare.
The car brand Mercedes is named after a ten-year-old girl, the daughter of a businessman who raced and sold the company's cars.
The first gasoline motorcycle, built by Gottlieb Daimler in 1885, had a wooden frame and wooden wheels.
In 1870 New York secretly built a one-block subway pushed by a giant fan, with a waiting room that had a piano and a fountain.
The word skyscraper was used for a ship's highest sail before it described tall buildings.
London's Crystal Palace, built for the Great Exhibition of 1851, used about 300,000 panes of glass and went up in only a few months.
The Crystal Palace's design was inspired by a giant water lily whose leaves were strong enough to hold up a child.
Concrete is the most used human-made material on Earth. Only water is consumed in bigger amounts.
Reinforced concrete was invented by a French gardener, Joseph Monier, who wanted stronger flower pots.
Before elevators, the top floors of buildings were the cheapest, for servants and the poor. Elevators turned them into luxury penthouses.
The snowboard began in 1965 as the Snurfer, two skis bolted together by a Michigan dad, Sherman Poppen, as a toy for his daughter.
In the 1770s a Swiss watchmaker built a doll the size of a small boy that writes real letters with a quill pen, and it still works today.
In the 1700s a mechanical duck toured Europe that appeared to eat grain and digest it, though the poop was secretly preloaded.
The first vending machines in modern times, in 1880s London, sold postcards at train stations.
The first coin-operated jukebox played in a San Francisco saloon in 1889, with four listening tubes that customers held to their ears.
The modern umbrella's lightweight steel frame was invented in 1852 by Samuel Fox, who used leftover steel from corsets.
Corrugated cardboard was first patented in 1856 as a lining for tall hats, years before anyone made shipping boxes from it.
The paper drinking straw was invented in 1888 by Marvin Stone, who was tired of rye grass straws leaving a grassy taste in his drink.
The bendy straw was invented in the 1930s by a man who watched his young daughter struggle to drink a milkshake through a straight straw.
The first charge card, Diners Club in 1950, was made of cardboard and was accepted at just 27 restaurants in New York.
The first lightweight folding baby stroller was designed in 1965 by an aircraft engineer who used ideas from airplane landing gear.
After a newspaper mistakenly ran his obituary calling him a merchant of death, dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel reportedly decided to fund the Nobel Prizes.
The first chewing gum sold in the United States, in the 1840s, was made from spruce tree resin.
The inventor of the Pringles can, Fredric Baur, asked for some of his ashes to be buried in one, and his family honored his wish.
The first shopping mall with a roof and climate control opened in Minnesota in 1956, designed to escape both summer heat and winter snow.
The Zamboni was invented in 1949 by Frank Zamboni, who ran a California ice rink and was tired of the slow job of smoothing the ice by hand.
Charles Goodyear said he discovered tough, weatherproof rubber when a sticky mix of rubber and sulfur hit a hot stove. He still died deep in debt.
Cellophane was invented in 1908 by a Swiss chemist who wanted a tablecloth that wine could not stain.
The sweetener sucralose was discovered in 1976 when a student was asked to test a chemical and thought he had been told to taste it.
Pyrex glass was first made for railway signal lanterns. It reached the kitchen after a scientist's wife baked a cake in a sawed-off glass battery jar.
The stain repellent Scotchgard was discovered in 1952 when a chemical spilled on a lab assistant's canvas shoe and simply would not wash off.
The Super Soaker water blaster was invented by Lonnie Johnson, a NASA engineer, while he was working on a new kind of heat pump.
Humans walked on the Moon in 1969, a year before the wheeled suitcase that finally caught on was patented.
The lava lamp was invented by Edward Craven Walker, who got the idea from a homemade egg timer of bubbling liquids he saw in an English pub.
During World War II, British pilots used ballpoint pens because fountain pens leaked at high altitude.
The Penny Black, the first postage stamp, was issued in Britain in 1840. British stamps still do not print the country's name, the only ones allowed to skip it.
The machine used to dig the first tunnel under the Thames was inspired by the shipworm, a creature that bores through wooden ships.
The first commercial oil well, drilled in Pennsylvania in 1859, struck oil just 21 meters down.
In 1807 Pall Mall in London became the first street in the world lit by gas lamps.
A tidal power station in France has made electricity from the rise and fall of the sea since 1966.
Most of Texas runs on its own power grid, largely cut off from the rest of the United States.
During the huge 2003 blackout in North America, so many lights went out that city dwellers could see the Milky Way, some for the first time.
Norway honors Johan Vaaler as the paper clip's inventor, but his 1899 design lacked the double loop: the classic paper clip came from Britain.
The abbreviation lb for pound comes from libra, the ancient Roman unit of weight.
The ancient Egyptian cubit was based on the length of a forearm, and the Great Pyramid was laid out in cubits.
Barbie is named after Barbara, the daughter of her creator Ruth Handler, and Ken is named after Barbara's brother.
China stretches across about five time zones, yet the whole country officially uses just one clock time.
Daylight saving time was first seriously proposed in 1895 by a New Zealand insect collector who wanted more daylight after work to hunt bugs.
In 1927 a swimmer wore Rolex's new waterproof Oyster watch during a 10-hour swim in the English Channel, and it came out still ticking.
The cuckoo clock comes from Germany's Black Forest, not from Switzerland, despite its famous Swiss reputation.
The grandfather clock got its name from a hit song of 1876, about a clock that stopped when its old owner died.
Salisbury Cathedral in England has a mechanical clock from around 1386 that still runs. It has no face and no hands; it just rings the hours.
Tarmac is short for tar macadam, named after Scottish engineer John McAdam, whose road surface of crushed stone spread worldwide.
In 1919 a U.S. Army convoy took 62 days to cross the country. A young officer on it, Dwight Eisenhower, later launched the interstate highway system as president.
In 1929 the airship Graf Zeppelin flew around the world in about 21 days, with passengers dining at tables with tablecloths.
In the 1890s Otto Lilienthal made around 2,000 flights in gliders he built himself, inspiring the Wright brothers.
In 1853 George Cayley's glider carried a man across a valley in England. The story goes that his coachman quit right after landing.
The first flight attendants, hired in 1930 by an American airline, all had to be trained nurses.
One of the first air traffic controllers, in 1929, directed planes by waving flags while sitting in a wheelbarrow.
Robert Fulton's first commercial steamboat in 1807 was mocked as Fulton's Folly, until it chugged up the Hudson River faster than sailboats.
As of 2024, the biggest cruise ship, Icon of the Seas, is about five times larger than the Titanic.
Edmond Halley, famous for his comet, also designed a diving bell in the 1690s and stayed underwater in it for over an hour.
The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, cut the cost of shipping goods between New York City and the Great Lakes by around 90 percent.
Workers digging the Brooklyn Bridge foundations under the river fell ill when they came up too fast, a mystery sickness now called the bends.
Frank Lloyd Wright's famous house Fallingwater is built right on top of a waterfall instead of facing it, so you hear the water rushing inside.
London's Big Ben tower leans slightly, its top sitting about half a meter off center.
The first passenger elevator in a public building opened in 1857 in a five-story New York store, climbing at about 12 meters a minute.
About 4,500 years ago, cities in the Indus Valley had covered drains and toilets in many homes, more advanced than most of Europe 3,000 years later.
Before glass windows were common, many homes covered window openings with oiled paper, cloth or thin sheets of animal horn.
Ancient Persians built tall wind towers that catch breezes and cool homes below, a kind of air conditioning with no electricity at all.
Archimedes is said to have designed a ship so huge that it was offered as a gift to the king of Egypt, because no harbor in Sicily could fit it.
Ancient Greeks built a track called the Diolkos to drag ships over land across the Isthmus of Corinth, a shortcut used for centuries.
The Corinth Canal, opened in 1893, is only about 21 meters wide at sea level, too narrow for most modern cargo ships to squeeze through.
London's Tower Bridge was once raised about 6,000 times a year for passing ships. Today it opens far less often.
Stainless steel was discovered in 1913, the story goes, when Harry Brearley noticed one of his test samples tossed on the scrap heap had not rusted.
The electric starter motor for cars was invented in 1911, partly because hand cranks caused so many injuries.
Car headlights started out as oil or acetylene lamps that drivers lit with a match.
The first car keys, ignition keys that also started the engine, appeared in 1949.
Cotton swabs were invented in the 1920s by Leo Gerstenzang after he saw his wife wrapping cotton around toothpicks to clean their baby.
Clarence Birdseye invented frozen food after watching Inuit fishermen in Labrador freeze fish instantly in bitter cold, and the fish tasted fresh months later.
Laszlo Biro's ballpoint pen became so popular in Argentina that people there still call any pen a birome.
The Tower of Hercules in Spain, built by the Romans about 1,900 years ago, is the oldest lighthouse still in use.
Christopher Wren, architect of St Paul's Cathedral in London, built it in about 35 years and lived to see it finished.
Many windmills in the Netherlands were used not to grind grain but to pump water off the land.
Some Dutch windmill keepers set the sails in special positions to send messages, like news of a birth or a death in the village.
The very first speed limit in the United States, in Connecticut in 1901, was 12 miles per hour in cities.
Safety glass was invented in 1903 after a French chemist dropped a glass flask coated with plastic and saw it crack without shattering.
The friction match was invented in 1826 by an English chemist after a stick coated in chemicals burst into flame when he scraped it on his hearth.
Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, was invented in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, who had already got rich selling a photo paper invention to Kodak's founder.
Archimedes' screw, a water-lifting spiral more than 2,000 years old, is still used today in some farms and sewage plants.
In the 1090s, China's Su Song built a water-powered clock tower over 10 meters tall that rang bells and moved puppets to announce the time.
In 1206 the inventor al-Jazari designed an elephant clock with a water timer inside and a mechanical bird that whistled every half hour.
The Montgolfier brothers, who built the first hot air balloons to carry people, ran a family paper-making business.
In 2000 a skydiver jumped with a parachute built from Leonardo da Vinci's 500-year-old design, and it worked.
Gutenberg's printing press was adapted from the screw presses used to squeeze grapes for wine.
Johannes Gutenberg went broke and lost his printing workshop to his main investor, soon after printing his famous Bible.
Some of the oldest ice skates were made from animal leg bones, strapped to people's feet thousands of years ago in northern Europe.
Inuit people carved snow goggles from bone or wood with thin slits to see through, protecting their eyes from blinding snow glare.
The zipper's first version, shown in 1893, was called a clasp locker, and it often popped open or jammed.
The first waterproof raincoats, sold by Charles Macintosh in the 1820s, went stiff in the cold and sticky in the heat.
Instant noodles were invented in 1958 by Momofuku Ando, who worked on them in a shed behind his house in Japan.
Black and Decker made a battery-powered drill for NASA so Apollo astronauts could drill into the Moon.
In 1906 a steam-powered car, the Stanley Steamer, set a land speed record of about 205 kilometers per hour.
In 1997 a jet car called ThrustSSC became the first car to break the sound barrier, reaching about 1,228 kilometers per hour.
The Plimsoll line painted on ship hulls shows how low they may safely sit in the water, ending the days of dangerously overloaded coffin ships.
India's Chand Baori stepwell has about 3,500 steps zigzagging down 13 stories to reach the water at the bottom.
Sweden's Icehotel is rebuilt from scratch every winter using ice blocks cut from a frozen river, then melts back into it in spring.
Turkey's ancient underground city of Derinkuyu goes down about 85 meters and could shelter thousands of people along with their animals.
Gustave Eiffel kept a private apartment near the top of his tower, where he entertained guests like Thomas Edison.
Beethoven was one of the first composers to mark his music with metronome speeds, soon after the metronome was invented in 1815.
Leonardo da Vinci sketched ball bearings around 1500, centuries before they became common in bicycles, cars and machines.
In 1965 two Amphicars, cars that could also float and drive like boats, crossed the English Channel.
In 1949 a car called the Aerocar could fold up its wings and tow them behind like a trailer. Only a handful were ever built.
The rocket belt jetpacks of the 1960s really flew, but they carried only enough fuel for about 20 seconds in the air.
Some old office buildings in Germany still have paternoster lifts: open cabins with no doors that loop nonstop, so you hop on and off as they pass.
As of 2024, La Paz in Bolivia has the world's biggest city cable car network, used by commuters like a subway in the sky.
The Golden Gate Bridge's main cables hold about 129,000 kilometers of wire, enough to wrap around the Earth more than three times.
London's Millennium Bridge closed two days after opening in 2000 because walkers' footsteps fell into step and made it sway.
Covered wooden bridges were built with roofs to keep the wooden deck dry, which could make a bridge last several times longer.
The Holland Tunnel under the Hudson River opened in 1927 with giant fans that replace all the air inside about every 90 seconds.
Chalk dug out for the Channel Tunnel was used to make a brand-new piece of England, a nature park called Samphire Hoe.
The treadmill was invented in 1818 as a punishment for prisoners, who climbed endless steps to power mills that ground grain.
The first electricity-making wind turbine was built in 1887 by a Scottish professor for his cottage. Villagers refused his spare power, reportedly calling it the work of the devil.
Seiko's first quartz wristwatch went on sale in 1969 for about the price of a small family car.
The first digital wristwatch, sold in 1972, cost about 2,100 dollars, more than many new cars at the time.
The S-shaped bend in the pipe under a toilet, patented in 1775, holds water that blocks sewer smells. Toilets still use it today.
There are about 15 different types of electric plugs used around the world, which is why travelers need adapters.
The flashlight got its name because early batteries were so weak it could only make short flashes of light.
Napoleon's surgeon Dominique Larrey invented fast, light horse carts to rush wounded soldiers to doctors, the ancestor of the ambulance.
Belisha beacons, the orange globes on poles at British crossings, appeared in 1934, years before the black and white zebra stripes were painted.
The first hand-cranked ice cream maker was invented in 1843 by Nancy Johnson, a woman in Philadelphia.
The espresso machine was first patented in 1884 in Turin, Italy, built to brew coffee fast for busy cafe customers.
The first electric kettle that switched itself off when the water boiled went on sale in 1955.
Wellington boots are named after the Duke of Wellington, who had his bootmaker make a new, simpler style of boot.
The first hot air balloons were reportedly heated by burning straw, wool and even old shoes, because the inventors believed smoke made them rise.
When the first automatic doors opened at shops in the 1950s and 60s, they used a mat that sensed people stepping on it.
The very first car accident in the United States happened in 1891 in Ohio, when a driver hit a tree root and crashed into a hitching post.
The tallest lighthouse in the world, in Saudi Arabia, is about 133 meters high, taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal.
When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its main span was about 50 percent longer than any suspension bridge built before it.
Toothpaste in squeezable tubes only appeared in the 1890s. Before that it was sold in jars, and everyone dipped their brush into the same one.
Movie theaters were among the first public places with air conditioning, and people flocked to summer films partly just to cool off.
The engines on the Boeing 777X are so huge that each one is wider than the body of a Boeing 737 airliner.
Tokyo's railways have hired platform staff to gently push passengers into packed rush-hour trains so the doors can close.
Gas-powered streetlights in many cities were switched on every evening by lamplighters, who walked their routes with long poles.
@microbes|Microbes
Your body holds roughly as many bacteria as human cells, so you are about half microbe by cell count.
Most of the bacteria in your body live in your large intestine, where a single gram can hold around 100 billion of them.
The microbes in your gut carry roughly 100 times more genes than your own body does.
Babies born the usual way get their first big dose of gut bacteria from their mother on the way out.
Your gut bacteria make vitamins your body cannot make by itself, including vitamin K.
Doctors cure some stubborn gut infections by transplanting poop from a healthy donor, and it works about 9 times out of 10.
Mice raised in totally germ-free bubbles grow up with weaker immune systems and oddly shaped guts.
Bacteria buried in seafloor mud for 100 million years woke up and began eating and dividing when scientists fed them in a lab.
Your skin microbes are so personal that scientists have matched computer keyboards to the people who typed on them.
Your mouth is home to roughly 700 kinds of bacteria, one of the most crowded neighborhoods in your body.
Dental plaque is a bacterial city, held together with sticky glue the bacteria build themselves.
In 1683 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek scraped the gunk off his own teeth and saw tiny creatures swimming in it, some of the first bacteria ever seen.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant, discovered bacteria with tiny homemade microscopes no bigger than a thumb.
Van Leeuwenhoek called the tiny creatures he saw "animalcules" and wrote that they moved about very prettily.
All the bacteria on Earth together outweigh all the animals, including every human, many times over.
There may be around a trillion kinds of microbes on Earth, and almost all of them have never been named.
For roughly 3 billion years, microbes were the only life on Earth, far longer than animals have existed.
The oxygen you breathe exists because tiny bacteria started pumping it into the air about 2.4 billion years ago.
When bacteria first filled the air with oxygen, it was likely poison to many of the microbes that had lived without it.
Yellow fever was the first human disease shown to be caused by a virus, in 1901, by a team that let mosquitoes bite volunteers.
In Shark Bay, Australia, bacteria still build the same kind of rock mounds they built billions of years ago.
One tiny ocean bacterium called Prochlorococcus may be the most common living thing that runs on sunlight, with octillions of cells.
About half of the oxygen made on Earth comes from tiny life floating in the ocean, not from forests.
A single liter of seawater can hold about a billion bacteria and ten times as many viruses.
A teaspoon of healthy soil can hold more microbes than there are people on Earth.
The lovely smell after rain is partly a chemical made by soil bacteria.
The 1918 flu is called Spanish flu, but it probably did not start in Spain: Spanish newspapers simply reported it while countries at war kept quiet.
Kefir grains are not grains at all, but rubbery clumps of bacteria and yeast that grow bigger as they ferment milk.
If one bacterium kept doubling every 20 minutes with unlimited food, its offspring would outweigh the Earth in about two days.
Coffee beans are fermented by microbes after the fruit is picked, and that step helps shape how your coffee tastes.
The largest known bacterium, from Caribbean mangroves, grows up to 2 centimeters long, about the size of an eyelash, and is visible without a microscope.
Every loaf of yeast bread is raised by a fungus: baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus that burps out gas bubbles.
Some of the smallest bacteria are so tiny that a few hundred could line up across the width of a human hair.
Bacteria can pass genes directly to each other, even to completely different species, like swapping trading cards.
Bacteria share antibiotic resistance genes with their neighbors, which is one reason resistance spreads so fast.
Many bacteria swim using a tail spun by a real rotary motor, which in some species turns faster than a race car engine.
The blue mold in Roquefort cheese was traditionally grown on loaves of rye bread left to go moldy in caves, then ground into powder.
E. coli finds food by swimming straight, randomly tumbling, and swimming longer whenever things smell better.
Some bacteria build chains of tiny magnets inside themselves and line up with Earth's magnetic field like compass needles.
The Hawaiian bobtail squid uses glowing bacteria as an invisibility cloak, matching moonlight so it casts no shadow.
Alfred Nobel made dynamite safe to handle by soaking nitroglycerin into a powder made of the fossil shells of tiny algae.
Bacteria vote with chemicals: many only act, like glowing or attacking, once enough of them are present to succeed.
Some bacteria turn into tough spores that can survive boiling, drying out and radiation, then wake up years later.
One bacterium, nicknamed Conan the Bacterium, can survive a radiation dose thousands of times stronger than what would kill a person.
After radiation smashes its DNA into hundreds of pieces, the bacterium Deinococcus glues it back together in hours.
Much of the world's iron ore formed when oxygen from early bacteria made iron in the ancient oceans rust and sink to the seafloor.
Bacteria left on the outside of the International Space Station survived years of vacuum, cold and harsh sunlight.
Microbes live in seafloor vents where the water is hotter than boiling but stays liquid under crushing pressure.
One microbe from a deep-sea vent has been grown in a lab at 122 C, hot enough to sterilize most medical tools.
A bacterium from a Yellowstone hot spring made modern DNA testing possible, since its enzymes survive the heat used to copy DNA.
Most of the oil we pump formed from tiny plankton that sank to the bottom of ancient seas millions of years ago.
The inventor of PCR said the idea came to him while driving at night on a winding California road.
The rainbow colors of Yellowstone's Grand Prismatic Spring are made by microbes, each color living at a different temperature.
Some microbes live happily in water about as acidic as car battery acid.
In 1996, NASA scientists said a meteorite from Mars held tiny fossil microbes; most experts now think the shapes formed without life.
Microbes have been found living in rock more than 2 kilometers beneath the seafloor.
Some microbes deep underground are so slow they may divide only once every few hundred or even thousand years.
Bacteria live nearly 3 kilometers down in a South African gold mine, fed by energy from radioactive rocks rather than sunlight.
Bacteria live in clouds, and some may help ice crystals form, giving a nudge to rain and snow.
Some bacteria help water freeze at warmer temperatures than normal, and ski resorts have used them to make snow.
Scientists drilled through about 800 meters of Antarctic ice and found a hidden lake full of bacteria living in total darkness.
Archaea look just like bacteria under a microscope, yet genetically they are as different from bacteria as you are.
A whole branch of life, the archaea, went unnoticed until 1977, when a scientist compared their genes.
Archaea were thought to live only in extreme places, but they turn out to be everywhere, even in your gut.
Much of the methane cows burp out is made by tiny archaea living in their stomachs.
No archaea have ever been confirmed to cause a disease in humans.
Your distant single-celled ancestors were probably archaea, according to genes found in deep-sea mud in the 2010s.
The first of these ancestor-like archaea took scientists about 12 years of patient work to grow in a lab.
The power plants inside your cells, the mitochondria, were once free-living bacteria swallowed over 1.5 billion years ago.
Mitochondria still carry their own tiny set of DNA, a leftover from when they were independent bacteria.
You inherit your mitochondria almost entirely from your mother, not your father.
The green parts of plant cells that catch sunlight were once free bacteria that got swallowed and kept as solar panels.
The idea that our cells contain captured bacteria was rejected by about 15 journals before it was finally published.
Some sea slugs steal the solar panels from algae they eat and keep them working inside their own bodies for months.
Aphids keep bacteria inside special cells to make nutrients that plant sap is missing, and neither can survive without the other.
No mammal can digest grass on its own: cows rely on trillions of microbes in their stomachs to do it.
There are about 10 million trillion trillion viruses on Earth, more than all the stars in the observable universe.
Lined up end to end, all the viruses on Earth would stretch about 100 million light years.
Every day, viruses in the ocean are thought to kill roughly 20 to 40 percent of all ocean bacteria.
Ocean viruses bursting bacteria release so many nutrients that they help feed the whole marine food web.
About 8 percent of your DNA is made of leftovers from ancient viruses that infected your ancestors.
A gene you got from an ancient virus helps build the placenta, so viruses helped make pregnancy possible.
Some giant viruses are bigger than some bacteria and can even be seen with an ordinary light microscope.
A giant virus found in a water tower in 1992 was mistaken for a bacterium for over ten years before anyone realized what it was.
Bacteria found in a camera brought back from the Moon in 1969 were long said to have survived there, but they most likely got in back on Earth.
Scientists revived a giant virus frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 30,000 years, and it could still infect amoebas.
Even viruses get sick: a tiny virus called Sputnik infects giant viruses and hijacks their factories.
Viruses that infect bacteria, called phages, look like tiny lunar landers with legs that grab the bacterium.
A phage injects its DNA into a bacterium like a syringe, then leaves its empty shell sitting outside.
Phages are the most abundant living things on Earth, if you count viruses as alive.
Doctors in the country of Georgia have used bacteria-killing viruses as medicine for about a century.
Phage therapy has saved patients whose infections resisted every antibiotic, using viruses picked to kill their exact bacteria.
Scientists still argue about whether viruses are alive, since they cannot grow or copy themselves without a host cell.
Watermelon snow is pink snow colored by cold-loving algae, and some people say it even smells a little like watermelon.
Many cold viruses grow best at slightly cooler temperatures, like those inside your nose.
More than 200 different viruses can cause what we call the common cold.
Smallpox killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone before it was wiped out.
Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated, declared gone by the World Health Organization in 1980.
Edward Jenner tested the first vaccine in 1796 using cowpox from a milkmaid's hand to protect a boy against smallpox.
Rinderpest, a deadly cattle virus, is the second disease ever eradicated, declared gone in 2011.
Before the polio vaccine, polio paralyzed hundreds of thousands of children every year worldwide.
Asked in 1955 who owned the patent on his polio vaccine, Jonas Salk said there was none: "Could you patent the sun?" he asked.
Polio cases worldwide have dropped by more than 99 percent since 1988.
Scientists rebuilt the 1918 flu virus in 2005 using genes recovered from victims, including one buried in Alaskan permafrost.
A virus that infects tulips caused the striped petals that sent tulip prices soaring during Dutch tulip mania in the 1600s.
The first virus ever discovered infected tobacco plants, found in the 1890s because it slipped through filters that trapped all bacteria.
The tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus ever photographed, revealing a tiny rod shape in 1939.
Many bacteria-killing viruses are so picky that they attack only one strain of one species and ignore everything else.
Viruses come in shapes like 20-sided dice, spirals, bullets and even lemons.
The rabies virus is shaped like a tiny bullet, and it reaches the brain by creeping along your nerves.
HIV copies its RNA genes into DNA backwards, breaking a rule biologists once thought could never be broken.
A fairy ring of mushrooms is one fungus spreading outward underground, and some rings are hundreds of years old.
Some caterpillar viruses make their hosts climb to the treetops before dying, so the virus rains down on leaves below.
The herpes virus that causes chickenpox hides in your nerves for decades and can come back as shingles.
Most adults carry several viruses that hide quietly in their bodies for life.
A virus that infects a fungus inside a grass can help the plant survive soil hotter than 50 C.
Some wasps use domesticated viruses to deliver genes into caterpillars, turning off their immune defenses.
Some viruses carry genes for photosynthesis and keep their ocean bacteria hosts harvesting sunlight while they multiply.
The smallest viruses are so tiny that dozens could line up across a single bacterium.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known: one case can spread to 12 to 18 unvaccinated people.
The measles virus can wipe out the immune system's memory of other germs, a problem called immune amnesia.
Bats carry many viruses without getting sick, partly thanks to their unusual immune systems.
The first mRNA vaccines were authorized in 2020, after decades of quiet research.
Katalin Kariko kept working on mRNA for decades despite being demoted and denied grants, then won the 2023 Nobel Prize.
mRNA from a vaccine breaks down within days and never enters the nucleus where your DNA is kept.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 after mold landed on a bacteria dish he had left out while on holiday.
A honey fungus in Oregon spreads under about 9 square kilometers of forest, making it one of the largest living things on Earth.
Penicillin was not mass-produced until World War II, about 15 years after Fleming first spotted it.
A moldy cantaloupe from a market in Peoria, Illinois, gave a penicillin strain that boosted production enormously.
Early penicillin was so precious that doctors collected it from patients' urine to reuse it.
The first patient treated with penicillin, a policeman in 1941, improved dramatically but died when the supply ran out.
In his Nobel speech in 1945, Fleming warned that misusing penicillin could breed resistant bacteria.
Bacteria resistant to penicillin were spotted even before the drug went into wide use.
Antibiotic-resistance genes have been found in 30,000-year-old permafrost, long before humans made any antibiotics.
Bacteria from a cave in New Mexico, sealed off for about 4 million years, resisted many modern antibiotics.
Most antibiotics we use come from soil microbes, which make them to fight their neighbors.
Streptomycin, the first drug to cure tuberculosis, came from a soil bacterium found in the 1940s.
Antibiotics do nothing against viruses, so they cannot cure a cold or the flu.
Drug-resistant infections were linked to more than a million deaths worldwide in 2019 alone.
Scientists found a new antibiotic, teixobactin, in 2015 by growing soil bacteria inside a tiny chip buried back in the dirt.
Most kinds of bacteria have never been grown in a lab: they simply refuse to live on a dish.
Life deep underground may weigh hundreds of times more than all humans combined, and almost all of it is microbes.
Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths in a maternity ward dramatically by making doctors wash their hands, and was mocked for it.
Before germ theory, many doctors believed diseases came from bad air, called miasma.
In some caves, colonies of bacteria hang from the ceiling in slimy, dripping strands that scientists really do call snottites.
Some of Pasteur's original swan-neck flasks are said to still be sterile more than 150 years later.
Pasteurization was first invented to stop wine and beer from spoiling, not milk.
Robert Koch proved in 1876 that a specific bacterium causes anthrax, the first time a germ was tied to a disease.
The agar used to grow bacteria in labs came from a kitchen: Fanny Hesse suggested it from her jelly recipes.
Petri dishes are named after Julius Petri, an assistant of Robert Koch who designed them in 1887.
Barry Marshall drank a broth of stomach bacteria to prove they cause ulcers, and won a Nobel Prize for it.
The wreck of the Titanic is slowly being eaten by bacteria that form rusty icicles, and one of them was named after the ship.
About half of all people carry the stomach bacterium that can cause ulcers, most without any symptoms.
The stomach ulcer bacterium survives acid by making ammonia to wrap itself in a tiny cloud of neutralized acid.
Tuberculosis has infected humans for thousands of years, and traces have been found in ancient Egyptian mummies.
About a quarter of the world's population carries the tuberculosis bacterium in a dormant form.
The Black Death bacterium killed an estimated third to half of Europe's population in the 1300s.
DNA from medieval plague victims proved that the Black Death was caused by the same bacterium as modern plague.
Typhoid Mary was a healthy cook who carried typhoid bacteria and infected dozens of people without ever feeling sick.
Dust storms carry microbes across whole oceans, and bacteria from African dust have been found floating in Caribbean air.
About 1,700 years ago, a Chinese doctor wrote about treating severe diarrhea with a drink made of poop and water.
The leprosy bacterium is one of the slowest-growing germs known, taking about two weeks to divide just once.
Armadillos are one of the few animals other than humans that can carry the bacterium that causes leprosy.
The bacterium behind tuberculosis divides only about once a day, which is why treatment takes months.
Clostridium botulinum makes one of the deadliest toxins known, yet tiny doses of it are used as Botox to smooth wrinkles.
Tetanus bacteria live harmlessly in soil and only cause trouble when they get deep into a wound away from air.
Lyme disease is named after the town of Lyme, Connecticut, where a cluster of cases was studied in the 1970s.
Some strains of Staph live in the noses of about a third of all people without causing harm.
Bacteria can survive for days or even weeks on dry surfaces like door handles and phones.
Copper surfaces kill many bacteria within hours, which is why some hospitals use copper door handles.
Soap does not just wash germs away; it can tear apart the fatty coat of many viruses.
Morning breath comes mostly from bacteria on the back of your tongue, which thrive overnight while your mouth makes less spit.
A used kitchen sponge can pack tens of billions of bacteria into a space the size of a sugar cube.
Bacteria can glue themselves into slimy films that are up to 1,000 times harder to kill with antibiotics.
Brewers made beer with yeast rescued from bottles in a 1797 shipwreck off Tasmania, still alive after more than 200 years.
Some bacteria eat plastic: one discovered in Japan in 2016 can digest the kind used in drink bottles.
Some bacteria eat oil, and they helped clean up after the Deepwater Horizon spill in 2010.
Some bacteria breathe metal: they can pass electrons onto iron or uranium the way we pass them to oxygen.
Cable bacteria link thousands of cells into living electrical wires up to several centimeters long in mud.
The smell of the seaside comes largely from a gas released when tiny ocean algae are eaten or die, and seabirds follow it to find food.
Some bacteria can turn dissolved gold into tiny gold nuggets as a way to protect themselves from its toxicity.
Bacteria make the holes in Swiss cheese by releasing carbon dioxide bubbles.
Yogurt is made by bacteria that turn milk sugar into acid, which makes the milk thicken.
Sourdough bread rises thanks to a team of wild yeasts and bacteria that can be kept alive for generations.
San Francisco's Boudin Bakery says it has kept the same sourdough starter alive since 1849, back in the days of the Gold Rush.
Chocolate gets its flavor partly from microbes that ferment the cacao beans before roasting.
