Some bacteria make plants grow tumors called galls by inserting their own genes into the plant's DNA.
Scientists turned that tumor-making bacterium into a tool for genetically engineering crops.
Your gut bacteria weigh roughly 200 grams in total, about as much as a mango.
A newborn baby's gut is nearly empty of microbes, yet within a few years it hosts trillions of them.
Cholera bacteria ride on tiny crustaceans, so in Bangladesh, filtering water through folded sari cloth cut cholera cases by about half.
Some bacteria can survive inside amoebas the way a burglar hides in a house, and Legionnaires' disease germs do just that.
Each time you kiss for 10 seconds, you can swap around 80 million bacteria with your partner.
Couples who live together share more skin and gut microbes than strangers, and even their dogs share some.
@math|Math
A well-shuffled deck of cards is almost certainly in an order that no deck in history has ever been in before.
There are about 8 x 10^67 ways to order a deck of 52 cards, far more than the number of atoms on Earth.
Put just 23 people in a room and there is a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday.
Roll a die six times and there is still about a 1 in 3 chance that you never see a six.
In a room of 23 people, the chance that someone shares YOUR birthday is only about 6%. You'd need 253 people to make it likely.
A soccer match has 23 people on the field counting the referee, so in about half of all games two of them share a birthday.
Pick a 3-digit number, subtract its reverse, then add that answer to its own reverse. You get 1089 every time (if the first and last digits differ by 2+).
Take a 4-digit number (not all digits the same), sort its digits high-to-low and low-to-high, and subtract. Repeat, and you always reach 6174 within 7 steps.
111,111,111 x 111,111,111 = 12,345,678,987,654,321: it counts up to 9 and back down again.
12,345,679 x 9 = 111,111,111. Multiply it by 18 instead and you get 222,222,222.
Euclid proved over 2,000 years ago that the prime numbers never run out, and his short proof still works perfectly today.
As of 2024, the biggest known prime number has over 41 million digits. Printed out, it would fill thousands of pages.
0.999... with the nines going on forever is not just close to 1. It is exactly equal to 1.
There are exactly as many even numbers as there are whole numbers, even though the evens seem to be only half of them.
Some infinities are bigger than others: there are more numbers between 0 and 1 than there are counting numbers in total.
A line 1 centimeter long contains exactly as many points as the whole of outer space.
A googol is bigger than the number of atoms in the entire observable universe.
A googolplex is 1 followed by a googol zeros. Even writing one zero on every atom in the universe, you couldn't write it down.
Fold a sheet of paper in half 42 times and, in theory, it would be thick enough to reach the Moon.
Ten factorial seconds, that is 10 x 9 x 8 x ... x 1 of them, adds up to exactly 6 weeks, to the second.
A million seconds is about 11 days. A billion seconds is nearly 32 years.
A trillion seconds ago, nobody had invented writing yet: it was about 31,700 years ago.
Multiply 142857 by 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 and you get the same six digits in the same circular order. Multiply it by 7 and you get 999999.
1 divided by 998001 spits out every three-digit number from 000 to 999 in order, skipping only 998.
1 divided by 81 is 0.012345679012345679..., counting up through every digit except 8.
Every whole number can be built by multiplying primes in exactly one way, which is why primes are called the atoms of numbers.
Add up all 37 numbers on a European roulette wheel, 0 through 36, and the total comes to exactly 666.
Some cicadas come out of the ground every 13 or 17 years, both prime numbers. One theory: it makes it hard for predators to match their cycle.
You can find a stretch of a million numbers in a row without a single prime in it.
Every even number above 2 seems to be two primes added together. It's been checked into the quintillions, but nobody can prove it.
Halve a number if even, triple it and add 1 if odd, and repeat. Every number ever tried ends at 1, but nobody can prove they all do.
Start the halve-or-triple-plus-one game at 27 and it takes 111 steps to reach 1, shooting up as high as 9,232 on the way.
A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors: 6 = 1 + 2 + 3. As of 2024, only 52 of them are known.
Nobody knows if an odd perfect number exists, but if one does, it has more than 1,500 digits.
220 and 284 are "amicable numbers": the divisors of each one add up exactly to the other.
In 1866, a 16-year-old found the friendly number pair 1184 and 1210, which the greatest mathematicians had overlooked for centuries.
Hardy called his taxi number, 1729, dull. Ramanujan said it was fascinating: the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
Any sandwich of bread, ham and bread can be cut with one straight slice that splits each of the three exactly in half. It's called the ham sandwich theorem.
153 = 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3. Only 88 numbers in our counting system equal their own digits powered up like that.
145 = 1! + 4! + 5!. Besides 1 and 2, the only other number that does this trick is 40,585.
3435 = 3^3 + 4^4 + 3^3 + 5^5: raise each digit to its own power, add them up, and you get the number back.
8 and 9 are the only neighbouring numbers that are both perfect powers. It took 158 years to prove there are no others.
2520 is the smallest number you can divide evenly by every number from 1 to 10.
Plato said the perfect city should have 5040 citizens, because 5040 divides evenly by every number from 1 to 10.
1 + 2 + 3 and 1 x 2 x 3 both equal 6. And 2 + 2 and 2 x 2 both equal 4.
Everyone knows 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2. Fewer know that 3^3 + 4^3 + 5^3 = 6^3.
10^2 + 11^2 + 12^2 = 365, and so does 13^2 + 14^2: the number of days in a year, twice.
Add up odd numbers starting from 1 and you always get a perfect square: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16.
Any number like 123123 or 456456 can always be divided by 7, 11 and 13.
37 x 3 = 111, 37 x 6 = 222, 37 x 9 = 333, and so on all the way to 37 x 27 = 999.
A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. Check any one you like.
2178 x 4 = 8712 and 1089 x 9 = 9801: both multiplications just flip the digits backwards.
Euler found a formula that spits out 40 prime numbers in a row before it finally fails.
Fermat guessed a formula always gave primes. Nearly a century later, Euler showed one of its numbers, 4,294,967,297, equals 641 x 6,700,417.
73 is the 21st prime and its mirror 37 is the 12th. And 21 = 7 x 3. It's a favourite of TV's Sheldon Cooper.
Prime numbers seem to "avoid" repeating their last digit: a prime ending in 1 is followed by another ending in 1 far less often than expected.
Pick two random whole numbers. There's about a 61% chance they share no common factor, and pi is hiding in that exact probability.
A guess about prime numbers held true for every number up to 906 million, then failed at 906,150,257.
Draw dots on a circle and connect them all: the pieces go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... and then 31, not 32.
Graham's number is so big the universe can't hold its digits, yet mathematicians know its last digit is 7.
3 to the power of 3 to the power of 3 is 7,625,597,484,987: three small 3s make over 7 trillion.
9 to the power of 9 to the power of 9 has about 370 million digits, enough to fill hundreds of books.
Add 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 forever and the total never goes past 2.
Add 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... and it grows forever, but you need over 272 million terms just to pass 20.
Add 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... (one over each square) forever, and somehow you get pi times pi divided by 6.
100 factorial (100 x 99 x 98 x ... x 1) ends in exactly 24 zeros.
0 factorial equals 1, because there's exactly one way to arrange nothing at all.
As of 2024, computers had worked out pi to more than 200 trillion digits. NASA uses only about 15 decimal places to fly its spacecraft.
About 37 decimal places of pi are enough to measure a circle the size of the observable universe to within the width of a hydrogen atom.
At the 762nd decimal place, pi suddenly has six 9s in a row. It's nicknamed the Feynman point.
Pi Day is March 14, written 3/14 in the US. It also happens to be Albert Einstein's birthday.
In 1897, the state of Indiana nearly passed a law that would have set a wrong value for pi. A visiting professor talked the senators out of it.
Archimedes trapped pi between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 by drawing shapes with 96 sides, more than 2,200 years ago.
In 5th-century China, Zu Chongzhi found that 355/113 is almost exactly pi. Nobody did better for about 900 years.
Ludolph van Ceulen spent much of his life calculating 35 digits of pi, and had them carved on his gravestone.
In 1873, William Shanks calculated pi by hand to 707 digits. In 1944 someone found he'd made a mistake at digit 528.
An ancient Egyptian scroll from about 1550 BC worked with a value of pi of about 3.16. Not bad for 3,500 years ago.
You can estimate pi by dropping needles on a floor of parallel lines and counting how many land across a line.
The Greek letter pi was first used for the circle number in 1706, by a Welsh math teacher named William Jones.
In 2015, Suresh Kumar Sharma of India recited 70,030 digits of pi from memory, a Guinness world record that took him over 17 hours.
Because pi is "transcendental", proven in 1882, you can never draw a square with exactly the same area as a circle using only a compass and ruler.
The Greeks tried for centuries to split any angle into three equal parts with only a compass and ruler. It was finally proven impossible in 1837.
Put 1 dollar in a bank paying 100% interest, added in tinier and tinier pieces, and after a year you'd have about 2.72 dollars, never more.
Drill a hole through the middle of a ball so the ring left over is 6 cm tall. That ring has the same volume whether the ball was an orange or the Earth.
In a Secret Santa draw, there's about a 37% chance that nobody picks their own name, almost no matter how big the group is.
e to the power of pi minus pi is 19.999099979..., so close to 20 it looks like a mistake.
e^(pi x sqrt 163) is 262,537,412,640,768,743.99999999999925, so close to a whole number that a 1975 April Fools' joke claimed it was one.
The imaginary number i raised to the power of i gives an ordinary real number: about 0.2079.
Euler's identity, e^(i x pi) + 1 = 0, links five of the most important numbers in math in one tiny equation. Many call it the most beautiful formula.
The ancient Romans built roads, aqueducts and an empire without ever having a symbol for zero.
The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero in the year 628, including what happens when you add or subtract it.
The Maya invented their own symbol for zero, completely independently of the rest of the world.
The digits we use, 0 to 9, came from India, travelled through the Arab world, and reached Europe around 1200.
Fibonacci's 1202 book helped convince Europe to drop Roman numerals and calculate with the digits 0 to 9.
The word "algorithm" comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century scholar from Baghdad.
"Digit" means finger, a reminder that we learned to count on our hands.
"Eleven" and "twelve" come from old Germanic words meaning roughly "one left over" and "two left over", after counting to ten on your fingers.
In Old Norse and Old English, a "hundred" often meant 120. Historians call it the "long hundred".
The word "sine" comes from a mistranslation: an Arabic word was misread as "pocket", which became the Latin sinus.
We have 60 minutes in an hour thanks to the Babylonians, who counted in sixties: 60 splits evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths.
Every whole number can be made by adding at most four perfect squares: 7 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1. Lagrange proved it works for all of them in 1770.
In French, 80 is "quatre-vingts", literally "four twenties", a leftover from counting in twenties.
The Oksapmin people of Papua New Guinea traditionally count using 27 points on the body, from one thumb up the arm, over the head and down the other side.
The Inca had no written numbers but kept detailed records with knotted strings called quipu, using a system of tens.
The ancient Egyptian symbol for a million was a kneeling god with his arms raised, as if amazed.
There is no year zero: the calendar jumps straight from 1 BC to AD 1.
1888 written in Roman numerals is MDCCCLXXXVIII, the longest year number in Roman numerals so far.
The symbols + and - first appeared in print in 1489. Before that, people wrote out "plus" and "minus" in words.
The equals sign was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines because "no two things can be more equal".
For centuries, European mathematicians refused to accept negative numbers, calling them absurd or fictitious.
"Imaginary numbers" got their name from Descartes in 1637, who meant it as a put-down. Today they help run electrical grids.
The infinity symbol was introduced by English mathematician John Wallis in 1655.
In 499, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata gave pi as 3.1416, correct to four decimal places.
In 14th-century India, Madhava discovered infinite formulas for pi, roughly 250 years before European mathematicians found them.
Babylonian astronomers tracked Jupiter with a geometry trick, measuring the area under a graph, that Europe only rediscovered about 1,400 years later.
A Babylonian clay tablet from about 1800 BC lists sets of numbers that form right triangles, like a 3,700-year-old math worksheet.
There are hundreds of known proofs of the Pythagorean theorem, including one by US President James Garfield.
Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth using nothing but shadows and the distance between two cities.
John Napier invented logarithms in 1614, turning hard multiplications into easy additions and saving astronomers years of work.
Leibniz published the binary system of 0s and 1s in 1703, more than 200 years before computers made it famous.
On your fingers in binary, each finger up or down, you can count from 0 to 1023 with just two hands.
A 2018 study found that honeybees seem to understand the idea of zero, ranking an empty set below one.
Babylonians already used a placeholder sign for "nothing here", but they didn't treat zero as a number you could calculate with.
Medieval Europe used counting boards with tokens; "the exchequer", the British treasury, is named after a checkered counting cloth.
In 1796, Gauss proved every whole number is a sum of at most three triangle numbers like 1, 3, 6 and 10. He wrote "Eureka!" in his diary.
A "score" means 20, which is why Lincoln's "four score and seven years ago" means 87 years.
On a game show, you pick 1 of 3 doors and the host opens a losing one. Switching to the other door doubles your chance of winning, from 1/3 to 2/3.
When Marilyn vos Savant explained the Monty Hall door puzzle in 1990, about 10,000 readers wrote in to say she was wrong. She was right.
The great mathematician Paul Erdos reportedly refused to believe the Monty Hall answer until he saw a computer simulation.
There are 292 ways to make change for a dollar using pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters and half-dollars.
Flip a coin 200 times and you will very likely see a streak of 6 or more heads or tails in a row. Real randomness is streakier than people expect.
Music apps made their shuffle LESS random, because listeners complained that truly random playlists repeated artists too often.
A 2023 experiment with over 350,000 coin flips found coins land the same side up as they started about 50.8% of the time.
The odds of being dealt a royal flush in 5-card poker are 1 in 649,740.
In Monopoly, Jail is the most visited square on the board, which makes the orange properties a few rolls beyond it some of the best buys.
You'd be dealt four of a kind about once every 4,165 poker hands.
Seven ordinary riffle shuffles are enough to mix a deck of cards properly. Fewer than that and patterns survive.
Do 8 perfect riffle shuffles in a row, splitting the deck exactly in half each time, and a deck of 52 cards returns to its starting order.
A deal where each bridge player gets all 13 cards of one suit has odds of about 1 in 2 x 10^27, yet newspapers report it happening. Usually the deck wasn't shuffled.
On a pair of dice, 7 is the most likely total: 6 of the 36 possible rolls add up to it.
Opposite faces on a standard die always add up to 7: 1 is opposite 6, 2 is opposite 5, and 3 is opposite 4.
There's a weird pair of dice, numbered 1-2-2-3-3-4 and 1-3-4-5-6-8, that gives exactly the same odds for every total as two normal dice.
There are sets of four dice where A usually beats B, B usually beats C, C usually beats D, and D usually beats A, like rock-paper-scissors.
On average, you need about 14.7 rolls of a die to see all six faces at least once.
Roll five dice at once and the chance they all match is 1 in 1,296.
A perfect March Madness bracket, guessed by coin flips, has odds of about 1 in 9.2 quintillion.
As of 2024, the odds of winning the Powerball jackpot with one ticket are about 1 in 292 million.
In 2009, Bulgaria's lottery drew the exact same six numbers in two draws in a row. With enough lotteries, the "impossible" becomes likely.
If you count a one-in-a-million event as a miracle, you'd expect about one per month just going about your day. That's Littlewood's law.
A medical test is 99% accurate and the disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. If you test positive, you most likely still don't have it: about 99% chance.
Toss a coin until you get two heads in a row: it takes 6 tosses on average. Waiting for heads-then-tails takes only 4.
Pick any three-flip pattern of heads and tails. Your opponent can always choose another that beats yours at least 2/3 of the time.
Break a stick at two random points. The three pieces can make a triangle only 1 time in 4.
Pick random numbers between 0 and 1 and add them until the total passes 1. On average it takes e, about 2.718 picks.
A drunk wandering randomly on a city grid will eventually find their way home. A drunk bird flying randomly in 3D has only about a 34% chance.
Roulette's single green zero gives the casino a 2.7% edge on every bet, and an American wheel's two zeros raise it to about 5.3%.
Doubling your bet after every loss feels foolproof, but one bad streak wipes you out. Casinos set table limits partly for that reason.
A game where you'd win on average an infinite amount of money is still one nobody would pay much to play. It's called the St. Petersburg paradox.
Two games that each lose money on their own can be alternated to make money. It's called Parrondo's paradox.
Choosing a partner, flat or employee from a line-up? Look at the first 37% without choosing, then take the next one better than all of those.
Given infinite time, a monkey hitting random keys would almost surely type the complete works of Shakespeare. In practice, not even a sentence.
100 prisoners must each find their own number in 100 boxes, opening 50. Random guessing almost never works, yet a clever loop trick wins 31% of the time.
Probability theory was born from gambling: in 1654, Pascal and Fermat exchanged letters about how to split the pot of an unfinished dice game.
Gerolamo Cardano, a 16th-century gambler and doctor, wrote the first book on probability, partly to win at dice.
Galileo was asked why three dice total 10 more often than 9. He showed 10 can be made 27 ways and 9 only 25.
Get 1% better every day for a year and you end up about 38 times better. Get 1% worse a day and only about 3% of you is left.
In the card game Spot It, any two cards share exactly one matching symbol. The trick comes from a branch of geometry about points and lines.
Guess a number from 1 to 100 using higher-or-lower hints and you'll never need more than 7 guesses.
Twenty yes-or-no questions are enough to pick out one thing from over a million possibilities.
A male honeybee has one parent and a female has two. Count a male bee's ancestors generation by generation and you get the Fibonacci numbers: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.
Tic-tac-toe has 255,168 possible games, but if both players make no mistakes, the game always ends in a draw.
Connect Four was solved in 1988: the first player can always win with perfect play, by starting in the middle column.
Checkers was solved in 2007 after 18 years of computing: with perfect play, the game is always a draw.
There are more possible games of chess than atoms in the observable universe.
After each chess player makes just one move, there are 400 possible board positions.
Computers have solved every chess endgame with 7 pieces or fewer. One has a forced checkmate that takes 549 moves.
The game of Go has about 2 x 10^170 possible legal board positions, far more than there are atoms in the universe.
A Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible positions, yet any of them can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.
Lining up every possible Rubik's Cube position side by side would stretch about 260 light-years.
Six standard 2x4 Lego bricks can be stacked together in 915,103,765 different ways.
There are about 6.67 sextillion possible filled-in Sudoku grids, so nobody will ever run out of new puzzles.
A Sudoku puzzle needs at least 17 starting clues to have just one solution. Computers checked every possibility to prove it in 2012.
In Mastermind, a smart enough player can always crack the secret code in 5 guesses or fewer.
Ten friends who rearranged themselves around a round table once a day would need about 994 years to try every seating.
The 26 letters of the alphabet can be arranged in about 4 x 10^26 different orders.
In 2012, a study of 3.4 million PINs found nearly 11% of people used 1234.
The German Enigma machine had about 158 quintillion possible settings, yet code breakers at Bletchley Park cracked it daily.
Online security relies on how hard it is to split huge numbers into primes. Multiplying is easy; going backwards could take longer than the age of the universe.
In 1973, a British spy agency mathematician secretly invented the method behind online encryption, years before it was published.
There are about 10^77 possible Bitcoin private keys, millions of times more than the number of atoms in the whole Milky Way.
Ask 1,000 randomly chosen people a question and you can usually estimate a whole nation's answer to within about 3 percentage points.
In 1936, a magazine polled 2.4 million people and predicted Roosevelt would lose. He won in a landslide; a sample of 50,000 picked right.
In 1906, Francis Galton found that the middle guess of 787 people at a fair was within 1% of an ox's real weight.
If Bill Gates walks into a bar, the average person in it becomes a billionaire, and nobody got any richer.
Most people have more legs than average, since a few people with fewer than two pull the average below 2.
On average, your friends have more friends than you do. It's true for most people, because popular people show up in more friend lists.
Moving one student from class A to class B can raise the average grade of both classes at once.
A treatment can look better in every group of patients yet worse overall, once the groups are combined. It's called Simpson's paradox.
In a 1981 study, about 93% of American drivers rated themselves better than the median driver. At most half of them can be.
In WWII, the Allies estimated German tank production from tank serial numbers. Spies said 1,400 a month; math said 246; the real figure was 245.
In real-world data like populations or bills, about 30% of numbers start with 1, but only about 5% start with 9. It helps catch tax fraud.
In most languages, the most common word appears about twice as often as the second, and three times as often as the third.
In WWII, statistician Abraham Wald advised armouring planes where returning bombers had NO bullet holes, since planes hit there never came back.
The t-test, used in science everywhere, was invented at the Guinness brewery by a chemist who published under the name "Student".
Florence Nightingale was a pioneering statistician; her charts helped prove most soldiers were dying of disease, not wounds.
A 2016 Facebook study found its users were linked to each other by an average of just 3.57 steps, fewer than the famous six degrees of separation.
Tie a rope snugly around the Earth's equator, then add just 1 meter to it. It would float about 16 cm above the ground all the way around.
Bees build hexagons for a reason: it was proven in 1999 that hexagons divide a surface into equal cells using the least wall material.
Only three regular shapes can tile a floor with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons.
There are only five perfectly regular 3D shapes, the ones used for dice: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.
A Mobius strip has only one side and one edge. Cut it down the middle and it stays in one piece, twice as long.
The recycling symbol, three arrows chasing each other, is drawn as a Mobius strip.
Some conveyor belts are made as Mobius strips so both "sides" wear out evenly and the belt lasts twice as long.
To a topologist, a coffee mug and a doughnut are the same shape: each has exactly one hole.
Gabriel's horn is a shape you could fill with a finite amount of paint, yet its surface is infinite, so you could never paint it.
A shape called the Koch snowflake has a never-ending perimeter, yet it fits inside a small circle.
The coastline of Britain gets longer the smaller your ruler, because you capture more and more nooks. Some say it has no true length.
Romanesco broccoli is a natural fractal: each bud is a small copy of the whole head, made of even smaller copies.
In theory, a solid ball can be cut into five pieces and rearranged into two balls, each the same size as the original. It's the Banach-Tarski paradox.
Any map, however complicated, can be coloured with just four colours so no neighbouring countries match. Proving it took a computer in 1976.
On a doughnut-shaped planet, some maps would need up to seven colours.
At any moment there are two exactly opposite points on Earth with the same temperature and air pressure.
You can't comb a hairy ball flat without leaving a tuft. So right now, somewhere on Earth, the wind is not blowing sideways at all.
Crumple a map of a city and drop it anywhere in that city: at least one point on the map will be directly above the spot it shows.
You can cut a bagel into two equal halves that are linked together like chain links, using just one twisting cut.
A wobbly four-legged table on an uneven floor can almost always be steadied by simply rotating it, not by stuffing paper under a leg.
Britain's 20p and 50p coins have curved edges that keep them the same width all the way around, just like a circle, so vending machines accept them.
A drill bit shaped like a curved triangle can drill almost perfectly square holes.
Round manhole covers can't fall into their own hole, no matter how you turn them. A square cover could slip in diagonally.
In 2023, an amateur shape hobbyist discovered "the hat", a single tile that covers a floor forever without the pattern ever repeating.
Penrose tilings never repeat. They were a puzzle curiosity until real crystals with the same kind of pattern were found in 1982.
For a long time, people knew only a few pentagon shapes that tile a floor. A homemaker, Marjorie Rice, found four new ones in the 1970s.
The fastest slide between two points isn't a straight line, it's a curve called a cycloid: the shape traced by a point on a rolling wheel.
A hanging chain forms a curve called a catenary. Flip it upside down and you get the strongest shape for an arch.
On the usual world map, Greenland looks as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is about 14 times larger.
It's impossible to make a flat map of the Earth without stretching or squashing something. A globe is the only honest map.
On a globe you can draw a triangle with three right angles: from the North Pole down to the equator, a quarter turn along it, and back up.
The shortest flight from New York to Tokyo heads north over Alaska, because straight lines on a globe look curved on a flat map.
You hold a pizza slice by bending its crust into a U because math says the tip then can't droop. It's Gauss's "remarkable theorem" at work.
Cut a pizza through any point with 8 slices at equal angles, then share alternating slices: both people get exactly the same amount of pizza.
A pizza with radius z and thickness a has volume pi x z x z x a: pizza.
Where soap bubbles meet, the films always join three at a time at equal angles of 120 degrees.
Every classic soccer ball has exactly 12 pentagons, and any ball made only of pentagons and hexagons like that needs exactly 12.
A cube can pass through a hole cut in an identical cube. It's called Prince Rupert's cube, after a 17th-century bet.
In 2025, mathematicians found the first convex shape proven unable to pass through a hole cut in a copy of itself.
There are exactly 11 different flat patterns of six squares that fold up into a cube.
You can fold paper, make one straight cut, and unfold any shape made of straight edges: a star, a swan, even your initials.
With paper folding, you can split any angle into three equal parts, something compass and ruler can't do.
Fold a strip of paper in half again and again, then unfold it at right angles: you get a jagged fractal called the dragon curve.
Flexagons, paper toys that flip to show hidden faces, were invented in 1939 by a student trimming his paper to fit an American binder.
A Japanese folding pattern lets a map open and close in one pull. It has also been used to fold solar panels for space.
A gomboc is a 3D shape that always rights itself, with no weight inside. Some tortoise shells work almost the same way.
The volume of a ball in higher dimensions peaks in 5 dimensions, then shrinks toward zero as dimensions keep rising.
In very high dimensions, nearly all of an orange's volume would be in its peel.
A 4D cube, a tesseract, has 8 cube-shaped faces, 24 squares, 32 edges and 16 corners.
In four dimensions, you can't tie a knot in a string: every knot just slips undone.
As of 2020, mathematicians had listed over 350 million different knots with 19 crossings or fewer.
Researchers in 1999 counted 85 ways to tie a necktie. A 2015 study with looser rules found 177,147.
In 1958, it was proven that a sphere can be turned inside out without tearing or creasing it, if the surface can pass through itself.
A line can wiggle so much that it passes through every single point in a square. Such "space-filling curves" were found in 1890.
Pringles crisps are shaped like a saddle, curving up one way and down the other. The same shape is used for strong, light stadium roofs.
The sunflower's seeds spiral both ways, usually in Fibonacci numbers like 34 and 55.
New leaves on many plants grow about 137.5 degrees around the stem from the last one, an angle that keeps them from shading each other.
Contrary to popular belief, the nautilus shell is not a golden spiral; its proportions are noticeably different.
The claims that the Parthenon and the Mona Lisa were designed around the golden ratio aren't backed by solid evidence.
A dartboard's numbers are arranged to punish sloppy throws: the top score, 20, sits between the lowly 1 and 5.
The Simpsons once showed 3987^12 + 4365^12 = 4472^12 as a joke. It's false, but the two sides agree in their first nine digits, enough to fool a calculator.
Fibonacci numbers secretly convert miles to kilometres: 5 miles is about 8 km, 8 miles about 13 km, and 13 miles about 21 km.
A4 paper is shaped so that folding it in half gives a sheet with exactly the same proportions, A5. The secret ratio is the square root of 2.
Two A4 sheets side by side make an A3, and an A0 sheet is exactly one square meter.
The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is shaped like an upside-down hanging chain, and it's as wide as it is tall: 192 meters.
Whisper at one focus of an oval-shaped room and someone at the other focus hears you clearly, even far away. The US Capitol has such a room.
Satellite dishes are parabolas because a parabola bounces every incoming parallel signal to the same single point.
Rainbows always appear at about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the Sun, which is why they're always circular arcs.
Snowflakes come in endless designs but almost always with six-fold symmetry, because of how water molecules link up in ice.
Lightning, river deltas, tree branches and your lungs all share the same branching fractal pattern.
Triangles are the only shape that can't be pushed out of shape without bending a side, which is why bridges and cranes are full of them.
Any flat polygon can be cut into pieces and rearranged into any other polygon of the same area. That's not true for 3D solids.
An equilateral triangle can be cut into just four pieces that rearrange into a perfect square.
A square can be tiled with smaller squares that are all different sizes. The smallest way uses 21 squares.
Roll a coin around another identical coin, and it makes two full turns, not one. Even a 1982 SAT question got this wrong.
Kepler guessed in 1611 that grocers stack oranges the densest way. It took until 1998, and a huge computer check, to prove him right.
A Futurama writer with a math PhD proved a brand-new theorem for a 2010 body-swapping episode. It's now known as the Futurama theorem.
Twelve identical balls can touch one central ball of the same size. Newton and a rival argued whether 13 might fit; it was settled in 1953.
In 2024, a mathematician posted a proof answering the "moving sofa problem": the biggest sofa that can turn a right-angled corridor corner.
The Sierpinski triangle, a fractal of triangles inside triangles, appears if you shade the odd numbers in Pascal's triangle.
In the 1990s, mathematician Daina Taimina crocheted the first physical models of hyperbolic space, a shape like curly lettuce or coral.
Frilly lettuce leaves, coral and sea slugs grow in hyperbolic shapes, which pack lots of edge into a small space.
The Menger sponge is a fractal cube with infinitely many holes: infinite surface area but zero volume.
The Mandelbrot set, one of math's most complex pictures, comes from repeating one tiny formula: square a number and add.
In 1637, Pierre de Fermat scribbled that he had a marvellous proof but the margin was too small to hold it. It took 358 years to prove.
Andrew Wiles read about Fermat's Last Theorem at age 10 in a library, and spent seven years secretly working on it as an adult before proving it.
When Wiles first announced his famous proof in 1993, a gap was found. It took him another year to fix it, and he almost gave up.
Grigori Perelman solved one of the hardest problems in math, then turned down both the Fields Medal and a 1 million dollar prize.
In 2016, computers solved a math puzzle with a proof 200 terabytes long, the largest proof ever written at the time.
There is no Nobel Prize for mathematics. The top award, the Fields Medal, is only given to mathematicians under 40.
In 2014, Maryam Mirzakhani became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, math's highest honour.
In 2022, Maryna Viazovska won the Fields Medal for finding the best way to pack spheres in 8 and 24 dimensions.
Terence Tao won a gold medal at the International Math Olympiad at age 13, the youngest gold medallist ever.
According to a famous story, young Gauss was told to add 1 to 100 and instantly answered 5050 by pairing 1+100, 2+99, and so on.
At 18, Gauss proved that a regular 17-sided shape can be drawn with just a compass and ruler, something nobody had managed in 2,000 years.
A man named Hermes spent about 10 years working out how to construct a regular polygon with 65,537 sides. His manuscript is kept in a trunk at a German university.
Srinivasa Ramanujan, mostly self-taught in India, mailed pages of formulas to Cambridge in 1913. G. H. Hardy said they must be true because no one could invent them.
Ramanujan found a formula for pi in which every extra term adds about 8 more correct digits.
Evariste Galois founded a whole branch of algebra and died after a duel at age 20, having scribbled down his ideas the night before.
Niels Henrik Abel proved there is no general formula for solving equations of degree five, and died at just 26.
Leonhard Euler went almost completely blind, yet kept producing mathematics at an astonishing rate, dictating it to helpers.
Euler's collected works fill more than 70 large volumes, and new volumes were still being printed in the 21st century.
Paul Erdos owned almost nothing and lived out of a suitcase, travelling between colleagues' homes for decades doing math.
Paul Erdos wrote around 1,500 papers with more than 500 co-authors. Mathematicians still brag about their "Erdos number".
A quip often linked to Paul Erdos says a mathematician is a machine for turning coffee into theorems. It was probably his friend Alfred Renyi's line.
Newton and Leibniz both invented calculus, and fought a bitter decades-long feud over who came first. Today we use Leibniz's notation.
Lewis Carroll, author of Alice in Wonderland, was a math lecturer at Oxford named Charles Dodgson.
Sophie Germain studied math in secret and corresponded with Gauss under a man's name, "Monsieur LeBlanc", fearing she'd be dismissed.
Emmy Noether proved that every symmetry in physics comes with a conservation law. Einstein praised her as a creative genius.
Hypatia of Alexandria was a renowned mathematician and teacher about 1,600 years ago.
NASA mathematician Katherine Johnson checked the computer's orbit numbers before John Glenn's 1962 flight. Glenn asked for her by name.
Florence Nightingale became the first female member of the Royal Statistical Society, in 1858.
Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no computer program can ever tell, for every program, whether it will eventually stop.
Kurt Godel proved that in any reasonable system of math, there are true statements that can never be proven within it.
Whether there is an infinity between the counting numbers and the real numbers can't be proved or disproved with standard math. Both answers are allowed.
In 1900, David Hilbert listed 23 great unsolved problems. Some have been solved, some proven unsolvable, and a few are still open.
The Konigsberg bridges puzzle asked if you could cross all seven bridges once each. Euler proved it impossible in 1736, founding a new field of math.
Omar Khayyam, famous today for his poetry, was also a top mathematician who helped make one of history's most accurate calendars.
John Nash, the mathematician from the film A Beautiful Mind, won the Nobel Prize in Economics for game theory.
Archimedes asked for a sphere inside a cylinder on his tomb, to celebrate proving the sphere has exactly 2/3 of the cylinder's volume.
According to legend, Archimedes' last words to a Roman soldier were "Do not disturb my circles".
According to legend, a follower of Pythagoras was thrown overboard for revealing that the square root of 2 can't be written as a fraction.
Hamilton was so thrilled by a new number idea in 1843 that he carved the formula into a Dublin bridge, where a plaque marks it today.
Mathematician John Conway invented the Game of Life, a "zero-player game" whose simple rules can simulate an entire computer.
Conway could tell the day of the week for any date in about two seconds, using a trick he invented called the Doomsday rule.
Martin Gardner wrote a famous puzzle column for 25 years and never took a math class after high school.
A bat and ball cost $1.10 together, and the bat costs $1 more than the ball. Most people say the ball is 10 cents. It's actually 5 cents.
A lily patch doubles every day and covers a pond in 48 days. It covered half the pond on day 47, not day 24.
100 kg of potatoes are 99% water. After drying to 98% water, they weigh just 50 kg.
Drive one mile at 30 mph. How fast must you drive the next mile to average 60 mph? It's impossible: your time is already used up.
Four people with one torch must cross a bridge in 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, two at a time. The best total is 17 minutes, not 19.
With 12 coins and one fake that's heavier or lighter, you can find the fake, and whether it's heavy or light, in just 3 weighings on a balance.
At any party, the number of people who shook hands an odd number of times is always even.
In any group of 6 people, there are always 3 who all know each other or 3 who are all strangers.
Guaranteeing 5 mutual friends or 5 mutual strangers needs a bigger party, and nobody knows how big: as of 2024, somewhere between 43 and 46 people.
A monk walks up a mountain one day and down the next, on the same path. There must be a spot he passes at the same time of day on both trips.
An ant crawls at 1 cm per second along a rubber band 1 km long that stretches by 1 km every second. Amazingly, the ant still reaches the end eventually.
In 1880, the sliding 15 puzzle swept America. Its famous challenge, swapping just the 14 and the 15, was mathematically impossible.
With just four identical books, you can stack them so the top book sticks out completely past the edge of the table.
A puzzle about a wolf, a goat and a cabbage crossing a river appears in a collection compiled about 1,200 years ago, around the time of Charlemagne.
Three friends pay 30 dollars for a room, get 5 back, keep 3 and tip 2. Where did the "missing" dollar go? Nowhere: the riddle just adds the wrong numbers.
Hilbert's Hotel has infinitely many rooms, all full. A new guest arrives? Everyone moves up one room, and room 1 is free.
Lottery numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are exactly as likely to win as any others, but thousands of people pick them, so the jackpot would be split thousands of ways.
Zeno argued that a runner could never catch a tortoise, since he must first reach where it was. Infinite sums solved it 2,000 years later.
There are exactly as many fractions as there are whole numbers, even though infinitely many fractions squeeze between 0 and 1.
In a 2010 study, pigeons playing the Monty Hall door game learned to switch doors and win more often. Most humans never did.
Nobody knows whether pi + e is a fraction or not, though almost everyone is sure it isn't.
Nobody has proven that every digit appears equally often in pi, even though it seems to be true for trillions of digits.
The number 0.12345678910111213... (writing all whole numbers in a row) contains every finite string of digits somewhere, including your phone number.
Taking turns ABBA instead of ABAB is fairer, since going first is an advantage. Football tried ABBA penalty shootouts in 2017.
In a computer, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, because computers store decimals in binary, which can't hold 0.1 exactly.
NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team used pounds and another used newtons.
In 2014, Gangnam Style was watched so many times it forced YouTube to upgrade its view counter, which maxed out at 2,147,483,647.
Pac-Man's level 256 is a garbled mess because the level counter overflows, like a car odometer rolling past its limit.
A grain of rice on the first chess square, doubled on each next square, totals over 18 quintillion grains, hundreds of years of the world's rice harvest.
Moving a 64-disk Tower of Hanoi at one move per second would take about 585 billion years, over 40 times the age of the universe.
Take 30 normal steps and you've walked 30 meters. Take 30 steps that each double in length and you'd circle the Earth about 26 times.
A million dollars in $100 bills weighs about 10 kilograms. A billion dollars would weigh about 10 tonnes.
If you spent 1,000 dollars a day, a million would last under 3 years, but a billion would last over 2,700 years.
A stack of a million one-dollar bills would be about 100 meters tall. A billion would be over 100 kilometers, reaching into space.
The Rule of 72: divide 72 by an interest rate and you get roughly how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years.
A mortgage at 7% over 30 years means paying back about 2.4 times the amount you borrowed.
The Gregorian calendar repeats exactly every 400 years, and that cycle happens to contain a whole number of weeks: 20,871.
Because the 400-year calendar cycle is fixed, the 13th of the month falls on a Friday slightly more often than on any other weekday.
The year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 wasn't and 2100 won't be: century years only leap if divisible by 400.
In 1582, ten days were removed from the calendar to fix accumulated drift: October 4 was followed by October 15.
Calendars from 2015 will match 2026 exactly, days and dates, because both years start on a Thursday and neither is a leap year.
You can count to 12 on one hand by touching your thumb to each finger segment. Some think this is where counting in dozens came from.
A chessboard has 204 squares, not 64, if you count every square of every size from 1x1 up to the whole 8x8 board.
A stack of a trillion pennies would be about 1.5 million km tall, four times the distance to the Moon.
There are more possible ways to arrange 20 books on a shelf than there have been seconds since the dinosaurs died, by over a thousand times.
A 4-digit lock has 10,000 combinations. At one try every 2 seconds, you'd go through them all in under 6 hours.
A 10-character password using letters, digits and symbols has around 50 quintillion possibilities.
To pick 6 numbers out of 49 there are 13,983,816 combinations. Buying one ticket a week, you'd expect to win once in about 270,000 years.
The chance of guessing all 6 numbers in a 6-from-49 lottery is lower than flipping a coin and getting 23 heads in a row.
A full house beats a flush in poker because it's rarer: about 1 in 694 hands versus 1 in 509.
Every calendar year has at least one Friday the 13th, and never more than three.
In Monopoly, rolling doubles three times in a row sends you to jail. That happens about once every 216 turns.
Snakes and Ladders is pure luck. With one player, the average game takes about 39 rolls on a classic board.
One 18-inch pizza has more pizza than two 12-inch pizzas, because doubling the width of a pizza quadruples how much you get.
A cone, a ball and a cylinder of the same width and height have volumes in the perfect ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
Ancient Egyptians wrote nearly every fraction as a sum of different "one over" fractions, so 3/4 was written as 1/2 + 1/4.
A clock's hour and minute hands overlap 22 times a day, not 24.
A clock's hour and minute hands form a perfect right angle 44 times every day, not 48 as you might guess.
"Forty" is the only number in English whose letters are in alphabetical order, and "one" is the only one in reverse order.
In American English, you can count from zero to nine hundred ninety-nine without ever using the letter A.
"Four" is the only number in English with exactly as many letters as its value.
Zero is an even number: it sits between two odd numbers and divides evenly by 2.
A dozen dozen is a "gross" (144), and a dozen gross is a "great gross" (1,728).
1 x 8 + 1 = 9, 12 x 8 + 2 = 98, 123 x 8 + 3 = 987... all the way up to 123456789 x 8 + 9 = 987654321.
1 x 9 + 2 = 11, 12 x 9 + 3 = 111, 123 x 9 + 4 = 1111... and the pattern keeps going to 111,111,111.
9 x 9 = 81, 99 x 99 = 9801, 999 x 999 = 998001, and 9999 x 9999 = 99980001.
To multiply a 2-digit number by 11, put the sum of its digits in the middle: 11 x 43 = 473. If the sum is 10 or more, carry the 1.
To square a number ending in 5, multiply the first digit by the next number up and stick 25 on the end: 35 x 35 = 1225.
Any number times 9 has digits that add up to a multiple of 9. Keep adding the digits and you'll always land on 9.
To multiply by 9 on your fingers, fold down finger number n: the fingers left of it are the tens, the ones right of it are the units.
Halve one number and double the other, again and again, then add up some rows: that's how Russian peasants, and ancient Egyptians, multiplied.
A long human life is surprisingly short in weeks: by your 77th birthday you've lived only about 4,000 of them.
Your 10,000th day alive comes at about 27 years and 4 months old.
Someone born on February 29 has only about a 1 in 1,461 chance of sharing that birthday with a random stranger.
A penny doubled every day for 30 days becomes over 5 million dollars. Most people would pick a million dollars up front instead.
Why earphones tangle: in a 2007 experiment, a string tumbled in a box for 10 seconds tied itself in a knot about half the time, once it was long enough.
In 2002, high school student Britney Gallivan folded a single very long strip of paper in half 12 times, smashing the supposed limit of 7.
Snap a chocolate bar of 24 squares into single squares: it takes exactly 23 snaps, no matter how you do it.
A knockout tournament of 64 teams always needs exactly 63 games, since every game knocks out one team.
"I cut, you choose" is perfectly fair for two people. A method for bigger groups where nobody ends up jealous took mathematicians until the 1990s.
Three straight cuts can split a round cake into 8 pieces, but a flat pancake into only 7.
Adding a new road can make everyone's trip slower. Cities have sometimes sped up traffic by closing roads instead.
If you wait for a bus at a random time, you wait on average longer than half the average gap between buses, because long gaps are more likely to catch you.
The average student sits in a bigger class than the average class size, because big classes hold more of the students.
In a building, the first elevator to arrive near the bottom floor is usually going down, simply because most of the building is above you.
In a supermarket with three checkout lines, your line is the fastest only 1 time in 3. No wonder the other line always seems quicker.
Have a coin you suspect is unfair? Flip twice: heads-tails counts as heads, tails-heads as tails, and redo any match. Now it's perfectly fair.
Many credit card numbers use a simple formula that catches every single-digit typo, invented in 1954 by an IBM scientist.
Any sound, from a violin to your voice, can be built by adding together pure tones. That's how MP3s and JPEG photos save space.
Music is ratios: an octave is a doubled frequency, and a perfect fifth vibrates at exactly 3 to 2.
We use 12 notes in an octave partly because 2 to the power of 7/12 is almost exactly 1.5, the perfect fifth.
Modern pianos are tuned so every interval except the octave is very slightly out of tune, so every key sounds equally good.
The Bible describes a round basin 10 cubits across and 30 cubits around, which treats pi as exactly 3.
The French Revolution briefly made clocks decimal: 10 hours a day, 100 minutes an hour, 100 seconds a minute. It lasted under two years.
The meter was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, which is why Earth is about 40,000 km around.
A nautical mile was originally one minute of latitude, one sixtieth of a degree, which is why sailors and pilots love it.
The word "million" comes from the Italian "milione", meaning "a big thousand". A thousand thousands needed a name of its own.
A knight can hop to every square on a chessboard exactly once and end where it started. There are over 13 trillion such loops.
There are exactly 92 ways to place 8 queens on a chessboard so that none of them can attack another.
In a 1600s bet, a gambler won by rolling at least one six in 4 throws, about 52% of the time, then lost betting on a double six in 24 throws, about 49%.
Getting a Yahtzee during a full turn, with up to three rolls, happens about 4.6% of the time.
You'd be dealt any one particular bridge hand of 13 cards about once in 635 billion deals.
Spread 3 beats as evenly as possible over 8 counts and you get the tresillo, the rhythm hiding in countless Latin and pop songs.
Take three socks from a drawer of only black and white socks and you're guaranteed a matching pair.
Two people in London have exactly the same number of hairs on their heads, guaranteed: there are far more Londoners than hairs on any head.
In any group of 13 people, at least two were born in the same month.
Every prime number bigger than 3 sits right next to a multiple of 6: 5 and 7 around 6, 11 and 13 around 12, 29 and 31 around 30.
An Egyptian papyrus from about 1850 BC correctly works out the volume of a pyramid with its top cut off.
Push pegs between two glass plates, dip them in soap, and the film forms the shortest network of roads linking them, with three-way 120 degree junctions.
Finding the shortest route through many cities is so hard that a million dollar prize awaits anyone who finds a fast method, or proves none exists.
A village barber shaves everyone who doesn't shave themselves. Who shaves the barber? A puzzle like this shook the foundations of math in 1901.
"This sentence is false" can't be true or false. Similar loops are behind some of the deepest discoveries in logic.
From a beach, with your eyes about 1.7 m up, the horizon is only about 4.7 km away.
A notched baboon bone from Africa, about 20,000 years old, may be one of the oldest counting tools ever found.
We count in tens almost certainly because we have ten fingers. The Maya, who counted fingers and toes, used twenties.
A temple wall in Gwalior, India, carved in 876, shows one of the oldest dated zeros written as a small circle.
Albrecht Durer hid the year 1514 in the bottom row of a magic square in one of his famous engravings.
Benjamin Franklin made up elaborate magic squares to pass the time during boring government meetings.
There's essentially only one 3x3 magic square using 1 to 9: every row, column and diagonal adds to 15. All others are just rotations or flips.
There are 880 different 4x4 magic squares, and over 275 million 5x5 ones.
Euler asked if 36 officers from 6 regiments and 6 ranks could stand in a square with no repeats in any row or column. It's impossible.
Euclid's Elements was used as a math textbook for over 2,000 years and is one of the most printed books in history.
Abraham Lincoln studied Euclid's geometry as an adult, to train himself to reason clearly.
At 12, Albert Einstein was given a geometry book he later called his "holy geometry booklet".
Napoleon Bonaparte has a geometry theorem named after him, about equilateral triangles drawn on the sides of any triangle.
Actress Danica McKellar, from The Wonder Years, co-authored a published math theorem while studying at UCLA.
Art Garfunkel, of Simon and Garfunkel, earned a master's degree in mathematics education.
Mathematician Kurt Godel told a judge, at his US citizenship hearing, that he'd found a logical flaw in the Constitution. Einstein was there.
Mathematician Persi Diaconis had a coin-tossing machine built that lands heads every single time, showing a coin toss is physics, not luck.
In 1952, codebreaker Alan Turing wrote equations showing how simple chemicals could paint spots and stripes on animals like leopards and zebras.
Crystals of the mineral pyrite grow as near-perfect cubes, straight out of the ground.
1 divided by 89 is 0.011235955..., which is the Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13... added up, each shifted one decimal place further along.
In 1846, astronomers found the planet Neptune by pointing a telescope where math said it had to be.
In 1801, the asteroid Ceres vanished behind the Sun. Young Gauss worked out its orbit, and it reappeared right where he predicted.
In 1961, Edward Lorenz rounded 0.506127 to 0.506 in a weather simulation and got a totally different forecast. It led to the "butterfly effect".
A QR code can still be read even if up to 30% of it is damaged or covered, thanks to error-correcting math.
Scratched CDs still play perfectly because the music is stored with extra math that rebuilds missing pieces.
Your phone's GPS works out where you are by measuring its distance from at least four satellites at once.
100 people board a plane; the first one sits in a random seat, and others take theirs or a random free one. The chance the last person gets their own seat is exactly 1/2.
A family has two children and at least one is a girl. The chance both are girls is 1 in 3, not 1 in 2.
Flip a coin 100 times. The chance of getting exactly 50 heads is only about 8%.
Guessing on a 10-question multiple-choice test with 4 options each, your chance of a perfect score is about 1 in a million.
A tiny 200 x 200 black-and-white screen can show 2^40,000 different pictures, a number with over 12,000 digits.
During WWII, Londoners believed German V-1 bombs were aimed at certain districts. A statistician showed the hits matched pure chance.
Ice cream sales and shark attacks rise and fall together. Ice cream doesn't attract sharks: both just go up in summer.
Athletes often slump after appearing on a magazine cover. It's not a jinx: they got there during an unusually good streak, which rarely lasts.
Very tall parents tend to have children a bit shorter than themselves, and very short parents taller ones. Francis Galton named it "regression to the mean".
Drop balls through a board of pegs and they pile up into a bell curve, the same shape that describes heights, test scores and measurement errors.
Take any number, scramble its digits, and subtract the smaller from the bigger: the answer is always divisible by 9. Magicians use it to read minds.
Blaise Pascal built a mechanical calculator at about 19, to help his father, a tax collector, with endless sums.
The Bernoulli family produced eight notable mathematicians across three generations, and they didn't always get along.
In 1940, G. H. Hardy proudly wrote that number theory had no warlike use. Decades later, it became the basis of military and online encryption.
Pierre de Fermat, one of history's great mathematicians, was a lawyer who did math only as a hobby.
In 1976, a "lost notebook" of Ramanujan's was found in a Cambridge library box, full of formulas still being unpacked today.
Claude Shannon, father of the digital age, also built a juggling machine and rode a unicycle through the halls of Bell Labs.
According to legend, the entrance to Plato's Academy said "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter".
According to legend, Descartes invented the coordinate grid while watching a fly crawl across his ceiling.
In 2015, a logic puzzle about "Cheryl's birthday" from a Singapore exam went viral, stumping adults around the world.
100 prisoners in a line each see the hats in front of them and must guess their own colour, black or white. With one clever plan, at least 99 survive.
In the classic "missing square" puzzle, rearranged pieces seem to leave a hole. The trick: the shapes aren't truly triangles, the edges bend slightly.
In a three-way duel, the worst shot can have the best chance of surviving, since the two good shots aim at each other first.
In a 1980 computer tournament of strategies for repeated cooperation games, the simplest winner was "copy whatever your opponent did last".
You can't connect three houses to three utilities on paper without lines crossing. On the surface of a coffee mug, you can.
A Klein bottle is a bottle with no inside or outside. You can't truly build one in our three dimensions without it passing through itself.
As of 2017, it's proven that exactly 15 kinds of five-sided tiles can cover a floor with no gaps, and no more will ever be found.
A die doesn't need to be a regular shape to be fair: 10-sided dice look like two pyramids stuck together, and they're perfectly fair.
Spinning a coin on a table instead of flipping it can be much less fair: some coins land one way far more often.
Squaring the number 1,111,111,111 gives 1,234,567,900,987,654,321: the pattern breaks once a carry sneaks in.
Every odd number can be written as the difference of two neighbouring squares: 7 = 16 - 9, 9 = 25 - 16.
Multiply any four consecutive numbers and add 1, and you always get a perfect square: 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 + 1 = 25.
Any three consecutive numbers multiplied together always give a multiple of 6.
If you write 2 to the power of any number, the last digit cycles forever through 2, 4, 8, 6.
There are 12,988,816 ways to cover a chessboard with 32 dominoes. Cut off two opposite corners, though, and there's no way at all.
An elephant has to be shaped very differently from a mouse because when you double an animal's size, its weight goes up 8 times but its bones only 4 times as strong.
In 1980, Shakuntala Devi multiplied two 13-digit numbers in her head in 28 seconds, earning a place in the Guinness Book of Records.
The ancient Greeks proved there are infinitely many primes, yet as of 2024 nobody can say whether there are infinitely many primes like 101 that read the same backwards.
Sudoku was invented in the US: it first appeared in 1979 in a Dell puzzle magazine as "Number Place", and got its Japanese name in 1984.
A Babylonian clay tablet about 3,800 years old works out the square root of 2 correctly to about six decimal places.
A strip of paper with a half twist, a Mobius strip, cut one third of the way in, makes two linked loops of different lengths.
"Geometry" literally means "earth measuring". Herodotus said it began with ancient Egyptians remeasuring fields after the Nile flooded.
2^4 and 4^2 are both 16, and it's the only pair of different whole numbers that swap like that.
In 2019, mathematicians finally wrote 42 as the sum of three cubes, the last number under 100 to be cracked. The numbers are 17 digits long.
The odds of being dealt a perfect hand in cribbage, 29 points, are about 1 in 216,580. Many lifelong players never see one.
Fold a paper triangle's top corner straight down to its long side, then fold the other two corners in to meet it: the three angles form a straight line, 180 degrees.
